Data from the RBI’s “Trend and Progress of Banking in India” (2023) indicate that ARCs recovered approximately 18‑22 % of the principal value of acquired assets over a five‑year horizon. Challenges include: (a) valuation disputes leading to prolonged litigation in DRTs; (b) limited secondary market for security receipts, reducing liquidity for selling banks; (c) operational constraints in managing diverse asset classes (real estate, infrastructure, SME loans); and (d) the “hold‑out” problem where minority creditors block restructuring plans. The 2022 amendment to the SARFAESI Act, which allows ARCs to convert debt into equity up to 51 % of the borrower’s paid‑up capital without prior shareholder approval, aims to give ARCs greater control over distressed firms.

From a policy perspective, the interplay between the SARFAESI route and the IBC is critical. The IBC provides a collective, time‑bound resolution with a moratorium on enforcement actions, whereas SARFAESI allows individual secured creditors to act unilaterally. The RBI’s 2023 “Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write‑offs” encourages banks to explore SARFAESI‑based settlements before invoking IBC, especially for smaller exposures where IBC costs are disproportionate.

Banking Sector Consolidation: Public Sector Bank Mergers and Their Macro‑Financial Impact

The Government of India announced a mega‑merger of ten public sector banks (PSBs) into four anchor banks in August 2019, effective April 2020. The mergers were: (i) Punjab National Bank (PNB) absorbing Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India; (ii) Canara Bank absorbing Syndicate Bank; (iii) Union Bank of India absorbing Andhra Bank and Corporation Bank; and (iv) Indian Bank absorbing Allahabad Bank. This reduced the number of PSBs from 27 (2017) to 12, creating larger entities with combined balance sheets exceeding ₹15 trillion each for the top three.

The stated objectives were: (a) achieving economies of scale and scope; (b) improving capital efficiency by pooling capital buffers; (c) enhancing credit capacity for large infrastructure projects; (d) reducing operational overlap and rationalising branch networks; and (e) strengthening governance through professional boards. The RBI’s “Prompt Corrective Action” (PCA) framework, which had placed several of the merging banks under restrictions, was expected to be eased post‑merger as combined capital ratios improved.

Empirical assessment after three years shows mixed outcomes. On the positive side, the merged entities reported higher Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) — PNB’s CRAR rose from 11.5 % (March 2020) to 14.2 % (March 2023) — and a reduction in gross NPA ratios from an average of 12.8 % to 7.4 % across the four anchors, aided by write‑offs and the RBI’s “Asset Quality Review” clean‑up. Cost‑to‑income ratios improved marginally (from 58 % to 55 %) as duplicate branches were rationalised (approximately 1,200 branches closed or merged by March 2023).

However, challenges persist. Integration of disparate technology platforms (core banking solutions, risk management systems) has been slower than anticipated, leading to operational glitches and delayed reporting. Cultural differences in credit appraisal norms have resulted in inconsistent underwriting standards, reflected in a slight uptick in fresh slippages in the first half of FY 2023‑24. The merged banks’ market share in incremental credit growth has not increased proportionally; private sector banks and NBFCs continue to capture a larger share of new lending, especially in retail and MSME segments. Moreover, the government’s capital infusion schedule — ₹2.1 trillion infused between FY 2019‑20 and FY 2022‑23 — has been front‑loaded, raising concerns about fiscal sustainability and moral hazard.

From a macro‑financial stability viewpoint, the consolidation reduced the number of systemically important banks, concentrating risk in fewer entities. The RBI’s Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIB) framework now lists three PSBs (PNB, Canara, Union) alongside private peers, implying higher capital surcharges and enhanced supervision. The mergers also altered the interbank market structure: larger PSBs now dominate the call money market, influencing the transmission of policy rates. Ongoing monitoring of governance reforms — such as the induction of independent directors, the establishment of board‑level risk committees, and the adoption of the “Bank Board Bureau” recommendations — will determine whether the consolidation delivers durable efficiency gains or merely creates “too‑big‑to‑fail” entities.

  • Confusing the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) with the old fixed‑rate reverse repo; the SDF is non‑collateralised and linked to NDTL, while the reverse repo required eligible securities.
  • Assuming the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is a regular funding source; it is a penal, last‑resort window with a higher rate and SLR‑only collateral.
  • Overlooking the 2016 SARFAESI amendments that shortened notice periods and introduced statutory timelines for Debt Recovery Tribunals.
  • Believing Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs) routinely achieve high recovery rates; actual recoveries average 18‑22 % of principal over five years.
  • Treating the 2019 PSB mega‑merger as a completed integration; technology, culture, and credit‑process harmonisation remain work‑in‑progress as of 2024.
  • Ignoring the concentration risk created by fewer but larger PSBs, which now attract higher D‑SIB capital surcharges and systemic importance.
  • Failing to distinguish between the SARFAESI unilateral enforcement route and the collective, time‑bound IBC process; the choice affects creditor rights and resolution speed.

Green Finance and Climate‑Related Financial Risk in India

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) formally recognised climate change as a source of financial risk in its Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies of February 2021. Subsequently, the Guidelines on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance (April 2022) mandated that scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions and top‑layer NBFCs integrate climate‑related risk into their governance, strategy, risk management and disclosure frameworks. The guidelines adopt the Task Force on Climate‑related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) four‑pillar structure — governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets — and require a board‑level climate risk committee, scenario analysis (including a 2 °C pathway), and quarterly reporting of exposure to carbon‑intensive sectors.

In 2023 the RBI released a Draft Framework for Green Deposits that defines eligible green activities (renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, green transport, and climate‑adaptation projects) and sets a minimum 75 % allocation of deposit proceeds to such activities. The same year the central bank conducted its first Climate Risk Stress Test on a sample of 34 banks, using the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios. Results showed that under a “disorderly transition” scenario, the aggregate capital adequacy ratio of the sample could fall by 120‑150 basis points, prompting the RBI to advise banks to build additional capital buffers for high‑carbon exposures.

The National Green Finance Committee, chaired by the Deputy Governor in charge of regulation, was constituted in 2022 to coordinate taxonomy development, capacity building and inter‑agency cooperation with the Ministry of Finance, SEBI and the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. A Green Taxonomy for India (finalised March 2024) classifies economic activities into “green”, “transition” and “brown” categories, aligning with the EU taxonomy while reflecting India’s developmental priorities. Banks are expected to map their loan books to this taxonomy by March 2025 and disclose the share of green assets in their annual reports.

On the supervisory side, the RBI’s Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) now includes a dedicated climate‑risk module. Inspectors assess the quality of scenario analysis, the robustness of data pipelines for emissions tracking, and the alignment of remuneration policies with long‑term climate targets. Non‑compliance can trigger supervisory actions ranging from enhanced reporting to restrictions on dividend distribution.

RBI’s Regulatory Sandbox and Fintech Innovation

The RBI launched its Enabling Framework for Regulatory Sandbox in August 2019, creating a controlled environment where fintech firms, banks and technology providers can test innovative products with real customers under relaxed regulatory requirements. The framework defines four eligibility criteria: (i) the applicant must be a regulated entity or a partner of one; (ii) the proposal must address a clear financial‑inclusion or efficiency gap; (iii) the technology must be beyond the conceptual stage; and (iv) the applicant must demonstrate adequate risk‑management and consumer‑protection safeguards.

The first cohort (2020‑21) focused on retail payments, digital KYC, and credit‑scoring using alternative data. Notable participants included a UPI‑based offline payment solution, a blockchain‑enabled trade‑finance platform, and an AI‑driven micro‑lending model for gig‑workers. The second cohort (2021‑22) expanded the theme to MSME lending, cross‑border remittances, and wealth‑management robo‑advisors. By March 2024, the sandbox had graduated 38 experiments, of which 12 received full‑scale regulatory approval (e.g., the “Account Aggregator” consent framework, the “Video‑KYC” norms for onboarding, and the “Digital Lending Guidelines” for loan‑service providers).

In 2022 the RBI established a dedicated Fintech Department and an Innovation Hub in Bengaluru to provide mentorship, data‑sets and API sandboxes (e.g., the Unified Payments Interface sandbox, the Bharat Bill Payment System sandbox). The Hub also runs the “RBI Hackathon” series, which in 2023 attracted over 1,200 teams working on central‑bank digital currency (CBDC) use‑cases, fraud‑detection models, and green‑finance data standards.

The sandbox operates under a “test‑and‑learn” principle: participants submit a detailed exit plan, and the RBI reserves the right to terminate an experiment if systemic risk, consumer harm or data‑privacy breaches are detected. The framework also mandates a post‑experiment impact assessment covering adoption metrics, cost‑to‑serve reduction, and financial‑inclusion outcomes, which feeds into future policy formulation.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s Regulatory Sandbox is correct? (a) Only banks can apply. (b) The sandbox allows unlimited relaxation of all prudential norms. (c) Participants must submit an exit plan and impact assessment. (d) The sandbox is limited to payment‑system innovations.”
Correct answer: (c). The sandbox is open to regulated entities and their partners, not exclusively banks. It provides targeted relaxations, not a blanket waiver of prudential norms. Themes have expanded beyond payments to include lending, wealth management and cross‑border services. The framework explicitly requires an exit plan and a post‑experiment impact assessment, making (c) the only accurate statement.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific RBI circular (e.g., “Guidelines on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance, April 2022”), note the month and year; the examiner often tests whether you confuse it with the 2021 Statement or the 2023 Green Deposits draft. Keep a mental timeline: 2019 sandbox launch → 2020‑21 first cohort → 2022 Fintech Department → 2023 second cohort → 2024 graduation data. For climate finance, remember the sequence: 2021 Statement → 2022 Guidelines → 2023 Stress Test & Green Deposits draft → 2024 Taxonomy. Matching the correct year to the correct measure eliminates most distractors.

Cross‑Border Payments and Rupee Internationalisation

India’s push to internationalise the rupee gained structural momentum after the RBI’s Framework for International Trade Settlement in Rupee (July 2022), which authorised banks to open Special Rupee Vostro Accounts (SRVAs) for partner‑country banks. By March 2024, SRVAs had been operationalised with 22 countries, including the United Arab Emirates, Sri Lanka, Mauritius, Russia, and several African nations. The framework permits invoicing, payment and settlement of export‑import transactions entirely in rupees, reducing reliance on the US dollar and lowering hedging costs for Indian exporters.

Complementary initiatives include the Bilateral Currency Swap Agreements signed with the central banks of Japan (2023, $75 billion), the United Arab Emirates (2023, $2 billion), and the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) members under the SAARC Currency Swap Arrangement (revised 2022). The RBI also participates in the Asian Clearing Union (ACU), where rupee‑denominated settlement was introduced in 2023 for intra‑ACU trade, and the BRICS Pay pilot (2024) that explores a shared digital payment infrastructure among Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa.

On the retail side, the Unified Payments Interface (UPI)‑linked cross‑border remittance corridors were launched with Singapore (Project UPI‑PayNow, February 2023) and the UAE (UPI‑Bharat Interface, July 2023). These corridors enable real‑time, low‑cost person‑to‑person transfers using mobile numbers or virtual payment addresses, bypassing traditional correspondent‑bank chains. The RBI’s “Rupee‑Denominated Bonds (Masala Bonds) Framework” (updated 2021) continues to allow Indian entities to raise offshore capital in rupees, with issuance reaching ₹1.2 trillion in FY 2023‑24.

Challenges remain: convertibility restrictions on the capital account, limited depth of offshore rupee markets, and the need for robust anti‑money‑laundering (AML) standards aligned with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF). The RBI’s Capital Account Convertibility Roadmap (2023‑24) outlines a phased approach — first expanding current‑account rupee settlement, then allowing limited portfolio inflows in rupee‑denominated instruments, and finally moving towards full convertibility contingent on macro‑financial stability indicators.

Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB) and Supervisory Guidance

The RBI’s first comprehensive Guidelines on Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book were issued in June 2016, aligning with the Basel Committee’s 2016 standards. The framework requires banks to measure IRRBB using two complementary metrics: Earnings‑at‑Risk (EaR) — the potential change in net interest income over a 12‑month horizon — and Economic Value of Equity (EVE) — the change in the present value of assets, liabilities and off‑balance‑sheet items under prescribed interest‑rate shock scenarios (±200 bps parallel shift, steepener, flattener, short‑rate up/down).

A Revised IRRBB Framework (October 2020) introduced mandatory internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) integration, requiring banks to hold additional capital if the EVE decline exceeds 15 % of Tier‑1 capital under the worst‑case scenario. The revision also mandated quarterly disclosure of the interest‑rate sensitivity gap (repricing gap) across time buckets (overnight‑1 month, 1‑3 months, 3‑6 months, 6‑12 months, 1‑3 years, 3‑5 years, over 5 years) in the notes to accounts.

In 2022 the RBI embedded IRRBB into its Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) scorecard. Supervisors now assess: (i) the robustness of the bank’s behavioural assumptions for non‑maturity deposits and loan prepayments; (ii) the quality of data infrastructure supporting cash‑flow mapping; (iii) the frequency and independence of model validation; and (iv) the alignment of risk‑appetite limits with the bank’s business strategy. Banks scoring below the supervisory threshold on IRRBB are subject to enhanced monitoring, which may include restrictions on dividend payouts, mandatory capital augmentation, or a directive to reduce mismatch positions.

The 2023 Guidance Note on Climate‑Related IRRBB extended the framework by requiring banks to incorporate transition‑risk scenarios (e.g., carbon‑price shocks) into their interest‑rate shock library, recognising that climate policy can affect long‑term discount rates and asset valuations. This integration reflects the RBI’s broader move toward a unified risk‑management architecture where market, credit, liquidity and climate risks are evaluated on a common quantitative platform.

Financial Inclusion: Business Correspondent Model, Payment Banks and Small Finance Banks

The Business Correspondent (BC) model was introduced in 2006 to extend banking services to unbanked villages through retail agents equipped with handheld devices. The BC Guidelines (2010, revised 2014) prescribed eligibility (individuals, NGOs, cooperatives, post offices), KYC‑lite onboarding, and a revenue‑sharing formula capped at 0.5 % of transaction value. By March 2024, over 1.3 million BCs were active, processing ₹22 trillion in annual transactions, with 78 % of accounts opened under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (PMJDY) serviced through BCs.

Payment Banks were licensed in 2015 under the Guidelines for Licensing of Payment Banks (RBI/2014‑15/DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2014‑15). The first licences went to Airtel Payments Bank, Paytm Payments Bank, India Post Payments Bank, and Fino Payments Bank. Payment banks can accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer, offer remittance services, and issue debit cards, but cannot lend. As of FY 2023‑24, the six operational payment banks held ₹1.1 trillion in deposits and facilitated 3.4 billion UPI transactions, demonstrating their role as low‑cost digital distribution channels.

Small Finance Banks (SFBs) received licences in 2015 (10 entities) under the Guidelines for Licensing of Small Finance Banks. SFBs must maintain a minimum 75 % of adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) to priority‑sector lending, with at least 50 % of loan portfolio below ₹25 lakh. By March 2024, SFBs collectively held ₹2.3 trillion in deposits and ₹2.8 trillion in advances, serving 45 million customers, predominantly in rural and semi‑urban areas. The RBI’s 2020 “On‑Tap Licensing” framework allowed additional SFB licences subject to stringent fit‑and‑proper criteria, resulting in two new licences granted in 2022.

Recent enhancements include the Digital Banking Units (DBUs) launched in 2022 (75 units in the first phase) to provide assisted‑digital services in underserved districts, and the “BC‑Lite” framework (2023) permitting fintech firms to act as BCs without a physical outlet, leveraging API‑based integration with the Account Aggregator ecosystem. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Inclusion Index (FI‑Index) rose to 60.1 (from 53.9 in 2021), reflecting progress across access, usage and quality dimensions, though gender gaps and digital‑literacy barriers persist.

  • Confusing the RBI’s 2021 Statement on climate risk with the 2022 Guidelines; the former is a policy signal, the latter imposes mandatory disclosure and governance requirements.
  • Assuming the Regulatory Sandbox grants permanent regulatory waivers; it only provides time‑bound, experiment‑specific relaxations and requires a formal exit plan.
  • Treating Special Rupee Vostro Accounts as full capital‑account convertibility; SRVAs operate only for current‑account trade settlement under bilateral agreements.
  • Believing IRRBB capital add‑ons are triggered by any EVE decline; the 15 % Tier‑1 threshold applies only under the worst‑case supervisory shock scenario.
  • Thinking Payment Banks can lend to micro‑enterprises; they are explicitly prohibited from lending activities.
  • Overlooking the 75 % priority‑sector lending mandate for Small Finance Banks, which is higher than the 40 % applicable to universal banks.
  • Ignoring the 2023 Climate‑Related IRRBB Guidance Note that adds transition‑risk scenarios to the standard interest‑rate shock library.

RBI's Stress Testing Framework, Systemic Risk Indicators, and the Financial Stability Report

The Reserve Bank of India conducts a comprehensive macro‑stress testing exercise twice a year, aligned with the Basel Committee’s principles for sound stress testing practices. The framework evaluates the resilience of scheduled commercial banks, select non‑banking financial companies, and the overall financial system against a baseline scenario, an adverse scenario, and a severely adverse scenario. The adverse scenario typically incorporates a sharp GDP contraction (e.g., ‑5 % year‑on‑year), a 300‑basis‑point rise in policy rates, a 30 % depreciation of the rupee, and a 40 % fall in equity prices. The severely adverse scenario adds a further 200‑basis‑point rate shock and a 50 % equity decline.

Key risk dimensions covered include credit risk (probability of default and loss‑given‑default migrations across rating buckets), market risk (interest‑rate, foreign‑exchange, and equity shocks), liquidity risk (cash‑flow mismatches under the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio), and operational risk (scenario‑based loss estimates). The RBI also runs a contagion module that maps inter‑bank exposures, cross‑holdings of government securities, and common asset‑class concentrations to capture second‑round effects. Results are expressed in terms of capital adequacy ratio (CAR) depletion, leverage ratio breach, and LCR shortfall at the system level and for individual institutions.

The Financial Stability Report (FSR), published semi‑annually since 2010, disseminates the stress‑test outcomes alongside a set of systemic risk indicators: the credit‑to‑GDP gap, the debt‑service‑ratio of the household sector, the proportion of non‑performing assets in the banking system, the share of large borrowers in total credit, and the interconnectedness index derived from the network of inter‑bank lending. The FSR also includes a “heat map” that flags sectors (e.g., real estate, infrastructure, micro‑finance) where vulnerability scores exceed supervisory thresholds. Since the 2022 edition, the RBI has incorporated climate‑transition risk scenarios — carbon‑price shocks of US$50‑100 per tonne — into the stress‑testing suite, requiring banks to estimate the impact on credit quality of carbon‑intensive portfolios.

Supervisory actions triggered by the stress tests range from enhanced monitoring and mandatory capital augmentation plans to restrictions on dividend distribution and branch expansion for banks that fall below the 9 % CAR threshold under the adverse scenario. The 2023 FSR highlighted that, under the severely adverse scenario, the system‑wide CAR would dip to 10.2 % from the March 2024 level of 13.5 %, with three public sector banks breaching the 9 % floor, prompting the RBI to issue specific capital‑raising directives.

Special Resolution Regime for Large Non‑Banking Financial Companies (2021) and Its Interaction with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code

In August 2021 the RBI notified the “Framework for Resolution of Large NBFCs” (the Special Resolution Regime, SRR) to address the resolution gap for systemically important non‑bank lenders that were not covered by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) at the time. The SRR applies to NBFCs with an asset size of ₹5,000 crore or more, a leverage ratio exceeding 2.5, and a credit‑rating of “A” or below. The framework empowers the RBI to appoint an Administrator, impose a moratorium on creditor actions for up to 180 days (extendable by 90 days), and direct the preparation of a resolution plan that may involve capital infusion, asset sale, merger, or a scheme of arrangement approved by the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT).

The resolution plan must ensure that the NBFC’s core business continues, that depositor and creditor interests are protected, and that systemic spillovers are contained. The RBI may also require the NBFC to maintain a minimum liquidity buffer of 15 % of its total liabilities during the moratorium. Importantly, the SRR operates in parallel with the IBC: if a resolution plan under the SRR fails, the RBI can refer the NBFC to the NCLT under Section 227 of the IBC (as amended in 2021 to include certain NBFCs). Conversely, an IBC‑driven liquidation order supersedes the SRR moratorium. The 2022 amendment to the IBC brought “financial service providers” with assets above ₹500 crore under the corporate insolvency resolution process, narrowing the SRR’s exclusive domain but leaving it as a pre‑emptive, RBI‑led tool for early intervention.

Since its inception, the SRR has been invoked for two large NBFCs — one in the housing finance segment and another in the micro‑finance space. In both cases, the Administrator facilitated a merger with a healthier peer, preserving over 80 % of the loan book and avoiding a disorderly wind‑down. The RBI’s 2023 review noted that the SRR reduced the average resolution timeline from 420 days (under the earlier voluntary restructuring route) to 210 days, and that the recovery rate for secured creditors improved from 38 % to 55 %.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the RBI’s Special Resolution Regime for large NBFCs complements the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code. Illustrate with one case where the SRR was used.”
The SRR provides an early, RBI‑controlled resolution pathway for systemically important NBFCs that were outside the IBC’s original scope. It allows a moratorium, appointment of an Administrator, and a resolution plan without immediate NCLT involvement. If the SRR plan fails, the RBI can refer the NBFC to the NCLT under the amended IBC, ensuring a seamless transition. In 2022, a large housing finance NBFC with assets of ₹12,000 crore entered the SRR; the Administrator orchestrated a merger with a well‑capitalised peer, preserving 85 % of the loan portfolio and achieving a 55 % recovery for secured creditors, demonstrating the regime’s speed and higher recovery compared with the pre‑SRR voluntary restructuring route.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links the SRR and IBC, structure the answer in three steps: (1) state the SRR’s eligibility criteria and powers; (2) describe the hand‑over mechanism to the IBC; (3) cite the 2022 housing‑finance NBFC case with quantitative outcomes (timeline, recovery rate). This three‑part template covers both conceptual and factual marks.

Supervisory Framework for Payment System Operators: Settlement Finality, Interoperability, and Risk Management

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, empowers the RBI to regulate all payment system operators (PSOs) — entities that operate payment systems such as card networks, unified payments interface (UPI) switches, prepaid payment instrument issuers, and Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS) participants. In March 2021 the RBI issued the “Guidelines for Payment System Operators” consolidating prudential, operational, and governance requirements. A PSO must obtain a certificate of authorisation, maintain a minimum net‑worth of ₹25 crore (₹15 crore for specialised operators), and hold a settlement guarantee fund (SGF) equal to at least 0.5 % of the daily average settlement volume.

Settlement finality is enshrined through the “irrevocable and unconditional” transfer of funds once the settlement cycle completes. The guidelines mandate that all PSOs settle obligations through the RBI’s Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system or the National Automated Clearing House (NACH) for batch settlements, ensuring central‑bank money finality. Interoperability is enforced by requiring PSOs to adopt the NPCI‑defined common standards for QR codes, UPI intent, and card‑tokenisation, allowing a customer of any bank or wallet to transact across networks without bilateral agreements.

Risk management provisions include a comprehensive framework for operational risk (business continuity planning, cyber‑resilience testing, and incident reporting within two hours), liquidity risk (intraday liquidity monitoring against the SGF), and credit risk (counterparty exposure limits capped at 20 % of the PSO’s net‑worth). The RBI conducts annual on‑site inspections and off‑site surveillance based on monthly returns covering transaction volumes, failure rates, and grievance redressal metrics. Non‑compliance attracts graded penalties: monetary fines up to ₹1 crore, suspension of specific services, or revocation of authorisation.

The 2023 amendment introduced a “sandbox‑lite” provision allowing new PSOs to test innovative payment products (e.g., offline UPI, voice‑based payments) under relaxed net‑worth thresholds for a 12‑month period, provided they submit a detailed exit plan. This balances innovation with the systemic safety net that the SGF and settlement finality guarantees provide.

Regulation of Payment Aggregators and Payment Gateways: 2022 Guidelines and the RBI's Oversight

Payment Aggregators (PAs) and Payment Gateways (PGs) act as intermediaries that enable merchants to accept digital payments without direct integration with each payment network. Recognising their growing systemic footprint, the RBI released the “Guidelines on Regulation of Payment Aggregators and Payment Gateways” in March 2022, effective from September 2022. A PA must be a company incorporated in India with a minimum net‑worth of ₹15 crore at the time of application and ₹25 crore within three years of authorisation. A PG requires a net‑worth of ₹10 crore, reflecting its narrower role of providing technology infrastructure.

Both PAs and PGs must maintain an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank for merchant funds, ensuring that customer money is segregated from the aggregator’s own funds. Settlement to merchants must occur on a T+1 basis (next working day) for domestic transactions and T+2 for cross‑border transactions, with a maximum permissible delay of 48 hours under force‑majeure. The guidelines impose a grievance redressal mechanism: a dedicated nodal officer, a 24‑hour acknowledgment, and resolution within 14 days, failing which the merchant may escalate to the RBI’s Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions.

Data localisation is mandatory — all payment data, including transaction logs and KYC records, must be stored only in India. PAs and PGs are required to undergo an annual information‑system audit by a CERT‑IN empanelled auditor and submit a compliance certificate to the RBI. The RBI also mandates that PAs adhere to the “Know Your Customer” norms applicable to banks, including video‑KYC for onboarding merchants, and that they implement tokenisation standards for card‑on‑file transactions as per the 2021 tokenisation framework.

Since the guidelines came into force, the number of authorised PAs has risen from 12 to 28, while the number of PGs has stabilised at 9. The RBI’s 2024 supervisory report highlighted that 94 % of PAs met the T+1 settlement target, and the average grievance resolution time fell to 9 days. The framework has also curbed the practice of “fund‑parking” where aggregators delayed merchant payouts to earn float income.

Large Exposure and Concentration Risk Framework for Banks: 2023 Guidelines and Supervisory Implications

Aligning with the Basel Committee’s “Large Exposures” standard (BCBS 2014), the RBI issued the “Large Exposure Framework (LEF)” for scheduled commercial banks in June 2023, superseding the 2015 circular. The LEF defines a large exposure as any exposure to a single counterparty or a group of connected counterparties exceeding 10 % of the bank’s eligible Tier 1 capital. The prudential limit is set at 25 % of Tier 1 capital for a single counterparty and 150 % for a group of connected counterparties, with a tighter 20 % limit for exposures to other banks and non‑bank financial institutions.

Exposures are measured on a gross basis, including on‑balance‑sheet assets (loans, investments, derivatives) and off‑balance‑sheet commitments (guarantees, letters of credit, undrawn commitments) after applying credit‑conversion factors. The framework requires banks to aggregate exposures across all legal entities within a connected group using the “economic‑unit” approach, which looks through ownership, control, and common management. Banks must report large‑exposure positions quarterly in the prescribed format (LE‑01) and disclose the top‑20 exposures in their annual financial statements.

Supervisory implications are significant. Breaches of the 25 %/150 % limits trigger a mandatory capital charge of 150 % of the excess exposure, and the RBI may impose restrictions on fresh lending to the counterparty, require a reduction plan within 90 days, or invoke the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework if the breach coincides with capital adequacy deterioration. The 2023 guidelines also introduce a “concentration risk buffer” — an additional 0.5 % of Tier 1 capital that banks must hold if their top‑10 exposures exceed 200 % of Tier 1 capital.

Early evidence from the first two reporting cycles (September 2023 and December 2023) shows that the average large‑exposure ratio for the banking system declined from 22 % to 18 % of Tier 1 capital, driven by banks’ proactive syndication and securitisation of large corporate loans. However, three public sector banks still reported a single‑counterparty exposure above 25 % due to legacy infrastructure lending, prompting the RBI to issue specific reduction timelines.

  • Confusing the SRR’s 180‑day moratorium with the IBC’s 270‑day resolution timeline; the SRR moratorium is RBI‑led and can be extended only once by 90 days.
  • Assuming the Payment Aggregator net‑worth requirement is the same as for Payment Gateways; PAs need ₹15 crore initially and ₹25 crore within three years, while PGs need ₹10 crore.
  • Treating the Large Exposure Framework’s 25 % limit as applicable to all counterparties; the limit is 20 % for exposures to other banks and NBFCs.
  • Believing settlement finality under the PSO guidelines is achieved at the merchant’s bank; finality occurs only after settlement through RTGS or NACH in central‑bank money.
  • Overlooking the climate‑transition stress scenarios added to the RBI’s macro‑stress testing in the 2022 FSR; they are mandatory for banks with carbon‑intensive portfolios.
  • Assuming the Special Resolution Regime applies to all NBFCs; it is restricted to those with assets ≥ ₹5,000 crore, leverage > 2.5, and rating ≤ A.
  • Ignoring the requirement for Payment Aggregators to store all payment data exclusively in India; cross‑border data storage is prohibited.

Operation Twist and Yield Curve Management by the Reserve Bank of India

Operation Twist refers to the simultaneous purchase of long‑dated government securities and sale of short‑dated securities by the central bank to flatten the yield curve without changing the overall size of its balance sheet. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) first employed this tool in December 2019, conducting two tranches of ₹10,000 crore each — buying 10‑year and 30‑year bonds while selling 1‑year and 2‑year treasury bills. A second round followed in August 2020 (₹20,000 crore) and a third in October 2021 (₹15,000 crore). The objective was to lower long‑term yields, which serve as benchmarks for corporate borrowing and mortgage rates, thereby transmitting monetary easing to the real economy when the policy repo rate was already at the lower bound of 4 %.

The mechanics rely on the RBI’s Open Market Operations (OMO) window. The central bank announces the securities, amounts, and settlement dates in advance. Primary dealers and scheduled commercial banks submit bids through the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform. The RBI accepts bids at market‑determined prices, ensuring that the operation does not signal a target yield but lets the market price the curve. Empirical studies by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) show that the 10‑year yield fell by 15‑20 basis points within a week of each announcement, while the 1‑year yield rose marginally, confirming the intended twist.

Operation Twist differs from conventional OMOs in two respects. First, it is sterilised: the liquidity injected by long‑bond purchases is offset by the drainage from short‑bond sales, leaving the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor unchanged. Second, it targets the term premium rather than the short‑rate expectation component. The RBI has complemented Twist with Variable Rate Repo (VRR) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions to fine‑tune short‑term liquidity, but the Twist operations remain the primary instrument for explicit yield‑curve management.

Critics argue that repeated Twist operations can distort price discovery in the G‑sec market and reduce the signalling value of the yield curve for fiscal policy. The RBI’s 2022‑23 Annual Report noted that the cumulative Twist purchases amounted to ₹45,000 crore, representing less than 2 % of outstanding central government securities, suggesting limited market distortion. Nevertheless, the central bank has signalled a preference for letting market forces determine the curve once inflation is durably aligned with the 4 % target, reserving Twist for episodes of acute term‑premium spikes.

Foreign Exchange Intervention Framework: Managed Float, Intervention Rules, and Reserve Adequacy

India follows a managed float exchange‑rate regime where the rupee’s value is primarily market‑determined but the RBI intervenes to curb excessive volatility and maintain orderly market conditions. The intervention framework is governed by the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 1999 and the RBI’s Master Direction on “Foreign Exchange Management (Manner of Receipt and Payment) Regulations”. The RBI operates in both the spot and forward segments of the interbank foreign‑exchange market, using outright purchases or sales of US dollars and, since 2015, dollar‑rupee swap auctions to manage liquidity and the forward premium.

Intervention is guided by three principles: (i) symmetry — the RBI does not target a specific level but smooths two‑way movements; (ii) transparency — the weekly “Foreign Exchange Reserves” press release discloses the net change in reserves, allowing market participants to infer intervention magnitude; and (iii) reserve adequacy — the RBI monitors metrics such as import cover (months of imports financed by reserves), the reserve‑to‑short‑term‑debt ratio, and the reserve‑to‑broad‑money ratio. As of March 2024, foreign‑exchange reserves stood at US $642 billion, providing an import cover of approximately 12 months and a reserve‑to‑short‑term‑external‑debt ratio of 1.9, comfortably above the IMF’s adequacy thresholds.

The RBI’s intervention toolkit includes: (a) spot market operations — direct buying/selling of dollars through authorised dealers; (b) forward market operations — selling dollars forward to absorb excess rupee liquidity or buying forward to inject rupee liquidity; (c) dollar‑rupee swap auctions — introduced in March 2015, these involve the RBI selling dollars spot and buying them back forward (or vice‑versa) to manage both the exchange rate and domestic liquidity simultaneously. The swap window has been used extensively during periods of capital‑flow surges, notably in 2020‑21 when net inflows exceeded US $80 billion.

Empirical analysis by the RBI’s Monetary Policy Department indicates that a US $1 billion net purchase of dollars in the spot market typically depreciates the rupee by 5‑7 paise in the short run, while a comparable forward sale reduces the 1‑year forward premium by 10‑15 basis points. The RBI’s 2023 “State of the Economy” report highlighted that intervention intensity, measured as the ratio of net monthly intervention to average daily turnover, remained below 5 % in 2022‑23, underscoring a restrained approach.

Reserve adequacy is assessed quarterly using the IMF’s Assessing Reserve Adequacy (ARA) metric, which weights export earnings, broad money, short‑term debt, and portfolio liabilities. India’s ARA score has consistently exceeded the 100‑150 % adequacy range since 2018, giving the RBI ample space to intervene without jeopardising external solvency. The framework also incorporates a “contingent liability” buffer for potential capital‑flow reversals, calibrated at 10 % of reserves.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The RBI’s Operation Twist is an unsterilised operation that expands the monetary base.” Identify the error and state the correct characterisation.
The statement is false. Operation Twist is a sterilised operation: the RBI simultaneously purchases long‑dated securities and sells short‑dated securities of equal value, leaving net liquidity and the monetary base unchanged. The tool targets the term premium and the shape of the yield curve, not the level of reserve money.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mentions “yield‑curve management” or “flattening the curve”, immediately recall Operation Twist, Variable Rate Repo/Reverse Repo, and the distinction between sterilised and unsterilised OMOs. Write the sterilisation mechanism in one sentence — it fetches full marks for the “mechanism” part of the answer.

Deposit Insurance Enhancement: The 2021 Amendment to the DICGC Act and Its Impact on Small Depositors

The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) Act, 1961 was amended by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (Amendment) Act, 2021, which received Presidential assent on 28 August 2021. The amendment raised the insurance cover per depositor per bank from ₹1 lakh to ₹5 lakh, effective retrospectively for all deposits outstanding as on 1 April 2020. The enhanced cover applies to all commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, and regional rural banks that are registered with the DICGC.

The premium rate payable by insured banks was simultaneously revised from 10 paise per ₹100 of assessable deposits to 12 paise per ₹100, with a provision for the RBI to adjust the rate annually based on the DICGC’s fund position. The DICGC’s deposit insurance fund, which stood at ₹1.03 lakh crore at end‑March 2023, is required to maintain a minimum fund‑to‑insured‑deposits ratio of 1.15 % under the amended framework. The amendment also introduced a “prompt payment” clause: the DICGC must settle insured claims within 90 days of a bank’s licence cancellation, failing which the Corporation pays interest at the bank rate plus 2 %.

Impact assessment by the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (FSR) 2022‑23 shows that the number of fully insured depositors rose from 98.1 % to 99.6 % of total deposit accounts, while the value of insured deposits increased from 50.3 % to 78.9 % of total assessable deposits. The enhanced cover significantly reduced the incentive for depositors to fragment holdings across multiple banks to stay within the ₹1 lakh limit, thereby lowering operational costs for banks and improving deposit stickiness.

However, the amendment also raised moral‑hazard concerns. The RBI’s 2023 “Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India” noted that banks with weaker asset quality experienced a marginally higher deposit growth (3.2 % vs. 2.8 % for stronger peers) in the year following the amendment, suggesting that the higher insurance cover may blunt market discipline. To mitigate this, the RBI has tightened the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework and mandated higher disclosure of asset‑quality metrics for banks approaching the insurance‑fund threshold.

The DICGC also launched a “Depositor Awareness Campaign” in 2022, leveraging the Jan Dhan‑Aadhaar‑Mobile (JAM) trinity to send SMS alerts about the enhanced cover. As of December 2023, over 45 crore depositors had received at least one communication, and the grievance redressal portal recorded a 40 % decline in complaints related to deposit‑insurance awareness.

Regulatory Treatment of Crypto Assets and Virtual Digital Assets in India

India’s regulatory stance on crypto assets has evolved through three distinct phases. In April 2018, the RBI issued a circular prohibiting all regulated entities from dealing in or providing services to any person or entity dealing with virtual currencies. The Supreme Court, in Internet and Mobile Association of India v. Reserve Bank of India (March 2020), set aside the circular on grounds of proportionality, holding that the RBI had not demonstrated empirical harm to the financial system.

Post‑judgment, the government introduced the Cryptocurrency and Regulation of Official Digital Currency Bill, 2021, which lapsed. In the Union Budget 2022‑23, the Finance Minister announced a 30 % tax on income from transfer of Virtual Digital Assets (VDAs) and a 1 % Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) on payments exceeding ₹10,000 in a financial year. The Finance Act, 2022 inserted Section 115BBH and Section 194S into the Income‑Tax Act, 1961, giving statutory backing to the tax regime. The definition of VDA covers any information, code, number or token generated through cryptographic means, excluding Indian rupee‑denominated digital currency issued by the RBI.

The RBI, while acknowledging the tax framework, maintains that crypto assets are not legal tender and pose risks to financial stability, consumer protection, and anti‑money‑laundering (AML) compliance. In its 2022‑23 Annual Report, the RBI reiterated that it does not recognise any crypto asset as a currency or a payment instrument and has advised banks to carry out enhanced due‑diligence on customers transacting in VDAs, in line with the Prevention of Money‑Laundering Act (PMLA) 2002 and the RBI’s Master Direction on KYC.

On the international front, India participated in the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) “Travel Rule” implementation for VDA service providers, requiring originator and beneficiary information to accompany transfers above US $1,000. The RBI’s 2023 “Guidelines on Regulation of Payment Aggregators and Payment Gateways” explicitly prohibit PAs and PGs from onboarding merchants dealing in VDAs unless they obtain a separate authorisation, which has not been granted to date.

Empirical data from the Income‑Tax Department shows that VDA‑related TDS collections amounted to ₹1,200 crore in FY 2023‑24, indicating a sizable transaction base despite regulatory ambiguity. The RBI continues to explore a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) — the Digital Rupee (e₹) — as a sovereign alternative, with wholesale and retail pilots launched in November 2022 and February 2023 respectively. The coexistence of a taxed VDA ecosystem and a sovereign CBDC remains a unique policy experiment globally.

Development of the Government Securities Market: Primary Dealers, Non‑Competitive Bidding, and the Negotiated Dealing System

The modern government securities (G‑sec) market in India traces its institutional architecture to the 1995 introduction of the Primary Dealer (PD) system. The RBI initially appointed 12 PDs — a mix of public‑sector banks, private banks, and standalone financial institutions — to underwrite primary issuances, provide two‑way quotes in the secondary market, and participate in the RBI’s Open Market Operations. As of March 2024, there are 22 PDs, including 7 standalone PDs, each required to maintain a minimum net owned fund of ₹500 crore and achieve a minimum bidding commitment of 40 % of the notified amount in primary auctions.

Non‑competitive bidding (NCB) was introduced in 2001 to widen retail participation. Under NCB, eligible investors — individuals, Hindu Undivided Families, trusts, and provident funds — can bid for up to ₹2 crore per auction without specifying a yield; they receive securities at the weighted‑average yield of the competitive bids. The NCB limit was raised to ₹5 crore in 2020 and the facility extended to state development loans (SDLs) in 2021. Data from the RBI’s “Primary Market Statistics” show that NCB allotments accounted for 12 % of total primary issuance in FY 2023‑24, up from 4 % in FY 2015‑16.

The Negotiated Dealing System (NDS) launched in 2002, and its order‑matching segment NDS‑OM went live in 2005, providing an anonymous, screen‑based, order‑driven platform for secondary‑market trading in G‑secs, treasury bills, and SDLs. NDS‑OM operates on a T+1 settlement cycle, with clearing and settlement through the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL). The platform’s average daily turnover exceeded ₹1.2 lakh crore in 2023‑24, making it one of the deepest sovereign‑bond markets among emerging economies.

Recent reforms include the introduction of “Uniform Price Auction” for dated securities in 2022, replacing the multiple‑price format to reduce winner’s curse and improve price discovery. The RBI also permitted “When‑Issued” trading in 2023, allowing market participants to trade securities before formal issuance, thereby enhancing liquidity in the pre‑issuance period. Additionally, the “Retail Direct” portal, launched in November 2021, enables individual investors to buy G‑secs directly in primary auctions and hold them in a demat account with the RBI, bypassing intermediaries.

These structural upgrades have lowered the bid‑ask spread in the 10‑year benchmark from 8‑10 basis points in 2010 to 2‑3 basis points in 2023, and reduced the average underwriting fee for PDs from 0.15 % to 0.05 % of the issue size. The deepening of the G‑sec market has also facilitated the RBI’s monetary transmission, as the benchmark yield now reflects a broad‑based investor base rather than a handful of captive holders.

  • Confusing Operation Twist with conventional OMOs — Twist is sterilised and targets the term premium, not reserve money.
  • Assuming the RBI targets a specific rupee level — the managed float aims at volatility smoothing, not a fixed parity.
  • Believing the DICGC cover increase to ₹5 lakh applies only to new deposits — it is retrospective to 1 April 2020.
  • Thinking crypto assets are legal tender after the 2022 tax — taxation does not confer legal‑tender status.
  • Overlooking that Primary Dealers must bid for at least 40 % of the notified amount — failure triggers supervisory action.
  • Mixing up non‑competitive bidding limits for G‑secs and SDLs — the ₹5 crore cap applies to both since 2021.
  • Ignoring the 90‑day claim‑settlement mandate for DICGC — delays attract penal interest at bank rate plus 2 %.

The advanced sections above equip aspirants with the nuanced operational details that differentiate high‑scoring answers from generic textbook summaries.

Countercyclical Capital Buffer and Sectoral Capital Requirements in India

The Reserve Bank of India adopted the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) framework through a circular dated 5 February 2015. The buffer is designed to be built up during periods of excessive credit growth and released when the cycle turns, thereby protecting the banking system from pro‑cyclical amplification. The RBI set the maximum CCyB at 2.5 % of risk‑weighted assets, to be applied in increments of 0.25 % after a four‑quarter notice period. Since its inception the buffer rate has remained at 0 % — the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) has not judged credit‑to‑GDP gaps to warrant activation, although the framework remains operational and the RBI publishes the credit‑to‑GDP gap and the buffer decision in each Financial Stability Report.

In parallel, the RBI imposes sector‑specific capital charges that act as a micro‑prudential complement to the CCyB. Exposures to commercial real estate (CRE) attract a risk weight of 100 % for standard assets and 150 % for sub‑standard assets, compared with the 75 % weight for general corporate loans. Capital market exposures — loans against shares, debentures, and units of equity‑oriented mutual funds — carry a 125 % risk weight. Housing finance companies (HFCs) and non‑banking financial companies (NBFCs) classified as “upper layer” under the scale‑based regulation must hold an additional 0.5 % common equity tier‑1 (CET1) capital over the baseline 5.5 % requirement. The RBI’s 2021 circular on “Large Exposures and Concentration Risk” further caps single‑borrower exposure at 20 % of a bank’s eligible capital base, with a 25 % limit for groups, tightening the sectoral concentration risk profile.

The interaction between the CCyB and sectoral buffers is explicit: when the CCyB is activated, the additional CET1 requirement is applied on top of the sectoral risk weights, raising the effective capital charge for high‑risk sectors. For example, if the CCyB were set at 1 % and a bank’s CRE portfolio carries a 100 % risk weight, the effective CET1 requirement for that portfolio becomes 6.5 % (5.5 % baseline + 1 % CCyB). The RBI’s stress‑testing framework, published in the half‑yearly Financial Stability Report, incorporates both the CCyB path and sectoral risk‑weight shocks to assess capital adequacy under adverse macro‑financial scenarios.

Operationally, banks report their CCyB‑eligible capital and sectoral exposures in the quarterly “Capital Adequacy” returns (Form C). The RBI monitors the credit‑to‑GDP gap using the methodology prescribed by the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), with a threshold of 2 % above the long‑run trend triggering a buffer review. As of the March 2024 Financial Stability Report, the credit‑to‑GDP gap stood at 1.3 %, well below the activation trigger, and the CCyB remained at 0 %. The RBI has signalled that any future activation would be communicated at least four quarters in advance, giving banks time to raise capital or adjust lending.

Standing Deposit Facility and Variable Rate Reverse Repo: Operational Details and Transmission Effects

The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) was introduced on 8 April 2022 as a non‑collateralised liquidity absorption tool, replacing the fixed‑rate reverse repo as the floor of the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor. The SDF rate was initially set at 3.75 %, 25 basis points below the policy repo rate (then 4.00 %). In the June 2022 monetary policy review the RBI aligned the SDF rate with the reverse repo rate at 3.35 %, making the SDF the primary instrument for absorbing surplus liquidity on an overnight basis. Banks can place any amount of funds in the SDF without providing government securities as collateral, a feature that distinguishes it from the reverse repo and the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF).

Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions were launched in March 2020 to manage durable liquidity over longer horizons (14‑day, 28‑day, and 56‑day tenors). The RBI announces the notified amount and the cut‑off rate; banks bid for the amount they wish to park at the prevailing rate. VRRR operations are conducted on the e‑Kuber platform and are typically used when the banking system holds excess liquidity that cannot be absorbed fully by the overnight SDF. In FY 2023‑24 the RBI conducted 48 VRRR auctions, absorbing an average of ₹1.2 lakh crore per auction, with cut‑off rates ranging between 3.30 % and 3.55 %. The VRRR cut‑off serves as a market‑determined benchmark for short‑term money‑market rates and feeds into the pricing of commercial paper, certificates of deposit, and the tri‑party repo market.

The transmission of SDF and VRRR rates to the broader money market operates through the interest‑rate corridor. The repo rate forms the ceiling, the SDF the floor, and the VRRR cut‑off anchors the term‑structure of interbank rates. When the RBI tightens policy, it raises the repo rate and typically lifts the SDF rate in tandem, narrowing the corridor and pushing up the weighted average call rate (WACR). Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that a 25 bps increase in the SDF rate leads to an average 18 bps rise in the 14‑day VRRR cut‑off and a 12 bps increase in the 91‑day treasury‑bill yield within two weeks, confirming the potency of the floor instrument.

Operationally, the RBI publishes a daily “Liquidity Operations” statement detailing the amount absorbed under SDF, the VRRR auction results, and the net liquidity injection or absorption. Banks’ participation in the SDF is voluntary but incentivised by the risk‑free return; in March 2024 the SDF absorbed ₹3.4 lakh crore, representing 68 % of total LAF absorption. The VRRR, by contrast, is used for calibrated liquidity management ahead of large government borrowing programmes or festival‑season cash demand. The coexistence of a collateral‑free floor (SDF) and a term‑based, market‑clearing instrument (VRRR) gives the RBI a flexible toolkit to steer short‑term rates without resorting to outright open‑market operations.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the Standing Deposit Facility and Variable Rate Reverse Repo together shape the short‑term interest‑rate corridor in India. Illustrate with the March 2024 liquidity data.”
The SDF, set at 3.35 % in March 2024, forms the corridor floor; banks placed ₹3.4 lakh crore in the SDF, establishing a risk‑free overnight rate. The 14‑day VRRR auction on 15 March 2024 cleared at a cut‑off of 3.48 % for ₹1.15 lakh crore, anchoring the term‑premium. The repo ceiling remained at 6.50 %. The corridor width (repo‑SDF) was 315 bps, while the term spread (VRRR‑SDF) was 13 bps, indicating ample liquidity but a modest term premium. The answer should note that the SDF absorbs surplus overnight funds without collateral, while VRRR drains durable liquidity at market‑determined rates, together steering the WACR and short‑term market yields.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the current SDF and repo rates (as of the latest monetary policy) and the typical VRRR tenors. In a descriptive answer, quote the latest liquidity‑operations numbers from the RBI’s weekly press release; this demonstrates up‑to‑date awareness and earns extra marks for data‑backed analysis.

Monetary Policy Transmission to Small and Medium Enterprises: Credit Guarantee Schemes and Bank Lending Behavior

Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) account for roughly 30 % of India’s gross value added and 40 % of exports, yet they historically face higher borrowing costs due to information asymmetry and collateral constraints. The RBI’s monetary transmission to this segment operates through both the interest‑rate channel and the credit‑availability channel. The interest‑rate channel works via the external benchmark lending rate (EBLR) system, which links all new floating‑rate loans to the repo rate, the 3‑month treasury‑bill yield, or the 6‑month MCLR. Since October 2019, all new SME loans above ₹10 lakh must be priced off an external benchmark, reducing the lag between policy rate changes and loan repricing to one reset cycle (typically one month).

The credit‑availability channel is amplified by government‑backed guarantee schemes. The Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), established in 2000, provides collateral‑free credit guarantees up to ₹2 crore per borrower. As of March 2024, CGTMSE had guaranteed ₹3.2 lakh crore of outstanding loans, covering 1.1 million units. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS), launched in May 2020 as part of the Atmanirbhar Bharat package, extended a 100 % guarantee on additional working‑capital loans up to 20 % of outstanding credit, with a cap of ₹5 crore per borrower. By December 2023, ECLGS had sanctioned ₹3.6 lakh crore, of which ₹2.9 lakh crore was disbursed, predominantly to micro‑enterprises in manufacturing and services.

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s “Quarterly Survey of Credit Conditions” shows that banks’ willingness to lend to micro‑enterprises improved from a net‑balance of –12 % in Q1 2020 to +8 % in Q4 2023, coinciding with the ECLGS rollout and the repo‑rate cuts of 2020‑21. However, the survey also flags a rising “risk‑aversion” index for small‑ticket loans (below ₹10 lakh), reflecting concerns over asset quality in the post‑pandemic period. The RBI’s 2022 circular on “Framework for Resolution of Stressed MSME Assets” introduced a one‑time restructuring window for MSME accounts with exposure up to ₹25 crore, allowing banks to extend moratoriums and convert debt to equity without classifying the account as an NPA, provided the resolution plan is implemented within 180 days.

Transmission effectiveness is also shaped by the “bank‑lending channel”. Public sector banks (PSBs), which hold 60 % of MSME credit, exhibit a higher pass‑through of policy rate cuts to lending rates (average 85 % within three months) compared with private sector banks (average 70 %). This differential arises from PSBs’ larger reliance on wholesale deposits linked to the repo rate and their mandate to meet priority‑sector lending targets (40 % of adjusted net bank credit). The RBI’s 2023 “Priority Sector Lending” guidelines raised the MSME sub‑target to 7.5 % of ANBC for PSBs, reinforcing the credit‑availability channel.

Supervisory Framework for Urban Cooperative Banks: Recent Reforms, Resolution Mechanisms, and Governance

Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) operate under a dual regulatory regime: the Reserve Bank of India for banking functions and the respective state registrar of cooperative societies for governance. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, brought UCBs squarely under RBI’s supervisory powers, enabling the central bank to supersede boards, issue directions, and initiate resolution without prior state‑government approval. As of March 2024, there are 1,531 UCBs with an aggregate deposit base of ₹5.8 lakh crore, accounting for 3.2 % of total scheduled commercial bank deposits.

The RBI’s 2021 “Revised Supervisory Action Framework (SAF) for UCBs” introduced a graded prompt‑corrective‑action (PCA) matrix similar to that for commercial banks, with three trigger thresholds based on capital‑to‑risk‑weighted‑assets ratio (CRAR), net NPA ratio, and profitability. A UCB breaching the first threshold (CRAR < 9 %, net NPA > 6 %, or two consecutive years of losses) faces restrictions on branch expansion, dividend declaration, and fresh lending to risky sectors. The second threshold (CRAR < 6 %, net NPA > 9 %) triggers mandatory board reconstitution and a capital‑raising plan within six months. The third threshold (CRAR < 3 %, net NPA > 12 %) empowers the RBI to supersede the board and appoint an administrator, paving the way for amalgamation or liquidation under the Banking Regulation Act.

In 2022 the RBI issued a “Governance Guidelines for UCBs” mandating a minimum of 51 % professional directors on the board, a fit‑and‑proper test for chief executives, and an independent audit committee with at least two members possessing banking or financial‑management experience. The guidelines also require UCBs to adopt a “Core Banking Solution” (CBS) compliant with the RBI’s “Cyber Security Framework” by March 2025, addressing the long‑standing technology gap that hindered real‑time monitoring.

Resolution mechanisms were strengthened through the “Scheme for Amalgamation of UCBs” notified in September 2023. The scheme provides a fast‑track process: the RBI can order amalgamation of a weak UCB with a stronger one (often a small finance bank or a commercial bank) within 90 days, with the deposit insurance cover of ₹5 lakh per depositor (enhanced by the 2021 DICGC amendment) remaining intact. The first such amalgamation under the new scheme occurred in January 2024, when the RBI merged the crisis‑hit “Maharashtra Urban Cooperative Bank” with “Equitas Small Finance Bank”, protecting ₹1,200 crore of depositor funds.

The combined effect of these reforms is visible in the improvement of aggregate UCB health indicators: the system‑wide CRAR rose from 10.2 % in March 2020 to 12.8 % in March 2024, while the gross NPA ratio fell from 9.4 % to 5.6 % over the same period. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report (March 2024) notes that the UCB sector no longer poses a systemic risk, but it cautions that concentration of deposits in a few large UCBs (the top 10 hold 45 % of sector deposits) warrants continued vigilance.

  • Assuming the CCyB is automatically activated when credit growth exceeds nominal GDP — the RBI must explicitly announce activation after a four‑quarter notice.
  • Confusing the SDF rate with the reverse repo rate — since June 2022 they are aligned, but the SDF remains a collateral‑free floor instrument.
  • Believing VRRR auctions are conducted at a fixed rate — the cut‑off is market‑determined and varies each auction.
  • Thinking ECLGS guarantees cover all MSME loans — the scheme applies only to incremental working‑capital facilities up to 20 % of outstanding credit.
  • Overlooking that UCBs are still subject to state cooperative‑society laws for member‑level governance — RBI’s supersession powers apply only to banking operations.
  • Assuming the PCA thresholds for UCBs are identical to those for commercial banks — the SAF uses distinct CRAR and NPA triggers calibrated for the cooperative sector.
  • Ignoring the 90‑day amalgamation timeline under the 2023 scheme — the RBI can complete a merger within three months, a key difference from the longer commercial‑bank resolution process.
The advanced sections above deepen the aspirant’s grasp of macro‑prudential tools, liquidity‑management instruments, SME‑focused transmission channels, and the evolving supervisory architecture for cooperative banks.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Housing Finance Market

The housing finance segment in India is dominated by scheduled commercial banks, housing finance companies (HFCs) registered with the National Housing Bank (NHB), and a growing cohort of non‑bank lenders that rely on bank borrowing. Transmission of policy rate changes to mortgage rates therefore travels through three linked channels: the marginal cost of funds based lending rate (MCLR) or external benchmark linked lending rate (EBLR) of banks, the cost of funds for HFCs that borrow heavily from banks and the capital markets, and the risk‑pricing adjustments that lenders make in response to changes in household income expectations and property‑price dynamics.

Bank‑linked transmission

Since October 2019 all new floating‑rate home loans from banks must be benchmarked to an external reference — the repo rate, the three‑month or six‑month treasury bill yield, or any other market‑determined benchmark published by Financial Benchmarks India. The spread over the benchmark is fixed at origination, so a 25‑basis‑point repo cut translates almost one‑for‑one into the loan rate after the next reset date, typically quarterly. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (2023) shows that the pass‑through to outstanding home‑loan portfolios averaged 78 % within four quarters during the 2019‑2022 easing cycle, higher than the 55 % observed for corporate term loans.

HFC funding channel

HFCs raise 60‑70 % of their resources through bank borrowings, non‑convertible debentures (NCDs) and commercial paper. When the policy corridor narrows, the weighted average cost of these liabilities falls, but the pass‑through is moderated by the credit‑spread component that reflects the HFC’s own rating and the market’s perception of real‑estate risk. The NHB’s 2022 “Review of Housing Finance” noted that a 50‑bps repo reduction lowered the average incremental cost of funds for the top ten HFCs by only 30‑35 bps because spreads on NCDs widened as investors demanded higher compensation for sectoral concentration risk.

Risk‑pricing and demand feedback

Lower mortgage rates improve affordability, but the elasticity of housing demand to interest‑rate changes is low in the short run (estimated at 0.15‑0.20 by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy). The stronger effect operates through the balance‑sheet channel: rising property values boost collateral values, reducing loan‑to‑value ratios and prompting banks to expand credit limits. Conversely, during tightening cycles, the RBI’s 2023 “Financial Stability Report” highlighted that a 100‑bps increase in the repo rate raised the gross NPA ratio of housing loans by 12‑15 bps within six quarters, primarily because of the lagged impact on borrower cash flows in the informal‑income segment.

Policy implications

The RBI’s 2024 “Monetary Policy Report” recommends that supervisors monitor the share of housing loans priced off external benchmarks versus legacy base‑rate/MCLR loans, because the latter exhibit sticky pass‑through. It also urges HFCs to diversify funding through securitisation and the recently permitted “covered bond” framework, which would make their cost of funds more directly responsive to policy rates.

RBI's Framework for Climate Risk Stress Testing and Scenario Analysis

In July 2023 the Reserve Bank released the “Draft Disclosure Framework on Climate‑Related Financial Risks” for scheduled commercial banks, followed by a final “Guidance Note on Climate Risk Stress Testing” in February 2024. The framework requires banks to integrate physical‑risk (flood, cyclone, heat‑wave) and transition‑risk (policy, technology, market) scenarios into their Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and to report results in the annual Financial Stability Report.

Scenario design

The RBI adopts the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) “Current Policies”, “Delayed Transition” and “Net Zero 2050” scenarios, calibrated for India using the Integrated Assessment Model (IAM) outputs from the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology. Physical‑risk scenarios map district‑level hazard projections (e.g., 1‑in‑100‑year flood depth) to bank loan portfolios using geocoded collateral data. Transition‑risk scenarios apply sector‑specific carbon‑price pathways (₹1,200‑₹2,500 per tonne CO₂ by 2030) to high‑emission sectors — thermal power, steel, cement, and commercial real estate.

Methodology and metrics

Banks must estimate the impact on three key metrics: (i) credit‑loss provisions under a 12‑month expected‑credit‑loss (ECL) horizon, (ii) risk‑weighted assets (RWA) inflation due to rating migrations, and (iii) liquidity‑coverage‑ratio (LCR) strain from deposit outflows in climate‑affected regions. The guidance prescribes a “bottom‑up” loan‑level approach for exposures above ₹5 crore and a “top‑down” portfolio‑level proxy for smaller tickets. Results are expressed as capital‑ratio depletion (percentage points of CET1) and as additional provisioning needs (₹ crore).

Supervisory integration

The RBI’s 2024 Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) will treat climate‑stress outcomes as a qualitative factor in the Pillar‑2 capital add‑on. Banks that project a CET1 depletion exceeding 150 bps under the “Delayed Transition” scenario must submit a remediation plan within 90 days, including sectoral exposure limits and green‑finance targets. The first round of submissions (March 2024) showed median CET1 depletion of 85 bps across the system, with three large public‑sector banks exceeding the 150‑bps threshold due to concentrated lending to coal‑based power projects.

Data and disclosure gaps

A persistent challenge is the absence of standardized, geocoded collateral data for agricultural and MSME loans, which together constitute 38 % of bank credit. The RBI has mandated that banks adopt the “India Climate Risk Data Template” (ICRDT) by March 2025, aligning with the forthcoming Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) Business Responsibility and Sustainability Reporting (BRSR) core metrics. Until the template is fully populated, supervisors rely on proxy‑based heat‑maps that may under‑state concentration risk in flood‑prone river basins.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the RBI’s climate‑risk stress‑testing framework translates physical‑risk hazards into capital‑ratio impact for a bank with a large agricultural loan book in the Gangetic plain.”
The answer should trace the chain: (1) the bank maps each loan to a district using the ICRDT; (2) NGFS physical‑risk scenarios provide district‑level flood‑depth and frequency projections; (3) a loss‑given‑default (LGD) model calibrated on historical flood‑damage data converts hazard intensity into expected credit losses; (4) the incremental ECL raises provisions, reducing CET1 capital; (5) the resulting CET1 depletion is compared against the 150‑bps supervisory trigger. Mention that the lack of granular collateral data forces the bank to use a top‑down proxy, which may under‑estimate the true capital impact.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question combines climate risk with capital adequacy, structure the answer in three layers: scenario → portfolio mapping → capital metric. Cite the specific RBI circular (February 2024 Guidance Note) and the NGFS scenario names. This signals that you know the regulatory architecture, not just the concept.

Digital Rupee Wholesale Pilot: Architecture, Settlement Finality, and Interoperability

The Reserve Bank launched the wholesale Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑W) pilot on 1 November 2022, initially involving nine banks for secondary‑market government‑securities settlement. By March 2024 the pilot expanded to 22 banks and included corporate‑bond repo, commercial‑paper settlement, and cross‑border trade‑finance use‑cases with the Monetary Authority of Singapore under the Project Ubin‑India link.

Ledger and consensus design

The CBDC‑W runs on a permissioned distributed ledger operated by the RBI’s “e₹‑W” node cluster. Consensus is achieved through a practical Byzantine Fault Tolerant (pBFT) protocol among the participating bank validator nodes, delivering finality within 2‑3 seconds. Unlike the retail CBDC (e₹‑R) which uses a token‑based model with offline capability, the wholesale variant is account‑based: each bank holds a CBDC‑W account at the RBI, and transfers are recorded as debit‑credit entries on the shared ledger.

Settlement finality and legal backing

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, was amended in 2023 to recognise CBDC‑W entries as “final and irrevocable” upon ledger commitment, equating them with Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) finality. This legal certainty eliminates the need for a separate netting‑and‑settlement cycle, reducing the settlement window for government‑securities trades from T+1 to intraday (T+0). The RBI’s 2024 “Wholesale CBDC Operational Guidelines” specify that a transaction is deemed final when the validator quorum (≥ 2/3 + 1 nodes) signs the block, and the originating bank receives a cryptographic receipt.

Interoperability with existing market infrastructure

The pilot integrates with the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL) for novation and with the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) for order routing. A “bridge smart contract” translates CBDC‑W transfer instructions into ISO 20022 messages understood by CCIL’s settlement engine. For cross‑border repo with Singapore, the RBI and MAS implemented a hashed‑time‑locked contract (HTLC) that atomically swaps e₹‑W for SGD‑CBDC on the respective ledgers, achieving delivery‑versus‑payment (DvP) without a correspondent‑bank intermediary.

Risk management and scalability

The RBI imposes a per‑bank CBDC‑W holding limit of ₹5,000 crore during the pilot, calibrated to 5 % of the bank’s net demand and time liabilities (NDTL). Real‑time monitoring dashboards track node‑health, latency, and queue depth. Stress tests conducted in January 2024 simulated a 10× volume surge (≈ 1.2 lakh transactions per minute) and confirmed that the pBFT consensus remained within the 3‑second finality target, though CPU utilisation on validator nodes approached 85 %, prompting a hardware‑upgrade roadmap for the production rollout.

Impact of Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio on Bank Asset‑Liability Management

The RBI implemented the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) in a phased manner from January 2015 (60 % minimum) to January 2019 (100 %). The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) became effective from October 2021 at a 100 % minimum for all scheduled commercial banks. Together, these standards reshape the structural liquidity profile of banks and influence pricing, product design, and balance‑sheet composition.

LCR‑driven shifts in high‑quality liquid assets (HQLA)

To meet the 100 % LCR, banks increased their holdings of Level 1 HQLA (government securities, cash, and RBI reserves) from an average of 18 % of total assets in March 2015 to 24 % in March 2024. The “LCR‑eligible” tag on government securities created a captive demand that compressed yields on the 10‑year benchmark by an estimated 15‑20 bps, as documented in the RBI’s 2023 “Annual Report”. Banks also reduced reliance on short‑term wholesale funding (certificates of deposit, commercial paper) because these outflows attract a 100 % run‑off factor under the LCR, raising the effective cost of such liabilities.

NSFR and the funding‑maturity profile

The NSFR requires that available stable funding (ASF) — weighted by stability factors (e.g., 100 % for regulatory capital, 90 % for retail deposits with maturity > 1 year) — covers required stable funding (RSF) assigned to assets based on their liquidity and maturity. Post‑NSFR, banks lengthened the average maturity of term deposits by 4‑6 months and increased the share of “core” retail deposits (savings and current accounts) from 58 % to 63 % of total deposits. Simultaneously, the share of long‑term infrastructure loans (RSF factor 85 %) in incremental credit fell from 12 % to 8 %, as banks re‑balanced toward assets with lower RSF weights such as short‑term working‑capital loans (RSF factor 50 %).

Pricing and product innovation

The marginal cost of maintaining LCR‑compliant HQLA buffers is now explicitly internalised in the “liquidity premium” component of the MCLR/EBLR calculation. Several large private banks introduced “LCR‑linked deposit” products offering a 10‑15 bps higher rate for deposits that qualify for the 90 % ASF factor, effectively passing the funding‑stability benefit to customers. On the asset side, banks have expanded “trade‑finance” and “supply‑chain finance” portfolios, which attract a 50 % RSF factor and generate fee income without materially increasing RSF.

Supervisory monitoring and stress‑testing

The RBI’s 2024 “Liquidity Stress Testing Framework” mandates quarterly scenario runs: (i) a 30‑day market‑wide stress with 30 % deposit outflow and 50 % HQLA haircut, (ii) a 90‑day idiosyncratic stress with 50 % wholesale‑funding roll‑over failure. Banks must report the projected LCR and NSFR trajectories and the contingency funding plan. The March 2024 Financial Stability Report noted that the system‑wide median LCR under the 30‑day stress remained above 115 %, while the NSFR dipped to 98 % for two mid‑size banks, triggering supervisory engagement on funding‑diversification plans.

Foreign Portfolio Investment Limits and Rupee Volatility

India’s foreign portfolio investment (FPI) regime, governed by the SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 and the RBI’s Foreign Exchange Management (Transfer or Issue of Security by a Person Resident Outside India) Regulations, 2017, sets sectoral caps and aggregate limits that directly influence rupee exchange‑rate dynamics. As of March 2024, the aggregate FPI limit in government securities stands at 6 % of outstanding stock, while the corporate‑bond limit is 15 % of outstanding stock, with a sub‑limit of 9 % for “long‑term” investors (pension funds, sovereign wealth funds) who enjoy a higher operational ceiling.

Limit mechanics and volatility transmission

When FPI inflows approach the aggregate cap, the RBI’s “voluntary retention route” (VRR) allows eligible investors to exceed the limit by up to 2 % of outstanding stock, provided they commit to a minimum three‑year holding period.
