Examiner's technique: Linking VRRR cut‑off to fund yield
A question asks: “If the RBI raises the VRRR cut‑off rate by 20 bps while keeping the policy repo rate unchanged, what is the most likely immediate impact on the portfolio yield of a money market mutual fund with a 70 % T‑bill allocation?”
The VRRR cut‑off acts as the de‑facto floor for the overnight call rate. A 20 bps increase lifts the call rate, which in turn raises the discount rate on newly issued T‑bills at the next auction. Since the fund holds 70 % in T‑bills that are marked‑to‑market daily, its portfolio yield will rise by roughly 14‑16 bps (70 % × 20 bps) within the auction cycle. The remaining 30 % in CP/CD will adjust only at rollover, so the immediate impact is dominated by the T‑bill leg.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the current corridor rates (SDF, repo, MSF) and the latest VRRR cut‑off from the RBI’s monthly bulletin. In a numerical question, compute the weighted‑average pass‑through using the fund’s disclosed asset allocation (available in the monthly factsheet). This turns a qualitative transmission question into a quick arithmetic problem.

Sovereign Green Bond Issuance: RBI's Operational Framework and Market Impact

India’s first sovereign green bonds (SGrBs) were auctioned on 25 January 2023, raising ₹16,000 crore across two tranches — a 5‑year ₹8,000 crore bond at 7.10 % and a 10‑year ₹8,000 crore bond at 7.29 %. The issuance followed the “Sovereign Green Bond Framework” released by the Ministry of Finance in November 2022, which defines a taxonomy aligned with the International Capital Market Association (ICMA) Green Bond Principles. Eligible expenditures include renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, and clean transportation. The RBI, as the government’s debt manager, conducts the auctions on the NDS‑OM platform using the uniform‑price method, with Primary Dealers required to bid for at least 5 % of the notified amount.

Proceeds are credited to the “Green Fund” maintained in the Public Account and are earmarked for projects certified by the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change. The RBI publishes a quarterly “Green Bond Allocation Report” detailing project‑wise utilisation; as of March 2024, 62 % of the FY 2022‑23 proceeds had been deployed, predominantly in solar‑power capacity addition (₹4,800 crore) and metro‑rail projects (₹2,200 crore). Secondary‑market liquidity remains modest: average daily turnover in the 10‑year SGrB was ₹1,200 crore in Q4 FY 2023‑24, with bid‑ask spreads of 8‑10 bps, tighter than comparable dated securities (12‑15 bps) due to the “greenium” — a yield discount of 3‑5 bps observed at issuance. The RBI’s 2023 “Guidelines for Market Making in Sovereign Green Bonds” obligate designated market makers to provide two‑way quotes for a minimum of ₹200 crore per session, supporting price discovery.

Cyber Resilience and IT Governance Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s cyber‑resilience architecture rests on three pillars: the 2021 “Cyber Security Framework for Banks”, the 2022 “Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices”, and the 2023 “Guidelines on Cyber Resilience for Payment System Operators”. The 2021 framework mandates a board‑level Cyber Risk Committee, a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the MD/CEO, and a minimum annual cyber‑security budget of 10 % of the IT spend. Banks must conduct a comprehensive vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) at least quarterly, and report any “critical” incident (impact on payment systems, data breach > 1 lakh records) to the RBI within 6 hours.

The 2022 Master Direction extends the governance requirements to all regulated entities (REs) — commercial banks, NBFCs‑ML, payment banks, small finance banks, and authorised payment system operators. It prescribes a “Three‑Lines‑of‑Defence” model: (i) business units own risk, (ii) risk‑management and compliance functions provide independent oversight, (iii) internal audit assures effectiveness. REs must maintain a “Technology Risk Appetite Statement” approved by the board, and submit a quarterly “IT Governance Report” covering project‑level milestones, legacy‑system decommissioning, and third‑party vendor risk scores. The 2023 guidelines for payment system operators add a mandatory “Business Continuity Plan (BCP) drill” every six months, with a recovery‑time objective (RTO) of 4 hours for critical payment systems (UPI, IMPS, RTGS). As of December 2023, the RBI’s supervisory dashboard showed 94 % compliance with the VAPT frequency norm, while 12 % of REs were issued “show‑cause” notices for delayed incident reporting.

Resolution Framework for Systemically Important Financial Institutions (SIFIs) in India

India’s resolution regime for Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIBs) was formalised through the RBI’s “Framework for Resolution of Systemically Important Banks” (July 2021) and the subsequent “Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for D‑SIBs” (March 2022). The current D‑SIB list (updated August 2023) comprises State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, and Punjab National Bank. The framework adopts the Financial Stability Board’s Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes, providing the resolution authority (RBI) with tools such as bail‑in, bridge institution, asset separation, and sale of business. Bail‑in powers are exercised under Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, allowing the RBI to write down or convert unsecured liabilities (including Tier‑2 capital instruments) to absorb losses.

Resolution planning is mandatory: each D‑SIB must submit a “Resolution Plan” (living will) annually, detailing legal entity structure, critical functions, inter‑connectedness, and funding‑liquidity strategies. The RBI’s “Resolution Planning Guidelines” (January 2023) require a minimum “Minimum Requirement for Own Funds and Eligible Liabilities” (MREL) of 8 % of risk‑weighted assets for D‑SIBs, phased in by March 2025. The PCA framework for D‑SIBs introduces graduated triggers — capital adequacy ratio (CAR) below 9 %, net NPA above 6 %, leverage ratio below 3.5 % — with corresponding restrictions on dividend distribution, branch expansion, and high‑cost deposits. In the event of a “point of non‑viability” (PONV), the RBI may invoke the “Special Resolution Regime” under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (Second Amendment) Act, 2021, enabling a time‑bound resolution (180 days, extendable by 90 days) with a dedicated Resolution Professional. The first live test of this architecture occurred during the 2022‑23 stress‑testing exercise, where a simulated 300 bps shock to the repo rate triggered a bail‑in of ₹12,000 crore of Tier‑2 bonds for a hypothetical D‑SIB, demonstrating operational readiness.

  • Confusing the WMA interest rate with the policy repo rate; WMA normal rate equals the repo rate, but special WMA carries a 25 bps premium.
  • Assuming all money market funds react identically to VRRR changes; funds with higher CP exposure exhibit a longer transmission lag.
  • Believing sovereign green bond proceeds can finance any infrastructure project; they are restricted to the taxonomy in the 2022 framework.
  • Thinking the 2021 Cyber Security Framework applies only to scheduled commercial banks; it covers all regulated entities including payment system operators.
  • Mixing up the MREL requirement for D‑SIBs with the Basel III capital conservation buffer; MREL is a separate loss‑absorbing capacity metric.
  • Assuming the bail‑in tool can be applied to insured deposits; deposit insurance (DICGC) protects deposits up to ₹5 lakh and is excluded from bail‑in.
  • Overlooking that the PCA triggers for D‑SIBs are stricter than for other banks (CAR < 9 % vs. 10.5 % for non‑D‑SIBs).

The advanced sections above integrate operational data, regulatory timelines, and transmission mechanics to equip aspirants for analytical and numerical questions in the examination.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has grown from a negligible segment in the early 2000s to a market size exceeding ₹40 lakh crore by March 2024. Transmission of the policy repo rate to corporate bond yields operates through three primary channels: the risk‑free rate channel, the credit‑spread channel, and the liquidity‑premium channel. When the RBI raises the repo rate, the overnight indexed swap (OIS) curve shifts upward, raising the risk‑free benchmark against which corporate bonds are priced. Simultaneously, higher short‑term rates increase the cost of funds for banks and primary dealers, widening the credit spread demanded by investors for lower‑rated issuers. The liquidity‑premium channel reflects the RBI’s open market operations (OMOs) and the special liquidity facility for corporate bonds introduced during the COVID‑19 pandemic; when the RBI absorbs liquidity via variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions, the supply of high‑quality collateral shrinks, pushing up yields on both government and corporate securities.

Empirical studies using daily data from the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL) show that a 25 basis‑point repo hike leads to an average 18‑22 bps increase in AAA‑rated 5‑year corporate bond yields within two weeks, while BBB‑rated yields rise by 30‑35 bps, reflecting the credit‑spread amplification. The RBI’s “Corporate Bond Purchase Programme” (CBPP) launched in April 2020, under which the central bank bought ₹1.2 lakh crore of investment‑grade bonds, compressed spreads by 40‑50 bps for eligible issuers. The programme was wound down in March 2022 as market conditions normalised. The introduction of the “Market Making Scheme” for corporate bonds in 2021, mandating designated market makers to provide two‑way quotes, improved price discovery and reduced bid‑ask spreads from an average of 30 bps to 12 bps for the most liquid issues.

Regulatory reforms have also shaped transmission. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) mandated a minimum 25 % public float for new issuances from 2019, enhancing secondary‑market depth. The RBI’s “Large Exposure Framework” (2023) caps bank exposure to a single corporate group at 20 % of Tier‑1 capital, limiting banks’ ability to absorb large primary issuances and pushing issuers toward broader investor bases. The “First Loss Default Guarantee” (FLDG) guidelines for digital lending platforms, while primarily aimed at fintech, indirectly affect corporate bond demand by altering the risk appetite of non‑bank investors. Finally, the upcoming “Corporate Bond Market Development Fund” (announced in the 2024‑25 Budget) aims to provide a backstop for market‑making activities, which should further smooth the pass‑through of policy rates to corporate borrowing costs.

RBI's Macroprudential Stress Testing of Interconnected Financial Institutions

The RBI’s macroprudential stress‑testing framework, formalised in the 2018 “Guidelines on Stress Testing for Banks” and extended to non‑bank financial companies (NBFCs) in 2020, evaluates the resilience of the financial system to severe but plausible adverse scenarios. The framework combines bottom‑up bank‑level solvency and liquidity stress tests with a top‑down system‑wide contagion analysis. The bottom‑up module requires each scheduled commercial bank and systemically important NBFC to project capital ratios, leverage ratios, and liquidity coverage ratios (LCR) under a baseline and three adverse scenarios: a 300 bps repo‑rate shock, a 5 % GDP contraction, and a 15 % depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar. Banks submit results quarterly; the RBI aggregates them in the semi‑annual Financial Stability Report (FSR).

The top‑down contagion module uses a network‑based “Interconnectedness Matrix” constructed from bilateral exposures in the interbank market, derivative positions, and common asset holdings. The RBI applies the CoVaR (Conditional Value‑at‑Risk) and SRISK (Systemic Risk) metrics to quantify spillover potential. In the 2023 FSR, the CoVaR for the banking system rose to 2.8 % of total assets under the severe interest‑rate shock, up from 1.9 % in 2022, reflecting increased reliance on short‑term wholesale funding. The “Contagion Index” — measuring the proportion of system capital that could be eroded by the failure of the largest five entities — stood at 12 % in March 2024, below the 15 % threshold that would trigger enhanced supervisory intervention.

Scenario design follows the “Macro‑Financial Scenario Framework” published by the RBI in 2021. Each scenario specifies paths for key macro variables (real GDP growth, CPI inflation, current account deficit, fiscal deficit, and the policy rate) over a 12‑quarter horizon. The RBI calibrates the severity using historical episodes: the 2008 global financial crisis, the 2013 taper tantrum, and the 2020 pandemic shock. The 2024 stress test introduced a “climate‑transition” scenario aligned with the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) “Delayed Transition” pathway, incorporating a carbon‑price shock of ₹2,500 per tonne CO₂ and a 10 % decline in fossil‑fuel‑related asset values. Results showed a modest 0.4 % additional capital shortfall for the banking sector, but a 1.2 % shortfall for NBFCs with high exposure to power‑generation assets.

Supervisory integration of stress‑test outcomes occurs through the “Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process” (SREP). Banks that breach the 9 % Common Equity Tier‑1 (CET1) threshold under the adverse scenario must submit a capital restoration plan within 30 days. For NBFCs, the RBI’s “Scale‑Based Regulation” (2022) links stress‑test results to layer‑specific capital and liquidity requirements. The 2023 “Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for D‑SIBs” incorporates stress‑test triggers: a projected CET1 below 8 % under the severe scenario activates dividend restrictions and limits on branch expansion. The RBI also publishes aggregate stress‑test summaries to enhance market discipline, a practice commended by the Financial Stability Board in its 2023 peer review.

Worked Example: Estimating Corporate Bond Yield Response
Assume the RBI raises the policy repo rate by 50 bps. The current 5‑year OIS rate is 6.80 %. The AAA corporate bond spread over OIS is 70 bps, and the BBB spread is 180 bps. Empirical elasticity suggests AAA yields move 0.85 × repo change, while BBB yields move 1.2 × repo change. Calculate the new yields for both ratings.
Step 1: Compute OIS shift = 0.50 % × 0.85 = 0.425 % (42.5 bps). New OIS = 6.80 % + 0.425 % = 7.225 %. Step 2: AAA new yield = new OIS + unchanged spread (70 bps) = 7.225 % + 0.70 % = 7.925 %. Step 3: BBB OIS shift = 0.50 % × 1.2 = 0.60 % (60 bps). New OIS for BBB = 6.80 % + 0.60 % = 7.40 %. BBB new yield = 7.40 % + 1.80 % = 9.20 %. Thus, AAA yield rises to 7.93 % and BBB yield to 9.20 %.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the transmission magnitude, first identify the relevant channel (risk‑free, credit‑spread, liquidity). Use the elasticity coefficients provided in the stem; if absent, apply the standard RBI‑published ranges (0.8‑0.9 for high‑grade, 1.1‑1.3 for low‑grade). Show the intermediate OIS shift calculation — examiners award partial marks for correct mechanics even if the final number has a rounding difference.

Exchange Rate Pass‑Through and Monetary Policy Effectiveness in India

India operates a managed float where the RBI intervenes to curb excessive volatility but allows the rupee to reflect market forces over the medium term. The exchange rate pass‑through (ERPT) to domestic prices measures the percentage change in the Consumer Price Index (CPI) resulting from a 1 % change in the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER). Empirical estimates using quarterly data from 2000‑2023 place the short‑run ERPT at 0.12‑0.15 and the long‑run ERPT at 0.22‑0.28 for headline CPI, with higher pass‑through for fuel (0.35‑0.40) and lower for services (0.05‑0.08). The asymmetry arises because import‑intensive sectors (energy, edible oils, capital goods) adjust prices quickly, while regulated prices and sticky wages dampen the overall effect.

The RBI’s sterilised foreign‑exchange interventions — selling dollars and simultaneously conducting OMOs to absorb the rupee liquidity — limit the monetary base expansion that would otherwise amplify ERPT. However, large‑scale interventions (e.g., the $100 billion purchase programme in FY 2021‑22) increase the RBI’s balance‑sheet exposure to exchange‑rate risk and can reduce the effectiveness of domestic rate changes. When the policy repo rate is raised, the interest‑rate differential attracts capital inflows, appreciating the rupee and partially offsetting the tightening via lower import prices. The net effect on inflation depends on the relative strength of the interest‑rate channel versus the exchange‑rate channel. In the 2022‑23 tightening cycle (repo from 4.00 % to 6.50 %), the NEER appreciated 3.2 %, contributing an estimated 0.4‑0.5 percentage‑point reduction in CPI inflation, while the direct interest‑rate channel contributed roughly 0.8‑1.0 percentage‑points.

Policy implications are twofold. First, the RBI’s “Flexible Inflation Targeting” (FIT) framework treats the exchange rate as an endogenous variable; the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) does not target a specific NEER level but monitors ERPT as part of its inflation forecast. Second, the RBI’s “Foreign Exchange Intervention Framework” (updated 2022) caps net intervention at 2 % of GDP per quarter unless exceptional circumstances arise, preserving reserve adequacy (import cover > 12 months) while allowing the rupee to act as a shock absorber. The 2023 “Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) misalignment” assessment indicated a 4‑5 % undervaluation, suggesting that further appreciation would not jeopardise export competitiveness but would enhance the disinflationary impact of rate hikes.

Household Balance Sheet Channel of Monetary Transmission

The household balance‑sheet channel captures how changes in the policy rate affect household debt service capacity, net worth, and consequently consumption and housing investment. In India, household debt‑to‑GDP rose from 11.5 % in 2015 to 37.1 % in March 2024, driven by mortgage loans (≈ 55 % of total), vehicle loans, and unsecured personal loans. The RBI’s “Survey of Household Finances” (2023) shows that the median debt‑service‑to‑income (DSTI) ratio for mortgage borrowers is 28 %, above the 25 % prudential threshold used by banks for new sanctions. A 100 bps repo increase raises the marginal cost of funds for banks by roughly 70‑80 bps, which is passed on to floating‑rate home loans with a lag of 1‑2 quarters. For a ₹50 lakh loan at 8.5 % over 20 years, a 75 bps rate hike increases the monthly EMI by ₹2,200, pushing the DSTI ratio above 30 % for many borrowers.

The wealth effect operates through asset prices. Higher rates depress equity valuations (the Nifty 50 price‑to‑earnings ratio fell from 24.5× in Dec 2021 to 19.8× in Dec 2023) and housing prices (the RBI’s House Price Index grew 2.1 % YoY in 2023 versus 7.4 % in 2021). Households holding financial assets experience a decline in net worth, reducing the marginal propensity to consume (MPC) out of wealth, estimated at 0.03‑0.04 for the top income quintile. Conversely, higher deposit rates increase interest income for savers, particularly senior citizens reliant on fixed deposits; the 2023‑24 hike in the senior‑citizen savings scheme rate from 7.4 % to 8.2 % added an estimated ₹12,000 crore to household interest income, partially offsetting the negative wealth effect.

Policy responses have targeted the balance‑sheet channel. The RBI’s “Risk‑Based Supervision” (2021) requires banks to conduct DSTI stress tests at the portfolio level, assuming a 200 bps rate shock. The “Credit Guarantee Scheme for Sub‑Prime Housing Loans” (2022) provides a 75 % guarantee on loans to borrowers with DSTI up to 35 %, encouraging lenders to maintain flow to vulnerable segments. The “External Benchmark Lending Rate” (EBLR) regime, mandatory from Oct 2019, links all new floating‑rate retail loans to the repo rate or the 3‑month T‑bill, ensuring faster and more symmetric transmission. Early evidence suggests that EBLR reduced the pass‑through lag from 4‑5 quarters to 1‑2 quarters, improving the predictability of household cash‑flow impacts for monetary policymakers.

Digital Public Infrastructure and Financial Inclusion: UPI, Bharat BillPay, and ONDC

India’s digital public infrastructure (DPI) stack — Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Bharat BillPay (BBPS), and the Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) — has transformed the last‑mile delivery of financial services. UPI, launched in April 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), processed 131 billion transactions worth ₹199 lakh crore in FY 2023‑24, accounting for 73 % of all retail digital payments by volume. The introduction of UPI 2.0 in August 2018 added features such as overdraft facilities, one‑time mandates, and invoice‑in‑the‑box, enabling credit‑linked payments and recurring bill settlements. The “UPI Lite” offline wallet (2022) extended access to feature‑phone users without internet connectivity, raising the active user base to 350 million by March 2024.

Bharat BillPay, operational since 2018, provides an interoperable bill‑payment platform covering electricity, water, gas, telecom, and municipal taxes. As of December 2023, BBPS onboarded 21,000 billers and processed 2.8 billion transactions annually, reducing the average bill‑payment cost for consumers by 40 % compared with traditional channels. The RBI’s “Bharat BillPay Operating Guidelines” (2021) mandate settlement finality within T+0 for participating banks, and the “Business Continuity Plan” drill requirement (2023) ensures a recovery‑time objective (RTO) of 4 hours for critical payment systems, aligning with the broader payment‑system resilience framework.

ONDC, piloted in April 2022 across five cities, aims to democratise e‑commerce by creating an open protocol for buyer‑seller discovery, logistics, and payments. By March 2024, ONDC had onboarded 36,000 sellers and 12 million buyers, with gross merchandise value (GMV) of ₹4,500 crore. The network leverages UPI for instant settlement and the Account Aggregator (AA) framework for consent‑based data sharing, enabling small merchants to access formal credit based on transaction history. The RBI’s “Regulatory Sandbox” cohort 5 (2023) included ONDC‑linked fintech solutions for inventory financing, demonstrating how DPI can close the credit gap for micro‑enterprises.

Despite rapid adoption, challenges persist. UPI’s zero‑merchant‑discount‑rate (MDR) model raises sustainability concerns for payment service providers; the RBI’s 2023 discussion paper on “Pricing of UPI Transactions” explores a tiered MDR structure. Interoperability between BBPS and state‑level bill‑payment platforms remains incomplete, leading to duplicate onboarding. ONDC’s success hinges on widespread adoption of the Beckn protocol and the resolution of data‑privacy issues under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023. The RBI’s “Financial Inclusion Index” (2024) rose to 64.2 from 53.9 in 2021, reflecting DPI’s contribution, but the gender gap in digital payment usage (female‑to‑male ratio 0.68) highlights the need for targeted literacy programmes.

  • Confusing the corporate bond purchase programme (CBPP) with the regular OMO; CBPP was a targeted, time‑bound intervention for investment‑grade bonds only.
  • Assuming the ERPT coefficient is uniform across all CPI components; fuel and edible oils exhibit significantly higher pass‑through than services.
  • Treating the household DSTI threshold as a regulatory cap; it is a supervisory benchmark used in stress tests, not a hard limit for loan sanction.
  • Believing UPI’s zero MDR applies to all payment modes; MDR is waived only for peer‑to‑peer and peer‑to‑merchant UPI transactions, not for card‑on‑UPI or credit‑line‑on‑UPI.
  • Mixing up the ONDC protocol with a marketplace; ONDC is an open network protocol, not a platform that holds inventory or processes payments directly.
  • Overlooking that the RBI’s macroprudential stress test includes a climate‑transition scenario only from the 2024 cycle onward.
  • Remember to verify the latest RBI circulars before the exam.

Banking Ombudsman Scheme: Structure, Jurisdiction, and Recent Amendments

The Banking Ombudsman Scheme (BOS) was introduced by the Reserve Bank of India in 1995 under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, to provide an expeditious and cost‑free dispute‑resolution mechanism for bank customers. The scheme is administered by the RBI through a network of 22 Banking Ombudsmen located in state capitals and major metropolitan centres. Each Ombudsman is a senior officer of the RBI, appointed for a term of three years, and operates independently of the banks against which complaints are filed.

Jurisdiction covers all scheduled commercial banks, regional rural banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and cooperative banks that are licensed by the RBI. The scheme entertains complaints relating to deficiency in banking services such as non‑payment or delayed payment of cheques, non‑adherence to prescribed working hours, failure to honour guarantee/letter of credit commitments, levy of charges without prior notice, and non‑observance of RBI directives on interest rates, KYC, and fair practices. As of the 2021 amendment, the pecuniary limit for compensation was raised from ₹20 lakh to ₹1 crore, and the Ombudsman can also award costs up to ₹1 lakh. The amendment also introduced a “deemed rejection” provision: if a bank fails to respond within 30 days, the complaint is deemed to be rejected, allowing the complainant to approach the Ombudsman directly.

The complaint process is entirely online through the RBI’s Complaint Management System (CMS). A complainant must first approach the concerned bank and wait for 30 days (or 45 days for credit‑card related grievances) before filing with the Ombudsman. The Ombudsman endeavours to settle the dispute through mediation; if mediation fails, a binding award is issued. The award is enforceable as a decree of a civil court. Banks may appeal to the Appellate Authority (the Deputy Governor in charge of consumer protection) within 30 days. The scheme also provides for a “Review” mechanism where the Ombudsman can review his own award on grounds of mistake or new evidence.

Recent enhancements include the 2022 “Integrated Ombudsman Scheme” which merged the Banking Ombudsman, the Ombudsman for Non‑Banking Financial Companies, and the Ombudsman for Digital Transactions into a single platform, simplifying access for customers. The integrated scheme also introduced a “Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre” to reduce turnaround time. The RBI’s Annual Report 2023‑24 notes that the integrated scheme received 4.2 lakh complaints, with a disposal rate of 96 % within the prescribed 90‑day timeline. The scheme’s effectiveness is monitored through the “Customer Service Index” published in the Financial Stability Report.

For examiners, the key distinctions are: (i) the scheme is statutory, not voluntary; (ii) the Ombudsman’s award is binding on the bank but not on the complainant; (iii) the pecuniary limit applies to compensation, not to the value of the underlying transaction; and (iv) the scheme does not cover disputes relating to loans sanctioned by non‑bank lenders unless they are NBFCs registered with the RBI.

Outsourcing and Cloud Services Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s regulatory stance on outsourcing was first articulated in the 2006 “Guidelines on Managing Risks and Code of Conduct in Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks”. The guidelines were substantially revised in November 2017 (Circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2017‑18) to align with the Basel Committee’s “Sound Practices for Managing Outsourcing Risk”. The 2017 framework mandates that banks retain ultimate responsibility for all outsourced activities, including those performed by sub‑contractors. It requires a board‑approved outsourcing policy, a comprehensive risk‑assessment before entering any arrangement, and a legally binding contract that specifies service‑level agreements, data‑confidentiality clauses, audit rights, and termination provisions.

In June 2021, the RBI issued a dedicated circular on “Cloud Services” (Circular DOR.No.BP.BC.112/21.04.048/2020‑21) recognising the growing adoption of public, private, and hybrid cloud models. The circular classifies cloud deployments into three tiers — “Non‑Critical”, “Critical”, and “Highly Critical” — based on the sensitivity of data and the impact of service disruption. For “Highly Critical” workloads (e.g., core banking, payment systems, customer‑identification data), the RBI insists on data localisation within India, encryption at rest and in transit, and a contractual right for the regulator to conduct on‑site inspections of the cloud service provider’s infrastructure. Banks must also maintain a “Cloud Exit Strategy” to ensure portability and avoid vendor lock‑in.

Key operational requirements include: (i) a due‑diligence checklist covering the provider’s financial health, security certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2), and compliance with Indian data‑protection laws; (ii) continuous monitoring through automated logs and periodic vulnerability assessments; (iii) incident‑reporting obligations — any breach affecting customer data must be reported to the RBI within six hours of detection; (iv) an annual independent audit of the outsourced/cloud arrangement, with the audit report submitted to the board and the RBI; and (v) a “Concentration Risk” limit — no single cloud provider may host more than 30 % of a bank’s critical workloads without prior RBI approval.

The framework also extends to NBFCs, payment system operators, and credit information companies through separate but substantively similar circulars (e.g., DNBS.PPD.No.01/66.15.001/2021‑22 for NBFCs). The RBI’s 2023 “Supervisory Framework for Cloud Adoption” introduced a “Cloud Readiness Assessment” tool that supervisors use during on‑site inspections. Banks that fail to meet the prescribed controls may face supervisory actions ranging from restrictive directions to monetary penalties under Section 47A of the Banking Regulation Act.

From an examination perspective, candidates should distinguish between “outsourcing” (delegation of a business process) and “cloud adoption” (use of a technology platform). The regulatory perimeter differs: outsourcing guidelines apply to any third‑party service, while cloud circulars specifically address data‑hosting models. Also, the 30 % concentration cap is a supervisory benchmark, not a statutory ceiling, and applies only to “Highly Critical” workloads.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Under the RBI’s 2021 Cloud Services circular, a bank may host its core‑banking database on a foreign public‑cloud provider provided the provider holds ISO 27001 certification.” Is this statement correct?
The statement is incorrect. For “Highly Critical” workloads such as core‑banking databases, the RBI mandates data localisation within India. A foreign public‑cloud provider, even with ISO 27001 certification, cannot host such data unless the data resides on infrastructure physically located in India and the contract grants the RBI on‑site inspection rights. The certification alone does not satisfy the localisation requirement.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes outsourcing and cloud concepts, first identify the workload classification (Non‑Critical, Critical, Highly Critical). Then apply the specific rule: localisation and inspection rights only for Highly Critical; due‑diligence and audit for all tiers. Remember the 30 % concentration cap is a supervisory benchmark, not a hard statutory limit.

Cybersecurity and IT Governance Guidelines for Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s first comprehensive cybersecurity circular was issued in June 2011 (DBS.CO.CSITE/BC.11/33.01.001/2010‑11), establishing a baseline framework that required banks to appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), formulate a board‑approved cybersecurity policy, and conduct periodic vulnerability assessments. The framework was substantially upgraded in June 2016 (Circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2015‑16) to incorporate the “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover). The 2016 circular mandated: (i) a dedicated Security Operations Centre (SOC) with 24×7 monitoring; (ii) implementation of multi‑factor authentication for all critical systems; (iii) encryption of sensitive data at rest and in transit; (iv) a formal incident‑response plan with defined escalation matrices; and (v) quarterly reporting of cyber incidents to the RBI’s Department of Banking Supervision.

In August 2020, the RBI issued a “Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” (MD‑ITG) that consolidated IT governance, cybersecurity, and business‑continuity requirements into a single supervisory document. The MD‑ITG requires banks to establish an IT Strategy Committee at the board level, a separate IT Steering Committee at the executive level, and a CISO reporting directly to the Managing Director/CEO. It also prescribes a “Three Lines of Defence” model: (1) business units owning risk; (2) risk‑management and compliance functions; (3) internal audit providing independent assurance. The direction introduces a “Cyber Crisis Management Plan” (CCMP) that must be tested through tabletop exercises at least annually.

For NBFCs, the RBI released a parallel “Master Direction – Information Technology Framework for NBFCs” in June 2021 (DNBS.PPD.No.01/66.15.001/2021‑22), which scales the requirements proportionately: NBFCs with asset size above ₹5,000 crore must comply with the full MD‑ITG, while smaller NBFCs follow a simplified “Baseline Cybersecurity Framework” covering CISO appointment, basic network segmentation, and incident reporting within 24 hours.

Key supervisory metrics include the “Cybersecurity Maturity Index” published in the Financial Stability Report, which rates entities on a five‑level scale (Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimising). The RBI’s 2023 supervisory findings highlighted that 68 % of scheduled commercial banks had reached at least the “Defined” level, whereas only 42 % of NBFCs above the threshold achieved the same. Common deficiencies cited were inadequate privileged‑access management, lack of automated log‑correlation, and insufficient testing of the CCMP.

Examination focus areas: (a) the distinction between the 2011 baseline circular and the 2016 framework (the latter introduces SOC, MFA, and quarterly reporting); (b) the three‑lines‑of‑defence model introduced in MD‑ITG; (c) the proportional application for NBFCs based on asset size; and (d) the requirement for annual tabletop testing of the Cyber Crisis Management Plan.

Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Governance in Financial Services

The RBI’s engagement with AI/ML began with a discussion paper released in October 2023 titled “Governance of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Financial Services”. The paper does not yet constitute a binding regulation but sets out supervisory expectations that are already being referenced in inspection questionnaires. The core principles are: (i) Model Risk Management — every AI/ML model used for credit scoring, fraud detection, algorithmic trading, or customer‑service chatbots must be documented in a Model Inventory, validated by an independent model‑validation team, and subjected to periodic back‑testing against out‑of‑sample data; (ii) Explainability and Transparency — decisions affecting customers (e.g., loan denial, credit‑limit reduction) must be explainable in plain language; black‑box models are permissible only where a documented “human‑in‑the‑loop” review is mandatory before final action; (iii) Data Governance — training data must be sourced lawfully, free from prohibited biases (gender, religion, caste), and stored in compliance with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; (iv) Accountability — the board must approve an AI/ML Governance Policy, designate a senior officer (Chief Data Officer or equivalent) as the accountable executive, and ensure that model‑performance metrics are reported to the board quarterly.

The discussion paper also introduces a “Risk‑Based Tiering” of AI/ML applications: Tier 1 (high impact, high autonomy) — e.g., automated loan underwriting, real‑time fraud blocking — requires full model validation, independent audit, and a pre‑deployment supervisory notification; Tier 2 (moderate impact) — e.g., marketing‑campaign optimisation — requires internal validation and documentation; Tier 3 (low impact) — e.g., internal productivity tools — requires only basic inventory registration. The RBI has indicated that a formal circular codifying these tiers is likely in the 2024‑25 policy cycle.

Supervisory integration: the RBI’s 2024 “Supervisory Framework for AI/ML” (draft) proposes that inspectors will assess (a) the existence of a Model Inventory, (b) the frequency of model‑drift monitoring (minimum monthly for Tier 1), (c) the presence of a “Model‑Change Management” process that treats any retraining as a new version requiring re‑validation, and (d) the adequacy of fallback mechanisms (e.g., rule‑based engine) when the AI/ML model is unavailable or produces anomalous outputs.

For candidates, the critical take‑aways are: the discussion paper is not yet law but reflects supervisory intent; the tiering concept mirrors the Basel model‑risk approach; explainability is a regulatory expectation, not a technical suggestion; and the board‑level accountability mirrors the three‑lines‑of‑defence model already embedded in MD‑ITG.

Co‑Lending Models between Banks and Non‑Banking Financial Companies

The RBI introduced the “Co‑Lending Model (CLM) for Banks and NBFCs” through a circular dated 5 November 2020 (DBR.No.BP.BC.63/21.04.048/2020‑21) to leverage the complementary strengths of banks (low‑cost funds) and NBFCs (origination reach). Under the model, a bank and an NBFC jointly extend a loan to a borrower, sharing credit risk in a pre‑agreed proportion — typically 80 % by the bank and 20 % by the NBFC, though the ratio may vary with board approval. The NBFC acts as the “originator” responsible for sourcing, appraisal, and documentation, while the bank provides the bulk of the funding and retains the legal title to the loan asset.

Key contractual requirements include: (i) a tripartite agreement among bank, NBFC, and borrower specifying the risk‑sharing ratio, interest‑rate split, and servicing responsibilities; (ii) a joint credit‑policy approved by both boards, covering eligibility, loan‑to‑value limits, and sectoral exposure caps; (iii) a “first‑loss” provision where the NBFC absorbs losses up to its share before the bank’s portion is impacted; (iv) a common escrow account for loan disbursement and repayment collection, managed by the bank; and (v) reporting obligations — the NBFC must report the co‑lended portfolio to the RBI’s Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC) and to the credit information companies.

The 2020 circular also permits “Co‑Origination” where the bank and NBFC jointly underwrite the loan at inception, and “Co‑Funding” where the NBFC originates and the bank funds later, provided the risk‑sharing ratio is fixed at origination. In 2022, the RBI clarified that the model extends to Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) and Microfinance Institutions (MFIs) registered as NBFCs, subject to the same governance standards. The 2023 “Scale‑Based Regulation” for NBFCs further requires that NBFCs in the Upper Layer obtain prior RBI approval for any co‑lending arrangement exceeding 10 % of their Tier‑I capital.

Supervisory monitoring focuses on: (a) concentration risk — the bank’s exposure to a single NBFC through co‑lending must not exceed 20 % of the bank’s Tier‑I capital; (b) asset‑quality segregation — co‑lended assets must be identified separately in the bank’s NPA classification; (c) interest‑rate risk — the blended yield must be allocated transparently to avoid mis‑pricing; and (d) operational risk — the NBFC’s outsourcing of collection to third parties must comply with the bank’s outsourcing guidelines.

Examination pointers: differentiate between “co‑origination” (joint underwriting) and “co‑funding” (sequential funding); remember the default 80‑20 risk split is a guideline, not a statutory rule; the first‑loss provision protects the bank but does not eliminate the NBFC’s capital requirement; and the model does not apply to loans originated solely by the bank without NBFC participation.

  • Assuming the Banking Ombudsman can adjudicate disputes involving non‑bank lenders that are not NBFCs registered with the RBI.
  • Treating the 30 % cloud‑concentration cap as a hard statutory limit applicable to all workload tiers.
  • Confusing the 2011 baseline cybersecurity circular with the 2016 framework; the latter introduces SOC, MFA, and quarterly incident reporting.
  • Believing the AI/ML discussion paper creates binding obligations; it only signals supervisory expectations pending a formal circular.
  • Thinking the co‑lending 80‑20 risk split is mandatory for every arrangement; boards may approve alternative ratios with proper justification.
  • Overlooking that the NBFC’s first‑loss share does not exempt it from maintaining its own capital adequacy for the co‑lended portfolio.
  • Missing the proportional application of MD‑ITG for NBFCs based on asset‑size thresholds (₹5,000 crore).
The advanced sections above complete the required coverage for this lesson.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has grown from a marginal segment in the early 2000s to a source of roughly 15 % of total non‑bank credit by 2023. Transmission of RBI policy rates to this market operates through four intertwined channels. First, the interest‑rate channel works via the risk‑free benchmark — primarily the 10‑year government security yield — which moves in step with the repo rate and liquidity operations. Second, the credit‑spread channel reflects the premium investors demand over the risk‑free rate; this premium is sensitive to the RBI’s outlook on growth and inflation because it shapes expectations of corporate default probabilities. Third, the portfolio‑rebalancing channel arises when the RBI conducts outright purchases of corporate bonds (the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme, CBPP, launched in March 2020 and extended in 2021) or provides liquidity through the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF). These operations lower yields on eligible papers and encourage investors to shift into slightly riskier issuances. Fourth, the signalling channel operates through forward guidance and the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC) communication; a credible commitment to low rates compresses term premia across the yield curve.

Empirically, a 25 basis‑point repo cut has historically reduced the 10‑year G‑sec yield by 15‑20 bps, while the spread on AAA‑rated corporate bonds narrows by an additional 5‑10 bps within a month, provided liquidity is ample. The CBPP‑1 (₹20,000 crore) and CBPP‑2 (₹30,000 crore) together absorbed about 2 % of outstanding corporate bonds, pulling the AAA‑G‑sec spread from 115 bps (Feb 2020) to 85 bps (Oct 2020). However, transmission is asymmetric: lower‑rated issuers (AA and below) experience muted spread compression because credit‑risk perception dominates the risk‑free rate effect. The RBI’s 2022 “Market Making Scheme” for corporate bonds, which designates primary dealers as obligatory market makers, aims to deepen secondary‑market liquidity and make the interest‑rate channel more effective for the entire rating spectrum.

Examiners often test the distinction between outright purchases (CBPP) and repo‑style liquidity (TLTRO, LTRO). Outright purchases expand the central bank’s balance sheet permanently and directly lower yields; repo operations are collateralised, temporary, and transmit mainly through the banking system. Another trap is assuming a one‑to‑one pass‑through from repo to corporate bond yields — credit spreads, issuance calendar, and foreign portfolio investor flows frequently decouple the two.

RBI's Liquidity Management during the 2020 COVID‑19 Crisis

When the nationwide lockdown was announced on 25 March 2020, the RBI unleashed a calibrated liquidity arsenal that injected roughly 8 % of GDP (≈ ₹18 lakh crore) into the financial system within three months. The sequence began with a 75 bps repo‑rate cut (to 4.40 %) and a 90 bps reverse‑repo reduction (to 3.35 %) on 27 March, followed by a 100 bps cash‑reserve‑ratio (CRR) cut (to 3 %) effective 28 March, releasing an estimated ₹1.37 lakh crore of primary liquidity. To address term‑funding stress, the RBI launched two Long‑Term Repo Operations (LTROs) of ₹1 lakh crore each (3‑year and 1‑year tenors) in April, and a Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operation (TLTRO) of ₹1 lakh crore in April‑May, earmarked for investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. A Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) of ₹50,000 crore was announced on 27 April to stem redemption pressures in debt‑oriented funds.

Simultaneously, the RBI announced a three‑month moratorium on term‑loan repayments (1 March‑31 May, later extended to 31 August) and a stand‑still on asset classification for accounts standard as on 1 March 2020. The “COVID‑19 Regulatory Package” also permitted banks to restructure eligible MSME and personal loans without downgrading asset quality, provided the resolution was invoked by 31 December 2020. On the communication front, the MPC adopted an explicit forward‑guidance stance, committing to keep the policy rate “accommodative as long as necessary” and signalling that the reverse‑repo rate would remain the effective floor for the interest‑rate corridor.

The combined effect was a swift shift from a deficit to a surplus liquidity regime: average daily net liquidity absorption by the RBI turned from ₹1.2 lakh crore (pre‑COVID) to a net injection of ₹3.5 lakh crore by June 2020. The weighted average call‑rate (WACR) fell below the reverse‑repo rate for the first time in years, confirming that the corridor had effectively collapsed. However, the moratorium and stand‑still created a “hidden NPA” problem that surfaced in the 2021‑22 asset‑quality review, prompting the RBI to introduce the “Resolution Framework for COVID‑19‑related Stress” (August 2020) with a one‑time restructuring window.

Worked Example
A 2021 mains question asked: “Explain the distinction between LTRO and TLTRO introduced by the RBI in 2020 and assess their relative effectiveness in transmitting policy easing to the corporate bond market.”
Answer outline: (1) Define LTRO — long‑term repo operations open to all eligible collateral (government securities, high‑quality corporate bonds) with no sectoral restriction; conducted in two tranches of ₹1 lakh crore each (3‑year and 1‑year). (2) Define TLTRO — targeted LTRO of ₹1 lakh crore where banks must deploy funds in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and NCDs within 30 days; tenor 1‑3 years. (3) Transmission: LTRO primarily expands banking‑system liquidity and lowers the marginal cost of funds, indirectly aiding corporate bond demand. TLTRO directly channels liquidity into the corporate bond market, evidenced by a 30‑40 bps compression in AAA‑G‑sec spreads within weeks of the first TLTRO auction. (4) Effectiveness: TLTRO had a more measurable impact on corporate bond yields and issuance volumes (₹1.2 lakh crore of fresh issuance in Q2 FY21), while LTRO’s effect was diffused across the broader credit market. (5) Caveat: both operations were collateralised and temporary; they did not address the underlying credit‑risk aversion that kept lower‑rated spreads elevated.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “liquidity measures during COVID‑19”, list them in chronological order (rate cuts → CRR cut → LTRO → TLTRO → SLF‑MF → moratorium → restructuring framework). Pair each tool with its primary transmission channel (interest‑rate, credit‑spread, term‑funding, forbearance). This structure earns both content and presentation marks.

The Role of the Financial Stability and Development Council in Macroprudential Coordination

The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) was constituted in December 2010 as an apex‑level forum to strengthen institutional mechanisms for financial stability, inter‑regulatory coordination, and financial sector development. Chaired by the Union Finance Minister, its members include the RBI Governor, the Chairpersons of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, the Chairman of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), and senior officials from the Department of Economic Affairs and the Department of Financial Services. The Council has no statutory powers; its recommendations are advisory, but they carry significant moral authority because all major regulators sit at the table.

Key macroprudential interventions coordinated through the FSDC include: (i) the 2015 recommendation to activate the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) framework, which the RBI operationalised in 2016; (ii) the 2017 endorsement of a resolution corporation for financial firms, a precursor to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016; (iii) the 2020 joint “COVID‑19 Regulatory Package” where the RBI, SEBI, and IRDAI aligned moratorium, asset‑classification stand‑still, and claim‑settlement relaxations; (iv) the 2021 oversight of the Special Resolution Regime for large NBFCs, ensuring that the RBI’s resolution powers under the IBC were complemented by SEBI’s market‑surveillance tools; and (v) the 2022‑23 guidance on climate‑related financial risk, urging regulators to adopt scenario‑analysis and disclosure standards consistent with the Task Force on Climate‑related Financial Disclosures (TCFD).

The FSDC operates through a Standing Committee chaired by the RBI Governor, which meets quarterly to monitor systemic risk indicators (credit‑to‑GDP gap, property‑price indices, inter‑bank exposure, shadow‑banking leverage). The Council also publishes a semi‑annual Financial Stability Report (FSR) that aggregates stress‑test results from banks, insurers, and NBFCs. A frequent examiner twist is to conflate the FSDC with the international Financial Stability Board (FSB). The FSB is a G20‑level body that sets global standards; the FSDC is a domestic coordination platform with no rule‑making authority. Another trap is assuming the FSDC can issue binding directives — its resolutions are implemented only when each regulator issues its own circular.

RBI's Framework for Cyber Resilience in Payment Systems

Cyber resilience for payment systems has evolved through three regulatory layers. The 2011 “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” set baseline controls (firewalls, intrusion detection, annual audits). The 2016 revision introduced a mandatory Security Operations Centre (SOC), multi‑factor authentication (MFA) for critical systems, and quarterly incident reporting to the RBI. In 2018, the RBI issued a dedicated “Cyber Security Framework for Payment System Operators (PSOs)”, extending the 2016 bank‑centric norms to non‑bank entities such as card networks, PPI issuers, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) ecosystem. The 2021 “Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls” consolidated these requirements and added: (a) board‑level oversight with a designated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO); (b) mandatory vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) at least annually; (c) encryption of data at rest (AES‑256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); (d) tokenisation of card‑on‑file data; (e) a 6‑hour incident‑reporting window for material breaches; and (f) a cap of 30 % on concentration of critical workloads in a single cloud service provider, aligned with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance (MD‑ITG).

The 2022 “Guidelines on Regulation of Payment Aggregators and Payment Gateways” further mandated that PAs/PGs adhere to the same cyber controls, maintain a separate escrow account for merchant settlements, and submit a quarterly compliance certificate signed by the CISO. The RBI also operates a Cyber Security Incident Reporting Portal (CSIRP) where regulated entities must log incidents; failure to report within the prescribed timeline attracts supervisory action under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007. Supervisory audits conducted in 2022‑23 revealed that 78 % of PSOs had a functional SOC, but only 52 % performed red‑team exercises annually, prompting the RBI to issue a 2023 advisory urging quarterly red‑team drills for systemically important PSOs.

Examiners often test the distinction between the 2011 baseline circular and the 2016 framework — the latter introduced SOC, MFA, and quarterly reporting, which are absent in the earlier version. Another common error is applying the 30 % cloud‑concentration cap to all workload tiers; the cap applies only to “critical” workloads as defined in MD‑ITG. Candidates should also remember that the 2021 Master Direction applies exclusively to payment system operators and payment aggregators/gateways, not to all NBFCs or banks (which remain governed by the 2016 bank framework).

  • Confusing the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (outright purchase) with LTRO/TLTRO (repo‑style liquidity) and assuming identical transmission effects.
  • Treating the 2020 moratorium as an automatic restructuring; it only deferred repayments and required a separate resolution plan under the August 2020 framework.
  • Equating the Financial Stability and Development Council with the international Financial Stability Board and attributing binding rule‑making power to the FSDC.
  • Applying the 2011 cyber‑security baseline to current payment‑system operators, ignoring the 2016 SOC, MFA, and quarterly reporting mandates.
  • Assuming the 30 % cloud‑concentration cap applies uniformly to all IT workloads rather than only to critical workloads defined under MD‑ITG.
  • Believing the RBI’s 2021 Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls extends to all regulated entities, while it is limited to payment system operators and payment aggregators/gateways.
  • Overlooking that the FSDC’s recommendations become effective only after each constituent regulator issues its own circular, making the Council a coordination body, not a legislative one.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Primary Dealers, Market Making, and RBI Liquidity Support

The corporate bond segment in India has historically been shallow, with outstanding issuance hovering around 16‑18 % of GDP. The Reserve Bank has therefore built a dedicated transmission architecture that bypasses the bank‑credit channel. The Primary Dealer (PD) system, comprising 21 entities as of March 2024, is the backbone. PDs are obligated to bid at every primary auction of government securities and, since 2015, to provide two‑way quotes in the secondary market for a minimum of 10 corporate bonds each. This market‑making commitment compresses bid‑ask spreads and creates a reference yield curve that feeds into the pricing of new issuances.

In April 2020 the RBI launched the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP), an outright purchase window of ₹1 lakh crore, later expanded to ₹2 lakh crore. Purchases are conducted through a uniform price auction on the NDS‑OM platform, with eligibility restricted to bonds rated AA and above, residual maturity up to 10 years, and a minimum issue size of ₹100 crore. The CBPP directly lowers yields on eligible paper by 15‑25 basis points on average, as evidenced by the 2021‑22 Financial Stability Report. The programme also signals the central bank’s willingness to absorb duration risk, anchoring long‑term expectations.

A complementary tool is the Corporate Bond Repo (CBR) introduced in July 2021. It allows banks and PDs to repo corporate bonds (rated A‑ and above) for overnight liquidity at the repo rate, effectively extending the LAF corridor to the corporate segment. The CBR has increased the repo‑eligible collateral pool by roughly ₹3.5 lakh crore, improving the liquidity premium on high‑grade corporate paper. The RBI also operationalised the Corporate Bond Market Development Fund (CBMDF) in 2022, seeded with ₹5,000 crore, to provide credit enhancement for lower‑rated issuers and to support market‑making by PDs during stress periods.

Transmission efficacy is monitored through the spread between the 10‑year G‑sec yield and the 10‑year AAA corporate bond yield. Since the CBPP inception, this spread has narrowed from a peak of 115 bps (March 2020) to a range of 55‑70 bps, indicating that policy rate cuts are being passed through to the non‑bank financing channel. However, the pass‑through remains asymmetric: rate hikes widen spreads faster than cuts narrow them, reflecting the credit‑risk premium embedded in corporate paper.

Key Takeaways for Examiners

  • Primary Dealers’ market‑making quota (minimum 10 bonds) is a regulatory requirement, not a voluntary practice.
  • CBPP purchases are outright, not repo‑style; they expand the RBI’s balance sheet and are accounted under “Other Assets”.
  • Corporate Bond Repo eligibility hinges on a minimum rating of A‑, unlike the LAF which accepts only sovereign collateral.
  • The CBMDF is a credit‑enhancement vehicle, not a direct purchase window.

RBI's COVID‑19 Special Liquidity Facilities: Design, Utilisation, and Transmission Effects

The pandemic triggered a suite of targeted liquidity operations that went beyond the regular Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF). The first was the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF), announced on 27 April 2020 with a corpus of ₹50,000 crore. It offered 90‑day repo funding against investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and certificates of deposit. By end‑June 2020, ₹30,000 crore had been drawn, stabilising net asset values of debt‑oriented funds and preventing fire‑sales.

Simultaneously, the RBI rolled out Targeted Long Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) in three tranches. TLTRO 1.0 (27 March 2020) provided ₹1 lakh crore of three‑year funding at the policy repo rate to all banks, with the condition that funds be deployed in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. TLTRO 2.0 (17 April 2020) earmarked ₹50,000 crore exclusively for NBFCs and MFIs, addressing the acute funding gap in the shadow‑banking sector. TLTRO 3.0 (5 May 2020) directed ₹50,000 crore toward small‑business lending via banks’ exposure to MSMEs. Cumulative utilisation of TLTRO 2.0 and 3.0 exceeded ₹1.2 lakh crore by September 2020.

A separate Special Liquidity Facility for NBFCs (SLF‑NBFC) of ₹30,000 crore was opened on 15 May 2020, allowing NBFCs to repo eligible collateral (rated BBB‑ and above) for 90‑day tenor. The facility was later extended to housing finance companies. The on‑tap liquidity window for banks, introduced in August 2020, permitted daily repo of up to 1 % of NDTL at the repo rate, providing a standing backstop.

Transmission evidence: the 10‑year AAA corporate bond yield fell from 7.45 % (pre‑pandemic) to 5.85 % by December 2020, a compression of 160 bps, while the policy repo rate was cut by 115 bps. The spread over G‑secs narrowed, confirming that the targeted operations succeeded in lowering the cost of market‑based finance for high‑grade issuers. For lower‑rated paper (A and BBB), spreads remained elevated, reflecting persistent credit‑risk aversion.

Examiner Focus Points

  • SLF‑MF was a repo facility, not a direct purchase; collateral eligibility was stricter than TLTRO.
  • TLTRO 2.0 and 3.0 had sector‑specific end‑use restrictions, unlike the generic TLTRO 1.0.
  • The on‑tap window is a standing facility, whereas TLTROs were announced with fixed auction dates.
  • Utilisation data are reported in the RBI’s monthly “Money Market Operations” press releases.
Worked Example
Explain how the RBI's Targeted Long Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) 2.0 differed from the regular LAF repo in terms of eligibility, tenor, and transmission objective.
TLTRO 2.0 was a three‑year repo auction conducted at the policy repo rate, open only to scheduled commercial banks, with the explicit condition that the borrowed funds be invested in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures issued by NBFCs and MFIs. In contrast, the regular LAF repo is an overnight (or 14‑day) facility available to all eligible banks against government securities, with no end‑use restriction. The transmission objective of TLTRO 2.0 was to channel durable liquidity directly into the shadow‑banking sector, thereby lowering funding costs for NBFCs/MFIs, whereas the LAF repo primarily manages short‑term inter‑bank liquidity and signals the policy stance.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “special liquidity facilities during COVID‑19”, list SLF‑MF, TLTRO 1.0/2.0/3.0, SLF‑NBFC, and the on‑tap window in chronological order. Pair each with its corpus, tenor, collateral, and target sector. This tabular recall earns full marks for both knowledge and structure.

RBI's Cyber Resilience Framework for Payment System Operators: Evolution, Mandatory Controls, and Supervisory Expectations

The regulatory journey began with the 2011 “Cyber Security Framework for Banks”, which mandated firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and annual IS audits. The 2016 revision added three critical pillars: a dedicated Security Operations Centre (SOC), multi‑factor authentication (MFA) for all critical systems, and quarterly incident reporting to the Department of Supervision. In 2018 the RBI issued a standalone “Cyber Security Framework for Payment System Operators (PSOs)”, extending the 2016 bank‑centric norms to non‑bank entities such as card networks, prepaid payment instrument (PPI) issuers, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) ecosystem.

The 2021 Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls consolidated and hardened these requirements. It introduced board‑level oversight with a designated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), mandatory vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) at least annually, encryption of data at rest using AES‑256 and in transit using TLS 1.2 or higher, tokenisation of card‑on‑file data, a six‑hour reporting window for material breaches, and a concentration cap of 30 % on critical workloads hosted with a single cloud service provider, aligned with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance (MD‑ITG). The 2022 “Guidelines on Regulation of Payment Aggregators and Payment Gateways” further mandated that PAs/PGs adhere to the same cyber controls, maintain a separate escrow account for merchant settlements, and submit a quarterly compliance certificate signed by the CISO.

Supervisory audits in 2022‑23 revealed that 78 % of PSOs had a functional SOC, yet only 52 % conducted red‑team exercises annually. In response, the RBI issued a 2023 advisory urging quarterly red‑team drills for systemically important PSOs. The Cyber Security Incident Reporting Portal (CSIRP) serves as the single reporting channel; failure to log incidents within the prescribed timeline attracts supervisory action under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007.

Common Examiner Traps

  • Confusing the 2011 baseline circular with the 2016 framework — the latter introduced SOC, MFA, and quarterly reporting, absent in the former.
  • Applying the 30 % cloud‑concentration cap to all IT workloads; the cap applies only to “critical” workloads as defined in MD‑ITG.
  • Assuming the 2021 Master Direction extends to all NBFCs or banks; it is limited to payment system operators and payment aggregators/gateways.
  • Overlooking that the FSDC’s recommendations become effective only after each constituent regulator issues its own circular, making the Council a coordination body, not a legislative one.

Impact of the 2023 Amendments to the Banking Regulation Act on Cooperative Banks: Governance, Capital, and Resolution

The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2023 received Presidential assent on 28 March 2023 and came into force on 1 April 2023. It significantly expands the Reserve Bank’s authority over both Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs). Key provisions include: (a) the power to supersede the board of a cooperative bank for up to 12 months and appoint an administrator, (b) mandatory Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 9 % for UCBs and 12 % for StCBs, aligned with Basel III, (c) introduction of a Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for cooperative banks with trigger points at 6 % CRAR, 3 % net NPA, and 0.25 % return on assets, (d) fit‑and‑proper criteria for directors and chief executives, requiring prior RBI approval, (e) compulsory audit by a qualified chartered accountant registered with the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India, and (f) a streamlined resolution mechanism under Section 45, allowing amalgamation or reconstruction without the prior consent of the state registrar.

The amendment also harmonises deposit insurance coverage: the 2021 DICGC Amendment raised the insured limit to ₹5 lakh per depositor, and the 2023 Act ensures that cooperative banks contribute to the DICGC fund on the same basis as commercial banks. Implementation challenges persist due to dual regulatory oversight — the Registrar of Cooperative Societies (state level) retains powers over incorporation, elections, and bye‑laws, while the RBI now exercises prudential supervision. The RBI’s 2023 “Supervisory Framework for Urban Cooperative Banks” operationalises the new PCA triggers and prescribes a timeline for capital augmentation: UCBs below 9 % CRAR must submit a capital restoration plan within 30 days and achieve compliance within 12 months.

Examiner Nuances

  • The 2020 amendment brought UCBs under RBI’s regulatory purview; the 2023 amendment strengthens enforcement (supersession, PCA, fit‑and‑proper).
  • State Cooperative Banks were already under RBI supervision; the 2023 Act extends the same governance tools to them.
  • Section 45 resolution now bypasses the state registrar’s approval, a shift from the pre‑2023 requirement.
  • Capital norms are phased: existing UCBs have a transition period until 31 March 2025 to meet the 9 % CRAR.

RBI's Outsourcing and Cloud Services Framework for Regulated Entities: 2023 Guidelines and Supervisory Expectations

Building on the 2015 “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks”, the RBI issued a comprehensive Master Direction on Outsourcing of IT Services in June 2023, applicable to commercial banks, NBFCs (upper and middle layers), and payment system operators. The framework mandates a board‑approved outsourcing policy that classifies activities into “core”, “critical”, and “non‑critical”. Core banking functions (e.g., core banking solution, KYC processing) cannot be outsourced. Critical activities may be outsourced only after a rigorous due‑diligence process covering financial soundness, information security posture, and geographic location of the service provider.

Contractual clauses must include: (i) data localisation — all customer data must reside in India, (ii) audit rights for the regulated entity and the RBI, (iii) business continuity and disaster recovery obligations with defined Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) and Recovery Point Objectives (RPO), (iv) concentration risk limits — no more than 30 % of critical workloads may be hosted with a single Cloud Service Provider (CSP), consistent with the MD‑ITG definition of “critical workloads”, (v) incident reporting within six hours of detection, and (vi) an annual independent audit of the outsourced activity, with the report submitted to the RBI within 30 days of completion.

The MD‑ITG, also released in 2023, introduces a CSP registration regime: CSPs seeking to host critical workloads must obtain a “Cloud Service Provider Registration” from the RBI, demonstrating compliance with ISO 27001, SOC 2 Type II, and data‑sovereignty requirements. The RBI conducts periodic thematic inspections of outsourcing risk, focusing on vendor concentration, sub‑contracting chains, and exit‑strategy adequacy. For NBFCs, a parallel set of guidelines was issued in November 2022, mirroring the bank framework but with proportionate thresholds based on asset size.

Key Supervisory Expectations

  • Boards must review outsourcing risk at least quarterly and document decisions in minutes.
  • Exit plans must be tested annually; a “fail‑over” drill is expected for each critical outsourced service.
  • Sub‑contracting beyond the first tier requires prior RBI approval.
  • Non‑compliance with the 30 % concentration cap triggers a supervisory letter and may restrict further outsourcing.
  • Assuming the 2015 outsourcing guidelines remain fully applicable; the 2023 Master Direction supersedes them and adds cloud‑specific controls.
  • Treating the 30 % cloud‑concentration cap as a blanket limit for all workloads; it applies only to critical workloads as defined in MD‑ITG.
  • Confusing the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (outright purchase) with LTRO/TLTRO (repo‑style liquidity) and assuming identical transmission effects.
  • Equating the 2020 moratorium with automatic restructuring; it only deferred repayments and required a separate resolution plan under the August 2020 framework.
  • Believing the RBI’s 2021 Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls extends to all regulated entities, while it is limited to payment system operators and payment aggregators/gateways.
  • Overlooking that the FSDC’s recommendations become effective only after each constituent regulator issues its own circular, making the Council a coordination body, not a legislative one.
  • Applying the 2011 cyber‑security baseline to current payment‑system operators, ignoring the 2016 SOC, MFA, and quarterly reporting mandates.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has grown from a negligible segment in the early 2000s to a market size exceeding ₹40 lakh crore by March 2024. Transmission of the RBI’s policy rate to this market operates through three interlocking channels: the risk‑free benchmark, the credit‑spread channel, and the liquidity‑premium channel. The introduction of the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR) for bank loans in 2019 created a direct link between the repo rate and the pricing of new bank credit, but corporate bonds continue to be priced off the Government‑Security (G‑Sec) yield curve plus a credit spread that reflects issuer‑specific risk and market liquidity.

When the RBI cuts the repo rate, the immediate effect is a fall in the short‑end of the G‑Sec curve via the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) and Open Market Operations (OMO). Primary dealers, who are mandated to bid in G‑Sec auctions, transmit the lower yields to the secondary market, compressing the risk‑free benchmark for corporate bonds. However, the credit‑spread channel often offsets part of the benchmark decline. During periods of heightened risk aversion — such as the COVID‑19 shock in March 2020 — spreads on lower‑rated issuers widened by 150‑200 basis points even as the 10‑year G‑Sec yield fell 80 bps. The RBI’s Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) and the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) launched in 2020 were designed to compress these spreads by providing banks with cheap, long‑tenor funds earmarked for investment in investment‑grade corporate paper.

The liquidity‑premium channel captures the cost of holding less‑liquid bonds. The RBI’s 2021 “Market Making in Corporate Bonds” guidelines required designated market makers to quote two‑way prices for a minimum of 5 % of the outstanding amount of each eligible ISIN. This reduced bid‑ask spreads from an average of 30‑40 bps to 10‑15 bps for the most liquid issuers, improving the pass‑through of policy rate changes to secondary‑market yields. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that a 25 bps repo cut translates into a 12‑15 bps decline in the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield within one month, but only a 5‑7 bps decline for AA‑rated paper, reflecting the persistent credit‑spread component.

Key structural reforms have further strengthened transmission. The 2022 “Framework for Issuance of Commercial Paper and Non‑Convertible Debentures” mandated a minimum credit rating of A3 for CP and a minimum issue size of ₹100 crore for NCDs, reducing fragmentation. The introduction of the “Electronic Book Building” platform for private placement in 2023 improved price discovery. Nevertheless, the market remains shallow for maturities beyond 10 years, limiting the effectiveness of long‑rate transmission to infrastructure financing.

RBI's Liquidity Management under the Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio

The Basel III liquidity standards — Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) — were adopted in India with a phased timeline: LCR became binding at 60 % in January 2015, rising 10 % annually to reach 100 % in January 2019; NSFR was made applicable from October 2021 at a 100 % minimum. Both ratios are calibrated on a consolidated basis for scheduled commercial banks, including foreign bank branches, and are reported monthly to the RBI.

The LCR requires banks to hold High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) sufficient to survive a 30‑day stressed cash‑outflow scenario. HQLA are classified into Level 1 (cash, central‑government securities, and RBI‑eligible securities) and Level 2A/2B (high‑rated corporate bonds, covered bonds, and certain equities) with haircuts of 0 %, 15 % and 50 % respectively. The RBI’s 2020 “Guidelines on LCR” introduced a “run‑off factor” of 5 % for retail deposits and 10 % for wholesale funding, reflecting Indian depositor behaviour observed during the 2013 taper‑tantrum episode. Banks must maintain the LCR on a daily average basis, and the RBI monitors compliance through the “LCR Return” submitted via the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS).

The NSFR addresses structural maturity mismatches by requiring Available Stable Funding (ASF) to exceed Required Stable Funding (RSF) over a one‑year horizon. ASF weights range from 100 % for Tier 1 capital and deposits with maturity ≥ 1 year, down to 0 % for liabilities with maturity < 6 months. RSF weights assign 100 % to loans to financial institutions with maturity < 1 year, 85 % to residential mortgages, and 65 % to performing corporate loans. The RBI’s 2021 “NSFR Framework” allowed a 5 % transitional carve‑out for “inter‑bank assets” until March 2023, acknowledging the high reliance of Indian banks on inter‑bank borrowing.

Operationally, the RBI uses the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) to manage surplus liquidity while allowing banks to meet LCR/NSFR without excessive holdings of low‑yield G‑Secs. The SDF, introduced in April 2022 at a rate 25 bps below the repo, provides a floor for the overnight rate and absorbs excess reserves. VRRR auctions, conducted at tenors of 14‑28 days, enable the RBI to fine‑tune the term structure of liquidity. In the first half of FY 2023‑24, the RBI absorbed an average of ₹2.3 lakh crore per fortnight through VRRR, keeping the weighted average call rate within the 6.00‑6.25 % corridor.

Supervisory integration is achieved through the “Liquidity Risk Monitoring Toolkit” (LRMT), which combines LCR, NSFR, and the “Liquidity Stress Testing” module. Banks failing to meet the LCR for three consecutive months are placed under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework’s liquidity trigger, which restricts dividend distribution and branch expansion. As of March 2024, only two small‑finance banks remained under the liquidity‑PCA trigger, reflecting broad compliance.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: “If the RBI reduces the repo rate by 25 bps while the banking system is holding excess reserves of ₹3 lakh crore, explain why the 10‑year AAA corporate bond yield may fall by less than 10 bps.”
The repo cut lowers the short‑end of the G‑Sec curve, but the 10‑year AAA corporate bond yield is anchored by the 10‑year G‑Sec yield plus a credit spread. Excess reserves keep the overnight rate near the SDF floor, limiting the pass‑through to longer tenors. Moreover, the credit‑spread component is driven by issuer‑specific risk and market liquidity, which are unchanged by a marginal repo move. The RBI’s VRRR operations absorb surplus liquidity at short tenors, preventing a sustained decline in term premiums. Consequently, the 10‑year AAA yield may move only 5‑8 bps, reflecting a muted term‑premium response and a sticky credit spread.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question links LCR/NSFR to monetary transmission, first identify the binding constraint (HQLA availability vs stable funding). Then trace the policy tool (repo, SDF, VRRR) to the specific ratio component it affects. Use the 30‑day LCR horizon for short‑rate pass‑through and the one‑year NSFR horizon for term‑structure effects. Cite the 2020 LCR run‑off factors and the 2021 NSFR carve‑out to demonstrate depth.

Impact of the 2023 Amendments to the Banking Regulation Act on Cooperative Banks

The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2023, which received Presidential assent on 11 August 2023, extended the RBI’s supervisory powers over Urban Cooperative Banks (UCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs) to a level comparable with scheduled commercial banks. The amendment inserted Section 56A, empowering the RBI to supersede the board of a UCB for up to 12 months if the bank fails to meet the 9 % Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) or breaches the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) thresholds. It also brought UCBs under the “fit‑and‑proper” criteria for directors, aligning them with the 2020 “Guidelines on Appointment of Directors”.

Prior to 2023, UCBs were regulated under a dual control regime: the Registrar of Cooperative Societies (state level) handled incorporation, elections, and bye‑laws, while the RBI exercised prudential supervision. The 2020 amendment had already subjected UCBs to the RBI’s licensing, audit, and inspection powers, but the 2023 amendment added enforcement teeth — the RBI can now issue directions for capital augmentation, restrict dividend payouts, and mandate merger with a stronger UCB or a commercial bank. The 2023 “Supervisory Framework for Urban Cooperative Banks” operationalised these powers, prescribing a 30‑day window for submission of a capital restoration plan and a 12‑month compliance horizon for banks below the 9 % CRAR.

The amendment also introduced a tiered PCA framework for UCBs mirroring the commercial‑bank PCA: Trigger 1 (CRAR < 9 % but ≥ 7.5 %) imposes restrictions on branch expansion and dividend; Trigger 2 (CRAR < 7.5 % but ≥ 6 %) adds curbs on lending to sensitive sectors; Trigger 3 (CRAR < 6 %) mandates supersession and a resolution plan. As of March 2024, 14 UCBs were under Trigger 1, three under Trigger 2, and one under Trigger 3, reflecting the framework’s immediate impact.
