These directions require banks to appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the board, conduct a quarterly vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) by an empanelled auditor, and report any “critical cyber incident” — defined as an event that compromises the confidentiality, integrity or availability of core banking data — within two hours of detection to the RBI’s Cyber Security and Information Technology Examination Cell (CSITEC). A six‑hour reporting window applies to non‑critical incidents. The 2023 master direction also introduces a “Cyber Risk Appetite Statement” that must be approved by the board annually and linked to the entity’s overall risk appetite framework.

Supervisory integration is achieved through the RBI’s “Supervisory Programme for IT and Cyber Risk” (SPITCR), which conducts thematic inspections on a rolling basis. In the 2023‑24 inspection cycle, 42 % of inspected banks were found to have gaps in vendor‑risk management for cloud providers, and 28 % lacked a tested cloud‑exit plan. The RBI has since issued show‑cause notices to three major private‑sector banks for non‑compliance with the two‑hour critical‑incident reporting norm, resulting in monetary penalties ranging from ₹1 crore to ₹5 crore.

For exam purposes, the key take‑aways are: (i) core banking functions cannot be outsourced to unregulated vendors; (ii) public cloud is allowed only for non‑critical workloads with data‑localisation and exit‑plan safeguards; (iii) critical cyber incidents must be reported within two hours, a stricter timeline than the six‑hour window often quoted in older study material; and (iv) the board‑level CISO and cyber‑risk appetite statement are now mandatory governance requirements.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s 2023 cloud framework is correct? (a) Public cloud can host core banking solutions. (b) Data localisation is optional for disaster‑recovery copies. (c) A cloud exit strategy must be executable within 180 days. (d) CSP empanelment by CERT‑In is not required.”
The correct answer is (c). The framework explicitly mandates a cloud exit strategy with a maximum transition period of 180 days. Core banking solutions must remain on‑premises or on a private cloud, so (a) is false. Primary data must reside in India; only a mirror copy for disaster recovery may be kept abroad, making (b) false. CSPs must be empanelled by CERT‑In, so (d) is false.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three‑tier classification — core vs non‑core outsourcing, critical vs non‑critical cloud workloads, and critical vs non‑critical cyber incidents — together with their respective reporting timelines (2 hours vs 6 hours) and approval requirements. A quick table in your notes will let you eliminate wrong options in under 30 seconds.

Resolution Framework for Stressed Assets in the Power Sector: The 2022 Prudential Framework and Its Interaction with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code

The power sector has historically accounted for a disproportionate share of banking sector NPAs, driven by fuel‑supply risk, regulatory tariff delays, and long gestation periods. Recognising the sector‑specific dynamics, the RBI issued the “Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets in the Power Sector” on 7 June 2022 (RBI/2022‑23/DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048). The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs‑D, and HFCs with exposure to generation, transmission, and distribution assets. It introduces a “Resolution Plan” that must be finalised within 180 days of the account being classified as a “stressed asset” (i.e., SMA‑2 or NPA), failing which the lender must initiate insolvency proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) within 30 days.

A key departure from the generic 2019 Prudential Framework is the “Change‑in‑Management” (CIM) provision. If the resolution plan entails a change in the promoter or management, the new promoter must bring in fresh equity of at least 25 % of the project cost, and the existing promoter’s stake must be diluted to below 10 %. This is stricter than the IBC’s “minimum 25 % equity” rule for resolution applicants and is designed to prevent promoter‑driven evergreening. The framework also mandates a “Fuel‑Supply Agreement (FSA) novation” clause: any resolution plan must secure a binding FSA with Coal India Limited or a gas supplier before the plan is submitted for lenders’ approval, addressing the single biggest operational risk for thermal plants.

Interaction with the IBC is governed by a “dual‑track” approach. Lenders may pursue the RBI framework and, in parallel, file an application under Section 7 of the IBC. If a resolution plan under the RBI framework is approved by 75 % of lenders by value and 60 % by number, it becomes binding on all creditors, including operational creditors, and the IBC application can be withdrawn. However, if the RBI‑framework plan fails to achieve the voting thresholds, the IBC process takes precedence. The National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) has, in multiple orders (e.g., Essar Power Gujarat Ltd., 2023), upheld the primacy of the IBC once the 180‑day RBI window expires without a viable plan.

Quantitative impact: As of March 2024, the RBI’s Financial Stability Report notes that power‑sector NPAs declined from ₹1.12 lakh crore (March 2022) to ₹0.78 lakh crore (March 2024), a 30 % reduction. Of the resolved accounts, 55 % were settled through the RBI framework (mostly via debt‑equity swaps and promoter dilution), 30 % through IBC liquidation or resolution, and 15 % through one‑time settlements (OTS) outside both frameworks. The average haircut for lenders under the RBI framework was 38 %, compared with 45 % under IBC liquidation, indicating a modest recovery advantage for the sector‑specific route.

For aspirants, the critical distinctions are: (i) the 180‑day resolution window with mandatory IBC filing thereafter; (ii) the 25 % fresh‑equity and promoter‑dilution requirements unique to the power‑sector framework; (iii) the mandatory FSA novation before plan submission; and (iv) the voting thresholds (75 % by value, 60 % by number) that differ from the IBC’s 66 % committee‑of‑creditors approval. Confusing these thresholds or the FSA requirement is a frequent source of error in both GS‑III and optional‑economy answers.

RBI’s Framework for the Regulation of Digital Lending Apps and Consumer Protection: 2022 Guidelines and the Self‑Regulatory Organisation

The proliferation of unregulated digital lending applications (DLAs) prompted the RBI to issue the “Guidelines on Digital Lending” on 2 September 2022 (RBI/2022‑23/DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048). The guidelines apply to all regulated entities (REs) — banks, NBFCs, and HFCs — that either directly operate a DLA or partner with a third‑party lending service provider (LSP). The core principle is “entity‑level accountability”: the RE remains fully responsible for the conduct of its LSP, including data privacy, fair‑practice code compliance, and grievance redressal. The RE must conduct a “due‑diligence” of the LSP before onboarding, covering technology stack, data‑storage location, and background of the LSP’s promoters.

Key operational requirements include: (i) all loan disbursements and repayments must flow through the RE’s bank account — no “pass‑through” accounts controlled by the LSP; (ii) the annual percentage rate (APR) must be disclosed upfront, inclusive of all fees, and cannot exceed the RE’s board‑approved risk‑based pricing ceiling; (iii) a “cooling‑off” period of 3 days after loan sanction during which the borrower can cancel without penalty; (iv) mandatory reporting of each loan to the Credit Information Companies (CICs) within T+1; and (v) a prohibition on automatic debit of the borrower’s account for repayment without explicit consent for each instalment.

To oversee compliance, the RBI mandated the formation of a Self‑Regulatory Organisation (SRO) for digital lending. In March 2023, the “Digital Lending Association of India” (DLAI) was recognised as the first SRO. The SRO’s charter requires it to maintain a public register of approved LSPs, conduct periodic audits of member REs’ digital lending portfolios, and issue a “Code of Conduct” that aligns with the RBI’s fair‑practice guidelines. The SRO can impose monetary penalties up to ₹25 lakh per violation and recommend suspension of an RE’s digital lending licence to the RBI. As of December 2023, the SRO had conducted 112 audits, issued 37 warnings, and levied penalties totalling ₹4.3 crore.

Consumer‑protection mechanisms are reinforced through the “Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021” (amended 2022) which now covers digital lending complaints. The pecuniary jurisdiction of the Ombudsman was raised to ₹20 lakh, and a dedicated “Digital Lending Grievance Redressal Portal” was launched on the RBI’s website, enabling borrowers to file complaints against both REs and LSPs. The portal mandates a 30‑day resolution timeline, extendable by 15 days with the Ombudsman’s approval.

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s 2023 “Survey on Digital Lending Practices” shows that 68 % of surveyed REs had fully complied with the APR‑disclosure norm, while 22 % still used pass‑through accounts — a violation that attracted supervisory action. The survey also highlighted that 41 % of borrowers were unaware of the cooling‑off right, underscoring the need for continued financial‑literacy drives. For exam answers, remember the three‑layer accountability chain: RE → LSP → SRO → RBI, and the specific numeric limits — APR ceiling, 3‑day cooling‑off, T+1 CIC reporting, ₹20 lakh Ombudsman limit, ₹25 lakh SRO penalty.

Impact of RBI’s Monetary Policy on Exchange Rate Pass‑Through and Imported Inflation: Empirical Evidence and Policy Implications

Exchange rate pass‑through (ERPT) measures the extent to which changes in the nominal exchange rate translate into domestic price changes, particularly for imported goods. In India, the RBI’s flexible inflation targeting (FIT) framework, adopted in 2016, targets headline CPI inflation at 4 % ± 2 %. The degree of ERPT determines how much of an external shock — such as a US‑Federal‑Reserve rate hike or a commodity‑price surge — feeds into domestic inflation, thereby influencing the monetary policy response.

Empirical studies by the RBI’s DEPR (2021, 2023) using quarterly data from 2000‑2022 estimate the short‑run ERPT to import prices at 0.38 and the long‑run ERPT to CPI at 0.22. The pass‑through to the wholesale price index (WPI) is higher, at 0.45 in the short run, reflecting the larger weight of traded goods in WPI. A 10 % depreciation of the rupee against the dollar therefore raises import prices by roughly 3.8 % within one quarter and pushes headline CPI up by about 2.2 % after four quarters, all else equal. The 2023 study also finds that ERPT has declined from 0.30 (CPI long‑run) in the pre‑FIT period (2000‑2015) to 0.22 post‑FIT, attributing the decline to improved anchoring of inflation expectations and a more credible policy framework.

The RBI manages ERPT through a combination of interest‑rate policy and foreign‑exchange intervention. When capital outflows threaten a sharp depreciation, the RBI may raise the policy repo rate to widen the interest‑rate differential, attracting portfolio inflows and stabilising the rupee. Simultaneously, it may sell dollars from its reserves — ₹5.6 lakh crore as of March 2024 — to smooth excessive volatility. The “managed float” regime allows the exchange rate to adjust to fundamentals while preventing disorderly movements. The 2022‑23 episode, where the rupee depreciated 11 % against the dollar, saw the RBI intervene to the tune of ₹1.2 lakh crore (net sales) and raise the repo rate by 250 basis points, which together limited the pass‑through to CPI to 1.8 % over the subsequent year, below the historical average.

Policy implications are twofold. First, a credible inflation‑targeting framework reduces ERPT by anchoring expectations, which means the RBI can tolerate a modest depreciation without triggering a large inflationary spiral. Second, the RBI’s communication strategy — forward guidance on the policy rate path and explicit statements on exchange‑rate policy — shapes market expectations and dampens speculative attacks. The 2023 “Monetary Policy Report” notes that a 100‑basis‑point surprise tightening reduces the one‑month ahead implied volatility of the rupee by 15 %, illustrating the signalling channel.

For exam preparation, retain the key numbers: short‑run ERPT to import prices ≈ 0.38, long‑run ERPT to CPI ≈ 0.22, decline from 0.30 to 0.22 post‑FIT, and the typical intervention magnitude (≈ ₹1‑1.5 lakh crore during a 10 % depreciation episode). Also remember that the RBI does not target the exchange rate directly; it targets inflation, and exchange‑rate movements are a transmission channel, not an objective.

  • Confusing the 180‑day resolution window in the power‑sector framework with the 210‑day IBC timeline — they are distinct and the RBI window triggers mandatory IBC filing.
  • Assuming public cloud can host core banking solutions; the 2023 framework restricts critical workloads to on‑premises or private cloud only.
  • Mixing up the two‑hour critical cyber‑incident reporting deadline with the six‑hour non‑critical deadline — a frequent trap in both GS‑III and IT‑security questions.
  • Believing the digital‑lending SRO can impose penalties up to ₹1 crore; the actual cap is ₹25 lakh per violation.
  • Treating the 0.38 short‑run ERPT to import prices as the pass‑through to CPI; the long‑run CPI pass‑through is only 0.22.
  • Overlooking the mandatory Fuel‑Supply Agreement novation clause in power‑sector resolution plans — a unique requirement not present in the generic IBC process.
  • Remember to verify the latest RBI circulars before the exam.

RBI's Governance Architecture: Central Board, Local Boards, and the Governor's Decision‑Making Powers

The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, establishes a two‑tier governance structure. At the apex sits the Central Board of Directors, chaired by the Governor and comprising up to four Deputy Governors, ten non‑official directors nominated by the Central Government, and four directors representing the Local Boards (Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai, New Delhi). The Central Board meets at least six times a year; a quorum of five directors is required. Its statutory functions include approving the Bank’s annual budget, appointing auditors, and sanctioning the issue of currency notes. The Governor, appointed for a three‑year term (extendable by two years under the 2020 amendment), exercises executive authority over monetary policy, regulation, and day‑to‑day management, but major policy decisions — such as changes to the policy repo rate — are taken by the independent Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), whose minutes are published within two weeks.

The four Local Boards advise the Central Board on regional economic conditions, banking development, and the functioning of the Bank’s offices in their jurisdictions. Each Local Board consists of five members appointed by the Central Government for four‑year terms. While they have no voting power on monetary policy, their recommendations feed into the Central Board’s deliberations on credit policy, financial inclusion, and the allocation of currency chests. The 2013 amendment to the RBI Act introduced a mandatory annual performance review of the Governor by the Central Board, enhancing accountability. In practice, the Governor’s decision‑making power is constrained by the MPC’s statutory mandate (inflation target 4 % ± 2 %) and by the Central Board’s oversight of the Bank’s balance sheet, risk management framework, and the appointment of senior officers (Deputy Governors, Executive Directors).

Recent governance reforms include the 2021 “Fit and Proper” criteria for directors, the 2022 introduction of a whistle‑blower mechanism for staff, and the 2023 directive requiring the Central Board to disclose its assessment of the Bank’s cyber‑resilience posture in the annual report. These changes aim to align the RBI’s governance with the Basel Committee’s “Corporate Governance Principles for Banks” while preserving the operational autonomy needed for credible monetary policy.

Priority Sector Lending: Evolution of Targets, Sub‑Targets, and Their Impact on Credit Allocation

Priority Sector Lending (PSL) originated in 1974 as a directive to channel credit to agriculture, small‑scale industry, and weaker sections. The framework was comprehensively revised in 2015 (Master Direction – Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification) and again in 2020 to address COVID‑19 disruptions. The current guidelines (updated March 2022) prescribe that domestic scheduled commercial banks allocate 40 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors, with specific sub‑targets: 18 % to agriculture (of which 8 % to small and marginal farmers), 7.5 % to micro enterprises, 10 % to weaker sections (including SC/ST, women, and minorities), and 5 % to export credit. In 2022 the RBI added renewable energy (solar, wind, biomass) and start‑ups (recognised by DPIIT) as eligible categories, reflecting a shift toward green and innovation‑driven lending.

As of March 2023, PSL accounted for roughly 41 % of total non‑food credit, with agriculture receiving the largest share (≈ 13 % of ANBC). The sub‑target for micro enterprises has driven a measurable increase in credit to firms with turnover below ₹5 crore — outstanding loans to this segment grew at a CAGR of 14 % between FY 2018‑23. However, banks often meet targets through priority sector lending certificates (PSLCs), tradable instruments that allow surplus lenders to sell compliance to deficit banks. In FY 2023, PSLC trading volume exceeded ₹2.3 lakh crore, indicating a robust secondary market but also raising concerns about the genuineness of underlying credit flow.

The RBI monitors compliance through quarterly returns (Form PSL‑1) and imposes penal interest of 2 % per annum on shortfalls. The 2023 “Statement on Developmental and Regulatory Policies” highlighted that while aggregate targets are met, regional disparities persist — northeastern states and certain union territories receive less than 20 % of their PSL entitlement. The central bank has therefore encouraged banks to adopt district‑level credit plans and to leverage the Business Correspondent network for last‑mile delivery.

Technique: Sub‑Target Calculation
A bank’s ANBC for FY 2023 is ₹1,20,000 crore. It has extended ₹22,000 crore to agriculture (including ₹9,000 crore to small/marginal farmers), ₹9,500 crore to micro enterprises, ₹11,000 crore to weaker sections, and ₹5,500 crore to export credit. Determine whether the bank meets each PSL sub‑target and compute the overall PSL compliance percentage.
Step 1 – Compute required amounts (percentage of ANBC):
Agriculture: 18 % × 1,20,000 = ₹21,600 crore (small/marginal farmers 8 % = ₹9,600 crore).
Micro enterprises: 7.5 % × 1,20,000 = ₹9,000 crore.
Weaker sections: 10 % × 1,20,000 = ₹12,000 crore.
Export credit: 5 % × 1,20,000 = ₹6,000 crore.
Step 2 – Compare actuals:
Agriculture actual ₹22,000 crore ≥ ₹21,600 crore (small/marginal ₹9,000 crore < ₹9,600 crore ✘).
Micro enterprises actual ₹9,500 crore ≥ ₹9,000 crore .
Weaker sections actual ₹11,000 crore < ₹12,000 crore ✘.
Export credit actual ₹5,500 crore < ₹6,000 crore ✘.
Step 3 – Overall PSL compliance: Total PSL extended = 22,000 + 9,500 + 11,000 + 5,500 = ₹48,000 crore. Required overall = 40 % × 1,20,000 = ₹48,000 crore. Compliance = 48,000 / 48,000 = 100 %.
Result: The bank meets the aggregate 40 % target but fails three sub‑targets (small/marginal farmers, weaker sections, export credit). Penal interest would apply on each shortfall.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the four core sub‑targets (18 %, 7.5 %, 10 %, 5 %) and the two newer categories (renewable energy, start‑ups). In numerical questions, first compute the required rupee amount for each sub‑target, then compare with the given actuals. Remember that overall compliance can be 100 % even when sub‑targets are missed — a classic trap. Practice at least three PSLC‑adjusted scenarios before the exam.

Resolution of Systemically Important Banks: The Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIB) Framework and Recovery Planning

The RBI introduced the Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIB) framework in July 2014, aligned with the Financial Stability Board’s (FSB) global SIB methodology. Banks are assessed on four indicators — size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity — using a weighted scoring model. The first list (2015) designated State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank as D‑SIBs. The 2023 list added Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, bringing the total to five. Each D‑SIB must maintain an additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital surcharge ranging from 0.20 % to 0.60 % of risk‑weighted assets, calibrated to its systemic importance bucket (Bucket 1: 0.20 %, Bucket 2: 0.40 %, Bucket 3: 0.60 %). As of March 2024, SBI and ICICI Bank fall in Bucket 3, HDFC Bank in Bucket 2, and Axis and Kotak in Bucket 1.

Beyond capital surcharges, D‑SIBs are required to submit annual recovery plans (living wills) detailing strategies for restoring viability under severe stress, and resolution plans outlining credible options for orderly wind‑down, including bail‑in mechanisms. The RBI conducts a supervisory review (SRP) of these plans every two years and may impose additional liquidity requirements (e.g., higher LCR or NSFR) if gaps are identified. The 2022 “Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for D‑SIBs” introduced graduated triggers — breach of the CET1 surcharge, leverage ratio below 3.5 %, or net NPA ratio above 6 % — leading to restrictions on dividend distribution, branch expansion, and high‑risk lending.

Cross‑border coordination is formalised through the Crisis Management Group (CMG) chaired by the RBI Deputy Governor (Supervision), with participation from the Ministry of Finance, SEBI, and the FSB. The 2023 Financial Stability Report noted that the D‑SIB framework has improved market discipline: CDS spreads for designated banks narrowed by 15‑20 bps relative to non‑D‑SIB peers after the 2021 bucket re‑classification. Nevertheless, the RBI continues to refine the methodology, proposing in its 2024 discussion paper to incorporate climate‑related financial risk as a fifth indicator.

RBI's Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves: Composition, Return Optimisation, and Risk Management

India’s foreign exchange reserves, managed by the RBI’s Department of External Investments and Operations (DEIO), stood at US $642.5 billion as of 29 March 2024. The portfolio comprises four main components: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) (≈ US $570 billion), Gold (≈ US $55 billion, 795 tonnes), Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) (≈ US $12 billion), and the Reserve Position in the IMF (≈ US $5 billion). FCA is invested predominantly in sovereign‑grade securities of the G‑7 economies, with a currency allocation of roughly 55 % USD, 20 % EUR, 10 % JPY, 8 % GBP, and the remainder in other reserve currencies including the Chinese yuan (added to the SDR basket in 2016).

The RBI follows a “safety‑liquidity‑return” hierarchy. Duration limits are set at a maximum of 10 years for USD‑denominated assets and 7 years for other currencies, with a portfolio‑average modified duration capped at 3.5 years to limit interest‑rate risk. Credit risk is controlled by restricting investments to issuers rated AA‑ or above by at least two major rating agencies. The DEIO employs a strategic asset allocation (SAA) model reviewed quarterly; tactical deviations are permitted within ±2 % of the SAA weights to capture short‑term market opportunities. In FY 2023, the reserve portfolio generated an average yield of 2.48 % (annualised), with gold contributing a 4.1 % return driven by price appreciation.

Reserves are deployed for market intervention (spot and forward sales/purchases) and for sterilisation via open market operations (OMOs) and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF). During the 2022‑23 depreciation episode, the RBI sold a net US $15 billion (≈ ₹1.2 lakh crore) while simultaneously conducting variable‑rate reverse repo auctions to absorb excess rupee liquidity. The 2023 “Reserve Management Guidelines” introduced a green‑bond allocation of up to 2 % of FCA, aligned with the RBI’s climate‑risk roadmap. Risk management is overseen by an internal Investment Committee and an external Audit Committee that reports to the Central Board annually.

Microfinance Regulation: The 2022 Master Direction and Borrower Protection

In March 2022 the RBI issued the Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Non‑Banking Financial Company – Micro Finance Institutions) Directions, 2022, replacing the 2011 guidelines. The framework applies to all NBFC‑MFIs (including those registered as Section 8 companies) and sets a uniform pricing ceiling: the interest rate charged to borrowers cannot exceed the lower of (a) the MFI’s cost of funds plus 10 percentage points, or (b) 24 % per annum. Processing fees are capped at 1 % of the loan amount, and no pre‑payment penalty may be levied for loans up to ₹2 lakh. The maximum loan size for a single borrower is ₹1.25 lakh (rural) or ₹2 lakh (urban), with a minimum tenure of 24 months for loans above ₹30,000.

The directions mandate transparent disclosure of the annualised percentage rate (APR) on the loan agreement and require MFIs to provide a cooling‑off period of three days during which the borrower can cancel the loan without penalty. A credit‑information reporting obligation to all four Credit Information Companies (CICs) within T+1 day of disbursement ensures real‑time visibility of borrower leverage. The RBI also introduced a grievance redressal mechanism with a dedicated Ombudsman for microfinance, empowered to award compensation up to ₹20 lakh per complaint.

Supervisory data from the March 2024 Financial Stability Report shows that the NBFC‑MFI portfolio grew to ₹3.1 lakh crore (≈ 2.3 % of total NBFC assets) with a gross NPA ratio of 2.8 %, down from 4.1 % in March 2021. The pricing cap has compressed net interest margins for larger MFIs by 150‑200 bps, prompting consolidation — the number of registered NBFC‑MFIs fell from 94 (March 2021) to 78 (March 2024). The RBI’s 2023 “Review of Microfinance Regulations” proposed a graduated pricing framework linked to the borrower’s credit‑score tier, but the final circular is awaited.

  • Confusing the Central Board’s advisory role with the MPC’s statutory rate‑setting authority — the Board does not vote on the repo rate.
  • Assuming the 40 % PSL target applies to total deposits rather than Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC).
  • Treating the D‑SIB capital surcharge as a substitute for the Countercyclical Capital Buffer; they are additive, not interchangeable.
  • Overstating the gold share in reserves — gold is ~8‑9 % of total reserves, not a majority.
  • Believing the 24 % interest‑rate ceiling for MFIs is a flat cap irrespective of the cost‑of‑funds benchmark; the lower of the two applies.
  • Mixing up the three‑day cooling‑off period for microfinance with the 14‑day “right to rescind” under the Consumer Protection Act for other loans.
  • Neglecting that PSLC trading volumes reflect compliance arbitrage, not necessarily incremental credit creation.
The advanced sections above complete the required coverage for this lesson.

RBI's 2019 Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets and Its Interaction with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code

The Reserve Bank of India replaced its 2017 revised framework with the Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets through a circular dated 7 June 2019. The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions (AIFIs) and non‑banking financial companies (NBFCs) with asset size above ₹500 crore. Its core pillars are early recognition, a time‑bound resolution process, and a mandatory inter‑creditor agreement (ICA) when multiple lenders are involved.

Early recognition requires lenders to classify an account as a special mention account (SMA) the moment a default of 1‑30 days occurs (SMA‑0), 31‑60 days (SMA‑1) or 61‑90 days (SMA‑2). Once an account slips into SMA‑2, the lender must initiate a 30‑day review period to assess viability. If the account is deemed viable, a resolution plan (RP) must be finalised within 180 days from the end of the review period. The RP may involve restructuring, change in ownership, or a combination thereof.

Inter‑creditor agreement (ICA) becomes mandatory when the aggregate exposure of lenders exceeds ₹100 crore. The ICA binds all signatories to the RP approved by lenders representing 75 % of the total outstanding credit facilities and 60 % of lenders by number. Dissenting lenders must either exit at a discount or accept the RP. The framework also prescribes provisioning norms: 20 % for accounts in the review period, 35 % if an RP is under implementation, and 100 % if the account is referred to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) without an RP.

The 2019 framework was designed to complement the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. If a viable RP cannot be agreed within 180 days, the lenders must refer the account to the NCLT under Section 7 (financial creditor) or Section 9 (operational creditor) of the IBC. The RBI’s circular explicitly states that the 180‑day timeline runs concurrently with the IBC’s 180‑day corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) period, preventing double counting. In practice, the ICA often serves as the pre‑IBC consensus mechanism, reducing the number of cases that actually enter the tribunal.

During the COVID‑19 pandemic, the RBI issued a COVID‑19 Regulatory Package (27 March 2020) that permitted a one‑time restructuring of eligible accounts without downgrading asset classification, extended the 180‑day RP window by 90 days, and relaxed ICA thresholds. The 2021 amendment (circular dated 4 June 2021) reinstated the original timelines but retained a “resolution framework for COVID‑19 related stress” for accounts that had availed the earlier relief. The framework’s effectiveness is reflected in the decline of gross NPAs of scheduled commercial banks from 9.3 % (March 2019) to 5.8 % (March 2024), although a portion of the improvement stems from write‑offs and the IBC’s own resolution outcomes.

Co‑Lending Models: RBI Guidelines, Risk Sharing, and Credit Expansion to Priority Sectors

The RBI first permitted co‑lending by banks and NBFCs through a circular dated 5 November 2020, later refined by the Co‑Lending Model (CLM) Master Direction issued on 24 September 2022. The model allows a bank and an NBFC (including a Housing Finance Company) to jointly originate, underwrite and service a loan, with the bank typically providing the bulk of the funding and the NBFC contributing the origination and collection expertise.

Risk‑sharing structure is fixed at a minimum of 80 %–20 % (bank:NBFC) for priority‑sector loans and 70 %–30 % for non‑priority‑sector loans. Both parties must conduct independent credit appraisal, but the final sanction requires a joint credit decision documented in a co‑lending agreement. The agreement must specify the allocation of recoveries, servicing responsibilities, and dispute resolution mechanisms. The RBI mandates that the NBFC’s share be senior to the bank’s share in the waterfall of recoveries, protecting the bank’s larger exposure.

Priority‑sector classification is a key incentive. Loans originated under the CLM that meet the RBI’s priority‑sector lending (PSL) criteria — agriculture, micro‑small‑medium enterprises (MSMEs), export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy and weaker sections — are counted toward the bank’s 40 % PSL target on an adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) basis. As of March 2024, the outstanding co‑lending portfolio stood at approximately ₹1.4 lakh crore, of which roughly 65 % qualified as PSL. The model has been particularly effective in the MSME segment, where NBFCs’ last‑mile reach complements banks’ low‑cost funds.

Operational safeguards include a cap on the NBFC’s exposure to a single borrower at 20 % of its Tier‑I capital, a requirement for the bank to hold the loan on its books (no synthetic securitisation), and quarterly reporting to the RBI on portfolio quality, delinquency ratios, and compliance with the ICA‑like co‑lending agreement. The 2022 Master Direction also introduced a “co‑lending scorecard” for supervisory assessment, weighting asset quality (40 %), governance (30 %), and outreach (30 %).

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (March 2024) shows that the gross NPA ratio of the co‑lending book was 1.9 %, lower than the industry average of 3.2 % for comparable MSME exposures. The model has also facilitated credit deepening in tier‑3/4 centres, where NBFC branch networks are denser than bank branches. However, challenges remain: alignment of differing risk‑appetite frameworks, data‑sharing standards, and the need for a unified technology platform for real‑time loan monitoring.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: "In the RBI's co‑lending model, the NBFC's share is senior to the bank's share in the recovery waterfall. Explain why this seniority is prescribed and its impact on the bank's provisioning."
The seniority protects the bank's larger (80 %) exposure by ensuring that the NBFC's 20 % share absorbs first losses. Consequently, the bank can apply a lower provisioning rate on its portion because the expected loss given default (LGD) is reduced. Under the RBI's provisioning norms, the bank's share is treated as a standard asset until the NBFC's tranche is fully written down, lowering the bank's overall provisioning burden and improving its capital adequacy.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes co‑lending with priority‑sector targets, first identify the risk‑sharing ratio (80:20 for PSL). Then recall that only the bank's share counts toward ANBC for the 40 % PSL target. A quick mental check: if the NBFC's share were senior, the bank's effective exposure is shielded, so provisioning is lighter — this is a favourite trap in numerical‑type questions.

Regulation of Digital Lending Applications: The 2022 RBI Guidelines and Enforcement Actions

The proliferation of unregulated digital lending apps prompted the RBI to issue the Guidelines on Digital Lending on 2 September 2022, followed by a Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Digital Lending) Directions, 2023 on 10 August 2023. The framework covers all regulated entities (REs) — banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators — that either directly lend through digital channels or partner with lending service providers (LSPs).

Key regulatory requirements include: (1) KYC and customer due diligence must be completed before any credit decision; (2) Transparent disclosure of the annualised percentage rate (APR), all fees, and the repayment schedule on the app interface; (3) Data privacy — borrower data cannot be shared with third parties without explicit consent, and data localisation norms apply; (4) Grievance redressal — a dedicated nodal officer and an escalation matrix culminating in the RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme; (5) Prohibition of unauthorised lending — only REs or their authorised LSPs may extend credit; (6) Loan servicing — collection practices must adhere to the RBI’s Fair Practices Code, banning coercive recovery.

The 2023 Master Direction introduced a “digital lending licence” concept for LSPs, requiring registration with the RBI, a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹2 crore, and a board‑approved IT security policy. It also mandated real‑time reporting of loan disbursements and repayments to the Credit Information Companies (CICs) within T+1 day, mirroring the microfinance reporting obligation.

Enforcement actions began in early 2023. The RBI, in coordination with the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, issued blocking orders under Section 69A of the IT Act against 5 prominent apps (e.g., “CashBean”, “KreditBee”, “MoneyTap”, “EarlySalary”, “PaySense”) for operating without a valid RE partnership, charging usurious rates exceeding 36 % APR, and misusing contact lists for harassment. Penalties ranged from ₹5 crore to ₹25 crore per entity. In March 2024, the RBI directed all REs to terminate agreements with any LSP not registered under the new framework by 30 June 2024.

Supervisory data from the Financial Stability Report (March 2024) indicates that the number of registered LSPs rose from 12 (September 2022) to 47 (March 2024), while complaints on the RBI’s Complaint Management System fell by 38 % year‑on‑year. The framework has also spurred the development of account aggregator‑based consent flows, enabling borrowers to share financial data securely with lenders, thereby reducing reliance on invasive permission requests.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Channels, Frictions, and Recent Evidence

Transmission of the RBI’s policy repo rate to the corporate bond market operates through three primary channels: the interest‑rate channel (repo → sovereign yields → corporate spreads), the liquidity channel (LAF/SDF operations → money‑market rates → primary‑dealer bidding), and the credit‑risk channel (policy stance → macro outlook → spread compression or widening). The RBI’s Open Market Operations (OMOs), Operation Twist (simultaneous purchase of long‑dated G‑secs and sale of short‑dated papers), and the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) launched in March 2020 are the main tools influencing these channels.

During the COVID‑19 easing cycle (March 2020‑February 2022), the repo rate was cut by 115 bps to 4 %. The 10‑year G‑sec yield fell from 6.7 % to 5.9 %, and the AAA corporate bond spread over the benchmark narrowed from 140 bps to 85 bps. The CBPP, which allowed the RBI to purchase up to ₹1 lakh crore of investment‑grade corporate bonds in the secondary market, directly compressed spreads by providing a backstop buyer. Primary dealers’ bidding volumes in the weekly G‑sec auctions rose 30 %, reflecting ample liquidity.

However, frictions persist. The corporate bond market remains illiquid — average daily turnover in the secondary market was only ₹4,500 crore in FY 2023, compared with ₹1.2 lakh crore in the G‑sec market. This illiquidity amplifies the bid‑ask spread and makes price discovery noisy, weakening the pass‑through. Moreover, credit‑rating concentration (over 70 % of outstanding bonds rated AA or above) limits differentiation, causing spreads to move in lockstep with sovereign yields rather than firm‑specific fundamentals.

The tightening cycle (May 2022‑February 2023) saw the repo rate rise by 250 bps to 6.5 %. The 10‑year G‑sec yield climbed to 7.4 %, but AAA corporate spreads widened only to 110 bps, indicating a partial transmission. The RBI’s Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) absorbed surplus liquidity, raising short‑term rates faster than long‑term yields — a classic “bear‑flattening” of the yield curve that dampened corporate bond issuance. Net issuance of corporate bonds fell 22 % in FY 2023 versus FY 2022.

Recent RBI research (Monetary Policy Report, April 2024) estimates the pass‑through elasticity of the repo rate to AAA corporate yields at 0.55 over a 12‑month horizon, lower than the 0.78 observed for the 10‑year G‑sec. The report recommends deepening the market‑making framework, expanding the corporate bond repo facility, and encouraging foreign portfolio investor (FPI) participation under the voluntary retention route to improve liquidity and transmission efficiency.

RBI's Cyber Resilience Framework for Regulated Entities: 2021 Master Direction and Supervisory Expectations

The RBI issued the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices on 7 June 2021, superseding the 2011 guidelines. The direction applies to all commercial banks, NBFCs (asset size ≥ ₹500 crore), payment system operators, and credit information companies. It establishes a board‑level cyber governance structure, mandatory Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) appointment, and a cyber crisis management plan (CCMP) that must be tested at least annually through tabletop exercises.

Core requirements include: (1) IT strategy committee at the board level, meeting quarterly; (2) Risk assessment covering confidentiality, integrity, availability, and regulatory compliance, updated after any material change; (3) Incident reporting — any cyber incident impacting critical systems must be reported to the RBI’s Department of Supervision within 6 hours of detection, with a detailed root‑cause analysis within 15 days; (4) Penetration testing — external red‑team exercises at least once a year, internal vulnerability scans quarterly; (5) Vendor risk management — due diligence on third‑party service providers, contractual right‑to‑audit clauses, and continuous monitoring of their security posture.

The 2023 amendment (circular dated 12 May 2023) introduced a Cyber Security Maturity Model (CSMM) with five levels — Initial, Managed, Defined, Quantitatively Managed, Optimising. REs are expected to achieve at least Level 3 (Defined) by March 2025. The RBI’s IT Examination (ITE) framework now incorporates CSMM scoring, and supervisory letters explicitly reference gaps in privileged access management, endpoint detection and response (EDR), and data‑loss prevention (DLP).

In 2024, the RBI issued a targeted circular on ransomware preparedness (dated 18 January 2024) mandating: (a) offline, immutable backups of critical data tested quarterly; (b) network segmentation to limit lateral movement; (c) a dedicated ransomware response playbook integrated into the CCMP; (d) mandatory cyber insurance coverage for losses exceeding ₹10 crore. The circular also required REs to participate in the National Cyber Exercise (NCX) conducted by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In).

Supervisory outcomes show progress: the Financial Stability Report (March 2024) reported that 92 % of scheduled commercial banks had a board‑approved CCMP, up from 68 % in 2021. However, only 54 % of NBFCs met the Level 3 CSMM threshold, prompting the RBI to issue prompt corrective action (PCA)‑like supervisory letters to laggards, restricting new digital product launches until compliance is demonstrated.

  • Confusing the 180‑day resolution window under the 2019 Prudential Framework with the IBC’s 180‑day CIRP period — they run concurrently, not sequentially.
  • Assuming the co‑lending risk‑sharing ratio is flexible; the RBI mandates a minimum 80:20 (bank:NBFC) for PSL loans and 70:30 for non‑PSL loans.
  • Believing digital lending apps can operate without a regulated entity partnership; the 2022/2023 guidelines require every loan to be originated by an RE or its registered LSP.
  • Overstating the pass‑through of repo rate to corporate bond yields — empirical elasticity is ~0.55, not 1‑to‑1.
  • Treating the 6‑hour incident reporting deadline as applicable only to banks; it applies to all REs covered by the 2021 Master Direction.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common mis‑statements.

RBI's Corporate Bond Repo Facility and Market‑Making Framework: Design, Operations, and Transmission Impact

The Reserve Bank introduced the Corporate Bond Repo Facility (CBRF) in October 2022 through a circular dated 21 October 2022 (DBR.No.BP.BC.45/21.04.048/2022‑23). The facility allows scheduled commercial banks, primary dealers, and eligible non‑bank financial companies to borrow funds by pledging listed corporate bonds rated AAA or AA as collateral. The initial haircut schedule was set at 5 % for AAA bonds and 10 % for AA bonds, with a maximum tenor of 90 days. In the April 2024 Monetary Policy Report the RBI disclosed that the outstanding repo volume under the CBRF reached ₹1.2 lakh crore, and the weighted average repo rate tracked the policy repo rate within a 5‑basis‑point band, confirming effective pass‑through.

Eligibility and Operational Mechanics

  • Only bonds listed on a recognised stock exchange with a minimum outstanding amount of ₹500 crore qualify.
  • Participants must maintain a minimum credit rating of AA from at least two SEBI‑registered credit rating agencies.
  • Haircuts are revised quarterly based on market volatility; the April 2023 revision raised the AA haircut to 12 % after a spike in spread volatility.
  • Market‑making obligations require primary dealers to quote two‑way prices for a minimum of 10 eligible ISINs during market hours, with a maximum bid‑ask spread of 15 bps for AAA and 25 bps for AA securities.

Transmission Impact

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) estimates the pass‑through elasticity of the repo rate to AAA corporate bond yields at 0.55 over a 12‑month horizon, compared with 0.78 for the 10‑year G‑sec. The CBRF narrowed the AAA‑G‑sec spread from 115 bps in September 2022 to 95 bps in March 2024, and corporate bond issuance rose 18 % year‑on‑year in FY 2024. The facility also reduced reliance on the overnight call market, lowering the weighted average call rate by 12 bps during the same period.

Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) during COVID‑19: Structure, Allocation, and Effect on Credit Flow

In response to the liquidity shock of March 2020, the RBI announced three tranches of Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) under circulars dated 27 March 2020, 17 April 2020, and 15 May 2020. The aggregate amount offered was ₹1 lakh crore, each tranche carrying a three‑year tenor at the prevailing policy repo rate (4.40 % at launch). Funds were earmarked for incremental lending to specific sectors: (i) MSMEs, (ii) NBFCs and HFCs with asset size ≥ ₹500 crore, and (iii) affordable housing loans sanctioned under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (PMAY). Banks could draw up to 100 % of their net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) subject to the sectoral caps.

Allocation and Utilisation

  • First tranche (₹25 000 crore) was fully subscribed; 68 % flowed to MSMEs, 22 % to NBFCs/HFCs, 10 % to affordable housing.
  • Second tranche (₹50 000 crore) saw 85 % utilisation; the share to NBFCs/HFCs rose to 35 % as liquidity stress in the shadow‑bank sector intensified.
  • Third tranche (₹25 000 crore) was 78 % utilised, with a higher proportion (18 %) directed to housing.

Credit‑Flow Impact

RBI’s Quarterly Statistics on Deposits and Credit (QSDC) show that bank credit to MSMEs grew 12.4 % year‑on‑year in Q2 FY 2021 versus 6.1 % in Q2 FY 2020. NBFC credit growth, which had contracted 4.3 % in Q1 FY 2021, turned positive at 3.7 % by Q4 FY 2021. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report (December 2021) attributed roughly 40 % of the incremental MSME credit to TLTRO‑linked lending. However, the report also flagged a rise in restructured advances under the Resolution Framework 2.0, indicating that part of the flow went to stressed borrowers.

Technique: Computing Cash Received under the Corporate Bond Repo Facility
A bank repos a AAA‑rated listed corporate bond with a market value of ₹100 crore under the RBI’s Corporate Bond Repo Facility. The applicable haircut for AAA bonds is 5 %. What is the cash amount the bank receives?
Cash received = Market value × (1 – haircut) = ₹100 crore × (1 – 0.05) = ₹95 crore. The bank therefore obtains ₹95 crore of liquidity while retaining the bond as collateral.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about any RBI liquidity facility, note three parameters: tenor, eligible collateral, and haircut schedule. These three together determine the cash margin and are the most frequently tested data points in both objective and descriptive papers.

RBI's On‑Tap Licensing Framework for Universal Banks and Small Finance Banks: Eligibility, Process, and Outcomes

The on‑tap licensing framework for universal banks was notified on 1 August 2016 (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.01.001/2016‑17) and for Small Finance Banks (SFBs) on 5 December 2019 (DBR.No.BP.BC.45/21.01.001/2019‑20). Both frameworks moved away from the earlier “stop‑and‑go” licensing windows to a continuous application process, subject to periodic review by the RBI’s Licensing Committee.

Universal Banks – Key Eligibility Criteria

  • Minimum net owned fund of ₹500 crore at the time of application.
  • Promoter group must have a track record of at least 10 years in banking, financial services, or a related regulated sector.
  • Fit‑and‑proper assessment of promoters, directors, and senior management as per the RBI’s 2015 guidelines.
  • Business plan demonstrating viability, financial inclusion targets, and compliance with the Basel III capital framework from day one.

Small Finance Banks – Key Eligibility Criteria

  • Minimum net owned fund of ₹200 crore (raised to ₹300 crore in the 2022 amendment).
  • Promoters may be individuals, corporate entities, or societies with at least 5 years of experience in financial inclusion or micro‑finance.
  • At least 75 % of net ANBC (Adjusted Net Bank Credit) must be directed to priority‑sector lending, with a minimum 50 % to the micro‑enterprise segment.
  • Mandatory listing within three years of commencement of operations.

Licences Granted (as of March 2024)

Under the universal‑bank on‑tap route, two licences have been issued (the most recent in 2022). For SFBs, ten licences have been granted since 2019, bringing the total number of operating SFBs to twelve. The RBI’s Annual Report 2023‑24 notes that the newly licensed SFBs collectively hold ₹1.1 lakh crore in deposits and have achieved a gross NPA ratio of 2.3 % within two years of operations, outperforming the industry average of 3.1 %.

Regulation of Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms: 2017 Directions, 2020 Amendments, and Supervisory Oversight

The RBI issued the Master Direction – Non‑Banking Financial Company – Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017 on 4 October 2017 (DNBR.PD.008/03.10.119/2017‑18). The framework brought P2P platforms under the NBFC regulatory perimeter, requiring registration as an NBFC‑P2P.

Core Regulatory Requirements

  • Minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore at the time of registration.
  • Leverage ratio capped at 1:1 (i.e., total outstanding loans cannot exceed NOF).
  • Exposure limits: a single lender cannot expose more than ₹10 lakh across all borrowers; a single borrower cannot borrow more than ₹10 lakh from all lenders on a platform.
  • Escrow account mechanism for fund transfer, with a designated bank acting as escrow agent.
  • Mandatory credit‑information reporting to all four Credit Information Companies (CICs).

2020 Amendments (Circular dated 24 September 2020)

  • Increased the per‑lender exposure cap to ₹50 lakh and per‑borrower cap to ₹10 lakh, subject to platform‑level aggregate limits.
  • Introduced a requirement for platforms to maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 % of risk‑weighted assets.
  • Mandated quarterly submission of loan‑level data to the RBI’s Department of Non‑Banking Supervision.

Supervisory Outcomes (as of December 2023)

There were 31 registered NBFC‑P2P platforms. Aggregate loan disbursements in FY 2023 stood at ₹18 500 crore, a 42 % increase over FY 2022. The RBI’s supervisory letters highlighted deficiencies in KYC compliance on 7 platforms and imposed monetary penalties totalling ₹3.2 crore. The Financial Stability Report (March 2024) flagged the sector’s growing interconnectedness with NBFCs as a systemic‑risk monitorable.

RBI's Financial Consumer Protection Framework: 2021 Guidelines, Grievance Redressal, and the Role of the Ombudsman

The Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Financial Consumer Protection) Directions, 2021 was issued on 30 June 2021 (DBR.No.BP.BC.57/21.04.048/2021‑22). It applies to all regulated entities (REs) – commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and credit information companies.

Four Pillars of the Framework

  • Transparency & Disclosure: Standardised Key Fact Statements (KFS) for all loan products, mandatory display of annualised percentage rate (APR) and total cost of credit.
  • Fair Practices: Prohibition of coercive recovery, mandatory cooling‑off period of 14 days for digital loans, and a cap on penal interest at 2 % per annum over the contracted rate.
  • Grievance Redressal: Every RE must appoint an Internal Ombudsman (IO) at the senior‑management level; the IO must resolve complaints within 30 days. Unresolved complaints can be escalated to the RBI’s Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2020 (revised 2022).
  • Data Privacy & Security: Alignment with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; REs must obtain explicit consent for data sharing and conduct annual privacy impact assessments.

2023 Amendment (Circular dated 12 May 2023)

  • Extended the framework’s coverage to all digital lending apps (DLAs) operating in partnership with REs.
  • Introduced a “Consumer Protection Scorecard” to be published annually on each RE’s website.
  • Empowered the RBI to impose a penalty of up to ₹1 crore per violation for non‑compliance with IO timelines.

Impact Assessment (FY 2024)

The RBI’s Consumer Protection Survey (January 2024) reported that 87 % of surveyed borrowers were aware of the KFS requirement, up from 62 % in 2021. The average resolution time for complaints handled by Internal Ombudsmen fell from 45 days (FY 2022) to 28 days (FY 2024). The Banking Ombudsman received 1.34 lakh complaints in FY 2024, a 12 % decline year‑on‑year, indicating improved first‑level redressal.

  • Confusing the corporate bond repo facility haircut schedule with the G‑sec repo haircut.
  • Assuming TLTRO funds could be used for any lending; they were sector‑specific.
  • Believing on‑tap licensing is open continuously; applications are accepted only during specified windows.
  • Thinking P2P platforms can lend without a net owned fund of ₹2 crore; the minimum is mandatory.
  • Overlooking that the 2021 Consumer Protection Directions apply to all regulated entities, not just banks.
  • Mixing up the Banking Ombudsman Scheme (2020) with the Internal Ombudsman requirement under the 2021 Directions.
  • Assuming the corporate bond repo facility is available for unlisted bonds; only listed bonds are eligible.

RBI's Digital Lending Guidelines and the Lending Service Provider Framework

The Reserve Bank of India issued the Guidelines on Digital Lending on 2 September 2022 (DoR.STR.REC.53/21.04.048/2022‑23) to address regulatory gaps exposed by the rapid growth of fintech‑driven credit. The framework applies to all regulated entities (REs) – commercial banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators – that originate, underwrite, or service loans through digital channels, including apps, web platforms, and APIs. The guidelines introduce three pillars: customer protection, data governance, and accountability of lending service providers (LSPs).

Customer Protection

Every digital loan must be accompanied by a standardized Key Fact Statement (KFS) that discloses the annualised percentage rate (APR), total cost of credit, repayment schedule, and penal charges. A mandatory cooling‑off period of 14 days allows borrowers to withdraw without penalty. Penal interest is capped at 2 % per annum over the contracted rate. REs must ensure that loan contracts are executed only after explicit, informed consent captured through a verifiable digital signature or OTP‑based authentication.

Data Governance

Data collected during the lending lifecycle – including device metadata, location, and contact lists – must be stored on servers located in India. REs are required to conduct a privacy impact assessment before launching a new digital lending product and to obtain separate consent for each distinct data‑processing purpose. The guidelines align with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and mandate that data be purged within 180 days of loan closure unless retention is required by law.

Lending Service Provider (LSP) Accountability

An LSP is any entity that provides credit‑underwriting, loan‑servicing, or collection services to an RE on a digital platform. The RE remains the principal and must enter into a written agreement with the LSP that specifies service‑level standards, data‑sharing protocols, and audit rights. The RE must conduct due‑diligence on the LSP’s financial soundness, technology stack, and compliance history before onboarding. Quarterly reporting of LSP‑level loan performance, grievance metrics, and breach incidents to the RBI’s Department of Supervision is mandatory.

Supervisory Outcomes

As of March 2024, the RBI had registered 112 LSPs across 47 REs. The first supervisory review (January‑March 2024) identified deficiencies in KFS compliance on 19 platforms and imposed monetary penalties totalling ₹4.7 crore. The Financial Stability Report (March 2024) flagged the growing interconnectedness between LSPs and NBFCs as a monitorable systemic risk, prompting the RBI to propose a consolidated exposure limit for RE‑LSP relationships in the next policy cycle.

RBI's Climate-Related Financial Risk Disclosure Framework and TCFD Alignment

In July 2023 the RBI released a Discussion Paper on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance, followed by the Draft Disclosure Framework in February 2024 (DoR.CLIM.REC.12/21.04.048/2023‑24). The framework requires all scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions, and top‑layer NBFCs to disclose climate‑related governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics in line with the Task Force on Climate‑related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations. The disclosures become mandatory from the financial year 2025‑26, with a phased rollout for smaller entities.

Governance and Strategy

Boards must designate a climate‑risk oversight committee and integrate climate scenarios into strategic planning. Institutions are expected to articulate how physical risks (floods, heatwaves) and transition risks (policy shifts, technology disruption) affect credit portfolios, investment books, and operational resilience. Scenario analysis must cover at least two pathways – a “orderly transition” (net‑zero by 2070) and a “disorderly transition” (delayed policy action) – using the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios adapted for the Indian context.

Risk Management and Metrics

Banks must embed climate risk into credit‑risk models, collateral valuation, and sectoral concentration limits. The framework prescribes quantitative metrics: (i) exposure to carbon‑intensive sectors as a percentage of total credit; (ii) green‑asset ratio (qualifying green loans and investments to total assets); (iii) climate‑adjusted probability of default for key portfolios. Qualitative disclosures include the methodology for scenario analysis, data sources, and limitations.

Supervisory Integration

The RBI will incorporate climate‑risk disclosures into its supervisory review and evaluation process (SREP) and the annual Financial Stability Report. Institutions failing to meet disclosure timelines may face supervisory letters, restrictions on dividend distribution, or enhanced capital requirements under Pillar 2. The framework also encourages voluntary adoption of the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) standards for cross‑border comparability.

Examiner's Twist
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the RBI's 2024 Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosure Framework is correct? (a) It applies only to public sector banks. (b) It mandates TCFD‑aligned disclosures from FY 2025‑26 for all scheduled commercial banks and top‑layer NBFCs. (c) It requires scenario analysis using only the NGFS 'current policies' scenario. (d) It exempts institutions with assets below ₹50,000 crore from any disclosure."
The correct answer is (b). The framework covers all scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions, and top‑layer NBFCs, with mandatory TCFD‑aligned disclosures from FY 2025‑26. It requires at least two scenarios (orderly and disorderly transition), not a single scenario. There is no blanket exemption based on asset size; smaller entities have a phased timeline but must eventually comply.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question references a recent RBI framework, first identify the regulated‑entity scope (banks, NBFCs, FIs) and the effective date. Then match the disclosure pillars (governance, strategy, risk management, metrics) to the answer choices. Eliminate options that narrow the scope incorrectly or cite a single scenario. The RBI’s phased approach is a frequent distractor – remember that “phased” does not mean “exempt”.

RBI's Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves: Composition, Investment Guidelines, and Adequacy Assessment

The RBI manages India’s foreign exchange reserves (FX reserves) under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999. As of March 2024, reserves stood at approximately US $642 billion, comprising four main components: Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) (≈ US $560 billion), Gold (≈ US $55 billion), Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) (≈ US $18 billion), and Reserve Position in the IMF (≈ US $9 billion). The FCA portfolio is invested in sovereign and high‑grade corporate bonds, short‑term deposits, and money‑market instruments across major reserve currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, JPY, CNY).

Investment Guidelines

The RBI’s Investment Policy for Foreign Currency Assets (last revised in 2021) mandates a minimum credit rating of AA‑ (or equivalent) for sovereign issuers and A‑ for corporate issuers. Duration limits are set to balance return and liquidity: the portfolio’s modified duration is kept within 2‑3 years. A strategic allocation to gold (around 8‑10 % of total reserves) provides a hedge against currency volatility. SDR holdings are maintained to meet IMF quota obligations and to diversify the reserve currency basket.

Adequacy Metrics

The RBI monitors reserve adequacy through multiple lenses: (i) Import Cover – reserves sufficient to finance 10‑12 months of merchandise imports; (ii) Reserve‑to‑Short‑Term‑External‑Debt Ratio – targeting a ratio above 1.5; (iii) Reserve‑to‑Broad‑Money (M3) Ratio – ensuring reserves exceed 20 % of M3; (iv) Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) for FX – a stress‑tested metric introduced in 2022 to assess the ability to meet 30‑day FX outflows under adverse scenarios. The RBI publishes these indicators in the quarterly Reserve Management Report and the annual Annual Report.

Intervention and Sterilisation

FX intervention is conducted through spot purchases/sales in the interbank market and, when necessary, through the Foreign Exchange Swap Window (introduced in 2020) to manage rupee volatility without altering domestic liquidity. Sterilisation of intervention flows is achieved via open market operations (OMOs), variable‑rate reverse repos, and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF). The RBI’s communication on intervention is limited to the monthly Bulletin and the Monetary Policy Report, preserving operational discretion.

Co-Lending Models between Banks and NBFCs: Regulatory Framework, Risk Sharing, and Supervisory Expectations

The RBI introduced the Co‑Lending Model (CLM) via a circular dated 5 November 2020 (DoR.FIN.REC.45/21.04.048/2020‑21) to leverage the comparative advantages of banks (low‑cost funds) and NBFCs (origination reach). The model permits scheduled commercial banks and eligible NBFCs (including HFCs) to jointly extend credit to priority‑sector and non‑priority‑sector borrowers, subject to a minimum risk‑sharing ratio of 80:20 (bank:NBFC) for priority‑sector loans and 70:30 for other loans.

Operational Requirements

Both partners must enter into a master agreement specifying credit‑assessment responsibilities, loan‑servicing arrangements, and dispute‑resolution mechanisms. The originating NBFC conducts the initial appraisal and KYC, while the bank performs an independent credit assessment before committing its share. Loan documentation is executed in the name of both lenders, and a single escrow account manages repayments. The NBFC acts as the lead servicer for collection and recovery, but the bank retains the right to step in upon breach of service‑level agreements.

Risk Management and Capital Treatment

For capital adequacy, the bank’s exposure is risk‑weighted based on the borrower’s rating, while the NBFC’s share follows its own regulatory capital framework. The RBI requires the bank to hold a provisioning coverage ratio (PCR) of at least 70 % on its portion of non‑performing co‑lended assets. Joint monitoring of early‑warning signals (overdue >30 days, covenant breaches) is mandatory, with monthly portfolio reviews reported to the respective boards.

Supervisory Outcomes

As of December 2023, 42 banks and 58 NBFCs had active co‑lending arrangements, with an outstanding co‑lended portfolio of ₹2.3 lakh crore. The RBI’s thematic inspection (Q4 FY2023) highlighted gaps in independent credit assessment by banks on 12 occasions and imposed supervisory letters requiring remedial action. The Financial Stability Report (March 2024) noted that co‑lending has improved credit flow to MSMEs and affordable housing but cautioned against concentration risk where a single NBFC dominates a bank’s co‑lending book.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Regulated Entities: Risk Management and Supervisory Oversight

On 27 April 2023 the RBI issued the Master Direction – Outsourcing of Financial Services by Regulated Entities (DoR.OUT.REC.78/21.04.048/2022‑23), replacing the 2017 guidelines. The direction applies to all REs – commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and credit information companies – and covers any arrangement where a third party performs a financial service that the RE would otherwise perform itself, including IT infrastructure, credit processing, debt collection, and customer support.

Governance and Due Diligence

REs must establish an Outsourcing Governance Framework approved by the board, with a designated senior‑management official accountable for outsourcing risk. Before onboarding a service provider, the RE must conduct due diligence covering the provider’s financial health, legal compliance, information‑security posture, business‑continuity plans, and sub‑contracting practices. A written contract must include: (i) clear service‑level agreements (SLAs) with measurable performance indicators; (ii) audit and inspection rights for the RE and the RBI; (iii) data‑localisation clauses ensuring that sensitive customer data resides in India; (iv) termination and exit‑management provisions.

Risk Management and Monitoring

REs are required to maintain a Register of Outsourced Activities and to conduct periodic risk assessments – at least annually – evaluating concentration risk (single provider exceeding 20 % of total outsourced spend), operational resilience, and regulatory compliance. Incident‑reporting timelines are aligned with the RBI’s Cyber Security Framework: material breaches must be reported within 6 hours, and a root‑cause analysis submitted within 30 days. The RE remains fully liable for the outsourced activity’s regulatory obligations.

Supervisory Oversight

The RBI’s Department of Supervision conducts thematic inspections focusing on critical outsourced functions (core banking, payment switching, credit underwriting). In the first inspection cycle (H2 FY2024), 27 REs received supervisory letters for deficiencies in SLA monitoring, inadequate exit‑strategy testing, and insufficient oversight of sub‑contractors. The RBI may impose restrictions on new outsourcing arrangements, require enhanced capital buffers, or direct the RE to bring critical functions in‑house if systemic risk is identified.

  • Confusing the 80:20 risk‑sharing ratio for priority‑sector co‑lending with the 70:30 ratio for non‑priority‑sector loans.
  • Assuming the Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosure Framework applies only to banks; it also covers all‑India financial institutions and top‑layer NBFCs.
  • Believing that the RBI’s FX reserve adequacy is judged solely by import cover; the RBI uses a suite of metrics including reserve‑to‑short‑term‑debt and FX LCR.
  • Thinking that LSPs under the Digital Lending Guidelines can operate without a written agreement with the regulated entity; the RE‑LSP contract is mandatory.
  • Overlooking that the Outsourcing Master Direction requires data localisation for all sensitive customer data, not just payment data.
  • Mixing up the cooling‑off period (14 days) under the Digital Lending Guidelines with the 30‑day grievance redressal timeline under the Consumer Protection Directions.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise regulatory knowledge in the examination.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and RBI Market‑Making Operations

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with issuance concentrated in high‑rated public sector entities and a limited secondary‑market turnover. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has sought to deepen this market because it provides an alternative funding channel for non‑bank corporates and improves the interest‑rate pass‑through from policy rates to the real economy. Transmission operates through three linked mechanisms: (i) the policy‑rate signal that shifts the risk‑free yield curve, (ii) the credit‑spread compression that follows improved liquidity, and (iii) the direct effect of RBI market‑making operations on bond prices and issuance costs.

Policy‑Rate Signal and Yield‑Curve Re‑pricing

When the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) changes the repo rate, the immediate impact is on the overnight indexed swap (OIS) curve and the government‑securities (G‑sec) yield curve. Corporate bond yields are priced as a spread over the corresponding G‑sec benchmark. A 25‑basis‑point repo cut typically lowers the 5‑year G‑sec yield by 15‑20 bps, and the corporate spread narrows by an additional 5‑10 bps as investors re‑balance toward higher‑yielding credit. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that the pass‑through to AAA‑rated corporate bonds is about 70 % within the first month, while lower‑rated issuers experience a lagged and smaller pass‑through because of credit‑risk premia.

RBI Market‑Making Operations

To address liquidity gaps, the RBI launched the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) in March 2020 and subsequently institutionalised a standing Market‑Making Scheme (MMS) for corporate bonds in August 2021. Under the MMS, designated primary dealers (PDs) quote two‑way prices for a basket of eligible bonds (minimum rating AA, minimum outstanding ₹500 crore). The RBI provides a back‑stop liquidity window: PDs can repo the purchased bonds at the prevailing repo rate plus a modest spread. This arrangement reduces the bid‑ask spread from an average of 30‑40 bps to 10‑15 bps, encouraging institutional investors such as mutual funds and insurers to hold corporate bonds to maturity.

Transmission to Issuance Costs and Credit Growth

Lower secondary‑market spreads feed directly into primary issuance. Data from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) show that the average coupon on new AAA issuances fell from 7.25 % in FY 2020‑21 to 6.55 % in FY 2022‑23, a 70‑bps decline that mirrors the combined effect of policy easing and improved market‑making. The cheaper funding has supported credit growth to the non‑bank corporate sector, which expanded at 12 % year‑on‑year in FY 2023‑24 versus 8 % in the pre‑CBPP period. However, transmission remains incomplete for lower‑rated issuers (A and BBB) where spreads remain elevated due to information asymmetry and limited investor base.

Challenges and Policy Implications

Key constraints include the absence of a robust credit‑default‑swap market for hedging, concentration of holdings among a few large mutual funds, and the need for a centralized trade‑reporting platform. The RBI’s 2023 discussion paper on a Corporate Bond Trade Repository aims to improve price discovery. For examiners, the critical takeaway is that monetary transmission to the corporate bond segment is a two‑stage process: policy‑rate pass‑through to the risk‑free curve, followed by liquidity‑enhancement measures that compress credit spreads. Questions often test the distinction between the indirect channel (yield‑curve shift) and the direct channel (RBI market‑making), and the relative speed of pass‑through across rating categories.

RBI’s Revised Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio Framework: Operational Details and Transmission Effects

The Basel III liquidity standards — the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and the Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) — were adopted in India in a phased manner. The LCR became binding for all scheduled commercial banks from January 2015, while the NSFR was made applicable from October 2021. In 2021 the RBI issued a revised LCR framework (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21) that aligned the definition of High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) with the Basel Committee’s 2017 revisions and introduced a differentiated run‑off factor for retail deposits based on digital‑banking intensity.

Key Revisions to the LCR

The revised LCR retains the 30‑day stress horizon but modifies three components: (i) Level 1 HQLA now includes sovereign‑guaranteed bonds issued by state governments, provided they meet the 0 % risk‑weight criterion; (ii) Level 2A assets (corporate bonds rated AA‑ or above) receive a 15 % haircut instead of the previous 20 %; (iii) the run‑off rate for stable retail deposits is reduced from 5 % to 3 % for banks where more than 60 % of retail deposits are sourced through digital channels, reflecting lower withdrawal volatility observed during the COVID‑19 period. The net effect is an estimated 2‑3 % reduction in the required HQLA stock for a typical large bank, freeing up ₹1.2‑1.5 lakh crore of government securities for market operations.

NSFR Operationalisation

The NSFR requires banks to maintain a stable funding profile over a one‑year horizon. The RBI’s 2021 guidelines (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.84/21.04.048/2020‑21) set the minimum NSFR at 100 % and prescribe Available Stable Funding (ASF) factors: 100 % for regulatory capital, 90 % for retail deposits with maturity > 1 year, 50 % for wholesale funding with residual maturity > 1 year, and 0 % for funding maturing within one year. Required Stable Funding (RSF) factors assign 5 % to unencumbered Level 1 HQLA, 15 % to performing loans to non‑financial corporates, and 100 % to non‑performing assets. Banks must report NSFR quarterly; the first reporting date was 31 December 2021.

Transmission to Money‑Market Rates and Credit Pricing

By lowering the HQLA requirement, the revised LCR reduces banks’ demand for short‑term government securities, exerting downward pressure on the overnight call‑money rate and the tri‑party repo rate. Empirical analysis in the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (March 2024) shows a 5‑bps decline in the weighted average call rate in the quarter following the LCR revision. On the NSFR side, the higher ASF weight for long‑term retail deposits incentivises banks to raise term deposits, which lengthens the liability profile and supports lower lending rates for infrastructure and housing loans. However, the NSFR also raises the cost of short‑term wholesale funding, prompting some banks to shift toward certificate‑of‑deposit issuance, which can tighten money‑market liquidity during periods of high credit demand.

Supervisory Monitoring and Reporting

The RBI’s Department of Supervision conducts quarterly LCR/NSFR stress tests using a 30‑day and a one‑year horizon respectively. Banks breaching the 100 % threshold are placed under enhanced monitoring and may face restrictions on dividend distribution and branch expansion. As of March 2024, all scheduled commercial banks reported LCR above 110 % and NSFR above 105 %, indicating comfortable compliance buffers. The next review cycle (2025) is expected to incorporate climate‑related liquidity risk factors, aligning with the RBI’s Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosure Framework.

Worked Example: LCR Impact on HQLA Composition
A bank holds ₹200 crore in Level 1 HQLA (central government securities), ₹80 crore in Level 2A HQLA (AA‑rated corporate bonds), and ₹50 crore in Level 2B HQLA (equity shares). Under the revised LCR, Level 2A haircut is 15 % and Level 2B haircut remains 50 %. The bank’s total net cash outflows over 30 days are ₹250 crore. Calculate the bank’s LCR and state whether it meets the 100 % minimum.
Adjusted HQLA = Level 1 (₹200 crore) + Level 2A after haircut (₹80 crore × 0.85 = ₹68 crore) + Level 2B after haircut (₹50 crore × 0.50 = ₹25 crore) = ₹293 crore. LCR = Adjusted HQLA ÷ Net cash outflows = ₹293 crore ÷ ₹250 crore = 1.172 = 117.2 %. The bank exceeds the 100 % requirement.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the effect of a revised LCR haircut on a bank’s HQLA, first compute the post‑haircut value for each asset class, then sum to get adjusted HQLA. Remember that only Level 1 and Level 2A/2B assets count; excess reserves and cash are Level 1. Practice the arithmetic with round numbers to avoid calculator errors under time pressure.

Fiscal Deficit Financing, Government Securities Market Development and Monetary Policy Coordination

The central government’s gross fiscal deficit (GFD) is financed primarily through dated securities (G‑secs) and treasury bills (T‑bills) issued in the primary market. The RBI acts as the debt manager under the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, and coordinates with the Ministry of Finance through the Quarterly Borrowing Calendar. The interaction between fiscal borrowing and monetary policy operates through three channels: (i) supply‑side pressure on G‑sec yields, (ii) the RBI’s open‑market operations (OMO) that sterilise or accommodate the borrowing, and (iii) the signalling effect of the borrowing calendar on inflation expectations.

Borrowing Calendar and Yield‑Curve Management

The annual borrowing calendar, announced in the Union Budget, specifies the weekly issuance schedule for dated securities across tenors (2‑year to 40‑year). In FY 2023‑24 the centre budgeted a gross market borrowing of ₹15.4 lakh crore, of which ₹13.5 lakh crore was dated securities. The RBI’s Primary Dealer (PD) system underwrites the issuance; any unsubscribed portion is devolved on the RBI, which then holds the securities in its investment portfolio. Large, front‑loaded borrowing can steepen the yield curve, raising long‑term rates relative to short‑term rates. To prevent excessive steepening, the RBI conducts Operation Twist — simultaneous purchase of long‑dated securities and sale of short‑dated securities — thereby flattening the curve without changing the policy repo rate.

OMO Sterilisation and Liquidity Management

When the government’s cash balances with the RBI rise (e.g., due to tax inflows), the RBI may conduct reverse repo or variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb surplus liquidity, keeping the weighted average call rate (WACR) near the repo rate. Conversely, during periods of heavy borrowing, the RBI may inject liquidity via outright purchase of G‑secs (OMO purchase) or through the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) at a rate below the repo rate.
