By March 2024, NARCL’s asset book had grown to ₹1.2 lakh crore (gross), with SRs issued to the selling banks and the guarantee invoked for the shortfall between recovery proceeds and the SR face value. The resolution strategy emphasises asset‑by‑asset resolution, leveraging the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) where feasible, and one‑time settlement (OTS) schemes for smaller exposures.

Key operational features differentiate NARCL from earlier Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs). First, the government guarantee on SRs eliminates the credit risk for selling banks, allowing them to derecognise the assets immediately and release capital. Second, IDRCL’s professional management team — drawn from banking, legal, and turnaround expertise — is empowered to take operational control of borrower entities, a power earlier ARCs lacked. Third, the NARCL‑IDRCL framework includes a resolution timeline of five years, with a mandatory review at the end of year three; if recovery falls below 40 % of the acquisition cost, the guarantee can be invoked for the shortfall.

Early outcomes indicate a recovery rate of approximately 28 % on the first tranche after 24 months, driven primarily by OTS agreements and a few successful IBC resolutions. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report (December 2023) noted that the bad‑bank structure has reduced the gross NPA ratio of PSBs from 9.8 % (March 2021) to 5.9 % (March 2024), but cautioned that the guarantee exposure creates a contingent fiscal liability that must be monitored. The government has indicated that the guarantee ceiling may be enhanced if the asset pipeline expands beyond the initial ₹2 lakh crore target.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: "If a public sector bank transfers a stressed loan of ₹500 crore to NARCL at 18 % of the outstanding amount, and the government guarantee covers 100 % of the Security Receipts issued, what is the immediate impact on the bank's Tier‑1 capital, assuming the loan was fully provisioned at 100 %?"
The bank derecognises the ₹500 crore loan and the associated 100 % provision (₹500 crore). It receives SRs worth ₹90 crore (18 % of ₹500 crore) backed by a government guarantee. The SRs are classified as investments and risk‑weighted at 0 % (sovereign guarantee). Consequently, the bank’s risk‑weighted assets fall by ₹500 crore, releasing Tier‑1 capital equivalent to the capital charge on that exposure (typically 8 % × ₹500 crore = ₹40 crore). The provision write‑back of ₹500 crore flows to the profit‑and‑loss account, boosting retained earnings and thus Tier‑1 capital by ₹500 crore, net of any tax effect. The net Tier‑1 capital increase is therefore approximately ₹540 crore (₹500 crore provision write‑back + ₹40 crore capital charge release), subject to the bank’s dividend policy and tax rate.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question combines NARCL mechanics with capital adequacy, first identify the accounting treatment (derecognition, provision write‑back, SR classification). Then apply the Basel III risk‑weight for sovereign‑guaranteed securities (0 %). Remember that the guarantee is a contingent liability for the government, not the bank, so it does not affect the bank’s leverage ratio. Practice a few numerical variants with different transfer discounts (15 %, 20 %) to internalise the capital impact.

RBI's Regulatory Framework for Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms

The Reserve Bank issued the Master Direction – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017 on 4 October 2017, bringing P2P platforms under the definition of Non‑Banking Financial Companies (NBFC‑P2P). The framework mandates registration with the RBI, a minimum net owned fund of ₹2 crore, and a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times the owned fund. Platforms must act as intermediaries only; they cannot lend from their own books, nor can they provide credit enhancement or guarantees to lenders.

Key operational safeguards include: (a) a cap of ₹50,000 per lender per borrower across all P2P platforms, with an aggregate exposure limit of ₹10 lakh per lender; (b) a borrower‑side limit of ₹10 lakh across all platforms; (c) mandatory credit‑assessment using a board‑approved algorithm, with the platform required to disclose the key parameters to both parties; (d) an escrow mechanism operated by a scheduled commercial bank to hold funds until matching is completed; and (e) a grievance redressal officer and a dispute resolution mechanism with a 30‑day turnaround.

In 2020 the RBI tightened the framework through a circular dated 24 June 2020, introducing a “fit‑and‑proper” criterion for promoters, requiring a minimum of three years’ experience in financial services, and mandating that platforms maintain a liquidity buffer of 5 % of outstanding loans in a designated bank account. The 2020 amendment also required platforms to report loan‑level data to the Credit Information Companies (CICs) on a monthly basis, enabling the integration of P2P credit histories into the mainstream credit‑scoring ecosystem.

As of March 2024, 23 entities held NBFC‑P2P registration. The aggregate loan book stood at ₹12,500 crore, with a 90‑day past‑due ratio of 2.3 %. The RBI’s Annual Report 2023‑24 highlighted that the leverage cap and exposure limits have prevented systemic spillovers, but flagged the risk of platform concentration — the top three platforms account for 68 % of the market. The central bank has indicated that a review of the ₹10 lakh borrower cap is under consideration to accommodate the growing demand for micro‑enterprise financing.

RBI's Cybersecurity and IT Governance Framework for Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s first comprehensive cybersecurity guideline for banks was issued in June 2011 (DBOD.No.BP.BC.57/21.04.048/2010‑11), prescribing a Cyber Security Policy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and a board‑level IT strategy committee. The framework was substantially upgraded by the Master Direction – Information Technology Framework for the NBFC Sector (June 2017) and the Cyber Security Framework for Banks (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2019‑20, dated 7 February 2020). The 2020 circular introduced a baseline cyber resilience requirement: banks must implement a Security Operations Centre (SOC) with 24×7 monitoring, conduct annual vulnerability assessments and penetration testing, and maintain an incident‑response plan tested through tabletop exercises at least twice a year.

For NBFCs, the RBI issued a separate Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices (November 2023), extending the baseline to all deposit‑taking NBFCs (NBFC‑D) and systemically important non‑deposit‑taking NBFCs (NBFC‑ND‑SI). The direction mandates a Board‑approved IT Strategy, a Risk Appetite Statement for technology risk, and the adoption of the ISO/IEC 27001 standard for information security management. Entities must submit a Cyber Security Return (CSR) quarterly, detailing incidents, root‑cause analysis, and remediation status.

Enforcement actions illustrate the supervisory seriousness. In 2022 the RBI imposed a monetary penalty of ₹2 crore on a private sector bank for failure to detect a credential‑stuffing attack that compromised 1.2 million customer accounts, citing non‑compliance with the SOC monitoring requirement. In 2023 a systemically important NBFC was directed to engage an external auditor for a comprehensive IT audit after a ransomware incident encrypted critical loan‑origination data for 72 hours. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report (June 2024) reported a 37 % year‑on‑year increase in reported cyber incidents across the regulated sector, underscoring the need for continuous investment in threat intelligence sharing through the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) and the Financial Sector Computer Emergency Response Team (Fin‑CERT).

Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosures and the RBI's Alignment with TCFD

The RBI released a Discussion Paper on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance in July 2021, signalling its intent to integrate climate‑related financial risks into supervisory expectations. This was followed by the Draft Guidelines on Climate‑Related Financial Risk Management and Disclosure in April 2022, which proposed alignment with the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) four pillars — governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics & targets. The final Master Direction – Climate‑Related Financial Risk Management and Disclosure was issued on 30 June 2023, applicable to all scheduled commercial banks, All‑India Financial Institutions (AIFIs), and top‑layer NBFCs (NBFC‑UL).

The direction requires entities to: (i) disclose the board’s oversight of climate risks and the role of a designated Climate Risk Officer; (ii) conduct scenario analysis using at least two climate pathways — a transition risk scenario (e.g., IEA Net‑Zero 2050) and a physical risk scenario (e.g., IPCC RCP 8.5) — and quantify the impact on credit portfolios, market risk, and liquidity; (iii) report a Climate Risk Heatmap at the sectoral level, identifying high‑exposure sectors such as thermal power, cement, and steel; and (iv) set measurable targets for financed emissions reduction, with a baseline year of FY 2022‑23 and a 2030 interim target consistent with the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi).

Implementation timelines are staggered: governance and strategy disclosures are mandatory from the financial year ending March 2025; scenario analysis and heatmap reporting from March 2026; and financed‑emissions targets from March 2027. The RBI has also established a Climate Risk Data Repository hosted by the Reserve Bank Information Technology (ReBIT) to standardise data templates and facilitate supervisory benchmarking. As of the March 2024 reporting cycle, 78 % of banks had appointed a Climate Risk Officer, and 62 % had completed the first round of scenario analysis, with the average projected credit loss under the transition scenario estimated at 1.4 % of gross advances.

  • Confusing the LCR’s 30‑day horizon with the NSFR’s one‑year horizon and applying the same HQLA eligibility criteria to both ratios.
  • Assuming NARCL’s government guarantee eliminates all fiscal risk; the guarantee is a contingent liability that materialises only if recoveries fall short of SR face value.
  • Treating P2P platforms as lenders rather than intermediaries, leading to erroneous capital‑adequacy calculations for the platform itself.
  • Overlooking the mandatory 24×7 SOC requirement for banks and the quarterly Cyber Security Return for NBFCs, which are distinct from the annual IT audit.
  • Believing the climate‑risk disclosure timeline is uniform; governance disclosures start FY 2025, scenario analysis FY 2026, and financed‑emissions targets FY 2027.
  • Mixing the ₹10 lakh borrower cap across all P2P platforms with the per‑platform ₹50,000 limit, resulting in double‑counting of exposure.
  • Ignoring the carve‑out for infrastructure loans under the NSFR, which reduces the RSF weight from 65 % to 50 % for qualifying assets.

Microfinance Institutions: RBI's 2022 Master Direction and Operational Constraints

The Reserve Bank issued the Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Regulatory Framework for Microfinance Loans) Directions, 2022, replacing the earlier 2011 guidelines and extending a uniform rule‑set to all regulated entities — scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, NBFC‑MFIs, and other NBFCs engaged in micro‑credit. The direction defines a microfinance loan as a collateral‑free loan to a household with annual income not exceeding ₹1.25 lakh in rural areas and ₹2 lakh in urban/semi‑urban areas. The maximum loan size is ₹1.25 lakh for the first cycle and ₹2 lakh for subsequent cycles, with a minimum tenure of 24 months for loans above ₹30 000. Pre‑payment penalties are prohibited.

Interest‑rate ceiling is the lower of two benchmarks: (i) 2.75 times the average base rate of the five largest commercial banks, or (ii) the entity’s cost of funds plus a margin cap of 10 % for NBFC‑MFIs and 12 % for other lenders. The cost‑of‑funds must be computed on a quarterly basis and disclosed on the entity’s website. Processing fees are capped at 1 % of the gross loan amount, and no additional charges (insurance premium, penalty interest, etc.) may be levied beyond the prescribed ceiling.

Household‑level indebtedness is monitored through a credit‑information‑company (CIC) database; a borrower cannot have more than two microfinance loans outstanding simultaneously, and total microfinance exposure per household must not exceed ₹1.25 lakh (rural) or ₹2 lakh (urban). Entities must conduct a compulsory credit‑bureau check before sanction and report each loan to at least one CIC within 30 days of disbursement. The direction also mandates a board‑approved policy for loan pricing, recovery practices, and grievance redressal, with a dedicated nodal officer for customer complaints.

Supervisory reporting includes a quarterly Microfinance Portfolio Return (MPR) detailing portfolio quality, sectoral distribution, and compliance with the income‑and‑loan‑size caps. The RBI’s 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report noted that the gross non‑performing asset ratio for the microfinance segment fell to 2.1 % from 3.4 % a year earlier, attributing the improvement to stricter underwriting and the income‑verification mandate. However, the report flagged concentration risk in a few states where portfolio growth outpaced income verification capacity.

Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms: Regulatory Architecture and Exposure Limits

The RBI brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending under its regulatory perimeter through the Master Direction – Non‑Banking Financial Company – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017, amended in 2020. A P2P platform must be registered as an NBFC‑P2P with a minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore and a leverage ratio (outside liabilities / owned fund) not exceeding 2. The platform acts solely as an intermediary; it cannot lend on its own books or provide credit enhancement.

Borrower‑side caps: an individual borrower may not owe more than ₹10 lakh across all P2P platforms, and exposure to a single platform is limited to ₹50 000. Lender‑side caps: an individual lender may not deploy more than ₹50 lakh across all platforms, with a per‑platform ceiling of ₹10 lakh. Institutional lenders (banks, NBFCs, mutual funds) are subject to separate exposure limits linked to their capital adequacy frameworks. All transactions must be routed through an escrow account maintained with a scheduled commercial bank, and the platform must settle funds within T+1 day.

Platforms are required to adopt a board‑approved credit‑assessment policy, perform KYC/AML checks on both borrowers and lenders, and disclose a standardised “Key Fact Statement” for each loan listing. The 2020 amendment introduced a mandatory credit‑score model validated by an external auditor, and a quarterly “P2P Lending Return” (PLR) capturing loan‑level data — amount, tenure, interest rate, repayment status, and default rates. The RBI also prescribed a grievance‑redressal mechanism with a 30‑day resolution timeline and an appellate authority at the platform level.

As of March 2024, 23 NBFC‑P2Ps held valid certificates of registration. The aggregate outstanding loan book stood at approximately ₹7,800 crore, with a 90‑day‑plus delinquency ratio of 1.8 %. The RBI’s 2023 supervisory circular highlighted that platforms using proprietary scoring models without external validation were more prone to under‑pricing risk, prompting a directive for annual model audits.

Examiner's trap
A P2P platform reports an aggregate borrower exposure of ₹12 lakh for a single borrower across two platforms (₹7 lakh on Platform A and ₹5 lakh on Platform B). The platform claims compliance because each individual platform exposure is below the ₹50 000 per‑platform limit. Is the platform compliant?
No. The RBI’s Master Direction caps a borrower’s total exposure across **all** P2P platforms at ₹10 lakh. The per‑platform ceiling of ₹50 000 is an additional restriction, not a substitute. Since the borrower’s combined exposure (₹12 lakh) exceeds the ₹10 lakh aggregate limit, the platform(s) are in violation. The correct answer must reference the aggregate borrower cap, not the per‑platform limit alone.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes aggregate and per‑platform limits, first identify the **global** cap (₹10 lakh for borrowers, ₹50 lakh for lenders) and then check the **individual** platform sub‑limits. A quick mental table — aggregate vs. per‑platform — prevents the common error of treating the sub‑limit as the only constraint.

Domestic Systemically Important Banks: Resolution Planning, Living Wills, and Capital Surcharges

Since 2015 the RBI has designated Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIBs) based on size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity. As of the 2023 assessment, State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, and HDFC Bank occupy Bucket 1 (additional CET1 surcharge of 0.6 % of risk‑weighted assets), while no bank currently falls in Bucket 2 (0.3 % surcharge). The surcharge is phased in over four quarters and must be maintained on a continuous basis.

In parallel, the RBI mandated that each D‑SIB submit a comprehensive resolution plan — commonly termed a “living will” — beginning FY 2017‑18. The plan must cover: (i) a strategic analysis of critical functions and shared services; (ii) a detailed mapping of legal entities, booking models, and cross‑border exposures; (iii) resolution strategies (bail‑in, bridge institution, asset separation) with estimated timelines; (iv) liquidity and capital adequacy projections under severe stress; and (v) operational continuity arrangements for payment‑system services. The RBI reviews these plans annually and may require remedial actions, such as restructuring of legal entities or enhancement of loss‑absorbing capacity.

The resolution‑planning framework draws on the Financial Stability Board’s Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes. Although the Financial Resolution and Deposit Insurance (FRDI) Bill, 2017 proposed a statutory Resolution Corporation, the bill lapsed. Consequently, the RBI relies on its powers under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (Section 45) and the RBI Act, 1934 (Section 35A) to direct D‑SIBs to maintain adequate “total loss‑absorbing capacity” (TLAC) — currently aligned with the Basel III TLAC standard of 18 % of RWA plus capital conservation buffer for G‑SIBs, adapted domestically as the D‑SIB surcharge plus the existing capital conservation buffer.

Supervisory outcomes: the 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report indicated that all three D‑SIBs met the CET1 surcharge requirement with a comfortable margin (average CET1 ratio 13.2 % vs. required 11.5 %). However, the RBI flagged gaps in cross‑border resolution coordination for one D‑SIB with significant overseas subsidiaries, urging the bank to finalise bilateral resolution‑cooperation agreements with host‑country authorities by March 2025.

Capital Flow Management: External Commercial Borrowings, FPI Limits, and Macroprudential Tools

India’s capital‑flow management framework combines price‑based and quantity‑based measures to balance financing needs with macro‑financial stability. The External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) framework, revised in 2019 and subsequently tweaked, classifies borrowings into three tracks: (i) Track I — automatic route up to US $750 million per financial year for eligible corporates, minimum average maturity 3 years (5 years for infrastructure); (ii) Track II — approval route for amounts above the automatic limit or for sectors under negative list; (iii) Track III — rupee‑denominated ECBs with a minimum maturity of 3 years. All ECBs are subject to an all‑in‑cost ceiling linked to the 6‑month LIBOR/ARR plus a spread cap of 450 bps for Track I and 500 bps for Track II.

Foreign Portfolio Investment (FPI) in debt is governed by the “Voluntary Retention Route” (VRR) and the “General Route”. Under the General Route, FPIs may invest up to 24 % of the outstanding stock of corporate bonds and 10 % of government securities (G‑secs) without prior approval. The VRR allows higher limits (up to 30 % for corporate bonds) provided the investor commits to a minimum retention period of three years and adheres to a prescribed investment‑duration profile. In 2020, the RBI introduced a temporary “FPI‑in‑Corporate‑Bonds” window with a 15 % limit to ease pandemic‑related funding stress, which was later merged into the VRR.

Macroprudential tools complement these quantity limits. The RBI employs the Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) to absorb surplus liquidity generated by large capital inflows, thereby preventing excessive credit growth and asset‑price inflation. In 2013, during the “taper tantrum”, the RBI imposed a minimum holding period of three years for FPI investments in G‑secs and raised the short‑term ECB all‑in‑cost ceiling. In 2022, the RBI tightened the “short‑term debt” limit for banks’ foreign currency exposure to 20 % of Tier‑1 capital, down from 30 %, to curb rollover risk.

The 2023‑24 Annual Report noted that net FPI inflows into debt turned positive at US $12.4 billion after two years of outflows, while ECB disbursements rose 18 % year‑on‑year to US $45 billion. The RBI’s capital‑flow‑management stance remains calibrated: the VRR limit for corporate bonds was raised to 30 % in April 2024, and the ECB automatic‑route ceiling is under review for a possible increase to US $1 billion, contingent on external‑sector resilience indicators.

RBI Governance, Accountability, and Parliamentary Oversight

The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, as amended, establishes the Central Board of Directors as the apex governance body. The Board comprises the Governor (chair), up to four Deputy Governors, ten non‑official directors appointed by the Central Government for a four‑year term, and two government officials (usually the Finance Secretary and the Secretary, Department of Financial Services). The Governor and Deputy Governors are appointed for a term not exceeding five years, with eligibility for re‑appointment. The Board meets at least six times a year; its minutes are not public, but key decisions — monetary policy, regulation, supervision — are communicated through press releases and the Annual Report.

Audit and financial accountability are layered. The RBI’s accounts are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) under Section 47 of the RBI Act. Additionally, the Central Board appoints two external auditors (typically large chartered‑accountant firms) for a statutory audit of the Bank’s financial statements, which are presented to Parliament along with the CAG’s report. The RBI also publishes a half‑yearly “Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India”, which serves as a supervisory transparency tool.

Parliamentary oversight operates through three channels: (i) the Governor’s appearance before the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Finance (typically twice a year) to discuss monetary policy, banking sector health, and regulatory initiatives; (ii) the submission of the Annual Report and the CAG’s audit report to both Houses of Parliament, triggering debate; (iii) the power of the Central Government to issue directions to the RBI under Section 7 of the RBI Act “in public interest”, a provision invoked only once (in 2018, for the resolution of a stressed NBFC). The RBI’s operational independence in monetary policy is safeguarded by the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) structure, where the Governor has a casting vote but no veto.

Recent governance enhancements include the 2021 amendment to the RBI Act mandating a “Risk Management Committee” of the Central Board, chaired by a Deputy Governor, to oversee enterprise‑wide risk (credit, market, operational, cyber, climate). The 2023 “Governance Review” circular required all regulated entities to adopt a “Board‑approved Risk Appetite Statement” and to appoint a Chief Risk Officer with direct reporting lines to the Board, aligning corporate governance with the RBI’s own framework.

  • Confusing the aggregate borrower cap (₹10 lakh) with the per‑platform cap (₹50 000) in P2P lending, leading to double‑counting of permissible exposure.
  • Assuming the microfinance interest‑rate ceiling is a single fixed percentage; it is the lower of a market‑linked benchmark and a cost‑of‑funds‑plus‑margin formula that varies quarterly.
  • Treating the D‑SIB capital surcharge as a one‑time add‑on rather than a continuous CET1 requirement that must be maintained alongside the capital conservation buffer.
  • Overlooking that the FRDI Bill’s Resolution Corporation never became law; resolution planning for D‑SIBs rests on existing Banking Regulation Act powers, not a statutory corporation.
  • Mixing the VRR and General Route FPI limits for corporate bonds; the VRR permits up to 30 % with a three‑year lock‑in, while the General Route caps at 24 % without lock‑in.
  • Believing the RBI’s Section 7 direction power is routinely used; it has been invoked only once and remains an exceptional, politically sensitive tool.
  • Ignoring the mandatory quarterly Microfinance Portfolio Return (MPR) and the P2P Lending Return (PLR), which are distinct from the annual supervisory returns filed by banks.

RBI’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process and Supervisory Review Process

The Basel III framework splits capital regulation into three pillars. Pillar 1 prescribes minimum capital ratios; Pillar 2 requires banks to conduct an Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) and the Reserve Bank to perform a Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP). In India the RBI issued the ICAAP guidelines in July 2017 (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2016‑17) and the SREP framework in March 2019 (DBR.No.BP.BC.115/21.04.048/2018‑19).

ICAAP obliges every commercial bank to develop a board‑approved capital plan that covers credit, market, operational, interest‑rate‑risk‑in‑the‑banking‑book (IRRBB), concentration, and strategic risks. The plan must be forward‑looking (typically three years), incorporate stress‑testing scenarios approved by the board, and demonstrate that internal capital targets exceed the regulatory minima by a comfortable margin. Banks submit the ICAAP document annually, together with a summary of the stress‑test results, to the Department of Supervision.

The SREP is the RBI’s counterpart. Supervisory colleges review the ICAAP, assess the quality of risk‑management frameworks, and assign a supervisory rating (CACS – Capital Adequacy, Asset Quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, Sensitivity). Based on the rating, the RBI may impose additional capital charges (Pillar 2 add‑ons), restrict dividend distribution, or require remedial action plans. The 2019 SREP circular introduced a “Supervisory Scorecard” that quantifies governance, risk culture, and data integrity, making the review more transparent.

Key interaction points include: (i) the ICAAP’s stress‑test outputs feed directly into the RBI’s macro‑stress‑testing exercise published in the Financial Stability Report; (ii) banks classified as Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIBs) undergo an enhanced SREP with a dedicated supervisory team; (iii) the RBI’s 2021 “Guidelines on Capital Planning and Stress Testing” mandated that ICAAP scenarios cover a severe COVID‑19‑type shock, a sharp rise in interest rates, and a simultaneous credit‑quality deterioration.

Failure to maintain a credible ICAAP can trigger Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) thresholds. For instance, a breach of the CET1 ratio below 7 % combined with a negative ICAAP assessment leads to mandatory capital augmentation within six months. The RBI also publishes a “Supervisory Action Framework” that maps ICAAP deficiencies to specific corrective measures, ensuring that the link between internal assessment and supervisory response is rule‑based rather than discretionary.

Macroprudential Loan‑to‑Value and Debt‑to‑Income Limits for Real Estate and Consumer Credit

Macroprudential tools target systemic risk arising from excessive leverage in specific sectors. The RBI has calibrated Loan‑to‑Value (LTV) caps for housing loans, commercial real estate (CRE) exposures, and, more recently, Debt‑to‑Income (DTI) limits for unsecured personal loans. The first LTV circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.71/21.04.048/2014‑15) set a maximum LTV of 80 % for housing loans up to ₹30 lakh and 75 % above that threshold. In 2018 the RBI tightened CRE LTV to 50 % for loans to developers and 60 % for loans to borrowers with existing CRE exposure, citing the build‑up of unsold inventory.

The 2020 “Guidelines on Responsible Lending” introduced a DTI ceiling of 40 % for new unsecured personal loans and credit‑card receivables, calculated on the borrower’s gross monthly income. Banks must verify income through salary slips, tax returns, or the Account Aggregator framework. The same circular mandated a minimum cooling‑off period of three months between successive unsecured loans to the same borrower.

In 2022 the RBI issued a sectoral capital requirement (DBR.No.BP.BC.124/21.04.048/2021‑22) that adds a 0.5 % risk‑weight surcharge on housing‑loan portfolios where the average LTV exceeds 75 % and a 1 % surcharge on CRE exposures with LTV above 60 %. The surcharge is applied on top of the standard risk weights and is reversible once the portfolio average falls below the threshold for two consecutive quarters.

Transmission of these limits works through both price and quantity channels. Higher LTV caps reduce the loan amount a borrower can obtain, dampening demand for property and curbing price momentum. DTI caps restrict the flow of unsecured credit to households with stretched balance sheets, lowering the probability of default spikes during income shocks. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that after the 2018 CRE LTV tightening, the year‑on‑year growth of CRE credit fell from 22 % to 9 % within four quarters, while non‑performing assets in the segment declined by 30 % over the same period.

Compliance is monitored through quarterly returns (Form LTV‑1 for housing, Form CRE‑1 for commercial real estate, and Form DTI‑1 for unsecured retail). The RBI’s 2023 “Supervisory Review of Macroprudential Measures” highlighted that 12 % of banks breached the DTI ceiling in at least one quarter during FY 2022‑23, resulting in supervisory letters and, in three cases, a temporary restriction on new unsecured lending.

Examiner’s trap
A question asks: “If a bank’s housing‑loan portfolio has an average LTV of 78 % and the bank’s CET1 ratio is 9.5 %, what additional capital charge does the RBI impose under the 2022 sectoral capital requirement?”
The 2022 circular prescribes a 0.5 % risk‑weight surcharge on housing‑loan exposures where the average LTV exceeds 75 %. The surcharge is applied to the risk‑weighted assets of that portfolio, not directly to the CET1 ratio. Therefore the bank must hold extra capital equal to 0.5 % of the risk‑weighted assets of the housing‑loan book. The CET1 ratio of 9.5 % is irrelevant to the calculation of the surcharge; it only matters for overall capital adequacy. The correct answer: an additional capital charge of 0.5 % of the housing‑loan risk‑weighted assets.
Exam‑day strategy
When a macroprudential question mixes LTV, DTI, and sectoral capital surcharges, first identify the instrument (LTV cap, DTI ceiling, or risk‑weight surcharge). Then locate the exact threshold (e.g., 75 % LTV for housing, 40 % DTI for unsecured). Remember that surcharges are expressed as a percentage of risk‑weighted assets, not as a direct CET1 add‑on. Practise converting a portfolio‑level breach into the incremental capital requirement using the formula: Incremental Capital = Surcharge % × Portfolio RWA.

Resolution Framework for Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks under Prompt Corrective Action

Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Payment Banks (PBs) operate under differentiated licences but are subject to the same Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework that applies to universal banks, with certain calibrated thresholds. The RBI’s 2017 PCA circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.101/21.04.048/2016‑17) defined three trigger metrics: Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR), Net NPA Ratio, and Return on Assets (RoA). For SFBs the CRAR trigger is set at 15 % (versus 9 % for universal banks) reflecting their higher risk profile, while the Net NPA trigger is 6 % (versus 6 % for universal banks) and RoA trigger is 0.25 % (versus 0.25 %).

Payment Banks, which cannot advance loans, are assessed on a modified set: Capital Adequacy (minimum 15 % CRAR), Leverage Ratio (minimum 3 %), and a “Liquidity Coverage Ratio” tailored to their high‑volume, low‑value transaction model. The 2021 PCA revision (DBR.No.BP.BC.138/21.04.048/2020‑21) introduced a “Graduated Restriction Matrix” that maps each breach level (Risk Threshold 1, 2, 3) to specific actions: (i) restriction on dividend distribution, (ii) prohibition on branch expansion, (iii) mandatory capital infusion within a defined timeline, and (iv) at the highest level, initiation of resolution proceedings.

Resolution options for SFBs and PBs differ from universal banks because of their limited asset base. The RBI’s 2022 “Resolution Framework for Differentiated Banks” (DBR.No.BP.BC.156/21.04.048/2021‑22) lists: (a) voluntary merger with a universal bank or another SFB/PB, subject to “fit‑and‑proper” clearance; (b) acquisition by a Non‑Banking Financial Company (NBFC) meeting the RBI’s “Large Exposure” norms; (c) conversion of the SFB licence to a universal bank licence, contingent on meeting the ₹500 crore net‑worth requirement and a clean supervisory record for three years; (d) orderly wind‑down with deposit insurance payout (DICGC coverage up to ₹5 lakh per depositor). For PBs, the wind‑down path is the most common, given the absence of loan assets.

The framework also mandates a “Resolution Planning” exercise every two years, where the board submits a Recovery Plan and a Resolution Plan. The Recovery Plan outlines actions to restore capital and liquidity (e.g., equity raise, asset sale, cost rationalisation). The Resolution Plan details the preferred exit route, valuation methodology, and the treatment of payment‑system obligations (e.g., settlement finality for wallet balances). The RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report noted that three SFBs submitted resolution plans in FY 2022‑23, of which two opted for merger and one for licence conversion.

Supervisory colleges monitor compliance through quarterly “PCA Monitoring Returns” (Form PCA‑SFB and Form PCA‑PB). Breaches trigger a “Supervisory Letter” that sets a 30‑day deadline for the board to present a capital restoration plan. Failure to meet the deadline escalates the bank to the next risk threshold automatically. The RBI also publishes an annual “PCA Status List” that names banks under each threshold, enhancing market discipline.

Transition from MIBOR to a Secured Overnight Benchmark and Adoption of SOFR Fallbacks

The Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate (MIBOR) has been the primary rupee interest‑rate benchmark since 1998, calculated from unsecured money‑market borrowing rates submitted by a panel of banks. Concerns about the reliability of submission‑based benchmarks after the global LIBOR scandals prompted the RBI to constitute a Working Group on Interest‑Rate Benchmarks in 2020 (Chair: Dr. Urjit Patel). The group’s final report (June 2021) recommended a transition to a transaction‑based, secured overnight rate derived from the tri‑party repo market (the “Indian Overnight Index Average”).

In March 2022 the RBI released a Consultation Paper on “Transition from MIBOR to a New Benchmark” outlining a three‑phase roadmap: (i) parallel run of the new secured overnight index alongside MIBOR for 12 months; (ii) cessation of MIBOR publication for tenors beyond overnight by end‑2023; (iii) full discontinuation of MIBOR by December 2024. The paper also mandated that all new derivative contracts reference the new index or, where international counterparties are involved, the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) with a spread adjustment.

The RBI’s 2023 “Guidelines on Fallback Provisions for Legacy MIBOR Contracts” (DBR.No.BP.BC.172/21.04.048/2022‑23) require banks and primary dealers to embed a contractual fallback clause that switches to SOFR (compounded in arrears) plus a fixed spread calibrated on the historical median difference between MIBOR and SOFR over a five‑year look‑back window. The spread is published by the Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India (FIMMDA) on a quarterly basis.

Market infrastructure has been upgraded to support the transition. The Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL) launched a “Secured Overnight Repo” (SOR) platform in July 2022, providing real‑time transaction data for the new index. The Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) now publishes the Indian Overnight Index Average (IOIA) daily at 10:00 am IST. As of March 2024, the IOIA has shown a stable spread of 3‑5 basis points over the policy repo rate, confirming its suitability as a risk‑free benchmark.

Supervisory oversight includes a quarterly “Benchmark Transition Report” submitted by all regulated entities, detailing the proportion of outstanding contracts migrated, the status of fallback clause insertion, and any operational issues. The RBI’s 2024 Annual Report noted that 78 % of the notional value of rupee‑denominated interest‑rate swaps had been migrated to the new index, while the remaining legacy contracts are covered by the SOFR fallback mechanism.

  • Confusing the ICAAP capital‑plan horizon (three years) with the SREP review cycle (annual) and assuming the same document serves both purposes.
  • Treating the LTV cap for housing loans as a single static number; the RBI applies tiered caps (80 % up to ₹30 lakh, 75 % above) and a separate CRE LTV schedule.
  • Assuming the DTI ceiling of 40 % applies to all retail credit; it is limited to unsecured personal loans and credit‑card receivables only.
  • Believing that PCA triggers for SFBs are identical to universal banks; SFBs face a higher CRAR threshold (15 %) and a distinct leverage‑ratio monitor.
  • Thinking the MIBOR cessation date is fixed at end‑2023; the RBI’s roadmap extends full discontinuation to December 2024 with a parallel‑run phase.
  • Mixing the SOFR fallback spread (published by FIMMDA) with the IOIA‑repo spread; they are calculated on different reference rates and look‑back windows.
  • Overlooking that Payment Banks cannot be resolved through merger with a universal bank unless the acquirer meets the RBI’s “fit‑and‑proper” and net‑worth criteria for a universal licence.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Services for Banks

The Reserve Bank of India issued the master direction on outsourcing of financial services by banks in November 2021 (RBI/2021‑22/115 DOR.CRE.REC.No.45/21.04.048/2021‑22). The direction replaces the 2006 guidelines and extends the supervisory perimeter to cover all material outsourcing arrangements, including information‑technology, back‑office, and customer‑facing activities. Banks are required to maintain a board‑approved outsourcing policy, conduct due‑diligence on service providers, and ensure that contracts contain explicit clauses on data confidentiality, audit rights, business‑continuity planning, and exit strategies. The RBI also mandated that banks report material outsourcing arrangements quarterly through the Off‑site Surveillance System (OSS) and that the chief risk officer certify compliance annually.

In March 2023 the RBI released a separate circular on “Guidelines on Cloud Services for Banks” (RBI/2022‑23/173 DOR.IT.REC.No.84/21.04.048/2022‑23). The circular recognises the growing adoption of public, private, and hybrid cloud models and sets out a risk‑based framework. Banks must classify cloud services as “critical” or “non‑critical” based on the impact of a service disruption on core banking functions. For critical services, the bank must retain the ability to switch providers within 30 days, maintain a secondary cloud environment, and ensure that data residency requirements under the Information Technology Act and the Personal Data Protection Bill (as enacted) are satisfied. The circular also requires a cloud‑specific business‑continuity plan, periodic penetration testing, and a contractual right for the RBI to inspect the cloud service provider’s infrastructure.

Both frameworks emphasise the “shared responsibility” model: the bank remains accountable for regulatory compliance, while the provider is responsible for the security of the underlying infrastructure. The RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report highlighted that 68 % of scheduled commercial banks had at least one critical cloud arrangement, and supervisory colleges have begun thematic inspections focusing on concentration risk with a single cloud vendor. Non‑compliance attracts supervisory actions ranging from a warning letter to restrictions on new outsourcing contracts.

Operationally, banks have responded by establishing dedicated vendor‑risk management units, adopting standardized contract templates approved by the Indian Banks’ Association, and investing in cloud‑agnostic application architectures to reduce lock‑in. The RBI’s 2024 Annual Report noted that the number of reported material outsourcing arrangements rose 12 % year‑on‑year, reflecting both increased digitisation and tighter reporting discipline.

From an examination perspective, candidates should be able to distinguish between the outsourcing master direction and the cloud‑services circular, identify the classification criteria for critical cloud services, and explain the supervisory consequences of concentration risk with a single cloud provider.

Banking Sector Exposure to Real Estate and Construction Sector Risk

The RBI’s prudential framework for real‑estate exposure was substantially revised through the circular dated 15 June 2022 (RBI/2021‑22/165 DOR.CRE.REC.No.71/21.04.048/2021‑22). The circular introduced tiered loan‑to‑value (LTV) caps for housing loans — 80 % for loans up to ₹30 lakh and 75 % for loans above that threshold — and a separate LTV schedule for commercial real‑estate (CRE) lending, capped at 60 % of the property value. It also mandated a minimum risk‑weight of 100 % for CRE exposures, irrespective of the external rating, and required banks to hold additional provisioning of 0.4 % on standard CRE assets.

Construction‑sector lending is governed by the “Prudential Norms for Advances to the Construction Sector” (RBI/2020‑21/89 DOR.CRE.REC.No.38/21.04.048/2020‑21). These norms prescribe a ceiling of 20 % of a bank’s net‑owned funds for aggregate exposure to a single builder group, and a sub‑limit of 10 % for unsecured advances. The RBI also requires quarterly monitoring of project‑level cash flows, escrow mechanisms for receivables, and independent valuation of collateral at least once a year.

The 2023 Financial Stability Report flagged that the share of real‑estate and construction loans in gross bank credit stood at 13.2 % as of March 2023, with a non‑performing asset ratio of 4.8 % for the segment — higher than the overall banking‑sector GNPA of 3.9 %. Stress‑test results indicated that a 200‑basis‑point rise in interest rates combined with a 15 % decline in property prices could push the segment’s GNPA above 7 %, triggering capital erosion for several mid‑size banks.

Supervisory actions have included the imposition of additional capital charges under Pillar 2 for banks with concentrated CRE portfolios, and the issuance of “Supervisory Letters” directing boards to submit de‑risking plans within 60 days. The RBI’s 2024 “Guidelines on Resolution of Stressed Real‑Estate Assets” (RBI/2023‑24/210 DOR.CRE.REC.No.95/21.04.048/2023‑24) further empower banks to invoke the SARFAESI Act, refer accounts to the National Company Law Tribunal under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, or sell assets to Asset Reconstruction Companies with a minimum recovery threshold of 30 % of the outstanding amount.

For answer‑writing, aspirants should be able to cite the LTV tiers, the risk‑weight treatment for CRE, the exposure ceilings for builder groups, and the supervisory tools (Pillar 2 capital add‑ons, SARFAESI, IBC) that the RBI employs to contain sectoral risk.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “The RBI’s 2022 circular on real‑estate exposure prescribes a uniform LTV of 75 % for all housing loans.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify.
False. The circular prescribes tiered LTV caps: 80 % for housing loans up to ₹30 lakh and 75 % for loans above ₹30 lakh. A single uniform cap does not exist.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific RBI circular, note the year and the key quantitative limits (LTV tiers, risk‑weights, exposure ceilings). A quick mental table of the 2022 real‑estate circular and the 2020 construction‑sector norms lets you eliminate options that quote a single LTV or an incorrect risk‑weight.

Foreign Portfolio Investment Limits and Rupee Volatility Management

The RBI, in coordination with the Securities and Exchange Board of India, manages foreign portfolio investment (FPI) in debt through a combination of quantitative limits and the voluntary retention route (VRR). The current framework, updated in the circular dated 6 April 2023 (RBI/2022‑23/189 DOR.FPI.REC.No.112/21.04.048/2022‑23), sets the aggregate FPI limit in government securities at 6 % of outstanding stock, with a sub‑limit of 2 % for state development loans. For corporate bonds, the limit is 9 % of outstanding stock, subject to a minimum residual maturity of three years.

The VRR, introduced in 2019 and refined in 2021, allows FPIs to invest beyond the statutory caps provided they retain the securities for a minimum period of three years and comply with a 75 % retention ratio. The RBI monitors VRR utilisation through the “FPI Debt Monitoring Report” published monthly on its website. As of March 2024, VRR accounted for approximately 1.8 % of total government‑security holdings by FPIs.

To dampen rupee volatility arising from sudden capital‑flow reversals, the RBI employs a mix of spot‑market intervention, forward‑market operations, and the “Market Stabilisation Scheme” (MSS). The MSS, revived in 2022, authorises the issuance of special treasury bills to absorb excess liquidity when net FPI inflows exceed a threshold of USD 5 billion in a quarter. The RBI’s 2023 Annual Report noted that MSS issuance of ₹1.2 lakh crore in FY 2022‑23 helped contain the rupee’s depreciation to 2.3 % against the US dollar despite a net FPI outflow of USD 12 billion.

Exchange‑rate management also leverages the “Foreign Exchange Intervention Framework” (circular dated 12 January 2022), which defines intervention bands, reporting obligations for authorised dealers, and a transparency regime that publishes net intervention data with a one‑month lag. The framework emphasizes a managed‑float regime where the RBI intervenes only to smooth excessive volatility, not to target a specific level.

Candidates should be able to differentiate between the statutory FPI caps and the VRR, explain the role of MSS in liquidity absorption, and describe how the intervention framework balances transparency with operational flexibility.

RBI's Approach to Green Taxonomy and Sustainable Finance Disclosure

In February 2023 the RBI released a discussion paper titled “Green Taxonomy for India” (RBI/2022‑23/210 DOR.GREEN.REC.No.15/21.04.048/2022‑23) seeking stakeholder comments on a classification system for environmentally sustainable economic activities. The proposed taxonomy aligns with the International Platform on Sustainable Finance (IPSF) core principles and defines “green” activities across six sectors: renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, green transport, and climate‑resilient infrastructure.

The paper outlines a three‑tier hierarchy — “core green”, “transition”, and “enabling” — with quantitative thresholds such as a minimum 80 % share of revenue from eligible activities for core‑green classification. It also proposes a “do‑no‑significant‑harm” (DNSH) test and minimum social safeguards. The RBI intends to embed the taxonomy into its supervisory framework by requiring banks to disclose the proportion of green‑classified exposures in their quarterly “Sustainable Finance Returns” (SFR), a new reporting template to be integrated with the existing Basel III Pillar 3 disclosures.

Parallel to the taxonomy, the RBI issued the “Guidelines on Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosures” in August 2023 (RBI/2023‑24/45 DOR.CLIMATE.REC.No.22/21.04.048/2023‑24). These guidelines adopt the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations and mandate scenario analysis for both physical and transition risks, with a minimum of two climate scenarios (a 1.5 °C pathway and a 3 °C pathway). Banks must publish the results in their annual reports from FY 2024‑25 onward.

The 2024 Financial Stability Report highlighted that 42 % of scheduled commercial banks had initiated internal green‑taxonomy mapping exercises, and the RBI’s supervisory colleges have begun thematic reviews of climate‑risk governance. The RBI also announced a “Green Deposit” framework (circular dated 10 October 2023) allowing banks to raise earmarked deposits for green projects, with a requirement that at least 75 % of the proceeds be allocated to taxonomy‑compliant assets.

For examination purposes, aspirants should recall the three‑tier classification, the DNSH principle, the TCFD‑aligned disclosure timeline, and the link between the green taxonomy and the new SFR reporting template.

Regulation of Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms in India

The RBI brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending platforms under its regulatory ambit through the “Master Direction – Non‑Banking Financial Company – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017” (RBI/2017‑18/123 DNBS.P2P.REC.No.1/21.04.048/2017‑18). The direction defines a P2P platform as an intermediary that facilitates loan transactions between individual lenders and borrowers without assuming credit risk on its own balance sheet. Platforms must obtain a Certificate of Registration (CoR) as an NBFC‑P2P, maintain a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹2 crore, and adhere to a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times.

Key operational safeguards include a cap of ₹50 lakh on aggregate exposure of a single lender across all P2P platforms, a borrower‑level cap of ₹10 lakh, and a mandatory credit‑assessment framework that uses at least two independent data sources. The RBI also requires platforms to maintain an escrow account for fund transfers, conduct quarterly audits of their matching algorithms, and submit a “P2P Lending Return” (Form P2P‑01) within 15 days of each quarter‑end.

In 2020 the RBI amended the directions (RBI/2020‑21/67 DNBS.P2P.REC.No.12/21.04.048/2020‑21) to introduce a “fit‑and‑proper” criterion for directors, enhance the grievance‑redressal mechanism with a 30‑day resolution timeline, and mandate that platforms participate in the RBI’s “Omni‑Channel Complaint Management System”. The 2023 “Guidelines on Digital Lending” (RBI/2022‑23/198 DOR.DIGITAL.REC.No.30/21.04.048/2022‑23) further extended the P2P framework to cover “first‑loss default guarantee” (FLDG) arrangements, requiring that any FLDG provided by the platform be limited to 5 % of the portfolio and be fully disclosed to lenders.

Supervisory data from the RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report shows that the number of registered NBFC‑P2P entities stood at 28, with aggregate loan‑origination volume of ₹18,500 crore in FY 2022‑23. The GNPA ratio for the segment was 2.1 %, lower than the overall NBFC average, attributed to the exposure caps and mandatory credit‑assessment norms.

Examinees should be able to cite the registration requirements, exposure caps, the 2020 amendment on governance, the FLDG ceiling, and the reporting template (Form P2P‑01) as distinguishing features of the P2P regulatory regime.

  • Confusing the 6 % FPI limit in government securities with the 9 % limit in corporate bonds; the two caps operate independently.
  • Assuming the VRR allows unlimited investment; the retention ratio and three‑year lock‑in are binding conditions.
  • Treating the green taxonomy’s “core green” threshold as a single 80 % revenue rule for all sectors; the DNSH test and social safeguards apply additionally.
  • Believing P2P platforms can hold credit risk on their balance sheet; they are prohibited from doing so under the master direction.
  • Mixing the LTV caps for housing loans (80 %/75 %) with the CRE LTV cap (60 %); they belong to separate circulars.
  • Overlooking that the MSS is triggered by net FPI inflows exceeding USD 5 billion in a quarter, not by rupee depreciation alone.

Priority Sector Lending: Target Architecture, Sub-Targets, and the 2020‑21 Recalibration

The Priority Sector Lending (PSL) framework remains the primary directed‑credit instrument in India, mandating that scheduled commercial banks allocate a prescribed share of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent of Off‑Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is higher, to designated sectors. The current architecture, codified in the RBI Master Direction Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification (September 2020), sets the overall target at 40 per cent of ANBC/CEOBE for domestic banks and 18 per cent for foreign banks with fewer than 20 branches. Within this envelope, granular sub‑targets operate: 18 per cent for agriculture (of which 8 per cent must flow to small and marginal farmers), 7.5 per cent for micro enterprises, and 10 per cent for weaker sections (including SC/ST, beneficiaries of government schemes, and small farmers). The 2020 recalibration expanded the definition of “agriculture” to include loans for post‑harvest infrastructure, renewable energy (solar pumps, compressed biogas), and loans to Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) up to ₹2 crore. The “micro enterprises” category was aligned with the MSMED Act, 2006 definition (investment ≤ ₹1 crore, turnover ≤ ₹5 crore), and a new “start‑up” category was introduced with a limit of ₹50 crore per borrower, provided the start‑up is DPIIT‑recognised. To manage shortfalls, banks must deposit the deficit amount in the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) with NABARD, the Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) fund, the MUDRA fund, or the National Housing Bank (NHB) fund, earning a below‑market rate of return (currently the bank rate minus 200 basis points). The Priority Sector Lending Certificate (PSLC) mechanism, operational on the e‑Kuber platform since 2016, allows banks with surplus PSL to sell certificates to deficit banks across four categories (Agriculture, Small/Marginal Farmers, Micro Enterprises, General), creating a price signal for directed credit. In FY 2022‑23, PSLC trading volume exceeded ₹6.2 lakh crore, with the “General” category commanding the highest premium (150‑200 bps over the repo rate), reflecting structural shortfalls in non‑agriculture segments. Examiners frequently test the distinction between ANBC (which excludes RIDF deposits) and CEOBE (which includes off‑balance sheet items like letters of credit and guarantees at credit conversion factors), and the fact that foreign banks with 20 or more branches must meet the 40 per cent target but with a sub‑target of 10 per cent for weaker sections instead of 18 per cent for agriculture.

Co‑operative Banking Reform: The 2020 Banking Regulation Act Amendments and Their Supervisory Consequences

The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (effective 1 April 2021) marked the most significant legislative overhaul of co‑operative banking since 1966, bringing Urban Co‑operative Banks (UCBs) and Multi‑State Co‑operative Banks (MSCBs) under a supervisory regime materially similar to that of commercial banks. The amendment empowers the RBI to supersede the board of a UCB/MSCB for up to 12 months (extendable by another 12 months) and appoint an administrator, a power previously available only for commercial banks under Section 36AA. It also enables amalgamation or reconstruction of a stressed co‑operative bank without imposing a moratorium, using a new Section 45(1A) that mirrors the commercial bank resolution pathway. On governance, the Act mandates that at least 51 per cent of directors on the board of a UCB/MSCB must have “special knowledge or practical experience” in banking, finance, law, or accountancy, and that the Chief Executive Officer (CEO) must satisfy a “fit and proper” criterion vetted by the RBI — a direct transplant of the commercial bank framework under Section 10A/10B. The 2021 amendment (Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2021) extended certain provisions to Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) that operate as “banking companies” (accepting deposits from non‑members), requiring them to obtain a licence and maintain CRR/SLR, though full prudential norms are being phased in. Supervisory data from the RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report shows that the Gross NPA ratio of UCBs declined from 10.2 per cent (March 2021) to 4.8 per cent (March 2023), attributed partly to the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework extended to UCBs in 2022 (trigger points: CRAR < 9 per cent, Net NPA > 6 per cent, leverage > 25 times). The RBI also issued the “Master Direction – Urban Co‑operative Banks – Exposure Norms and Statutory/Other Restrictions” (2022), capping single borrower exposure at 15 per cent of Tier I capital and group exposure at 25 per cent, with a sub‑limit of 10 per cent for unsecured exposures. A critical nuance for examiners: the 2020 Act does not apply to State Co‑operative Banks (StCBs) and District Central Co‑operative Banks (DCCBs), which remain under the dual control of the Registrar of Co‑operative Societies (state government) and NABARD/RBI for banking functions. This duality creates regulatory arbitrage — StCBs/DCCBs are not subject to the CEO fit‑and‑proper test or the 51 per cent professional director rule — a gap the RBI has flagged in its 2022 “Vision Document for Co‑operative Banks”.

Examiner's trap: PSL shortfall deployment vs. ANBC computation
A bank has ANBC of ₹1,000 crore and a PSL achievement of 36 per cent (₹360 crore). The shortfall of ₹40 crore is deposited in RIDF. What is the bank's ANBC for the next reporting quarter, and does the RIDF deposit earn the repo rate?
ANBC for the next quarter excludes the RIDF deposit (per Master Direction, RIDF/SIDBI/MUDRA/NHB deposits are deducted from bank credit for ANBC computation). Thus ANBC falls to ₹960 crore (₹1,000 crore – ₹40 crore). The RIDF deposit earns the bank rate minus 200 bps, not the repo rate. This lower return is a deliberate disincentive for chronic shortfalls. A common error is to assume ANBC remains unchanged or that the deposit earns market rates.
Exam‑day strategy: PSL and co‑operative banking
Memorise the four PSLC categories and the current premium hierarchy (General > Micro Enterprises > Agriculture > Small/Marginal Farmers). For co‑operative banks, create a two‑column table: “UCBs/MSCBs (post‑2020 Act)” vs. “StCBs/DCCBs (dual control)” listing CEO fit‑and‑proper, board composition, supersession powers, and PCA applicability. The RBI’s 2022 Vision Document and the 2023 FSR chapter on co‑operative banks are the authoritative sources for recent data points.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Partial Credit Enhancement, Market Making, and the RBI’s Corporate Bond Purchase Programme

While the interest‑rate and credit channels of monetary transmission to bank lending are well documented, the corporate bond market channel has acquired systemic significance as non‑bank financing now accounts for roughly 25 per cent of total credit flow to the commercial sector (RBI Financial Stability Report, 2023). The transmission mechanism operates through three interacting levers. First, the Partial Credit Enhancement (PCE) framework, introduced in 2014 and revised in 2019 (RBI/2018‑19/181 DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2018‑19), allows banks to provide credit enhancement up to 20 per cent of the bond issue size (capped at 50 per cent of the issue for infra bonds), enabling lower‑rated issuers to access the market at investment‑grade yields. The enhancement is treated as a contingent liability for the bank (100 per cent risk weight) and must be unconditional and irrevocable. Second, the market‑making obligation for Primary Dealers (PDs) in corporate bonds, mandated by SEBI (2018) and reinforced by the RBI’s 2021 “Guidelines on Market Making in Corporate Bonds”, requires PDs to quote two‑way prices for designated liquid bonds, compressing bid‑ask spreads and improving price discovery. Third, the RBI’s direct intervention via the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) — announced in October 2020 and operationalised through on‑tap Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO 2.0) and outright secondary‑market purchases — provided a backstop during the COVID‑induced dislocation. Under TLTRO 2.0 (₹1 lakh crore, March 2021), banks could borrow at the repo rate for up to three years on condition that funds were deployed in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures, with at least 50 per cent allocated to mid‑sized corporates (turnover ₹250‑500 crore). The outright CBPP (₹1 lakh crore, April‑June 2021) saw the RBI purchase bonds in the secondary market via the NDS‑OM platform, with a portfolio weighted towards AAA/AA rated issuers. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR Working Paper 2022) found that the announcement of TLTRO 2.0 compressed spreads on AA‑rated 5‑year bonds by 45‑60 bps within two weeks, while the outright purchases reduced the term premium on 10‑year corporate bonds by 25 bps. A critical limitation: the PCE framework remains underutilised — only 12 banks had active PCE exposures as of March 2023, totalling ₹8,400 crore — because the 100 per cent risk weight and provisioning requirements make it capital‑intensive. Examiners often test the distinction between TLTRO (collateralised lending to banks against corporate bonds) and outright CBPP (RBI’s own balance‑sheet purchase), and the fact that PCE can only be provided by scheduled commercial banks, not by NBFCs or AIFs.

The Liquidity Management Framework: From Structural Deficit to Surplus and the RBI’s Evolving Toolkit (2014‑2024)

India’s structural liquidity position has undergone three distinct regime shifts since 2014, each reshaping the RBI’s operating toolkit. Phase I (2014‑2016): Persistent deficit. Average daily net liquidity absorption via the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) hovered around ₹1.2‑1.5 lakh crore. The repo rate was the de facto policy rate, with the reverse repo fixed at 100 bps below. Open Market Operations (OMOs) were predominantly purchase‑side (₹2.3 lakh crore net purchases in FY 2015‑16) to offset the deficit. Phase II (2017‑2019): Demonetisation‑induced surplus. The withdrawal of ₹15.4 lakh crore in specified bank notes (November 2016) flooded the system with surplus liquidity, peaking at ₹4.8 lakh crore net absorption in January 2017. The reverse repo became the operative rate (the “floor” of the corridor), and the RBI introduced the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) — issuing ₹2.5 lakh crore of MSS bills in 2017‑18 — to sterilise the surplus. The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) at 100 bps above repo served as the ceiling. Phase III (2020‑2022): COVID surplus and the new corridor. Proactive liquidity injection (LTROs, TLTROs, FX swaps, OMOs) pushed surplus absorption to ₹7.2 lakh crore (September 2021). The RBI recalibrated the corridor in April 2022 by introducing the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) at 3.75 per cent (25 bps below the then repo rate of 4.00 per cent), which became the new floor — uncollateralised, unlike the reverse repo. The reverse repo was retained at 3.35 per cent but ceased to be the primary absorption tool; instead, the RBI shifted to Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions (14‑day and 28‑day tenors) as the main liquidity absorption instrument, with the SDF serving as a backstop for residual surplus. Phase IV (2023‑2024): Return to deficit. As credit growth outpaced deposit growth (credit‑deposit ratio > 78 per cent), the system slipped into deficit (net injection of ₹1.1 lakh crore via LAF in March 2024). The repo rate (6.50 per cent) regained its status as the operative rate. The RBI now uses Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auctions for fine‑tuning injection, while the SDF remains the floor and MSF (6.75 per cent) the ceiling. Two structural drivers merit attention: (i) government cash balances — the single‑day swing in Centre’s cash balance at the RBI can exceed ₹2 lakh crore during tax‑collection months, requiring intraday liquidity management via the Ways and Means Advances (WMA) limit (₹1.5 lakh crore for H1 FY 2024‑25) and Special Drawing Facility (SDF) against government securities; (ii) foreign exchange intervention — every dollar purchased injects ~₹83 crore of rupee liquidity, and the RBI’s net FX purchases of $32 billion in FY 2023‑24 added ~₹2.6 lakh crore of durable liquidity, partially offset by VRRR auctions. For examination purposes, aspirants must be able to trace the operative rate in each phase (repo → reverse repo → SDF → repo) and explain why the SDF, being uncollateralised, expands the RBI’s absorption capacity beyond the stock of government securities held by banks.

RBI’s Supervisory Framework for Financial Market Infrastructures: Systemic Importance, Settlement Finality, and the 2023 Payment System Operator Guidelines

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS Act) empowers the RBI to designate, regulate, and oversee Financial Market Infrastructures (FMIs) — payment systems, central counterparties (CCPs), central securities depositories (CSDs), and trade repositories. The RBI adopts the CPMI‑IOSCO Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures (PFMI) as the supervisory benchmark. India’s Systemically Important Payment Systems (SIPS) are: (i) RTGS (Real Time Gross Settlement) — systemically important due to high‑value interbank and government securities settlements (daily volume ~₹3.5 lakh crore); (ii) CCIL (Clearing Corporation of India Ltd.) — the CCP for foreign exchange (FX‑Clear), government securities (GC‑Clear), and money market (Repo‑Clear) segments, providing novation and multilateral netting; (iii) NPCI (National Payments Corporation of India) — operator of retail payment systems (UPI, IMPS, NACH, RuPay, NETC) processing >12 billion transactions/month. The 2023 Guidelines on Supervisory Framework for Payment System Operators (RBI/2022‑23/198 DOR.PAY.REC.No.30/21.04.048/2022‑23) introduced a tiered supervisory approach: Tier 1 (SIPS) — continuous supervision, on‑site inspection annually, mandatory compliance with all 24 PFMI principles, and a requirement to maintain a minimum net‑worth of ₹500 crore (for CCPs) or ₹100 crore (for payment system operators). Tier 2 (prominent retail systems like card networks, PPI issuers with >10 crore transactions/month) — periodic off‑site monitoring, thematic inspections, and a net‑worth floor of ₹25 crore. Tier 3 (other authorised operators) — returns‑based surveillance. A pivotal operational change: the guidelines mandate settlement finality at the point of irrevocable transfer in the books of the settlement bank (for RTGS, finality is immediate; for UPI, finality occurs at the end of the settlement cycle, currently every 30 minutes). The 2022 amendment to the PSS Act (effective 2023) explicitly protects settlement finality from insolvency proceedings — a “zero‑hour” rule ensuring that completed settlements cannot be unwound. On interoperability, the RBI mandated (March 2022) full interoperability across KYC‑compliant Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs), UPI, and card networks by March 2024, requiring PPI issuers to participate in a common network (UPI or card rails) and prohibiting closed‑loop wallets for new customers. The Cheque Truncation System (CTS) operates on a grid‑based architecture (three grids: North, South, West) with T+1 settlement finality, and the 2021 “CTS 2010” standard mandates image‑based clearing with MICR‑code‑free processing. Examiners frequently test the distinction between a CCP (CCIL, which novates trades and mutualises counterparty risk) and a payment system operator (NPCI, which facilitates message exchange and settlement but does not novate), and the fact that the RBI’s oversight of CCIL extends to its risk‑management model (margin methodology, default fund sizing) under the PFMI, whereas for NPCI the focus is on operational resilience, cyber‑security, and consumer protection.

  • Confusing the PSL sub‑target for agriculture (18 per cent) with the weaker‑sections sub‑target (10 per cent); they are distinct and both binding.
  • Assuming the 2020 Banking Regulation Act amendments apply to State Co‑operative Banks and DCCBs; they do not — dual control persists.
  • Treating TLTRO (collateralised bank borrowing) and outright Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (RBI’s own balance‑sheet purchase) as identical instruments; they differ in risk‑bearing and exit mechanics.
  • Believing the reverse repo rate remained the operative floor throughout 2020‑2022; the SDF (April 2022) replaced it as the floor, and VRRR became the primary absorption tool.
  • Stating that NPCI novates UPI transactions; NPCI is a payment system operator, not a CCP — settlement finality rests with the settlement banks, not NPCI.
  • Overlooking that PCE can only be provided by scheduled commercial banks, not by NBFCs, AIFs, or foreign portfolio investors.
  • Mixing the MSS trigger (net FPI inflows > USD 5 billion in a quarter) with the VRRR trigger (surplus liquidity conditions assessed daily); they operate on different time horizons and metrics.

RBI's Lender of Last Resort Operations: Emergency Liquidity Assistance and the 2020 COVID‑19 Special Liquidity Facilities

The Reserve Bank of India derives its lender‑of‑last‑resort (LOLR) mandate from Section 17(3) of the RBI Act, 1934, which permits the Bank to provide advances to scheduled commercial banks against eligible collateral when the financial system faces a systemic liquidity shock. The COVID‑19 pandemic triggered a series of calibrated LOLR interventions that went beyond the routine Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF). In March 2020 the RBI announced a Special Liquidity Facility (SLF) for Mutual Funds of ₹50,000 crore, backed by high‑quality corporate bonds and commercial paper, to prevent fire‑sales in the debt‑fund segment. The facility was operated through a 90‑day repo window at the prevailing policy repo rate and was fully subscribed within days, signalling acute stress in the short‑term funding market.

Simultaneously, the RBI launched Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) in two tranches (TLTRO 1.0 in March 2020 for ₹1 lakh crore and TLTRO 2.0 in April 2020 for ₹50,000 crore). Unlike the SLF, TLTROs provided three‑year funds at the policy repo rate, but banks were required to deploy the proceeds exclusively in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. The conditional deployment clause was a novel macro‑prudential tool that linked liquidity provision to credit flow to the corporate sector. By September 2020 the RBI had also opened a Special Liquidity Facility for NBFCs and HFCs (₹30,000 crore) to address the funding gap faced by non‑bank lenders after the IL&FS episode.

The operational design of these facilities showcased three distinguishing features: (i) collateral elasticity – the RBI accepted a broader basket of assets, including AA‑rated corporate bonds, which were normally ineligible under the LAF; (ii) tenor extension – moving from overnight to three‑year funding reduced rollover risk for banks; and (iii) targeted end‑use – the TLTRO deployment condition ensured that liquidity reached the real economy rather than remaining parked in government securities. The RBI’s 2021‑22 Annual Report noted that the combined SLF and TLTRO operations lowered the weighted average call‑money rate by 45 basis points and compressed corporate bond spreads by 30‑40 bps within two months of launch.

Exit management was built into each facility: the SLF matured in 90 days with a rollover option, TLTROs carried a three‑year maturity with a premature redemption clause linked to the bank’s net‑stable‑funding‑ratio (NSFR) compliance, and the NBFC facility was wound down once the RBI’s Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) became the floor rate in April 2022. The experience reinforced the principle that LOLR actions must be time‑bound, collateral‑transparent, and accompanied by a clear exit roadmap to avoid moral hazard and balance‑sheet encumbrance.

Transmission of Monetary Policy to the Corporate Bond Market via the RBI's Corporate Bond Purchase Programme

In October 2020 the RBI unveiled the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) as part of its unconventional monetary policy toolkit. The programme authorised outright purchases of investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) in the secondary market up to an aggregate ceiling of ₹1.5 lakh crore. Purchases were conducted through a multiple‑price auction on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, with the RBI acting as a price‑taker to avoid market distortion. The first auction, held on 29 October 2020, saw bids worth ₹12,000 crore against a notified amount of ₹10,000 crore, indicating strong demand for central‑bank liquidity in the corporate bond segment.

The transmission channel operates through three mechanisms. First, the portfolio‑rebalancing effect – by removing high‑quality bonds from the market, the RBI forces investors to shift into slightly lower‑rated paper, compressing credit spreads across the rating spectrum. Second, the signalling effect – the announcement itself lowered the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield by 18 bps within a week, as market participants priced in a sustained accommodative stance. Third, the liquidity‑premium reduction – the RBI’s presence as a committed buyer improves secondary‑market depth, reducing the bid‑ask spread from an average of 12 bps to 7 bps for the targeted issuers.

Empirical assessment by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) in the 2021‑22 Monetary Policy Report showed that the CBPP contributed an estimated 12‑15 bps reduction in the weighted average cost of new corporate bond issuance during the first six months. However, the programme’s impact was asymmetric: high‑rated issuers (AAA/AA+) experienced a larger spread compression than lower‑rated (A‑rated) paper, reflecting the eligibility filter. The RBI deliberately limited purchases to the top two rating buckets to contain credit risk on its balance sheet, a design choice that differentiates the CBPP from the earlier Open Market Operations (OMO) in government securities, where the central bank bears sovereign risk only.

Exit strategy was embedded in the programme’s design: purchases cease once the notified amount is exhausted, and the RBI holds the bonds to maturity, receiving coupon payments and principal redemption. As of March 2023 the outstanding CBPP portfolio stood at ₹1.2 lakh crore, with an average residual maturity of 4.2 years. The RBI has indicated that any future scaling will be contingent on a reassessment of market liquidity conditions and the evolution of the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) rate, ensuring that the CBPP remains a temporary, crisis‑management instrument rather than a permanent market‑making function.

Technique: Distinguishing CBPP from TLTRO in Transmission Questions
A question asks: "Which of the following statements correctly differentiates the RBI's Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) from the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO)?" Options: (a) CBPP provides funds to banks; TLTRO purchases bonds directly. (b) CBPP involves outright purchase of bonds by RBI; TLTRO lends to banks against collateral with end‑use restrictions. (c) Both are conducted at the reverse repo rate. (d) CBPP is limited to government securities; TLTRO targets corporate bonds.
Correct answer: (b). The CBPP is an outright secondary‑market purchase of investment‑grade corporate bonds by the RBI, expanding its own balance sheet. TLTRO, by contrast, is a collateralised repo lending window where the RBI provides three‑year funds to banks at the policy repo rate, conditional on deployment in corporate debt. CBPP does not lend to banks, and TLTRO does not involve direct bond purchases by the RBI. Both operate at the policy repo rate, not the reverse repo rate, and neither is limited to government securities.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question compares unconventional tools, first identify the balance‑sheet impact: outright purchase (asset‑side expansion) versus repo lending (liability‑side expansion with collateral). Then check for end‑use conditions, eligibility filters, and maturity profile. A quick mental table (Tool | RBI Balance‑Sheet Effect | Counterparty | End‑Use | Tenor) eliminates three options in seconds.

Impact of the 2023 Amendments to the Banking Regulation Act on Governance of Cooperative Banks

The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2023 (effective 1 April 2023) extended the RBI’s supervisory powers over Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs) and State Cooperative Banks (StCBs) / District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCBs) in three critical areas. First, the amendment brought Section 35A powers — directions in public interest, including supersession of the board and appointment of an administrator — within the RBI’s reach for all cooperative banks, removing the earlier requirement of state‑government concurrence. Second, it mandated minimum capital adequacy of 9 per cent (Tier‑1 7 per cent) for UCBs with deposits above ₹100 crore, aligning them with the Basel‑III framework applicable to scheduled commercial banks. Third, it introduced a fit‑and‑proper criteria for directors and chief executives, requiring RBI approval for appointments and empowering the RBI to remove persons deemed unfit.

The legislative change was prompted by the 2020‑21 crisis in several large UCBs (e.g., Punjab & Maharashtra Cooperative Bank, Sri Guru Raghavendra Sahakari Bank) where governance failures and political interference led to depositor losses. The amendment also clarified that the dual‑control structure (state registrar for incorporation, RBI for banking regulation) persists, but the RBI’s directions now prevail in matters of prudential regulation, asset classification, and resolution. Importantly, the 2023 Act does not extend the 2020 Banking Regulation Act amendments (which applied only to UCBs) to StCBs/DCCBs; those entities continue to be governed by the respective state cooperative societies acts for organisational matters.

Operationally, the RBI issued a Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Supervisory Framework for Cooperative Banks) 2023 in June 2023, detailing the prompt corrective action (PCA) matrix for UCBs, the timeline for capital augmentation (12 months from breach), and the process for board supersession. By December 2023, the RBI had invoked supersession powers in three UCBs, appointing administrators and initiating merger talks with stronger peers.
