  • Overlooking the mandatory 70 % hedge ratio for Track I/II ECBs; many candidates cite a 50 % figure from the pre‑2018 regime.
  • Assuming the microfinance interest‑rate ceiling of 24 % still applies to NBFC‑MFIs; the 2022 Master Direction replaced it with a cost‑plus formula.
  • Thinking BC commissions can be charged to borrowers as a separate “service fee”; the 2022 BC Framework explicitly forbids any extra charge to the customer.
The advanced sections above integrate regulatory text, quantitative benchmarks, and supervisory expectations that are routinely examined in descriptive and case‑study questions.

Digital Lending Guidelines 2022: Scope, Cooling‑Off Period, and Compliance

The Reserve Bank of India issued the Digital Lending Guidelines on 2 September 2022 (RBI/2022‑23/XX) to bring uniformity to the rapidly expanding digital credit ecosystem. The circular applies to all regulated entities (REs) — commercial banks, small finance banks, payments banks, NBFCs, housing finance companies, and any other entity authorised to lend under the RBI Act. It explicitly covers loans originated through the RE’s proprietary mobile app, web portal, or any third‑party platform that acts as a lending service provider (LSP). The guidelines do not apply to pure marketplace platforms that merely match borrowers with lenders without assuming credit risk.

Key Provisions

  • Direct Disbursement: Loan amounts must be credited directly to the borrower’s bank account. No intermediary — including the LSP — may hold, route, or park funds.
  • Cooling‑Off Period: A mandatory 72‑hour (3‑day) window after disbursement during which the borrower may cancel the loan without any penalty, prepayment charge, or impact on credit score. The RE must honour the cancellation and refund any interest accrued for those days.
  • Data Privacy and Consent: Explicit, informed consent is required before accessing a borrower’s data (including contact list, location, or device identifiers). Data collected must be limited to what is necessary for credit assessment and must be stored in India.
  • Transparency of Charges: All fees — processing, documentation, penal interest — must be disclosed upfront in a standardised Key Fact Statement (KFS). The annual percentage rate (APR) must be displayed prominently.
  • Grievance Redressal: REs must appoint a dedicated nodal officer for digital lending complaints and resolve them within 30 days. Escalation to the RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme is permitted thereafter.

Compliance Timeline and Supervisory Expectations

Existing digital lending arrangements were required to be aligned with the guidelines by 30 November 2022. The RBI’s Department of Supervision conducts thematic inspections focusing on the cooling‑off implementation, data‑localisation adherence, and the integrity of the KFS. Non‑compliance attracts supervisory action under the Scale‑Based Regulation framework, including restrictions on new digital loan sanctions.

RBI’s Co‑Lending Framework: Operational Mechanics and Risk Sharing

The co‑lending model (CLM) was first introduced in September 2020 (Circular DBR.No.BP.BC.72/21.04.048/2020‑21) and substantially revised in November 2022 to deepen credit flow to priority sectors, especially agriculture, MSMEs, and affordable housing. The framework permits scheduled commercial banks (SCBs) and eligible NBFCs (including HFCs) to jointly originate, underwrite, and service loans. The bank acts as the lead lender and the NBFC as the co‑lender.

Risk‑Sharing Structure

  • Exposure Split: Minimum 80 % of the loan amount must be funded by the bank; the NBFC may contribute up to 20 %. For loans to micro‑enterprises (up to ₹10 lakh), the NBFC share can be raised to 30 % with board approval.
  • Credit Risk Allocation: Both parties bear credit risk in proportion to their funded share. The bank’s portion is subject to its own provisioning norms; the NBFC follows its applicable provisioning framework.
  • Interest Rate: A single blended interest rate is charged to the borrower. The rate is determined by the bank, but the NBFC’s cost of funds is factored into the pricing through a mutually agreed spread.

Operational Workflow

  1. Origination: The NBFC sources and conducts preliminary appraisal. The bank performs independent credit assessment and final sanction.
  2. Documentation: A single loan agreement is executed, naming both lenders. Security creation (mortgage, hypothecation) is done in favour of a security trustee representing both parties.
  3. Disbursement: Funds are released jointly — the bank transfers its share to the borrower’s account; the NBFC transfers its share to the same account or to the bank’s escrow, which then credits the borrower.
  4. Servicing and Recovery: The bank typically handles repayment collection, monitoring, and NPA classification. The NBFC receives its share of recoveries net of expenses.

Prudential Safeguards

The RBI mandates that the bank’s board approve a co‑lending policy covering due‑diligence on the NBFC’s financial health, governance, and IT systems. The NBFC must maintain a minimum Capital Adequacy Ratio of 15 % and a Net NPA ratio below 6 % to remain eligible. Quarterly reporting to the RBI on co‑lending portfolio quality, sectoral distribution, and compliance with the 80‑20 split is compulsory.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “In the RBI’s co‑lending model, the NBFC can fund up to 30 % of the loan for all priority‑sector categories.” State whether this is true or false and justify.
False. The 30 % NBFC share is permitted only for loans to micro‑enterprises up to ₹10 lakh, subject to board approval. For all other priority‑sector categories (agriculture, affordable housing, etc.) the NBFC’s maximum share remains 20 %. The 80‑20 split is the default rule; the higher NBFC participation is an explicit exception, not a general provision.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the two‑tier exposure limits (80‑20 default, 70‑30 for micro‑enterprises) and the eligibility thresholds (CAR ≥ 15 %, Net NPA < 6 %). In descriptive answers, cite the September 2020 circular and the November 2022 revision; examiners reward precise regulatory references.

Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Regulation: Registration, Prudential Norms, and Consumer Protection

The RBI brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending under a formal regulatory perimeter through the Non‑Banking Financial Company – Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017, subsequently updated in 2020. Only entities incorporated in India and registered as an NBFC‑P2P with the RBI may operate a P2P platform. The registration process requires a minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore, a fit‑and‑proper promoter test, and a robust technology architecture certified by a CERT‑IN empanelled auditor.

Prudential Norms

  • Leverage Ratio: The platform’s total outstanding loans across all lenders cannot exceed 2 times its NOF.
  • Exposure Limits: A single lender’s exposure to a single borrower is capped at ₹50,000; aggregate exposure of a lender across all borrowers cannot exceed ₹10 lakh. Borrower‑side caps are ₹10 lakh per platform and ₹50 lakh across all platforms.
  • Escrow Arrangement: Funds must flow through an escrow account maintained with a scheduled commercial bank. The platform cannot hold or use lender funds for its own operations.
  • Provisioning: Platforms must maintain a contingency provision of 0.25 % of the outstanding loan portfolio, rising to 0.40 % if the portfolio NPA exceeds 3 %.

Consumer Protection Measures

The directions mandate a Fair Practices Code covering transparent disclosure of interest rates, fees, and recovery procedures. Borrowers must receive a loan agreement in a language they understand. The platform must provide a 30‑day cooling‑off period for borrowers to withdraw without penalty — distinct from the digital lending cooling‑off period. Grievance redressal must be resolved within 15 days, with escalation to the RBI Ombudsman for Digital Transactions. Data localisation is compulsory: all borrower and lender data must reside on servers located in India.

Large Value Payment Systems: RTGS, NEFT, and UPI Architecture

India’s high‑value payment infrastructure rests on three pillars — the Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system, the National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT) system, and the Unified Payments Interface (UPI). Each serves distinct value‑size and speed requirements while sharing a common settlement finality framework overseen by the RBI.

RTGS

Launched in March 2004, RTGS processes individual transactions of ₹2 lakh and above on a real‑time, gross basis. Settlement occurs continuously during business hours (07:00–18:00 on working days) with finality at the moment of credit to the beneficiary’s account. Participants include all scheduled commercial banks, select primary dealers, and the RBI itself. The system operates on the INFINET secure messaging network and uses the ISO 20022 message standard since the 2020 upgrade.

NEFT

NEFT, operational since November 2005, settles transactions in half‑hourly batches (48 cycles per day). There is no minimum or maximum transaction limit, making it suitable for both retail and corporate payments. Settlement finality is achieved at the end of each batch. NEFT participants are the same as RTGS, plus regional rural banks and cooperative banks that meet eligibility criteria.

UPI

UPI, launched in April 2016 by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), enables instant push‑and‑pull payments between bank accounts using a virtual payment address (VPA). It operates 24 × 7, including holidays, with a per‑transaction cap of ₹1 lakh (₹2 lakh for verified merchants). UPI’s architecture is built on the Immediate Payment Service (IMPS) rails and leverages the UPI Switch for routing. Interoperability is mandated: all banks and authorised payment system providers must connect to the UPI Switch. The RBI’s 2022 directive extended UPI to feature phones via USSD (*99#) and introduced UPI‑Lite for low‑value offline transactions up to ₹200.

Settlement Finality and Risk Management

All three systems settle in central bank money, ensuring payment versus payment (PvP) finality. The RBI’s Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 provides the legal basis for irrevocability once settlement occurs. Systemic risk is mitigated through participant collateral requirements, real‑time monitoring of intraday liquidity, and the RBI’s Standing Liquidity Facility for settlement banks.

Resolution of Stressed Assets in the Power Sector: The 2018 Circular and Subsequent Amendments

In February 2018 the RBI issued a landmark circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.101/21.04.048/2017‑18) mandating a time‑bound resolution framework for stressed assets in the power sector. The circular required lenders to initiate a resolution plan within 180 days of default, failing which the account would be referred to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC). The move aimed to address the large stock of non‑performing assets (NPAs) in thermal power projects, many of which suffered from fuel supply uncertainties and power purchase agreement (PPA) disputes.

Key Features of the 2018 Framework

  • 180‑Day Timeline: Lenders had to finalise a resolution plan — including restructuring, change in ownership, or asset sale — within 180 days from the date of first default.
  • Independent Credit Evaluation: An independent credit evaluation (ICE) by a credit rating agency was mandatory for exposure above ₹500 crore.
  • Inter‑Creditor Agreement (ICA): All lenders were required to sign an ICA binding them to the majority decision (75 % by value).

Judicial Intervention and the 2019 Revised Circular

The Supreme Court, in its September 2019 judgment in Association of Power Producers v. Union of India, struck down the 180‑day mandatory referral to NCLT as ultra vires the RBI Act. In response, the RBI issued a revised circular in June 2019 (DBR.No.BP.BC.45/21.04.048/2019‑20) that retained the resolution framework but made the NCLT referral discretionary. The revised circular introduced a “Resolution Plan” to be implemented within 180 days, with a further 90‑day extension permissible. It also allowed lenders to pursue a “One‑Time Settlement” with borrowers without invoking IBC.

2020 Prudential Framework and Current Status

The RBI’s 2020 Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets (circular dated 7 August 2020) superseded the sector‑specific circulars, providing a unified approach for all sectors, including power. Under this framework, the 180‑day timeline remains, but the mandatory ICA threshold was lowered to 60 % by value, and the ICE requirement was made applicable for exposures above ₹1,000 crore. The framework also introduced a “Resolution Professional” appointment mechanism for cases entering IBC. As of March 2024, the power sector’s gross NPA ratio has declined from 12.5 % (March 2018) to 5.8 %, reflecting the combined effect of resolution plans, asset sales to renewable energy players, and improved fuel supply arrangements.

  • Assuming the digital lending cooling‑off period applies only to loans above ₹1 lakh; the 72‑hour window is universal for all digital loans irrespective of ticket size.
  • Confusing the co‑lending 80‑20 split with the 70‑30 split for all priority‑sector loans; the higher NBFC share is restricted to micro‑enterprises up to ₹10 lakh.
  • Believing P2P platforms can hold lender funds in their own wallets; the escrow mandate requires funds to reside in a bank‑maintained escrow account.
  • Thinking NEFT operates in real‑time like RTGS; NEFT settles in half‑hourly batches, not continuously.
  • Assuming the 2018 power‑sector circular’s mandatory NCLT referral is still in force; the Supreme Court invalidated it, and the 2019 revision made referral discretionary.
  • Overlooking that UPI‑Lite transactions are limited to ₹200 per transaction and ₹2,000 daily, not the standard ₹1 lakh UPI limit.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and Credit Spreads

The corporate bond market in India has grown from a negligible share of total credit in the early 2000s to roughly 18 % of outstanding non‑food credit by March 2024. Transmission of the policy repo rate to this segment operates through three intertwined channels: the primary‑dealer conduit, the open‑market‑operation (OMO) purchase programme, and the risk‑pricing feedback loop. Primary dealers, mandated to underwrite government securities, also act as market‑makers for high‑rated corporate paper. When the RBI lowers the repo rate, the cost of funds for primary dealers falls, narrowing the bid‑ask spread on corporate bonds and encouraging fresh issuance.

The RBI’s targeted OMO purchase of corporate bonds, launched in April 2020 under the “Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds” and later extended as the “Corporate Bond Purchase Programme” (CBPP), directly injected liquidity into the secondary market. The CBPP allowed the RBI to buy up to ₹1 lakh crore of investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) through a auction‑based mechanism. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research shows that the average credit spread on AA‑rated 5‑year paper compressed by 45‑55 basis points within three months of the first auction, while the spread on AAA paper narrowed by 30‑40 basis points. The effect was strongest for issuers with existing banking relationships, reflecting the credit‑channel amplification where lower bank lending rates reduce the opportunity cost of holding corporate debt.

A second transmission leg works through the “risk‑pricing feedback loop”. As the policy rate falls, the yield curve flattens, reducing the term premium embedded in corporate bond yields. Lower term premiums improve the attractiveness of longer‑dated corporate paper, prompting issuers to extend maturities. This maturity extension, in turn, reduces rollover risk for the banking sector, feeding back into easier bank credit conditions. However, the loop can reverse sharply if inflation expectations become unanchored; the 2022‑23 tightening cycle saw corporate bond spreads widen by 70‑80 basis points despite a modest 150‑basis‑point repo hike, illustrating the asymmetric sensitivity of the risk‑pricing channel.

Operation Twist, conducted between December 2020 and March 2021, simultaneously sold short‑dated government securities and bought long‑dated ones. By pulling down the 10‑year sovereign yield by roughly 35 basis points, the operation lowered the benchmark against which corporate spreads are quoted, delivering an indirect transmission boost. The RBI’s 2023 “Standing Deposit Facility” (SDF) and “Variable Rate Reverse Repo” (VRRR) auctions further refined the interest‑rate corridor, ensuring that the marginal cost of funds for primary dealers remains closely aligned with the policy rate, thereby preserving the primary‑dealer conduit.

Key take‑aways for examiners: (1) transmission to corporate bonds is not automatic; it depends on primary‑dealer balance‑sheet capacity and the depth of the secondary market; (2) targeted purchase programmes have a measurable but time‑bound impact on spreads; (3) the risk‑pricing feedback loop can amplify or dampen the initial impulse depending on inflation credibility.

RBI’s Liquidity Management during the COVID‑19 Pandemic: Special Liquidity Facilities and Their Exit

The onset of the COVID‑19 lockdown in March 2020 triggered an unprecedented surge in demand for rupee liquidity as banks faced deposit outflows, a sharp rise in government borrowing, and a freeze in money‑market activity. The RBI responded with a layered toolkit that combined conventional instruments (repo, reverse repo, marginal standing facility) with three bespoke facilities: the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF), the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO), and the On‑Tap Liquidity Window for Non‑Banking Financial Companies (NBFC‑LTRO).

The SLF‑MF, announced on 27 April 2020, provided ₹50 000 crore of 90‑day repo funding to mutual funds against investment‑grade corporate bonds and commercial paper. The facility was rolled over twice, ultimately reaching ₹1 lakh crore, and was fully unwound by September 2021 as redemption pressures eased. The TLTRO, launched on 17 April 2020, offered three‑year funds at the prevailing repo rate (then 4.40 %) to banks on condition that the proceeds be deployed in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. Three tranches totalling ₹2.5 lakh crore were conducted; the last tranche matured in March 2023. The NBFC‑LTRO, opened on 15 May 2020, extended ₹1 lakh crore of three‑year funding to eligible NBFCs and housing finance companies, with a mandatory 50 % deployment in fresh lending to micro‑, small‑ and medium‑enterprises (MSMEs).

Exit management was calibrated to avoid a sudden liquidity shock. The RBI adopted a “graduated unwind” strategy: (i) cessation of fresh auctions once the targeted amount was subscribed; (ii) allowing existing operations to mature naturally; (iii) using variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb excess liquidity as the economy recovered. By June 2022, the net liquidity injection from all pandemic‑era facilities had turned negative, with the banking system moving into a surplus of ₹3.2 lakh crore. The RBI’s 2022‑23 Monetary Policy Report noted that the orderly exit prevented a spike in short‑term rates and kept the weighted average call rate (WACR) within the policy corridor throughout the transition.

Two lessons stand out for policy analysis: first, the combination of targeted long‑term funding with deployment conditions can direct liquidity to specific credit segments without distorting the overall money‑market rate structure. Second, a transparent exit roadmap — communicated through the Monetary Policy Statement and the Financial Stability Report — anchors market expectations and reduces the risk of a “taper tantrum” in domestic rupee markets.

Worked Example: Assessing Facility Impact
A question asks: “Explain how the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) differed from the regular Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) repo in terms of tenor, collateral, and transmission objective during the COVID‑19 period.”
The regular LAF repo is an overnight (or 14‑day) collateralised lending window where banks pledge government securities to meet short‑term liquidity needs; its primary objective is to keep the overnight call rate within the policy corridor. TLTRO, by contrast, offered three‑year funds at the repo rate, accepted a broader collateral set (investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, NCDs), and explicitly required banks to deploy the proceeds in designated corporate debt instruments. Thus, TLTRO targeted the credit‑channel transmission to the corporate bond market, whereas LAF repo targets the interest‑rate channel for overnight rates.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “transmission channels” or “liquidity tools”, map each tool to its primary channel (interest‑rate, credit, balance‑sheet, exchange‑rate) and note any conditionalities (tenor, collateral, deployment rules). Use a two‑column table in your answer sheet: Tool → Channel → Key Condition. This structure earns full marks for clarity and completeness.

Digital Lending Guidelines 2022: Consumer Protection, Data Governance, and the Cooling‑Off Period

The Reserve Bank’s “Guidelines on Digital Lending” issued on 2 September 2022 (RBI/2022‑23/112) constitute the first comprehensive regulatory framework for lending conducted through digital platforms, including fintech apps, NBFC‑owned lending apps, and bank‑partnered marketplaces. The guidelines apply to all regulated entities (REs) — scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators — that originate, underwrite, or service loans via digital channels.

Three pillars dominate the framework. First, the “cooling‑off period” mandates that borrowers be given a minimum 72‑hour window after loan disbursement during which they may cancel the loan without any penalty, interest, or fee. This period is universal, applying irrespective of ticket size, and overrides any contractual clause to the contrary. Second, data governance provisions require REs to obtain explicit, informed consent before accessing a borrower’s contact list, location, or device identifiers. Data collected must be stored on servers located in India, and any sharing with third parties (including credit bureaus) must be disclosed in the loan agreement. Third, the guidelines prescribe a “Key Fact Statement” (KFS) to be presented in a standardized format before loan acceptance, covering the annualised percentage rate (APR), all fees, repayment schedule, and the cooling‑off right.

Enforcement mechanisms include a graded supervisory approach: (i) a mandatory self‑assessment report to be filed within 90 days of the guideline’s effective date; (ii) quarterly returns on loan‑level data (disbursements, cancellations, complaints); (iii) a dedicated grievance redressal officer for digital lending complaints, with a 30‑day resolution timeline. Non‑compliance attracts penalties under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI Act, 1934, including possible restriction on digital lending operations.

Early supervisory feedback (RBI’s 2023‑24 Annual Report) indicates that the cooling‑off period led to a 12 % cancellation rate in the first quarter of implementation, predominantly in sub‑₹50 000 tickets, suggesting that the provision curbs impulsive borrowing. However, industry representations have highlighted operational challenges in verifying the 72‑hour window for loans disbursed via UPI‑linked instant credit lines, prompting the RBI to issue a clarificatory FAQ in January 2023 confirming that the clock starts at the moment of credit to the borrower’s account.

For examination purposes, remember: the guidelines do not create a new licensing category; they overlay existing RE licences. The cooling‑off period is a consumer‑protection tool, not a prudential capital requirement. Data localisation is a sovereign‑data‑security measure, distinct from the Personal Data Protection Bill provisions.

Macroprudential Policy Coordination: The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) and Inter‑Agency Mechanisms

The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC), constituted in December 2010 under the Chairmanship of the Union Finance Minister, serves as the apex inter‑agency forum for macroprudential oversight in India. Its membership includes the RBI Governor, the Chairpersons of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, the Finance Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, and the Chief Economic Adviser. The Council’s mandate spans (i) monitoring systemic risk across banking, insurance, pension, and securities markets; (ii) coordinating regulatory responses to emerging vulnerabilities; (iii) fostering financial sector development and inclusion; and (iv) overseeing the implementation of the G‑20‑endorsed “Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes”.

Operationally, the FSDC is supported by a Sub‑Committee chaired by the RBI Governor, which meets quarterly and produces the “Financial Stability Report” (FSR) — a semi‑annual publication that assesses stress‑test results, credit‑growth trends, and cross‑border spillovers. The 2023‑24 FSR highlighted three coordinated actions: (a) the activation of the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) at 0.5 % for scheduled commercial banks, effective from March 2024, based on a joint RBI‑SEBI assessment of credit‑to‑GDP gaps; (b) a synchronized tightening of sectoral exposure limits for real‑estate and infrastructure lending, with the RBI issuing a circular and SEBI aligning its Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) norms; (c) a joint communication protocol for “systemically important financial institutions” (SIFIs) that mandates simultaneous disclosure of leverage ratios, liquidity coverage ratios, and resolution‑plan status.

Beyond the FSDC, bilateral Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) institutionalise day‑to‑day coordination. The RBI‑SEBI MoU (2018, renewed 2022) covers information sharing on large exposures, market‑abuse surveillance, and the regulation of credit‑default‑swap (CDS) references. The RBI‑IRDAI MoU (2020) addresses insurance‑company investments in bank‑issued Tier‑2 bonds and the treatment of insurance‑linked securities in bank capital calculations. These MoUs enable real‑time data exchange, reducing the lag between a stress signal in one segment and a supervisory response in another.

A notable test of this architecture occurred during the 2022‑23 “NBFC liquidity stress” episode. The FSDC Sub‑Committee convened an emergency meeting in October 2022, leading to a coordinated package: the RBI extended the TLTRO‑NBFC window, SEBI relaxed the minimum subscription requirement for NBFC‑issued commercial paper, and the Ministry of Finance announced a partial credit guarantee scheme for AA‑rated NBFC bonds. The combined effect stabilized short‑term funding markets within six weeks, as reflected in the narrowing of the 91‑day commercial paper spread from 180 bps to 70 bps.

Examiners often probe the distinction between “micro‑prudential” (entity‑level) and “macro‑prudential” (system‑level) tools, and the institutional locus of each. The FSDC is the macro‑prudential coordinator; the RBI retains micro‑prudential authority over banks and NBFCs, while SEBI and IRDAI exercise micro‑prudential powers over their respective sectors. Understanding this division avoids the common error of attributing macro‑prudential decisions solely to the RBI.

  • Confusing the 72‑hour cooling‑off period with a 48‑hour “right to rescind” that applies only to certain credit‑card products.
  • Assuming the TLTRO tenor was one year; it was three years with a mandatory deployment condition.
  • Believing the FSDC can issue binding directives to regulators; it issues recommendations that regulators implement through their own statutory powers.
  • Thinking the Countercyclical Capital Buffer is automatically activated at a fixed credit‑to‑GDP threshold; activation requires a joint assessment and a formal FSDC Sub‑Committee decision.
  • Overlooking that the Digital Lending Guidelines apply to bank‑partnered fintech apps, not only to standalone NBFC lending apps.
  • Mixing up the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) with the Standing Liquidity Facility (SLF) for banks; the former was a pandemic‑specific, time‑bound window.
  • Remember that each advanced topic links a specific instrument to a defined transmission channel and a measurable outcome, which is the core of examiner expectations.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the Role of the RBI’s Market Operations

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with outstanding issuance hovering around 15‑17 % of GDP compared with over 100 % in advanced economies. This structural thinness weakens the interest‑rate channel because banks remain the dominant source of term finance for non‑financial firms. The RBI has therefore supplemented conventional policy‑rate changes with targeted market operations that directly affect corporate bond yields. The most prominent intervention was the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) launched in March 2020 as part of the COVID‑19 response. Under the CBPP the RBI purchased investment‑grade corporate bonds in the secondary market through a series of open‑market operations, initially capped at ₹1 lakh crore and later expanded to ₹2 lakh crore. Purchases were conducted via the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, ensuring price discovery and transparency.

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that the CBPP compressed the spread between AAA‑rated corporate bonds and the corresponding government‑security benchmark by 30‑45 basis points within three months of launch. The compression was most pronounced for issuers in the infrastructure and manufacturing sectors, which rely heavily on long‑tenor funding. Importantly, the programme also improved primary‑market issuance conditions: the average coupon on new AAA issuances fell by roughly 25 bps in the quarter following the first purchase window, and the volume of fresh issuance rose by 18 % year‑on‑year.

Beyond the CBPP, the RBI’s regular Open Market Operations (OMOs) and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) influence the corporate bond curve indirectly by shaping the short‑end of the risk‑free yield curve. When the RBI conducts variable‑rate repo auctions to inject durable liquidity, the resulting decline in the overnight call‑money rate pulls down the entire term structure, lowering the discount rate used in corporate bond valuation models. Conversely, variable‑rate reverse repo auctions absorb surplus liquidity, steepening the curve and raising corporate borrowing costs. The transmission is amplified when banks, flush with liquidity, increase their holdings of corporate bonds to meet the Held‑to‑Maturity (HTM) and Available‑for‑Sale (AFS) portfolio limits prescribed under Basel III.

A critical nuance is the interaction between the RBI’s market operations and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) regulatory framework. SEBI’s 2021 circular on “Enhanced Disclosure and Investor Protection for Corporate Bonds” mandated granular reporting of secondary‑market trades, which improved price transparency and allowed the RBI to calibrate purchase volumes more precisely. Moreover, the introduction of the “Corporate Bond Repo” segment on the NDS‑OM platform in 2022 enabled banks to repo corporate bonds with the RBI, creating a direct link between the policy corridor and corporate‑bond funding costs.

Examiners often test the distinction between “direct purchase” programmes (CBPP) and “indirect liquidity” tools (OMO, SDF). A correct answer should note that direct purchases target specific credit‑risk segments and can be tapered without altering the policy rate, whereas indirect tools work through the banking system and affect all asset classes simultaneously. Another frequent trap is to assume that the CBPP permanently lowered corporate‑bond yields; in practice, yields reverted once the purchase window closed and global risk‑off episodes (e.g., the 2022 US‑Fed tightening cycle) re‑asserted themselves.

RBI’s Sterilisation Operations and Management of Capital‑Flow Volatility

Large and volatile capital inflows pose a dual challenge: they appreciate the rupee, hurting export competitiveness, and they expand domestic liquidity, complicating inflation targeting. The RBI’s sterilisation toolkit is designed to neutralise the liquidity impact of foreign‑exchange interventions while allowing the exchange rate to adjust in a managed‑float framework. The principal instruments are the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), Cash Management Bills (CMBs), and variable‑rate reverse repo auctions under the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF).

The MSS was introduced in 2004 under Section 17 of the RBI Act, authorising the issuance of dated government securities solely for sterilisation purposes. Unlike regular dated securities, MSS bonds are not counted towards the government’s market borrowing programme and are held in a separate MSS account. During the 2008 global financial crisis the RBI issued ₹1.2 lakh crore of MSS securities to absorb the surge in dollar inflows that followed the US‑Fed’s quantitative easing. A second large‑scale deployment occurred in 2013‑14 after the “taper tantrum”, when portfolio outflows reversed and the RBI sold dollars, injecting rupee liquidity that was subsequently mopped up through ₹80 000 crore of MSS issuance.

Cash Management Bills, introduced in 2010, provide a flexible, short‑tenor (91‑day, 182‑day, 364‑day) instrument for fine‑tuning liquidity. CMBs are issued at a discount and redeemed at par, and they do not form part of the dated‑security stock. Their auction calendar is announced weekly, allowing the RBI to respond quickly to unexpected forex intervention volumes. In the first half of 2020‑21, when the RBI purchased over US$ 100 billion to prevent excessive rupee appreciation, it simultaneously issued CMBs worth ₹2.5 lakh crore, keeping the weighted average call‑rate within the policy corridor.

Variable‑rate reverse repo auctions (VRRR) have become the workhorse of daily sterilisation since the 2016‑17 monetary‑policy framework shift to a flexible inflation‑targeting regime. The RBI announces a notified amount and a cut‑off rate; banks bid for the amount they wish to park. The cut‑off rate typically aligns with the reverse repo rate, but the RBI can set a higher cut‑off to absorb excess liquidity more aggressively. During the 2022‑23 tightening cycle, the RBI conducted VRRRs of up to ₹4 lakh crore per fortnight, pushing the weighted average call‑rate close to the repo rate and signalling a firm stance.

A key analytical point is the “sterilisation cost” — the interest differential between the foreign‑exchange assets (largely US Treasury yields) and the rupee‑denominated sterilisation instruments. When US yields rise faster than Indian rates, the cost widens, eroding the RBI’s net interest income. The 2023‑24 Annual Report noted a sterilisation cost of approximately ₹12 000 crore for the year, reflecting the 300‑bps spread between the 10‑year US Treasury (4.5 %) and the 10‑year Indian G‑sec (7.5 %). Examiners may ask candidates to compute the approximate cost given a hypothetical inflow of US$ 10 billion and a 200‑bps spread; the correct approach is to multiply the rupee equivalent of the inflow by the spread and adjust for the average tenor of sterilisation instruments.

Worked Example: Sterilisation Cost Calculation
Assume the RBI intervenes to purchase US$ 10 billion when the exchange rate is ₹82/US$. The RBI sterilises the resulting rupee liquidity entirely through 91‑day Cash Management Bills yielding 6.5 % per annum, while the US Treasury 91‑day bill yields 4.5 %. Estimate the quarterly sterilisation cost in rupees.
Step 1: Convert the dollar inflow to rupees: 10 billion × 82 = ₹820 billion. Step 2: Compute the interest differential per annum: 6.5 % − 4.5 % = 2 % (200 bps). Step 3: Quarterly cost = ₹820 billion × 2 % ÷ 4 = ₹4.1 billion. Therefore, the RBI incurs an approximate sterilisation cost of ₹4.1 billion for the quarter.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “primary sterilisation instrument” in a given year, match the episode to the tool: 2008‑09 → MSS; 2013‑14 → MSS + CMB; 2020‑21 → CMB + VRRR; 2022‑23 → VRRR dominant. Memorise the chronological sequence rather than the legal provisions; the examiner tests application, not statute recall.

Resolution Regime for Systemically Important Financial Institutions: The SIFI Framework and Cross‑Border Coordination

The global financial crisis highlighted the “too‑big‑to‑fail” problem, prompting the Financial Stability Board (FSB) to develop the Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes. India transposed these principles through a layered approach: the RBI’s Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIB) framework (2014, revised 2020), the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) 2016 for non‑bank entities, and the 2021 Special Resolution Regime for large NBFCs. A D‑SIB is identified using a two‑step indicator‑based methodology — size, interconnectedness, substitutability, and complexity — with a bucketing system that imposes additional Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital surcharges ranging from 0.2 % to 0.8 % of risk‑weighted assets. As of March 2024, State Bank of India, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank occupy the highest bucket (0.8 %).

Resolution planning for D‑SIBs is governed by the RBI’s “Resolution Planning Guidelines” (2017, updated 2022). Each D‑SIB must submit a credible resolution plan (living will) annually, detailing strategies for rapid and orderly resolution — including bail‑in, bridge‑bank, and asset‑separation tools — without recourse to public funds. The RBI evaluates plans against the “Resolution Assessment Framework” and can impose corrective actions such as restrictions on dividend distribution or branch expansion if the plan is deemed non‑credible. The 2023 assessment found that two D‑SIBs had material gaps in cross‑border resolvability, prompting the RBI to engage with host‑country supervisors under the FSB’s “Cross‑Border Crisis Management” (CBCM) framework.

Cross‑border coordination is operationalised through the “Resolution Colleges” convened by the home supervisor (RBI for Indian banks) and attended by host supervisors from jurisdictions where the bank has material operations (e.g., the UK Prudential Regulation Authority for SBI’s London branch). The colleges meet at least annually and produce a “Joint Resolution Plan” that aligns bail‑in triggers, loss‑allocation rules, and communication protocols. India’s participation in the FSB’s “Resolvability Assessment Process” (RAP) since 2021 has led to concrete improvements: the RBI mandated that all D‑SIBs maintain a minimum “Total Loss‑Absorbing Capacity” (TLAC) of 18 % of RWA plus capital buffers, effective January 2025, aligning with the FSB’s TLAC standard.

For non‑bank SIFIs — large NBFCs and Housing Finance Companies (HFCs) — the 2021 Special Resolution Regime (SRR) created a dedicated “Resolution Corporation” under the RBI’s aegis, empowered to invoke “Resolution Tools” (transfer of assets, bridge institution, bail‑in) without invoking the IBC. The SRR applies to NBFCs with asset size above ₹50 000 crore or those designated by the RBI. The first test came in 2022 when a systemically important NBFC faced a liquidity crunch; the Resolution Corporation facilitated a structured sale of its loan book to a consortium of banks, preserving financial stability while imposing losses on subordinated creditors.

Examiners frequently confuse the D‑SIB capital surcharge with the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB). The surcharge is a permanent structural requirement based on systemic importance, whereas the CCyB is a time‑varying macroprudential tool activated by the FSDC Sub‑Committee. Another trap is to assume that the IBC applies to banks; it does not — bank resolution remains under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI’s resolution planning framework.

Macroprudential Tools Targeting Real‑Estate and Construction Sector Exposures

Real‑estate lending has historically been a source of systemic risk in India, contributing to the 2008‑09 NPA surge and the 2018‑19 NBFC stress episode. The RBI has deployed a suite of sector‑specific macroprudential instruments that go beyond generic capital‑adequacy norms. The key measures are: (i) sectoral exposure limits, (ii) loan‑to‑value (LTV) caps, (iii) risk‑weight adjustments, and (iv) provisioning overlays.

In 2015 the RBI issued a circular capping bank exposure to the commercial real‑estate (CRE) segment at 20 % of Tier 1 capital, with a sub‑limit of 10 % for residential real‑estate (RRE) projects. The 2020 revision tightened the CRE limit to 15 % and introduced a 10 % sub‑limit for “high‑risk” CRE (projects with construction‑stage funding exceeding 70 % of project cost). Breaches trigger supervisory action under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework.

LTV caps were first introduced for housing loans in 2010 (maximum 80 % for loans up to ₹30 lakh, 75 % above that). The 2021 circular extended LTV limits to CRE loans: 60 % for land acquisition, 70 % for construction finance, and 80 % for completed‑property loans. The caps are calibrated to the risk‑weight framework: loans exceeding the LTV threshold attract a 150 % risk weight instead of the standard 100 % (or 75 % for affordable housing). This risk‑weight escalation directly raises the capital charge, discouraging aggressive leverage.

Provisioning overlays add a forward‑looking dimension. The 2022 “Prudential Framework for Real‑Estate Exposure” required banks to maintain an additional 0.5 % provision on standard CRE assets and 1 % on standard RRE assets where the borrower’s debt‑service‑coverage ratio (DSCR) falls below 1.2. The overlay is reversible; it is released when the DSCR improves for two consecutive quarters. Early evidence from the 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report indicates that the overlay contributed to a 12 % decline in fresh CRE disbursements and a 7 % improvement in the weighted‑average DSCR of the CRE portfolio.

Coordination with the National Housing Bank (NHB) and the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs ensures that macroprudential tightening does not choke affordable‑housing supply. The 2023 “Affordable Housing Fund” (AHF) window, refinanced by the NHB at a concessional rate, is exempt from the LTV and provisioning overlays, provided the end‑use certification is verified. This carve‑out illustrates the policy trade‑off between financial stability and developmental objectives — a nuance examiners often probe through case‑study questions.

  • Confusing the D‑SIB capital surcharge (structural) with the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (cyclical).
  • Assuming the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code applies to bank resolution; it does not.
  • Treating the Market Stabilisation Scheme as a regular government borrowing instrument rather than a sterilisation‑only tool.
  • Believing the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme permanently lowered corporate‑bond yields; yields reverted after the purchase window closed.
  • Overlooking the LTV carve‑out for affordable‑housing loans under the NHB’s Affordable Housing Fund.
  • Mixing up the 91‑day Cash Management Bill tenor with the 364‑day Treasury Bill when computing sterilisation cost.
  • Attributing macroprudential decisions solely to the RBI; the FSDC Sub‑Committee is the formal decision‑making body.

These advanced topics illustrate how specific instruments, institutional mandates, and cross‑border arrangements interact to shape monetary‑policy transmission, financial‑stability outcomes, and examinable analytical frameworks.

RBI's Framework for Co‑Lending Models and Their Impact on Credit Flow

The Reserve Bank of India introduced the co‑lending model (CLM) in November 2020 through a circular that permitted banks to partner with registered Non‑Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) for joint origination and funding of priority‑sector loans. Under the framework, the bank and the NBFC share the credit risk in a pre‑agreed proportion — typically 80:20 or 70:30 — while the NBFC retains the customer interface, loan sourcing, and servicing responsibilities. The bank’s portion is funded at its marginal cost of funds, giving the NBFC access to cheaper liquidity than it could raise on its own balance sheet. The circular mandates a tripartite agreement, a common credit appraisal process, and a joint monitoring mechanism, with the bank acting as the lead lender for reporting to the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC).

Since inception, the model has been extended to housing finance companies (HFCs) and to loans under the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS). Data from the RBI’s Quarterly Statistics on Deposits and Credit show that co‑lending disbursements crossed ₹1.2 lakh crore by March 2024, with the bulk flowing to micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and affordable housing. The risk‑sharing arrangement improves the NBFC’s capital adequacy because only its share of the exposure counts toward its risk‑weighted assets, while the bank benefits from portfolio diversification and priority‑sector lending (PSL) fulfilment without expanding its branch network.

Supervisory safeguards include a cap on the NBFC’s exposure to a single borrower at 20 % of its Tier I capital, a requirement that the NBFC’s net‑owned fund (NOF) be at least ₹25 crore, and a prohibition on co‑lending for speculative real‑estate or capital‑market exposure. The RBI also conducts periodic thematic inspections focusing on the quality of the joint credit appraisal, the adequacy of the NBFC’s internal audit, and the timeliness of data submission to CRILC. In 2023 the RBI issued a clarificatory FAQ stating that the bank’s share of the loan must be classified as a standard asset unless the joint account turns non‑performing, at which point both partners recognise the NPA in their respective books according to the agreed risk‑sharing ratio.

Empirical studies by the Indian Institute of Banking and Finance (IIBF) indicate that co‑lending has reduced the average cost of funds for participating NBFCs by 120–150 basis points and shortened loan‑processing turnaround times by 30 %. However, challenges remain: operational integration of disparate IT systems, alignment of recovery procedures, and the risk of “evergreening” where the NBFC rolls over its share while the bank’s portion stays standard. The RBI’s 2024 discussion paper on “Enhancing the Co‑Lending Framework” proposes a standardised data‑exchange protocol, a common credit‑score threshold, and a mandatory independent audit of the joint portfolio every two years.

RBI's Regulation of Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms: Licensing, Prudential Norms, and Consumer Protection

The RBI brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending platforms under its regulatory perimeter in October 2017 through the “Non‑Banking Financial Company – Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017”. A P2P platform must obtain a Certificate of Registration (CoR) as an NBFC‑P2P, maintain a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹2 crore, and adhere to a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times its owned fund. The directions cap the aggregate exposure of a single lender across all P2P platforms at ₹50 lakh and the exposure of a single borrower at ₹10 lakh, with a per‑platform limit of ₹10 lakh for lenders and ₹5 lakh for borrowers.

Prudential norms require platforms to conduct KYC and credit‑assessment of borrowers using a board‑approved algorithm, to disclose the expected rate of return, default rates, and fees to lenders before each transaction, and to maintain an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank for fund flows. The platform cannot guarantee returns, provide credit enhancement, or cross‑sell insurance products. A quarterly return on the platform’s portfolio quality, including the 90‑day past‑due ratio, must be filed with the RBI. In 2021 the RBI tightened the framework by mandating a minimum 1 % provision on standard assets and a 25 % provision on sub‑standard assets, aligning P2P provisioning with the broader NBFC framework.

Consumer‑protection measures include a mandatory grievance‑redressal mechanism with a designated nodal officer, a 30‑day resolution timeline, and the right of lenders to approach the RBI Ombudsman for Digital Transactions if unsatisfied. Platforms must publish a “Fair Practices Code” on their website, detailing loan‑pricing methodology, data‑privacy safeguards, and the process for loan‑recovery. The RBI’s 2022 supervisory circular highlighted instances of platforms mis‑representing default rates and using aggressive recovery agents; it directed all NBFC‑P2Ps to appoint an independent compliance officer and to undergo an annual information‑system audit by a CERT‑IN empanelled auditor.

As of March 2024, 23 entities hold a valid CoR, with aggregate loan‑origination of approximately ₹18,500 crore during FY 2023‑24. The sector’s 90‑day delinquency ratio averaged 3.8 %, lower than the 5.2 % observed in the unregulated marketplace lending segment prior to regulation. The RBI’s 2023 discussion paper on “Digital Lending – Regulatory Approach” proposes extending the P2P framework to cover “loan‑service‑provider” models where a fintech originates loans on behalf of a bank or NBFC, thereby closing regulatory arbitrage.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s P2P lending regulations is correct? (a) Platforms may guarantee a minimum return to lenders. (b) The aggregate exposure limit for a lender across all platforms is ₹10 lakh. (c) Platforms must maintain a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹2 crore. (d) The leverage ratio for NBFC‑P2Ps is capped at 5 times owned fund.”
The correct answer is (c). The 2017 directions prescribe a minimum net‑owned fund of ₹2 crore for NBFC‑P2Ps. Statement (a) is prohibited — platforms cannot guarantee returns. Statement (b) misstates the lender cap, which is ₹50 lakh across all platforms, not ₹10 lakh. Statement (d) is incorrect; the leverage ratio ceiling is 2 times owned fund, not 5 times.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three key numeric thresholds for P2P: ₹2 crore NOF, ₹50 lakh lender aggregate cap, and 2× leverage. When a question mixes P2P limits with those for NBFC‑MFIs or small finance banks, isolate the P2P‑specific figures to avoid confusion.

RBI's Approach to Financial Benchmark Administration: Transition from MIBOR to FBIL and Alternative Reference Rates

Financial benchmarks underpin the pricing of derivatives, loans, and securities. Until 2015 the Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate (MIBOR), administered by the Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India (FIMMDA), served as the primary rupee interest‑rate benchmark. Concerns about the robustness of MIBOR — thin underlying transaction volume and susceptibility to manipulation — prompted the RBI to mandate the creation of an independent benchmark administrator. In 2015 the Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL) was incorporated as a joint venture of the RBI, banks, and market participants, and was recognised as a “Benchmark Administrator” under the RBI’s “Financial Benchmarks (Administration) Directions, 2019”.

FBIL now publishes the Mumbai Interbank Forward Offer Rate (MIFOR), the FBIL Overnight MIBOR, the FBIL 3‑Month and 6‑Month MIBOR, and the Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR)‑linked rupee benchmarks. The transition plan, announced in 2020, required all new rupee‑denominated floating‑rate loans and derivative contracts to reference FBIL‑administered rates by 31 December 2021, with legacy contracts encouraged to migrate by 30 June 2023. The RBI also directed banks to incorporate fallback clauses referencing the FBIL Overnight MIBOR or the RBI’s policy repo rate in case the primary benchmark becomes unavailable.

The shift aligns India with the global move from IBOR‑type benchmarks to transaction‑based, risk‑free rates. FBIL’s methodology uses a volume‑weighted average of eligible transactions in the unsecured overnight call money market (for the overnight rate) and the secured market repo segment (for term rates). The administrator follows the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) Principles for Financial Benchmarks, including governance by an independent oversight committee, transparent methodology documentation, and periodic external audits.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the RBI’s “Framework for Benchmark Administration” which mandates quarterly reporting of input data quality, conflict‑of‑interest policies, and business‑continuity arrangements. In 2022 the RBI imposed a penalty on a major bank for using a discontinued MIBOR tenor in its loan‑pricing engine after the migration deadline, underscoring the enforceability of the transition. The RBI’s 2023 consultation paper on “Alternative Reference Rates for Rupee Derivatives” explores the feasibility of a term‑SOFR‑linked rupee benchmark to support the development of a robust interest‑rate derivatives market.

RBI's Cybersecurity and IT Governance Framework for Regulated Entities: Guidelines, Audits, and Incident Reporting

The RBI’s “Cyber Security Framework in Banks” (2016) and its subsequent “Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” (2023) constitute the cornerstone of cyber‑resilience for scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and other regulated entities. The framework adopts a risk‑based approach: entities must classify information assets, conduct a comprehensive threat‑vulnerability assessment, and implement a layered defence comprising perimeter security, network segmentation, endpoint protection, and continuous monitoring through a Security Operations Centre (SOC).

Governance requirements include a board‑approved IT strategy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting to the board’s Risk Management Committee, and an annual IT‑risk appetite statement. The 2023 Master Direction mandates that banks conduct a “Cyber Crisis Management Plan” drill at least once a year, simulate ransomware and distributed‑denial‑of‑service (DDoS) attacks, and document lessons learned. Entities must also maintain a “Cyber Incident Reporting” mechanism: any material breach — defined as unauthorised access to critical systems, data exfiltration exceeding 1 GB, or service disruption beyond four hours — must be reported to the RBI’s Department of Supervision within six hours of detection, followed by a detailed root‑cause analysis within 30 days.

Audit obligations are stringent. Banks must engage a CERT‑IN empanelled auditor for an annual independent information‑system audit covering the entire IT estate, including cloud services, third‑party vendors, and mobile‑banking applications. The audit report, along with a management‑action‑plan, is submitted to the RBI within 45 days of the financial‑year end. The RBI also conducts thematic “Cyber Security Assessment” inspections, focusing on privileged‑access management, patch‑management latency, and the effectiveness of the SOC’s threat‑intelligence feeds.

In 2022 the RBI issued a circular on “Outsourcing of IT Services” requiring regulated entities to retain full accountability for outsourced functions, conduct due‑diligence on vendor cyber‑posture, and include “right‑to‑audit” clauses in contracts. The 2024 “Guidelines on Cloud Adoption” permit the use of public‑cloud infrastructure for non‑core workloads provided data‑localisation, encryption‑at‑rest, and contractual audit‑rights are satisfied. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report 2023‑24 noted a 27 % year‑on‑year increase in reported cyber incidents, with phishing and credential‑stuffing accounting for 62 % of cases, prompting the regulator to propose a mandatory “Cyber Hygiene Scorecard” for all supervised entities from FY 2025‑26.

RBI's Monetary Policy Transmission to the External Sector: Exchange Rate Pass‑Through, Trade Balance, and Capital Flows

Monetary‑policy actions influence the external sector through three primary channels: the exchange‑rate channel, the trade‑balance channel, and the capital‑flow channel. When the RBI raises the policy repo rate, the immediate effect is a widening of the interest‑rate differential vis‑à‑vis major reserve currencies, attracting short‑term portfolio inflows and exerting upward pressure on the rupee. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) estimates the short‑run exchange‑rate pass‑through (ERPT) to import prices at 0.35–0.45, implying that a 1 % appreciation reduces import‑price inflation by 35–45 basis points within two quarters.

The trade‑balance channel operates with a lag. A stronger rupee makes exports less competitive and imports cheaper, widening the trade deficit. However, the magnitude depends on the price elasticity of export and import demand. RBI studies using the “Export‑Import Elasticity Framework” find that a 1 % real effective exchange‑rate (REER) appreciation reduces export volumes by 0.6 % and increases import volumes by 0.4 % over a four‑quarter horizon, contributing to a modest deterioration in the current‑account balance.

Capital‑flow dynamics are shaped by the RBI’s sterilisation operations. When inflows surge, the RBI intervenes in the spot market, purchasing foreign currency and releasing rupee liquidity. To prevent excess liquidity from undermining the policy stance, the RBI conducts variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions, issues Cash Management Bills (CMBs), and uses the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS). The effectiveness of sterilisation is measured by the “sterilisation coefficient” — the ratio of net RBI absorption to gross intervention. Data for FY 2023‑24 show a coefficient of 0.78, indicating that roughly 78 % of intervention‑induced liquidity was mopped up.

The RBI’s “Flexible Inflation Targeting” framework explicitly recognises the exchange‑rate as a secondary consideration. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) minutes of 2023‑24 reveal that members weighed the risk of excessive rupee volatility against the primary inflation objective, opting for a calibrated rate‑hike path complemented by forward guidance on liquidity normalisation. The 2024 “External Sector Report” highlights that the rupee’s REER remained within a ±5 % band around its 36‑month average, suggesting that the combined policy‑rate and intervention toolkit has contained disorderly movements while allowing the exchange rate to act as a shock absorber.

  • Confusing the co‑lending risk‑sharing ratio (bank:NBFC) with the priority‑sector lending sub‑target for MSMEs.
  • Assuming P2P platforms can hold borrower funds in their own accounts; regulations require an escrow account with a scheduled commercial bank.
  • Believing the MIBOR transition deadline applied only to new contracts; legacy contracts were also expected to migrate by June 2023.
  • Thinking the RBI’s cyber‑incident reporting window is 24 hours; the Master Direction mandates a six‑hour initial report for material breaches.
  • Overlooking that the sterilisation coefficient measures the proportion of intervention liquidity absorbed, not the total volume of foreign‑exchange reserves.
  • Treating the exchange‑rate pass‑through coefficient as a fixed constant; it varies with the degree of invoice‑currency pricing and the share of imported inputs in domestic production.
  • These traps highlight the need for precise regulatory knowledge and careful reading of RBI circulars.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing of IT Services and Cyber Resilience Framework

The Reserve Bank of India issued a comprehensive circular in April 2022 on “Outsourcing of IT Services” that made regulated entities (REs) fully accountable for any outsourced function. The circular mandates that REs conduct due‑diligence on the vendor’s cyber‑posture, include a “right‑to‑audit” clause in every contract, and retain the ability to terminate the arrangement without jeopardising critical operations. In 2024 the RBI followed up with “Guidelines on Cloud Adoption” permitting the use of public‑cloud infrastructure for non‑core workloads provided data‑localisation, encryption‑at‑rest, and contractual audit‑rights are satisfied. Both documents stress that the board of the RE remains responsible for the overall risk management framework, including vendor concentration risk and exit‑strategy planning.

The 2022 circular also introduced a mandatory “Cyber Hygiene Scorecard” to be reported annually from FY 2025‑26. The scorecard captures metrics such as patch‑management latency, privileged‑access management maturity, and the effectiveness of the Security Operations Centre’s threat‑intelligence feeds. The RBI’s Financial Stability Report 2023‑24 highlighted a 27 % year‑on‑year rise in reported cyber incidents, with phishing and credential‑stuffing accounting for 62 % of cases. This data drove the regulator to propose a supervisory escalation matrix where REs scoring below a defined threshold face enhanced monitoring, mandatory third‑party penetration testing, and possible restrictions on new digital product launches.

Operationally, REs must maintain an updated inventory of all outsourced IT assets, classify them by criticality, and map each to a business‑continuity plan. The circular requires a minimum of quarterly vendor‑risk reviews and an annual independent audit of the vendor’s control environment. Contracts must specify service‑level agreements (SLAs) for incident response times — typically four hours for critical incidents — and define clear escalation paths to the RE’s chief information security officer (CISO). The RBI also expects REs to conduct tabletop exercises simulating vendor failure scenarios at least once a year.

From a supervisory perspective, the RBI’s Department of Supervision (DoS) evaluates compliance through on‑site inspections and off‑site returns. The 2024 cloud guidelines add a requirement that any data processed in a public cloud must reside in India, and that encryption keys remain under the RE’s control. The regulator has signalled that non‑compliance will attract penalties under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and may trigger the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for banks. The combined effect of these measures is to shift the industry from a reactive “incident‑response” posture to a proactive “cyber‑resilience” culture.

For aspirants, the key take‑aways are: (i) accountability cannot be outsourced; (ii) the right‑to‑audit clause is non‑negotiable; (iii) the Cyber Hygiene Scorecard will become a supervisory benchmark from FY 2025‑26; and (iv) cloud adoption is allowed only under strict data‑localisation and key‑management conditions. These points frequently appear in case‑study questions on operational risk and in descriptive answers on the evolving regulatory architecture.

Retail Central Bank Digital Currency Pilot: Architecture, Offline Capability, and UPI Interoperability

The RBI launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑R) pilot in December 2022 across four cities — Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru, and Bhubaneswar — expanding to nine additional cities by March 2024. The pilot uses a two‑tier architecture: the RBI issues the digital rupee to participating banks (the “issuance layer”), which then distribute it to end‑users through their existing mobile‑banking apps (the “distribution layer”). The ledger is a permissioned distributed‑ledger technology (DLT) platform operated by the RBI, with consensus achieved through a practical Byzantine Fault Tolerance (pBFT) protocol among a set of validator nodes run by the central bank and selected banks.

A distinguishing feature of the retail pilot is its offline‑payment capability. The RBI specified a “dual‑mode” design where the CBDC wallet can execute proximity payments via Near‑Field Communication (NFC) or QR‑code scanning without an active internet connection, relying on a secure element in the user’s device to store a limited‑value offline balance. The offline limit is set at ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000 cumulative per day, after which the wallet must reconnect to the online ledger for settlement and balance refresh. This design addresses financial‑inclusion concerns in areas with intermittent connectivity.

Interoperability with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) was demonstrated in the pilot’s second phase. Users can scan a UPI QR code from a CBDC wallet and the transaction is routed through the NPCI’s UPI switch, with the CBDC ledger settling the net position between the issuing bank and the acquiring bank in near‑real time. The settlement finality is achieved within the same T+0 cycle, leveraging the existing Real‑Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) infrastructure for inter‑bank obligations. The RBI has mandated that all participating banks support both CBDC‑R and UPI QR codes in their merchant acquisition terminals.

From a monetary‑policy perspective, the retail CBDC provides the RBI with a direct transmission channel to household liquidity. Because the digital rupee is a liability of the central bank, it does not create commercial‑bank credit risk, and its velocity can be observed in real time. The pilot’s data shows an average daily transaction volume of 1.2 million and a value of ₹350 crore by end‑March 2024, with a median transaction size of ₹250. The RBI has indicated that a full‑scale rollout will be calibrated based on the pilot’s impact on currency‑in‑circulation, bank deposit substitution, and the effectiveness of offline limits in preventing double‑spending.

Exam‑relevant nuances include: (i) the two‑tier issuance‑distribution model mirrors the existing currency‑distribution framework; (ii) offline limits are a risk‑mitigation tool, not a permanent feature; (iii) UPI interoperability is achieved at the QR‑code level, not by merging the two ledgers; and (iv) the pilot’s legal basis is the RBI Act, 1934, amended by the Finance Act, 2022, which explicitly recognises “digital rupee” as legal tender. Questions often test the distinction between wholesale and retail CBDC, the role of the secure element, and the settlement finality mechanism.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the RBI’s retail CBDC pilot achieves settlement finality for a UPI‑QR transaction initiated from a CBDC wallet, and why the offline‑payment limit is necessary.”
The transaction flows from the payer’s CBDC wallet to the merchant’s UPI QR code. The NPCI UPI switch validates the QR, forwards the payment request to the acquiring bank, which then sends a settlement instruction to the RBI’s CBDC ledger. The ledger, operating on a permissioned pBFT consensus, debits the issuing bank’s CBDC account and credits the acquiring bank’s CBDC account in the same T+0 cycle, achieving finality. The offline limit (₹2,000 per transaction, ₹10,000 daily) caps exposure to double‑spending when the wallet is disconnected from the ledger; once the limit is reached, the wallet must go online to synchronise balances, ensuring the central bank’s ledger remains the single source of truth.
Exam‑day strategy
When a CBDC question appears, first identify the tier (wholesale vs retail) and the ledger type (permissioned DLT vs centralised). Then map the transaction flow: wallet → QR/UPI → switch → ledger → settlement. Remember the offline caps and the legal tender status under the amended RBI Act. Use the two‑tier architecture diagram mentally to structure a concise answer.

Regulation of Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms: Escrow Mechanism, Capital Adequacy, and Consumer Protection

The RBI’s “Master Direction – Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017” established the regulatory perimeter for P2P platforms, later amended in 2021 to tighten prudential norms. A P2P platform must be a non‑banking financial company (NBFC) registered with the RBI, with a minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore. The platform cannot hold borrower funds in its own accounts; all funds must flow through an escrow account maintained with a scheduled commercial bank. The escrow arrangement ensures that the platform acts only as a matchmaker, eliminating the risk of misappropriation.

Capital adequacy for P2P NBFCs is governed by a leverage ratio: the total outstanding loans facilitated through the platform cannot exceed 1.5 times the NOF. This cap limits the platform’s ability to scale aggressively without proportionate equity. Additionally, the platform must maintain a minimum capital‑to‑risk‑weighted‑assets ratio (CRAR) of 15 %, aligned with the broader NBFC framework. The RBI also requires a board‑approved “Fair Practices Code” covering transparent disclosure of interest rates, fees, and recovery procedures.

Consumer‑protection provisions mandate that the platform provide a standardised Key Fact Statement (KFS) to every borrower before loan origination, detailing the annualised percentage rate (APR), processing charges, and prepayment penalties. Grievance redressal must be resolved within 30 days, with an escalation matrix to the RBI’s Ombudsman Scheme for Non‑Banking Financial Companies. The platform is prohibited from offering guaranteed returns or using coercive recovery tactics. Data‑privacy obligations follow the Information Technology Act, 2000, and the platform must obtain explicit consent before sharing borrower data with lenders.

On the lender side, the RBI caps individual exposure to a single borrower at ₹50,000 across all P2P platforms, and aggregate exposure of a lender across all borrowers at ₹10 lakh. These limits aim to prevent concentration risk and protect retail lenders from excessive loss. The platform must report monthly transaction data to the RBI’s Department of Non‑Banking Supervision, including loan‑level details, default rates, and recovery metrics. The 2021 amendment introduced a requirement for platforms to appoint a Chief Compliance Officer (CCO) and to conduct an annual independent audit of the escrow mechanism.

For examination purposes, remember: (i) P2P platforms are NBFC‑P2P, not banks; (ii) escrow with a scheduled commercial bank is mandatory; (iii) leverage ratio 1.5× NOF and CRAR 15 %; (iv) borrower‑level exposure cap ₹50,000, lender‑level cap ₹10 lakh; (v) KFS, 30‑day grievance window, and Ombudsman escalation. Questions often test the distinction between P2P and marketplace lending, the role of the escrow account, and the applicability of the SARFAESI Act (which does not apply to P2P loans).

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Agricultural Credit Market through Priority Sector Lending and the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund

The RBI’s monetary policy influences agricultural credit primarily via the priority‑sector lending (PSL) framework. Banks are required to allocate 18 % of their Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to the agriculture sector, with a sub‑target of 8 % for small and marginal farmers. When the policy repo rate changes, the marginal cost of funds for banks shifts, altering the pricing of PSL loans. However, the transmission is mediated by the Interest Subvention Scheme (ISS), which provides a 2 % interest subvention on short‑term crop loans up to ₹3 lakh, and an additional 3 % subvention for prompt repayment, effectively capping the farmer’s effective rate at 4 % per annum for timely borrowers.

The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), managed by NABARD, acts as a refinancing window for banks that extend long‑term loans for rural infrastructure — irrigation, warehousing, and rural roads. RIDF loans are priced at a fixed spread over the prevailing repo rate, typically 1.5 % to 2 %. When the RBI eases policy, the RIDF lending rate declines, lowering the cost of long‑term capital for agricultural projects. Conversely, a tightening cycle raises RIDF rates, but the impact is partially offset by the government’s budgetary allocation to the fund, which can be increased to maintain flow.

The Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme, linked to the PSL target, provides a revolving credit facility with a drawing limit based on the scale of finance for the crop. The interest rate on KCC is benchmarked to the bank’s one‑year MCLR (or external benchmark after 2019) plus a spread. Monetary‑policy rate cuts transmit quickly to KCC rates because most banks have adopted the external benchmark (repo‑linked) for new PSL loans. Empirical studies by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research estimate a pass‑through of 0.65 % to KCC rates within two quarters of a 100‑basis‑point repo change.

Non‑performing assets in the agriculture portfolio remain a concern. The RBI’s “Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets” applies to farm loans, but the sector benefits from the “One‑Time Settlement” (OTS) scheme and the “Farm Loan Waiver” announcements by state governments, which can distort credit discipline. The RBI has urged banks to use the “Asset Classification and Provisioning” norms consistently and to leverage the “Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises” (CGTMSE) for allied activities such as dairy and poultry, which are classified under agriculture.

Key points for answers: (i) PSL target 18 % ANBC, sub‑target 8 % for small/marginal farmers; (ii) ISS caps effective farmer rate at 4 % for prompt repayment; (iii) RIDF refinances long‑term rural infrastructure at repo‑linked rates; (iv) KCC rates benchmarked to external benchmark, pass‑through ≈ 0.65; (v) stressed‑asset resolution uses OTS and CGTMSE, but loan waivers create moral hazard. Questions may ask to trace the transmission chain from repo → MCLR/external benchmark → KCC/ISS → farmer cost, and to evaluate the role of RIDF in smoothing long‑term credit.

  • Confusing the P2P platform’s escrow requirement with a bank’s own escrow for loan disbursement; the regulation mandates a scheduled commercial bank escrow, not an internal account.
  • Assuming the retail CBDC offline limit applies to the wholesale pilot; the wholesale pilot has no offline mode and settles only on the DLT ledger.
  • Treating the Cyber Hygiene Scorecard as a voluntary self‑assessment; from FY 2025‑26 it becomes a mandatory supervisory return with escalation consequences.
  • Believing the Interest Subvention Scheme covers all agricultural loans; it applies only to short‑term crop loans up to ₹3 lakh and requires prompt repayment for the additional 3 % benefit.
  • Overlooking that the RIDF lending rate is a fixed spread over the repo rate, not a direct pass‑through of the policy rate; budgetary top‑ups can decouple the two.
  • Thinking the SARFAESI Act can be invoked for P2P loan recovery; the Act applies only to secured creditors of banks and financial institutions, not to P2P platforms.
  • Assuming the Kisan Credit Card interest rate is fixed by the RBI; it is benchmarked to the bank’s external benchmark rate plus a spread, so monetary‑policy changes transmit through the benchmark.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the Primary Dealer System

The corporate bond market in India remains shallow relative to bank credit, but it is the principal channel through which large, rated firms access long‑term funds without intermediation. The Reserve Bank influences this market through three linked mechanisms: the policy repo rate, the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) that sets the short‑term cost of funds for primary dealers, and the statutory liquidity ratio (SLR) that determines banks’ appetite for holding government securities versus corporate paper. Primary dealers (PDs) — currently 22 entities — are mandated to bid at every government securities auction and to provide two‑way quotes in the secondary market. Their borrowing cost is anchored to the weighted average call rate (WACR), which tracks the repo rate closely. When the RBI cuts the repo rate, the WACR falls, reducing PDs’ funding cost and narrowing the spread they demand on corporate bonds. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research shows a pass‑through of roughly 0.45 percentage points to the 10‑year AAA corporate bond yield within two quarters of a 100‑basis‑point repo move, compared with 0.65 percentage points for the 10‑year G‑sec yield.

A second transmission leg operates through banks’ balance sheets. Lower repo rates reduce the marginal cost of funds based lending rate (MCLR) and, for banks that have adopted the external benchmark, the repo‑linked lending rate (RLLR). Cheaper bank credit improves the credit quality of corporate issuers, which in turn compresses credit spreads on their bonds. However, the effect is asymmetric: during tightening cycles, spreads widen faster than they compress during easing because investors demand a higher risk premium for potential downgrades. The RBI’s “Market Making Scheme” for corporate bonds, introduced in 2021, obliges designated market makers to quote firm bids and offers for a minimum size, improving liquidity and making the spread more responsive to policy signals.

Third, the SLR requirement creates a portfolio substitution effect. Banks must hold a prescribed share of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) in approved securities, predominantly government bonds. When the repo rate falls, the yield on government securities declines, making them less attractive relative to corporate bonds of comparable maturity. Banks therefore rebalance toward corporate paper, pushing up demand and lowering yields. The RBI’s periodic “Open Market Operations (OMO) Purchase” of government securities injects durable liquidity, reinforcing the portfolio shift. Conversely, OMO sales drain liquidity and can reverse the flow.

Key frictions remain. The corporate bond market suffers from low retail participation, fragmented settlement (T+1 for government securities versus T+2 for corporate bonds), and a limited repo market for corporate paper. The RBI’s 2023 “Corporate Bond Repo” framework, which allows repos against listed corporate bonds with a minimum rating of AA, aims to deepen the collateral pool and improve price discovery. Until the repo market for corporate bonds attains critical mass, the transmission from repo to corporate yields will remain incomplete, especially for lower‑rated issuers.

RBI’s Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Services for Banks: Operational Resilience and Supervisory Expectations

In April 2023 the RBI issued a comprehensive master direction on outsourcing of financial services by regulated entities (REs), superseding the 2017 circular and extending its scope to cloud‑based arrangements. The direction classifies outsourcing into “material” and “non‑material” based on the potential impact on the RE’s ability to conduct its business, meet regulatory obligations, or protect customer data. Material outsourcing includes core banking functions, payment processing, credit underwriting, and any activity that involves access to customer‑identifiable information. For each material arrangement, the RE must obtain prior approval from its board, conduct a risk assessment covering concentration, legal, and exit‑strategy risks, and maintain a register that is subject to supervisory review.

Cloud services receive a dedicated annex.
