The RBI requires REs to adopt a “shared responsibility model” in which the cloud service provider (CSP) is responsible for the security of the cloud infrastructure, while the RE retains accountability for data governance, encryption key management, and incident response. CSPs must be empaneled by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In) and comply with the MeitY “Cloud Services Empanelment” criteria. Data localisation provisions mandate that all payment‑system data and any data classified as “critical” under the Personal Data Protection Bill (as drafted) reside on servers located in India. The direction also obliges REs to conduct annual penetration testing of the cloud environment and to retain audit logs for a minimum of five years.

Supervisory expectations are articulated through the “Outsourcing Risk Management Framework” (ORMF). The ORMF requires REs to establish a dedicated outsourcing governance committee, chaired by a senior executive, that reports quarterly to the board. The committee must monitor service‑level agreements (SLAs), track key risk indicators (KRIs) such as downtime, data‑breach incidents, and vendor financial health, and ensure that exit plans are tested at least once every two years. The RBI’s on‑site inspection checklist now includes verification of the outsourcing register, evidence of board‑level approvals, and the results of the most recent cloud‑security audit.

Non‑compliance attracts graduated supervisory actions ranging from a written warning to restriction on new outsourcing arrangements, and in severe cases, the imposition of a monetary penalty under Section 47A of the Banking Regulation Act. The 2023 direction also aligns with the Basel Committee’s “Principles for Outsourcing” and the Financial Stability Board’s “Guidance on Outsourcing and Third‑Party Risk Management”, ensuring that Indian banks’ practices are comparable with global standards.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s 2023 outsourcing master direction is correct? (a) Only core banking functions are classified as material outsourcing. (b) Cloud service providers must be empaneled by CERT‑In and comply with MeitY criteria. (c) Data localisation applies only to payment‑system data. (d) Exit plans need to be tested only once in five years.”
Correct answer: (b). The direction explicitly requires CSPs to be CERT‑In empaneled and to meet MeitY empanelment criteria. Statement (a) is wrong because material outsourcing also covers payment processing, credit underwriting, and any activity with access to customer‑identifiable information. Statement (c) is incomplete; localisation also covers data classified as critical under the draft Personal Data Protection Bill. Statement (d) misstates the frequency — exit plans must be tested at least once every two years, not five.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific RBI circular (e.g., “April 2023 master direction on outsourcing”), focus on the three pillars: classification (material vs non‑material), cloud‑specific annex (CERT‑In, MeitY, localisation), and supervisory framework (ORMF, board committee, testing frequency). Eliminate options that narrow the scope (only core banking) or extend timelines (five‑year exit test). The RBI’s language is precise — “at least once every two years” and “prior board approval” are recurring keywords.

External Commercial Borrowing Framework: Monetary Policy Transmission and Hedging Requirements

The External Commercial Borrowing (ECB) framework governs Indian entities’ access to foreign currency loans, bonds, and trade credits. The RBI, in consultation with the Ministry of Finance, sets the “all‑in‑cost” ceiling — the maximum permissible spread over the relevant benchmark (typically 6‑month LIBOR/SOFR or the USD Secured Overnight Financing Rate) — which is revised periodically to reflect global monetary conditions. As of the latest revision (January 2024), the ceiling for ECBs with a maturity of three to five years stands at 450 basis points over the benchmark, while longer‑tenor borrowings (above five years) are allowed a ceiling of 500 basis points. These ceilings act as a transmission channel: when the US Federal Reserve raises rates, the benchmark rises, and the all‑in‑cost ceiling rises in tandem, preserving the spread but increasing the absolute cost for Indian borrowers.

Hedging requirements constitute the second transmission leg. The RBI mandates that entities with ECB exposure exceeding USD 20 million (or equivalent) must hedge at least 70 % of their principal and interest cash flows through forward contracts, options, or cross‑currency swaps. The hedge ratio is monitored quarterly through the “ECB‑2” return. When domestic interest rates fall relative to foreign rates, the forward premium on the rupee narrows, reducing the cost of hedging and making ECBs relatively cheaper. Conversely, a widening interest‑rate differential increases the forward premium, raising the effective cost of foreign borrowing and encouraging a shift toward rupee‑denominated debt.

The framework also distinguishes between “automatic route” and “approval route” ECBs. Automatic‑route borrowings — up to USD 750 million per financial year for eligible corporates — require only post‑facto reporting, whereas approval‑route borrowings (e.g., for infrastructure projects, start‑ups, or entities with existing high leverage) need prior RBI clearance. The approval route allows the RBI to impose additional conditions such as a higher hedge ratio, a lower all‑in‑cost ceiling, or a mandatory rupee‑denominated tranche, thereby fine‑tuning the transmission of global monetary conditions to specific sectors.

Recent developments include the introduction of the “Green ECB” category (2022) which permits a 25‑basis‑point concession on the all‑in‑cost ceiling for borrowings earmarked for climate‑friendly projects, provided the issuer obtains a second‑party opinion aligned with the International Capital Market Association’s Green Bond Principles. The RBI also liberalised the “Trade Credit” window in 2023, extending the maximum tenor for supplier’s credit from one year to three years for capital goods imports, with a corresponding hedge requirement of 50 %. These measures aim to diversify funding sources while keeping the overall external debt sustainability indicators — debt‑to‑GDP, debt‑service‑to‑exports, and short‑term‑debt‑to‑reserves — within the thresholds prescribed by the IMF’s Debt Sustainability Framework.

Digital Lending Guidelines 2022: Lending Service Providers, Data Governance, and the Role of the Account Aggregator

The RBI’s “Guidelines on Digital Lending” issued in September 2022 (updated March 2023) constitute the first comprehensive regulatory architecture for algorithm‑driven credit delivery. The guidelines define a “Lending Service Provider” (LSP) as any entity — including fintech platforms, non‑bank financial companies, and banks’ own digital arms — that performs one or more of the following functions on behalf of a regulated entity (RE): customer acquisition, credit underwriting, loan disbursement, collection, or recovery. Every LSP must be onboarded through a written agreement that specifies data‑sharing protocols, liability allocation, and audit rights. The RE remains the “principal” and is fully accountable for the LSP’s conduct, including compliance with the Fair Practices Code, the Interest Rate Risk in the Banking Book (IRRBB) norms, and the KYC/AML framework.

Data governance is the cornerstone. The guidelines prohibit LSPs from storing borrowers’ personal data beyond the minimum period necessary for the contracted function. All data must be encrypted at rest and in transit, and access logs must be retained for five years. Crucially, the guidelines mandate the use of the Account Aggregator (AA) framework for consent‑based sharing of financial data. An AA, licensed by the RBI, acts as a fiduciary that fetches a borrower’s bank statements, GST returns, and credit‑bureau reports only after explicit, revocable consent. The RE must integrate with at least one AA before launching a digital lending product, ensuring that the borrower’s data footprint is auditable and that the “data minimisation” principle is observed.

Algorithmic transparency requirements obligate REs to document the credit‑scoring model’s variables, weightages, and validation results. Any model change that materially alters the approval rate or pricing must be approved by the RE’s board risk committee and reported to the RBI within 30 days. The guidelines also introduce a “cooling‑off” period of 30 days for borrowers who have been denied credit, during which the RE cannot re‑approach the same borrower with a revised offer unless a material change in the borrower’s profile is documented.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the “Digital Lending Return” (DLR), a quarterly filing that captures portfolio‑level metrics: number of loans originated via LSPs, average ticket size, NPA ratio by LSP, and incidence of customer complaints. The RBI’s 2023 supervisory circular on “Outsourcing and Cloud Services” (discussed earlier) applies mutatis mutandis to LSPs that host their platforms on cloud infrastructure, reinforcing the shared‑responsibility model. Penalties for non‑compliance include restriction on new LSP onboarding, monetary fines under Section 47A, and, in egregious cases, revocation of the RE’s licence to conduct digital lending.

  • Confusing the all‑in‑cost ceiling for ECBs with the domestic MCLR spread; the ceiling is a spread over an external benchmark (SOFR/LIBOR), not over the repo rate.
  • Assuming that the 70 % hedge requirement applies to all ECB borrowers; it triggers only when the outstanding ECB exposure exceeds USD 20 million.
  • Believing that LSPs can independently store borrower data indefinitely; the guidelines require data minimisation and a maximum retention period tied to the contracted function.
  • Overlooking that the Account Aggregator framework is mandatory for digital lending, not optional; REs must integrate with at least one licensed AA before product launch.
  • Thinking that the cooling‑off period applies only to rejected applications; it also applies when a borrower withdraws consent during the AA‑mediated data fetch.
  • Misreading the outsourcing master direction as applying only to banks; it covers all regulated entities, including NBFCs, payment system operators, and housing finance companies.
  • The RBI’s 2023 outsourcing direction requires exit‑plan testing at least once every two years, not once in five years.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Rural Credit Market through Priority Sector Lending and the Kisan Credit Card Scheme

Priority Sector Lending Targets and Sub‑Targets

The Reserve Bank of India mandates that scheduled commercial banks allocate 40 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors, with a sub‑target of 18 % for agriculture (including 8 % for small and marginal farmers). These targets are reviewed annually and were last revised in the Master Direction – Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification (2023). The RBI monitors compliance through quarterly returns and imposes penal interest on shortfalls, which creates a direct link between monetary policy stance and the quantum of credit flowing to rural borrowers.

Kisan Credit Card (KCC) Scheme Evolution

Launched in 1998 on the recommendations of the R. V. Gupta Committee, the KCC provides short‑term credit for cultivation, post‑harvest expenses, and consumption needs. The scheme was revamped in 2020: the interest subvention was raised to 2 % per annum for loans up to ₹3 lakh, and an additional 3 % prompt‑repayment incentive was introduced, effectively bringing the farmer’s cost to 4 % per annum. In 2022 the RBI extended KCC coverage to animal husbandry and fisheries, and allowed digital onboarding through the Account Aggregator framework, reducing turnaround time from 15 days to 48 hours.

Transmission Mechanism

When the RBI eases the policy repo rate, banks’ marginal cost of funds falls. Because PSL quotas are binding, banks cannot simply redirect the cheaper funds to corporate borrowers; they must deploy a portion to agriculture. The KCC’s interest‑subvention formula is linked to the bank’s base rate (now the external benchmark), so a repo‑rate cut translates almost one‑for‑one into lower KCC rates. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (2023) shows a 25 bps repo cut raises KCC disbursements by 3‑4 % within two quarters, confirming a strong interest‑rate channel in the rural segment.

Data‑Driven Monitoring

The RBI’s “Priority Sector Lending – Quarterly Data” portal publishes bank‑wise disbursement, outstanding, and NPA ratios for agriculture. The 2023 Financial Stability Report highlighted that the agriculture NPA ratio fell from 9.8 % (March 2021) to 7.2 % (March 2023), coinciding with the repo‑rate easing cycle of 2020‑21 and the KCC subvention enhancement. This granular data enables the MPC to assess the real‑economy impact of its decisions beyond aggregate credit growth.

RBI's Regulatory Framework for Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms and Account Aggregator Integration

Licensing and Capital Requirements

The RBI issued the “Master Direction – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017” and updated it in 2021. A P2P platform must obtain a Certificate of Registration, maintain a minimum net owned fund of ₹2 crore, and adhere to a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times its owned fund. The platform’s exposure to a single borrower is capped at ₹50 lakh and to a single lender at ₹10 lakh, limiting concentration risk.

Governance and Conduct Standards

Platforms are required to appoint a Chief Compliance Officer, conduct annual independent audits of their credit‑scoring algorithms, and publish a “Fair Practices Code” on their website. The 2021 amendment mandated that all loan agreements be executed electronically with timestamped audit trails, and that platforms maintain a grievance redressal mechanism with a 30‑day resolution window.

Account Aggregator (AA) Integration

Following the Digital Lending Guidelines (September 2022), every P2P platform must integrate with at least one RBI‑licensed Account Aggregator before launching a new product. The AA fetches the borrower’s bank statements, GST returns, and credit‑bureau reports only after explicit, revocable consent. This consent‑based data pull replaces the earlier practice of screen‑scraping and ensures compliance with the “data minimisation” principle. The platform must log every AA‑mediated data request and retain the logs for five years.

Supervisory Reporting and Penalties

Registered P2P platforms file a quarterly “P2P Lending Return” capturing loan‑origination volume, average ticket size, NPA ratio by vintage, and customer‑complaint metrics. Non‑compliance attracts monetary penalties under Section 47A of the RBI Act, restriction on new borrower onboarding, and, in severe cases, cancellation of the registration certificate. The 2023 supervisory circular on “Outsourcing and Cloud Services” extends the shared‑responsibility model to P2P platforms that host their technology stack on cloud infrastructure.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s P2P lending framework is correct? (a) Platforms may store borrower data indefinitely for analytics. (b) The leverage ratio ceiling is 5 times owned fund. (c) Integration with an Account Aggregator is optional. (d) The single‑borrower exposure limit is ₹50 lakh.”
The correct answer is (d). The 2021 Master Direction caps a platform’s exposure to any single borrower at ₹50 lakh. Statement (a) violates the data‑minimisation rule; (b) misstates the leverage ceiling (2 times, not 5); (c) is false because AA integration has been mandatory since the 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes P2P norms with digital‑lending rules, isolate the regulatory source: the 2017/2021 Master Direction governs licensing, capital, and exposure limits; the 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines govern AA integration, data retention, and cooling‑off periods. Tag each statement to its source before deciding.

The RBI's Framework for Managing Systemic Risk from Interconnectedness: Network Analysis, Contagion Metrics, and the Systemic Risk Survey

Interbank Network Mapping

The RBI’s Financial Stability Report (FSR) publishes a half‑yearly “Interbank Exposure Matrix” that captures bilateral lending, borrowing, and derivative positions among scheduled commercial banks, primary dealers, and large NBFCs. Since the 2019 FSR, the RBI has applied the DebtRank algorithm to estimate the systemic impact of a hypothetical default by each node. The 2023 FSR reported that the top five banks accounted for 62 % of total interbank assets, and a simultaneous shock to their capital buffers could raise the system‑wide capital shortfall by 1.8 % of risk‑weighted assets.

Contagion Metrics and Stress Scenarios

Beyond DebtRank, the RBI monitors the “Co‑Risk” measure (pairwise conditional probability of distress) and the “Systemic Expected Shortfall” (SES) for each institution. The 2022 macro‑stress test incorporated a “twin‑shock” scenario: a 300 bps rise in the repo rate combined with a 15 % depreciation of the rupee. Results showed that the SES for the banking sector increased from 0.9 % to 2.4 % of GDP, prompting the MPC to flag liquidity‑risk buffers in its policy statement.

Systemic Risk Survey (SRS)

Since 2015 the RBI conducts a quarterly Systemic Risk Survey covering banks, insurers, mutual funds, and market infrastructure institutions. Respondents rank risks on a five‑point scale. The March 2024 SRS highlighted “cyber‑risk” and “climate‑transition risk” as the top two emerging threats, each scoring above 4.0 for the first time. The survey feeds directly into the RBI’s Macroprudential Policy Committee’s deliberations on countercyclical capital buffers and sectoral capital surcharges.

Policy Tools Deployed

Based on network analysis, the RBI has calibrated the “Large Exposure Framework” (2023) to limit a bank’s exposure to a single counterparty group to 20 % of Tier‑1 capital, with an additional 5 % for systemically important counterparties. The “Countercyclical Capital Buffer” (CCyB) was activated at 0.5 % in April 2023 after the SRS indicated a credit‑cycle upturn. The RBI also introduced a “Systemic Risk Surcharge” of 25 bps on the risk‑weighted assets of the five Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIBs) in the 2023‑24 budget.

Evolution of the RBI's Government Cash Management: Cash Management Bills, Treasury Bills, and the Ways and Means Advances Framework

Cash Management Bills (CMBs)

Introduced in 2010, CMBs are short‑dated (typically 7‑91 days) discount instruments issued by the RBI on behalf of the central government to meet temporary cash mismatches. Unlike regular Treasury Bills, CMBs are not part of the notified borrowing calendar; they are announced ad‑hoc via press release and auctioned on the NDS‑OM platform. The 2021 revision allowed tenors up to 182 days and introduced a “green shoe” option for oversubscription up to 20 % of the notified amount.

Treasury Bills (T‑Bills) Structure

The RBI issues three benchmark T‑Bill tenors — 91‑day, 182‑day, and 364‑day — on a weekly auction cycle. The 2022 auction calendar increased the share of 364‑day bills from 15 % to 25 % of total T‑Bill issuance to lengthen the government’s debt maturity profile. Non‑competitive bidding was extended to all three tenors in 2020, allowing retail investors and provident funds to participate without quoting a yield.

Ways and Means Advances (WMA) Framework

Under Section 17(5) of the RBI Act, the central government can draw WMAs up to a limit set by the RBI in consultation with the Ministry of Finance. The limit was ₹1.2 lakh crore for 2022‑23 and raised to ₹1.5 lakh crore for 2023‑24. The “Special WMA” window, collateralised by government securities, carries the repo rate; the “Normal WMA” is unsecured and priced at the repo rate plus 25 bps. The 2021 amendment introduced a “hard‑stop” trigger: if the government’s WMA utilisation exceeds 75 % of the limit for five consecutive working days, the RBI may restrict further drawdowns until the utilisation falls below 60 %.

Coordination with Monetary Operations

CMBs and T‑Bills are the primary instruments through which the RBI manages durable liquidity. When the banking system faces a surplus, the RBI conducts Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions using T‑Bills as collateral; during deficits, it injects liquidity via Variable Rate Repo (VRR) or outright purchase of CMBs. The 2023 “Operation Twist” episode demonstrated this coordination: the RBI simultaneously sold short‑dated CMBs and bought long‑dated government securities to flatten the yield curve while keeping the WMA utilisation within the prescribed band.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Services for Regulated Entities: Operational Resilience, Data Localization, and Exit‑Plan Testing

Scope and Applicability

The “Master Direction – Outsourcing of Information Technology Services by Regulated Entities” (issued April 2023) applies to all RBI‑regulated entities: commercial banks, NBFCs, HFCs, payment system operators, and small finance banks. It supersedes the 2017 outsourcing circular and extends the regulatory perimeter to cloud‑service providers (CSPs) that host critical systems such as core banking, payment gateways, and data‑analytics platforms.

Data Localization and Sovereignty

Regulated entities must ensure that all “critical data” — defined as customer‑identifiable information, transaction logs, and risk‑model inputs — resides on servers physically located in India. CSPs are required to provide a contractual undertaking that data will not be replicated or processed outside Indian jurisdiction without prior RBI approval. The 2023 direction also mandates encryption‑at‑rest using AES‑256 and encryption‑in‑transit using TLS 1.3.

Operational Resilience Requirements

Entities must conduct a “Business Impact Analysis” (BIA) for each outsourced critical function, define Recovery Time Objectives (RTO) not exceeding four hours for payment systems and eight hours for core banking, and test the recovery plan at least annually. The direction introduces a “Shared Responsibility Matrix” that delineates the CSP’s duties (infrastructure availability, patch management) from the entity’s duties (application‑level controls, access management).

Exit‑Plan Testing and Contractual Safeguards

Every outsourcing agreement must contain an exit‑plan clause specifying data‑return formats, transition timelines (maximum 180 days), and the CSP’s obligation to assist in migration. The RBI requires the regulated entity to perform a full exit‑plan drill at least once every two years, documenting the results and submitting a summary to the Department of Supervision. Failure to test attracts a penalty of up to ₹1 crore under Section 47A.

Supervisory Reporting and Penalties

Regulated entities file a quarterly “Outsourcing Return” detailing the number of critical functions outsourced, CSP‑wise risk ratings, incident‑response metrics, and exit‑plan test outcomes. The RBI’s 2023 supervisory review found that 12 % of banks had not conducted the biennial exit drill; those banks were directed to complete the drill within 90 days and faced a supervisory letter. Repeated non‑compliance can lead to restriction on new outsourcing arrangements.

  • Confusing the KCC interest‑subvention rate with the repo rate; the subvention is a fixed 2 % plus a 3 % prompt‑repayment incentive, not a floating spread.
  • Assuming P2P platforms can operate without an Account Aggregator; AA integration has been mandatory since the September 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines.
  • Believing the DebtRank metric is the sole contagion indicator; the RBI also uses Co‑Risk and Systemic Expected Shortfall in its FSR.
  • Thinking Cash Management Bills are part of the regular T‑Bill calendar; CMBs are ad‑hoc, non‑calendar instruments issued for temporary cash mismatches.
  • Overlooking that the outsourcing master direction requires a biennial exit‑plan drill, not a one‑time test at contract inception.
  • Misreading the WMA “hard‑stop” trigger as a permanent ceiling; it only restricts further drawdowns until utilisation falls below 60 %.

Retail Central Bank Digital Currency Pilot: Architecture, Offline Capability, and Financial Inclusion Implications

The Reserve Bank of India launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑R) pilot in December 2022, initially covering four cities and four banks. The pilot uses a two‑tier architecture: the RBI issues the digital rupee to participating banks (the “issuance layer”), and banks distribute it to end‑users through existing mobile‑banking applications (the “distribution layer”). Each token is a cryptographically signed liability of the RBI, denominated in rupees, and carries a unique serial number that enables traceability while preserving user‑level pseudonymity.

Offline capability is a design priority for financial inclusion. The pilot incorporates a “near‑field communication” (NFC) based offline wallet that allows peer‑to‑peer transfers without internet connectivity, subject to a per‑transaction ceiling of ₹2,000 and a daily cumulative limit of ₹10,000. The offline wallet stores a limited set of signed tokens locally; when the device reconnects, the wallet synchronises with the RBI’s ledger, and any double‑spend attempts are rejected. This mechanism mirrors the offline functionality tested in the Bahamas’ Sand Dollar and China’s e‑CNY pilots.

From an inclusion perspective, the CBDC‑R aims to reduce reliance on physical cash in remote areas where ATM density is low. The pilot’s onboarding flow leverages the Jan Dhan‑Aadhaar‑Mobile (JAM) trinity: a beneficiary’s Aadhaar‑linked bank account is used for KYC, and the digital rupee wallet is provisioned instantly. Early data from the pilot (as reported in the RBI’s 2023‑24 Annual Report) indicate that 12 % of wallet activations occurred in districts classified as “aspirational” by NITI Aayog, suggesting traction among underserved populations.

Supervisory oversight focuses on three pillars: (i) operational resilience of the issuance layer, tested through quarterly disaster‑recovery drills; (ii) consumer protection, enforced via a mandatory dispute‑resolution window of 48 hours for failed offline transactions; and (iii) anti‑money‑laundering compliance, requiring banks to report any single‑day wallet load exceeding ₹50,000 to the Financial Intelligence Unit. The RBI has signalled that a nationwide rollout will be contingent on achieving a 99.9 % transaction‑success rate in the pilot and on the finalisation of the Digital Rupee (Retail) Regulations, currently under public consultation.

RBI's Co‑Lending Framework: Risk Sharing, Credit Assessment, and Supervisory Oversight

In September 2022 the RBI issued the “Co‑Lending Model (CLM) Guidelines” to formalise risk‑sharing arrangements between banks and Non‑Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), including Housing Finance Companies (HFCs). Under the CLM, a bank and an NBFC jointly originate a loan, with the bank contributing a minimum of 20 % of the credit exposure and the NBFC the remainder. The loan is recorded on the balance sheets of both entities in proportion to their share, and the NBFC acts as the “originator‑servicer”, handling customer acquisition, documentation, and collections.

The framework mandates a “joint credit appraisal” process: the bank’s credit committee must independently assess the borrower’s repayment capacity, while the NBFC provides the initial credit scoring model. Both parties must agree on the final risk rating before disbursement. This dual‑appraisal requirement addresses the earlier concern that banks merely acted as passive fund providers, relying entirely on NBFC‑generated scores.

Risk‑sharing is operationalised through a “first‑loss” and “pro‑rata” structure. The first‑loss tranche, typically 5‑10 % of the loan amount, is absorbed by the NBFC; losses beyond that are shared pro‑rata according to the exposure split. The guidelines also prescribe a “minimum holding period” of 12 months for the bank’s share, preventing immediate securitisation and ensuring skin‑in‑the‑game.

Supervisory oversight includes quarterly reporting of co‑lending portfolios to the Department of Supervision, with granular data on sectoral distribution, ticket size, and delinquency buckets. The RBI’s 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report noted that co‑lending exposures grew 38 % year‑on‑year, reaching ₹1.2 lakh crore, with the bulk concentrated in micro‑enterprise and affordable‑housing segments. The report flagged concentration risk in a few large NBFCs and recommended enhanced monitoring of the first‑loss coverage ratio.

To mitigate operational risk, the CLM requires a legally binding “Co‑Lending Agreement” that specifies data‑sharing protocols, dispute‑resolution mechanisms, and exit clauses. The agreement must be vetted by the bank’s legal and compliance functions and filed with the RBI within 30 days of execution. Non‑compliance attracts penalties under Section 47A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “In the RBI’s Co‑Lending Model, what is the minimum bank share, the first‑loss tranche responsibility, and the mandatory holding period for the bank’s portion?”
The correct answer: the bank must hold at least 20 % of the loan; the first‑loss tranche (typically 5‑10 %) is borne by the NBFC; and the bank’s share cannot be sold or securitised for a minimum of 12 months. Cite the September 2022 Co‑Lending Model Guidelines and the 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report for the growth figure.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question on co‑lending appears, first identify the three quantitative pillars (bank share, first‑loss, holding period). Then check whether the stem asks for a qualitative aspect such as “joint credit appraisal” or “reporting frequency”. Matching the pillar to the stem eliminates distractors quickly.

Green Taxonomy and Sustainable Finance Disclosure Requirements for Regulated Entities

In February 2023 the RBI released the “Draft Framework for Green Taxonomy and Sustainable Finance Disclosures” for public consultation, aiming to align Indian financial institutions with global standards such as the EU Taxonomy and the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD). The taxonomy classifies economic activities into three tiers: “Green” (substantial contribution to climate mitigation or adaptation), “Transition” (activities moving towards low‑carbon pathways), and “Brown” (high‑carbon activities). Each tier carries a defined eligibility threshold expressed in terms of greenhouse‑gas intensity (kg CO₂e per unit of output) and a “do‑no‑significant‑harm” (DNSH) criterion covering biodiversity, water, and pollution.

Regulated entities — commercial banks, NBFCs, HFCs, and All‑India Financial Institutions — are required to map their loan portfolios and investment books against the taxonomy on a quarterly basis. The mapping must be disclosed in the notes to accounts and in a dedicated “Sustainable Finance Report” published alongside the annual financial statements. The first mandatory reporting cycle begins with the quarter ending March 2025, giving institutions a two‑year preparation window.

The framework introduces a “Green Asset Ratio” (GAR), defined as the proportion of on‑balance‑sheet assets classified as Green or Transition to total assets. Banks with a GAR below 5 % are expected to submit a board‑approved transition plan within six months, outlining targets for green lending, capacity building, and risk‑management enhancements. The RBI will monitor GAR trends through its supervisory returns and may impose additional capital surcharges under Pillar 2 for persistent under‑performance.

To support implementation, the RBI has partnered with the Indian Banks’ Association (IBA) and the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to develop a common data‑template and a taxonomy‑mapping toolkit. Pilot testing with five large banks in 2023‑24 revealed that 68 % of corporate loan exposures could be classified automatically using existing sectoral codes, while the remaining 32 % required borrower‑level granular data, prompting the RBI to mandate enhanced ESG data collection from large corporate borrowers (turnover > ₹500 crore) starting FY 2024‑25.

International alignment is reinforced through the RBI’s participation in the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) and the Basel Committee’s “Principles for the Effective Management and Supervision of Climate‑Related Financial Risks”. The final taxonomy, expected to be notified by end‑2024, will be reviewed every three years to incorporate scientific updates and policy shifts such as the National Green Hydrogen Mission.

Phased Capital Account Convertibility: Liberalised Remittance Scheme, External Commercial Borrowings, and Macro‑Financial Stability

India’s journey toward full capital account convertibility has been calibrated through a sequence of liberalisation steps, each accompanied by macro‑prudential safeguards. The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), introduced in 2004 and progressively relaxed, now permits resident individuals to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for permissible current and capital account transactions, including overseas education, medical treatment, and portfolio investment. The 2023 amendment added a “purpose‑code” reporting requirement for remittances exceeding USD 10,000, enabling the RBI to monitor capital‑flight risks in real time.

External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) framework, overhauled in 2018 and refined in 2021, classifies borrowings into three tracks based on end‑use, maturity, and hedging requirements. Track I (minimum average maturity 3 years) covers working‑capital and general corporate purposes; Track II (minimum 5 years) targets capital‑expenditure in infrastructure and manufacturing; Track III (minimum 10 years) is reserved for long‑gestation projects such as renewable energy. All ECBs above USD 20 million equivalent must be hedged for at least 70 % of the principal, and the RBI monitors the aggregate ECB‑to‑GDP ratio, which stood at 2.3 % in March 2024.

The RBI’s “Capital Account Management” framework integrates these channels with the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) and the Monetary Policy Framework. A key macro‑financial stability tool is the “Capital Flow Management Measures” (CFMs) kit, which includes variable‑rate minimum retention periods for portfolio inflows, sectoral caps on non‑resident deposits, and the ability to impose temporary “stand‑still” clauses on short‑term debt rollovers during stress episodes. The 2020 COVID‑19 episode saw the RBI activate a 90‑day stand‑still on certain short‑term ECBs, preventing a disorderly outflow.

Empirical analysis in the RBI’s 2022‑23 “Report on Currency and Finance” shows that incremental liberalisation under the LRS and ECB tracks has been associated with a modest increase in gross capital inflows (average 0.4 % of GDP per year) without a statistically significant rise in exchange‑rate volatility, attributed to the concurrent deepening of the domestic bond market and the RBI’s active intervention policy. However, the report cautions that the growing share of non‑resident portfolio investment in government securities (now 12 % of outstanding) creates a transmission channel for global risk‑off episodes, warranting continued vigilance and a calibrated pace for further liberalisation.

  • Confusing the retail CBDC offline transaction ceiling (₹2,000 per transaction) with the daily cumulative limit (₹10,000).
  • Assuming the bank’s minimum share in co‑lending is 10 % instead of the prescribed 20 %.
  • Overlooking that the first‑loss tranche in co‑lending is borne by the NBFC, not shared pro‑rata.
  • Misstating the Green Asset Ratio threshold for mandatory transition plans as 10 % rather than 5 %.
  • Believing the LRS limit is USD 200,000; the current ceiling is USD 250,000 per financial year.
  • Thinking ECB Track I requires a minimum maturity of 5 years; the correct minimum is 3 years.
  • Neglecting the RBI’s authority to impose temporary stand‑still clauses on short‑term ECBs during systemic stress.

RBI's Framework for Resolution of Large Stressed Assets: The National Asset Reconstruction Company (NARCL) and India Debt Resolution Company (IDRCL)

The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was incorporated in July 2021 under the Companies Act, 2013, with an authorised capital of ₹6,000 crore and an initial paid‑up capital of ₹1,500 crore. The shareholding pattern is calibrated to ensure public‑sector dominance while allowing private participation: public‑sector banks hold 51 % and private‑sector banks and financial institutions hold the remaining 49 %. NARCL operates as an asset reconstruction company (ARC) registered under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002.

NARCL acquires stressed assets through a structured 15:85 consideration model. The selling bank receives 15 % of the agreed value in cash upfront, while the balance 85 % is issued as security receipts (SRs) backed by a government guarantee of ₹30,600 crore announced in the 2021‑22 Budget. The guarantee covers the principal amount of SRs, reducing the risk for the transferring bank and improving the marketability of the receipts. As of March 2024, NARCL had acquired assets with a book value of approximately ₹50,000 crore across sectors such as power, steel, textiles and infrastructure.

India Debt Resolution Company Limited (IDRCL) was set up as a separate asset‑management entity to manage the resolution process for assets acquired by NARCL. IDRCL’s capital structure mirrors NARCL’s: 51 % held by NARCL and 49 % by private investors, including alternative investment funds. IDRCL is responsible for operational turnaround, asset monetisation, and eventual sale or restructuring, charging a management fee and a performance‑linked upside. The two‑tier structure separates acquisition risk (NARCL) from resolution expertise (IDRCL), addressing the conflict‑of‑interest concerns that plagued earlier ARC models.

Interaction with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) is carefully delineated. NARCL can participate as a financial creditor in the Committee of Creditors (CoC) and may vote on resolution plans, but it is not classified as a “resolution applicant” under Section 25(2)(h) of the IBC. This distinction prevents NARCL from directly proposing resolution plans while still allowing it to influence outcomes. The SARFAESI Act continues to provide the enforcement backbone for secured creditors, enabling NARCL to take possession and sell secured assets without court intervention where the borrower defaults.

The framework also includes a sunset clause: the government guarantee on SRs is valid for five years from issuance, after which NARCL must either redeem the receipts or extend the guarantee with fresh approval. This time‑bound guarantee incentivises timely resolution and limits fiscal exposure. The RBI monitors NARCL’s asset quality through quarterly returns and conducts thematic inspections to ensure compliance with provisioning norms applicable to ARCs under the Master Direction – Reserve Bank of India (Asset Reconstruction Companies) Directions, 2017.

RBI's Supervisory Framework for Cyber Resilience and Technology Risk in Banks and NBFCs

The Reserve Bank’s approach to cyber resilience has evolved from a set of advisory guidelines to a comprehensive supervisory framework anchored in three key circulars. The “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” (June 2016) established baseline controls such as a board‑approved cyber security policy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and mandatory incident reporting within six hours of detection. The 2021 “Guidelines on Cyber Security for Banks and NBFCs” expanded the scope to non‑bank financial companies, introducing a proportionate approach: systemically important NBFCs (asset size ≥ ₹5,000 crore) must adopt the full framework, while smaller NBFCs follow a scaled‑down version.

The 2023 “Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” consolidated IT governance, business continuity, and cyber risk into a single regulatory instrument. It mandates annual independent penetration testing, quarterly vulnerability assessments, and a cyber crisis management plan (CCMP) tested through tabletop exercises at least once a year. Boards are required to review cyber risk dashboards quarterly, and the CISO must report directly to the board or a board‑level committee, ensuring top‑level accountability.

Incident reporting has been tightened: any material cyber incident — defined as one affecting confidentiality, integrity, or availability of critical systems or customer data — must be reported to the RBI’s Department of Supervision within six hours, followed by a detailed root‑cause analysis within 15 days. The RBI maintains a confidential Cyber Incident Repository and shares anonymised threat intelligence with regulated entities through the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In) coordination channel.

Supervisory tools include thematic IT examinations, cyber‑risk focused on‑site inspections, and a scoring model that feeds into the Supervisory Action Framework (SAF). Persistent deficiencies trigger escalated actions ranging from mandatory remedial action plans to restrictions on new digital product launches. In 2024, the RBI issued a specific circular on ransomware preparedness, requiring entities to maintain offline backups, conduct ransomware simulation drills, and report ransom payments (if any) to law‑enforcement agencies.

For payment system operators, the “Framework for Cyber Security and Resilience of Payment Systems” (2022) adds requirements for end‑to‑end encryption, tokenisation of card data, and real‑time fraud monitoring. The RBI also conducts periodic “Red Team” exercises on critical payment infrastructure such as the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) and the Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS) to assess systemic resilience.

Application of NARCL Structure in a Case Study
A public‑sector bank sells a non‑performing asset with a book value of ₹500 crore to NARCL under the 15:85 structure. Calculate the cash component received by the bank upfront and describe the nature of the remaining consideration.
Under the 15:85 structure, the bank receives 15 % of ₹500 crore = ₹75 crore in cash immediately. The balance 85 % (₹425 crore) is issued as security receipts (SRs) backed by a sovereign guarantee of ₹30,600 crore announced in the 2021‑22 Budget. These SRs are tradable instruments representing the bank’s residual claim on the recovered proceeds from the underlying asset.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the 15:85 split and the ₹30,600 crore guarantee figure; use the mnemonic “15 cash, 85 receipts, 30.6k guarantee”. In questions on cyber resilience, recall the six‑hour reporting window and the three‑tier circular hierarchy (2016 → 2021 → 2023).

RBI's Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves: Composition, Investment Guidelines, and Risk Management

Foreign exchange reserves are managed by the Reserve Bank under Section 40 of the RBI Act, 1934, and the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999. As of end‑March 2024, the reserves stood at approximately US$ 642 billion, comprising Foreign Currency Assets (FCA) of US$ 570 billion, gold holdings of 803 tonnes (valued at US$ 55 billion), Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) of US$ 18 billion, and the Reserve Position in the IMF of US$ 5 billion. The FCA portfolio is invested primarily in sovereign or sovereign‑guaranteed securities of G‑10 countries, highly rated supranational bonds, and short‑term deposits with central banks and the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).

Investment guidelines are codified in the RBI’s “Investment Policy for Foreign Exchange Reserves” (last revised 2022). The policy sets a strategic asset allocation: 70‑80 % in high‑quality government securities (duration 1‑3 years), 10‑15 % in agency and supranational bonds, 5‑10 % in short‑term deposits, and a small tactical allocation to gold‑linked instruments. Credit risk limits restrict exposure to any single sovereign issuer to 10 % of FCA and to any single non‑sovereign counterparty to 2 %. Counterparty limits for deposit placements are capped at 5 % of FCA per institution.

Risk management is overseen by the RBI’s Internal Risk Management Committee, which monitors market risk (duration, currency composition), credit risk (issuer ratings, concentration), and liquidity risk (ability to meet intervention needs within 48 hours). The RBI publishes a weekly Statistical Supplement showing reserve composition, and a quarterly “Management of Foreign Exchange Reserves” report detailing returns. For FY 2023‑24, the annualised return on FCA was 2.4 %, while gold revaluation gains contributed an additional 0.6 % to overall reserve returns.

Reserves are deployed for three primary objectives: (i) maintaining confidence in monetary and exchange‑rate stability, (ii) providing a buffer against external shocks, and (iii) meeting the country’s external payment obligations. Intervention operations are conducted through the spot and forward markets, with the RBI typically selling dollars to curb excessive rupee depreciation and buying dollars to prevent sharp appreciation. The RBI also uses the “Market Stabilisation Scheme” (MSS) to sterilise liquidity arising from large intervention purchases.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing, Cloud Services, and Third‑Party Risk Management for Regulated Entities

The “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks” (April 2021, updated November 2022) establish a principles‑based framework applicable to commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and NBFCs‑ML. The guidelines require board approval for any material outsourcing arrangement, defined as one where the service provider’s failure could materially affect the bank’s financial condition, reputation, or regulatory compliance. A comprehensive risk assessment covering operational, legal, concentration, and exit risks must be documented before contract execution.

Contractual clauses mandated by the RBI include: (a) data confidentiality and ownership provisions ensuring that customer data remains the bank’s property; (b) audit and inspection rights for the bank and the RBI; (c) business continuity and disaster‑recovery obligations of the service provider; (d) clear exit‑strategy provisions with a maximum transition period of 180 days. Banks must maintain an updated inventory of all outsourced activities and report material changes to the Department of Supervision within 15 days.

Cloud‑specific guidance was issued in the 2022 update, requiring banks to use only Cloud Service Providers (CSPs) empanelled by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under the “MeitY Cloud Empanelment Framework”. Data localisation rules under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, mandate that payment‑system data be stored exclusively in India. For non‑payment data, banks may use overseas CSPs provided they meet the RBI’s data‑privacy and sovereign‑control requirements, including contractual clauses for lawful access by Indian regulators.

Third‑party risk management extends beyond outsourcing to include fintech partnerships, API integrations, and vendor‑managed services. The RBI’s “Master Direction on Information Technology Governance” (2023) introduces a “Vendor Risk Tiering” model: Tier‑1 vendors (critical infrastructure, core banking) require annual on‑site assessments; Tier‑2 vendors (support functions) require biennial assessments; Tier‑3 vendors (commodity services) are monitored through automated risk dashboards. Concentration risk limits cap exposure to any single vendor group at 15 % of total outsourcing spend.

Non‑compliance attracts supervisory actions under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, including monetary penalties, restriction on new outsourcing contracts, and, in severe cases, removal of key managerial personnel. The RBI also conducts thematic inspections on outsourcing risk, with findings published in the annual “Trend and Progress of Banking in India” report.

RBI's Supervisory Framework for Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks: Capital, Governance, and Prudential Norms

Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Payment Banks (PBs) were licensed in 2015 under differentiated banking guidelines to further financial inclusion. SFBs require a minimum paid‑up equity capital of ₹200 crore, while PBs require ₹100 crore. Promoter shareholding is capped at 40 % for both categories, with a mandatory dilution to 26 % within 12 years for SFBs and 15 years for PBs. The “fit and proper” criteria for promoters and directors are aligned with those for universal banks, including a clean track record, financial soundness, and no adverse regulatory orders.

Governance norms mandate a minimum of 50 % independent directors on the board, a separate Risk Management Committee, and a Chief Risk Officer reporting directly to the board. SFBs must comply with the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) applicable to scheduled commercial banks; PBs are required to maintain CRR only, with SLR exemption. Both categories are subject to the Basel III capital framework, with a minimum Common Equity Tier‑1 (CET1) ratio of 5.5 % and a total Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) of 9 % (including the Capital Conservation Buffer).

Asset‑side restrictions differentiate the two models. SFBs can extend loans up to 10 % of their loan portfolio to a single borrower and 15 % to a borrower group, with at least 75 % of adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) directed to priority‑sector lending. PBs are prohibited from undertaking any lending activity; they may only accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer and provide payments, remittances, and distribution of simple financial products such as mutual funds and insurance. Both SFBs and PBs are covered under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) with the standard insurance limit of ₹5 lakh per depositor.

Recent regulatory developments include the 2023 “Guidelines for Merger of Small Finance Banks” allowing voluntary amalgamation with another SFB or a universal bank subject to RBI approval, and a pathway for SFBs to transition to universal banks after five years of satisfactory performance, provided they meet the universal bank licensing criteria. The RBI conducts annual on‑site inspections and quarterly off‑site returns (Form X for SFBs, Form Y for PBs) covering asset quality, liquidity coverage ratio, and compliance with priority‑sector targets. Supervisory intervention follows the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework adapted for differentiated banks, with triggers based on CAR, net NPA ratio, and leverage ratio.

  • Confusing NARCL’s 15:85 structure with the typical ARC model and forgetting the sovereign guarantee on security receipts.
  • Assuming the cyber‑security framework applies uniformly to all NBFCs without recognising the proportionate approach for smaller entities.
  • Mixing up the composition of foreign exchange reserves by treating SDRs as part of gold holdings.
  • Overlooking that Payment Banks cannot undertake any lending activity, unlike Small Finance Banks.
  • Believing that outsourcing guidelines require all cloud providers to be empanelled directly by the RBI, while empanelment is done by MeitY.
  • Remember to verify the latest RBI circulars before the exam.

Outsourcing and Cloud Risk Management Framework for Banks

The Reserve Bank of India issued the Master Direction on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks in April 2023, replacing the 2017 guidelines and extending the regulatory perimeter to cover cloud‑based arrangements. The direction classifies vendors into three tiers based on criticality: Tier‑1 vendors provide core banking, payment‑system infrastructure, or data‑centre services and are subject to annual on‑site assessments; Tier‑2 vendors support functions such as application development and require biennial assessments; Tier‑3 vendors supply commodity services and are monitored through automated risk dashboards. A concentration‑risk cap limits exposure to any single vendor group to 15 % of the bank’s total outsourcing spend.

Data‑localisation requirements differentiate payment‑system data from other data. Payment‑system data must be stored exclusively in India, while non‑payment data may reside on overseas cloud service providers (CSPs) provided the bank ensures contractual clauses that grant Indian regulators lawful access and meet the RBI’s data‑privacy and sovereign‑control standards. The RBI does not empanel CSPs directly; empanelment is performed by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under the MeitY Cloud Empanelment Framework. Banks must conduct due‑diligence on the CSP’s certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2) and include exit‑strategy clauses in contracts.

Third‑party risk management now extends beyond traditional outsourcing to cover fintech partnerships, API integrations, and vendor‑managed services. The Master Direction on Information Technology Governance (2023) mandates a board‑approved IT strategy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting to the board, and a vendor‑risk‑tiering model aligned with the outsourcing direction. Non‑compliance attracts supervisory actions under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, including monetary penalties, restriction on new outsourcing contracts, and, in severe cases, removal of key managerial personnel. The RBI also conducts thematic inspections on outsourcing risk, with findings published in the annual Trend and Progress of Banking in India report.

Cyber Resilience and Information Technology Governance in Banks

The RBI’s Cyber Security Framework for Banks (June 2021) set a baseline for cyber resilience, requiring banks to adopt a risk‑based approach, establish a Security Operations Centre (SOC), and conduct periodic vulnerability assessments and penetration testing. The framework mandates a board‑level Cyber Risk Committee, a designated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) with direct reporting lines to the board, and an incident‑response plan that includes mandatory reporting of material cyber incidents to the RBI within six hours of detection.

The subsequent Master Direction on Information Technology Governance (2023) integrates cyber resilience into broader IT governance. It prescribes a three‑line‑of‑defence model: business units own risk, the risk‑management function provides oversight, and internal audit provides independent assurance. Banks must maintain a comprehensive IT asset inventory, enforce privileged‑access management, and implement multi‑factor authentication for all critical systems. The direction also requires annual independent cyber‑security audits by CERT‑In‑empanelled auditors and the submission of a Cyber‑Security Posture Report to the RBI.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the RBI’s Cyber‑Security Supervisory Framework, which includes off‑site returns (Form CS‑1), on‑site inspections focusing on threat‑intelligence integration, and thematic reviews of ransomware preparedness. Banks that fail to meet the prescribed maturity levels face graded supervisory actions ranging from advisory letters to restrictions on digital‑product launches. The framework aligns with international standards such as the Basel Committee’s Cyber‑Resilience Principles and the Financial Stability Board’s Guidance on Cyber‑Risk Management.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the RBI's 2023 Master Direction on IT Governance is correct? (a) It requires banks to empanel cloud service providers directly with the RBI. (b) It mandates a board‑approved IT strategy and a CISO reporting to the board. (c) It exempts Tier‑3 vendors from any risk assessment. (d) It allows payment‑system data to be stored overseas if encrypted."
The correct answer is (b). The 2023 Master Direction explicitly requires a board‑approved IT strategy and a Chief Information Security Officer reporting directly to the board. Statement (a) is false because CSP empanelment is done by MeitY, not the RBI. Statement (c) is false; Tier‑3 vendors are monitored through automated dashboards, not exempt. Statement (d) contradicts the data‑localisation rule that payment‑system data must reside in India.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question references the 2023 IT Governance direction, first identify whether it pertains to board‑level responsibilities, vendor‑tiering, or data‑localisation. Eliminate options that assign RBI the role of CSP empanelment or that relax payment‑data localisation. The presence of a CISO reporting to the board is a hallmark of the 2023 direction and a frequent correct‑answer cue.

Business Correspondent Model: Evolution, Compensation Structure, and Supervisory Oversight

The Business Correspondent (BC) model was introduced in 2006 under the RBI/2005‑06/DBOD.No.BL.BC.58/22.01.001/2005‑06 circular to extend banking services to unbanked areas through non‑bank intermediaries. The 2014 Master Direction on Business Correspondents formalised eligibility criteria, requiring BCs to be entities such as NGOs, cooperatives, or companies with a minimum net worth of ₹10 lakh. The direction capped the number of BC outlets per bank at 15 % of its total branches in a district to prevent concentration.

Compensation for BCs comprises a fixed monthly fee (typically ₹5,000‑₹10,000) plus a variable component linked to transaction volumes — usually 0.5 %‑1 % of the transaction value for deposits and 0.2 %‑0.5 % for withdrawals. The 2022 Guidelines on Compensation and Incentive Structures for Business Correspondents mandated that the variable component not exceed 50 % of total compensation to avoid mis‑selling. Banks must disclose the compensation structure in their annual reports and ensure that BC agents are not incentivised to push specific financial products.

Supervisory oversight was strengthened by the 2023 Master Direction on Outsourcing, which treats BC arrangements as outsourcing contracts. Banks are required to conduct due‑diligence on BCs, monitor transaction‑level data through the Core Banking Solution, and submit quarterly BC‑performance returns (Form BC‑1). The RBI’s Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework for differentiated banks also applies to BC‑related deficiencies, with triggers based on transaction‑failure rates exceeding 5 % and customer‑complaint ratios above 2 %.

Corporate Bond Market Transmission: RBI's Purchase Programme and Market Making

The RBI launched the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) in March 2020 as part of its COVID‑19 liquidity measures, initially allocating ₹10,000 crore for outright purchases of investment‑grade corporate bonds in the secondary market. The programme was expanded in October 2020 to ₹20,000 crore and further to ₹50,000 crore in April 2021, with eligibility extended to bonds rated AA and above. Purchases are conducted through the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, ensuring transparent price discovery.

In addition to outright purchases, the RBI introduced a Corporate Bond Market Making Scheme in 2021, designating select Primary Dealers (PDs) as market makers for specified corporate‑bond ISINs. Market makers are required to provide two‑way quotes with a maximum spread of 15 bps for AAA‑rated bonds and 25 bps for AA‑rated bonds, and to maintain a minimum quote size of ₹5 crore. The scheme aims to deepen secondary‑market liquidity, reduce bid‑ask spreads, and improve the transmission of policy rates to corporate borrowing costs.

Empirical analysis by the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (December 2022) showed that the CBPP compressed corporate‑bond yields by 30‑45 bps relative to comparable government‑security yields, and that the market‑making scheme reduced average bid‑ask spreads from 45 bps to 18 bps for AAA bonds. The RBI continues to calibrate the programme size based on market conditions, with a built‑in sunset clause that requires a review every six months.

Resolution of Stressed Assets: Asset Reconstruction Companies, SARFAESI Act, and the National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL)

The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002 empowered banks and financial institutions to enforce security interests without court intervention, provided the borrower’s account is classified as a non‑performing asset (NPA). The Act also laid the regulatory foundation for Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), which acquire NPAs from banks at a discount and attempt recovery through restructuring or asset sale. The RBI’s Guidelines for ARCs (2003, revised 2017) prescribe a minimum net owned fund of ₹100 crore, a leverage ratio not exceeding 5 times, and a requirement to hold at least 15 % of the security receipts issued for each acquisition.

In 2021, the government established the National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) as a “bad bank” to aggregate large stressed assets from public‑sector banks. NARCL follows a 15:85 structure: it pays 15 % of the acquisition value upfront in cash and issues security receipts (SRs) for the remaining 85 %. The SRs carry a sovereign guarantee, making them eligible for inclusion in banks’ Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) holdings. The companion entity, India Debt Resolution Company Limited (IDRCL), manages the resolution process, while NARCL holds the assets.

The interaction between NARCL and the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016 is governed by a memorandum of understanding that allows NARCL to refer accounts to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) if resolution through the ARC route fails. As of March 2024, NARCL had acquired stressed assets worth approximately ₹83,000 crore, with a recovery rate of around 35 % on resolved accounts. The RBI monitors NARCL’s compliance with ARC guidelines, including the 15 % SR‑holding requirement and the leverage cap, through quarterly returns and on‑site inspections.

  • Confusing the 15:85 cash‑SR structure of NARCL with the typical ARC model where the entire consideration is paid via security receipts.
  • Assuming the sovereign guarantee on NARCL’s security receipts applies to all ARC‑issued receipts.
  • Overlooking that the SARFAESI Act does not apply to agricultural land or to loans below ₹1 lakh.
  • Believing that the CBPP purchases are conducted through primary‑market auctions rather than the NDS‑OM secondary‑market platform.
  • Mixing up the compensation caps for Business Correspondents (variable component ≤ 50 % of total) with the older uncapped incentive structures.
  • Thinking that the RBI directly empanels cloud service providers; empanelment is done by MeitY.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common mistakes.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Government Securities Market: Primary Dealer System and Auction Dynamics

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducts its open‑market operations primarily through the government securities (G‑sec) market, where the primary dealer (PD) system acts as the backbone of primary issuance and secondary‑market liquidity. Introduced in 1995, the PD framework designates a set of banks and financial institutions that are obligated to bid at every primary auction, provide two‑way quotes on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, and maintain a minimum turnover ratio. As of March 2024 there are 22 PDs, each required to hold a minimum net owned fund of ₹500 crore and to achieve a bidding commitment of at least 0.5 % of the notified amount in each auction.

Auction mechanics follow a uniform‑price (Dutch) format for dated securities and a multiple‑price format for treasury bills. The RBI announces the notified amount, the cut‑off yield, and the amount accepted. The cut‑off yield becomes the benchmark for the day’s secondary‑market yields and feeds directly into the marginal cost of funds based lending rate (MCLR) and the external benchmark lending rate (EBLR) used by banks. When the RBI wishes to tighten liquidity, it can increase the notified amount or set a higher cut‑off, pushing yields up; conversely, a lower cut‑off or a larger devolvement on PDs signals easing.

The transmission chain is amplified by the PDs’ market‑making obligations. PDs must quote bid‑ask spreads not exceeding 5 bps for the 10‑year benchmark and 10 bps for off‑the‑run securities. This ensures that any shift in the policy repo rate is reflected quickly in G‑sec yields, which in turn anchor the pricing of corporate bonds, interest‑rate swaps, and the cost of funds for banks. Empirical work published in the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (December 2022) showed that a 25 bps repo‑rate change translates into a 18‑22 bps movement in the 10‑year G‑sec yield within two weeks, with the PD quoting discipline accounting for roughly 60 % of the pass‑through.

Recent refinements include the introduction of the “Green Shoe” option in 2021, allowing the RBI to accept up to 10 % additional subscription above the notified amount at the cut‑off yield, and the shift to a T+1 settlement cycle for primary issuances in 2023, reducing settlement risk and improving the velocity of liquidity injection. The RBI also conducts variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions that absorb surplus liquidity at rates linked to the prevailing repo rate, providing a finer instrument for short‑term liquidity management without disturbing the primary‑dealer auction calendar.

RBI's Oversight of the Unified Payments Interface: Settlement Finality, Interoperability, and Risk Controls

The Unified Payments Interface (UPI), launched by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) in April 2016, has become the dominant retail payment rail, processing over 10 billion transactions per month by early 2024. The RBI’s regulatory oversight is exercised through the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and the “Framework for Regulation of Payment System Operators” issued in 2021. This framework mandates that all payment system operators, including NPCI, obtain a certificate of authorisation, adhere to settlement finality rules, and maintain a robust risk‑management architecture.

Settlement finality in UPI is achieved through the “Immediate Payment Service” (IMPS)‑style real‑time gross settlement (RTGS) at the NPCI’s central switch. Each transaction is irrevocable once the payer’s bank sends a debit confirmation and the payee’s bank receives a credit confirmation. The RBI requires that the settlement finality point be no later than the end of the business day, and NPCI’s architecture meets this by completing the debit‑credit cycle within seconds. The framework also obliges NPCI to publish a daily settlement‑finality report, which the RBI reviews during its quarterly on‑site inspections.

Interoperability is enforced by the “UPI Interoperability Guidelines” (2022), which require all participating banks and payment service providers (PSPs) to accept UPI IDs issued by any other PSP. The guidelines also standardise the technical APIs, QR‑code specifications, and dispute‑resolution timelines (T+1 for failed transactions, T+3 for chargebacks). To mitigate concentration risk, the RBI capped the market share of any single third‑party app at 30 % of total UPI volumes in 2023, a measure aimed at preventing systemic dependence on a single platform.

Risk controls include a mandatory “Transaction‑Level Risk Scoring” engine that evaluates velocity, device fingerprint, and beneficiary‑history patterns in real time. PSPs must maintain a minimum net‑worth of ₹25 crore and a capital adequacy ratio of 15 % of risk‑weighted assets, aligned with the Basel III leverage ratio for payment operators. The RBI’s 2023 “Cyber Resilience Framework for Payment System Operators” further requires NPCI and PSPs to conduct annual red‑team exercises, maintain a 24×7 security operations centre, and report any breach within six hours.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about UPI settlement finality is correct? (a) Settlement finality occurs at the end of the next business day. (b) Settlement finality is achieved when the payer’s bank sends a debit confirmation. (c) Settlement finality is achieved only after the payee’s bank acknowledges credit. (d) Settlement finality is guaranteed by the RBI’s RTGS system."
The correct answer is (c). Under the RBI’s Framework for Regulation of Payment System Operators (2021) and NPCI’s UPI procedural guidelines, a UPI transaction becomes irrevocable only after both the debit confirmation from the payer’s bank and the credit confirmation to the payee’s bank are completed. The settlement finality point is defined as the moment the payee’s bank receives the credit, not merely the debit initiation. Option (a) describes a deferred‑net settlement, which UPI does not use. Option (b) is incomplete because the debit alone does not guarantee the payee’s credit. Option (d) conflates UPI’s real‑time switch with the separate RTGS system used for large‑value payments.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question mixes UPI, IMPS, and RTGS settlement concepts, first identify the payment system referenced. UPI and IMPS are real‑time retail rails with instant finality; RTGS is a wholesale gross‑settlement system with finality at the point of settlement. Remember the 30 % market‑share cap for third‑party UPI apps (2023) and the T+1/T+3 dispute timelines — these are frequent numeric traps.

Resolution of Stressed Assets in the Power Sector: The Role of the National Company Law Tribunal and the RBI's Prudential Norms

The power sector has historically accounted for a disproportionate share of banking sector NPAs, peaking at roughly 30 % of total stressed assets in 2018. The RBI’s February 2018 circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.101/21.04.048/2017‑18) mandated that any account with a default of more than 90 days be referred to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) within 180 days, failing which the bank must initiate resolution under the IBC. This circular was later struck down by the Supreme Court in April 2020 (Dharani Sugars vs. Union of India) on the grounds of excessive delegation, but the RBI re‑issued a revised framework in June 2019 (Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets) that retained the 180‑day timeline while granting lenders flexibility to choose between restructuring, change of ownership, or liquidation.

Under the revised framework, the “Resolution Plan” must be approved by 75 % of creditors by value and 60 % by number, and then submitted to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) for sanction. The NCLT’s role is to ensure procedural fairness, verify that the plan meets the “fair value” test, and confirm that the resolution applicant is not a related party. For power assets, the NCLT has frequently invoked Section 29A of the IBC to bar defaulting promoters from bidding, leading to the entry of new strategic investors such as Tata Power, Adani Power, and JSW Energy.

The RBI’s prudential norms also require banks to maintain a higher provision coverage ratio (PCR) for power‑sector exposures — 50 % for sub‑standard assets and 100 % for doubtful assets — compared with the standard 15 % and 25 % respectively. Additionally, the “Large Exposure Framework” (2023) caps a bank’s exposure to a single power‑generation company at 20 % of its Tier‑1 capital, with an additional 5 % allowed for infrastructure projects that meet the “green” classification under the RBI’s Green Finance taxonomy.

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (December 2023) indicates that the average recovery rate for power‑sector accounts resolved through the IBC stood at 38 % of admitted claims, higher than the 28 % average for all sectors. However, the time‑to‑resolution remains elevated at 420 days on average, reflecting the complexity of fuel‑supply agreements, power‑purchase agreements, and regulatory approvals from state electricity regulatory commissions.

Impact of the Foreign Portfolio Investor Limits on Domestic Bond Yields and Exchange Rate Pass‑Through

Foreign Portfolio Investor (FPI) participation in Indian government and corporate bonds is governed by the “Voluntary Retention Route” (VRR) introduced in 2019 and the “FPI Investment Limits” notified under the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) 2000. As of March 2024, the aggregate FPI limit in central government securities stands at 6 % of outstanding stock, while the limit for state development loans (SDLs) is 2 %. Corporate bond limits are set at 15 % of the outstanding stock for each issuer, with a sub‑limit of 9 % for “long‑term” investors (holding period > 1 year).

When the RBI raises the FPI limit — for example, the increase from 4 % to 6 % for G‑secs in October 2020 — the immediate effect is a compression of yields by 10‑15 bps as foreign demand absorbs supply. Conversely, the imposition of a “short‑term” investment cap (the 9 % sub‑limit) in 2021 led to a widening of the 10‑year G‑sec yield by about 8 bps as short‑horizon investors reduced positions. The transmission to the exchange rate operates through the capital‑flow channel: higher FPI inflows appreciate the rupee, reducing imported inflation and allowing the RBI to maintain a lower repo rate. A 2022 RBI working paper estimated that a 1 % increase in FPI holdings of G‑secs is associated with a 0.3 % appreciation of the INR/USD rate over a three‑month horizon, with a pass‑through elasticity of 0.12 to domestic CPI inflation.

The RBI manages volatility through the “FPI Investment Monitoring Framework” (2022), which requires custodians to report daily positions and triggers a “limit breach” alert when utilisation exceeds 95 % of the prescribed ceiling. In such events, the RBI may temporarily suspend fresh purchases or invoke the “Market Stabilisation Scheme” (MSS) to absorb excess liquidity. The interplay between FPI limits, the VRR, and the MSS creates a multi‑layered toolkit that the RBI calibrates to balance yield stability, exchange‑rate management, and domestic monetary autonomy.

RBI's Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Adoption for Regulated Entities: Operational Resilience and Concentration Risk

In April 2023 the RBI issued the “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services and Cloud Adoption” (RBI/2022‑23/112), superseding the 2017 outsourcing circular. The guidelines apply to all scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and other regulated entities (REs). They introduce a risk‑based classification of outsourcing arrangements into “Critical”, “Material”, and “Non‑Material” based on the potential impact on the RE’s ability to conduct core banking functions, protect customer data, and meet regulatory obligations.

For “Critical” outsourcing — defined as any arrangement whose failure would cause a severe disruption to payment, settlement, or credit‑risk processes — the RE must obtain prior RBI approval, conduct a comprehensive due‑diligence covering the service provider’s financial soundness, cyber‑security posture, and geographic concentration of data centres. The RE must also maintain a “Business Continuity Plan” (BCP) that includes a tested fail‑over to an alternate provider within 24 hours. The guidelines cap the aggregate exposure to a single cloud service provider (CSP) at 30 % of the RE’s total IT spend, and require that at least two CSPs be used for critical workloads.

Data‑localisation requirements remain in force: all payment‑system data must be stored only in India, while non‑payment data may be stored abroad provided the RE obtains a “Data‑Processing Addendum” that ensures compliance with the Information Technology (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules, 2011 and the forthcoming Personal Data Protection Bill. The RBI also mandates an annual “Cloud‑Risk Assessment” by an independent auditor, with findings reported to the board’s Risk Management Committee.

Concentration risk is addressed through the “Inter‑Connectedness Dashboard” that the RBI publishes quarterly, mapping the top‑10 CSPs used by REs and their market‑share thresholds. As of December 2023, the three largest CSPs accounted for 68 % of total cloud spend by Indian banks, prompting the RBI to issue a supervisory letter urging diversification. The guidelines also require REs to include “exit clauses” in contracts, specifying data‑portability formats, transition timelines (maximum 180 days), and liability for service‑level breaches.

  • Confusing the 30 % market‑share cap for third‑party UPI apps with the 30 % CSP concentration limit for cloud outsourcing.
  • Assuming the RBI’s 2018 February circular on stressed assets remains operative after the Supreme Court’s 2020 ruling.
  • Treating the FPI short‑term sub‑limit (9 %) as the overall corporate‑bond ceiling (15 %).
  • Believing that settlement finality in UPI occurs at the debit‑confirmation stage rather than after credit confirmation.
  • Overlooking the requirement for a minimum of two cloud service providers for critical workloads under the 2023 outsourcing guidelines.
  • Mixing up the Green Shoe option (10 % additional subscription) with the VRRR auction mechanism.
  • Assuming the NCLT’s approval of a resolution plan is automatic once the 75 % creditor threshold is met, ignoring the fair‑value test.

These advanced sections complete the required depth for the current pass.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, but a series of regulatory reforms since 2015 have deepened its role as a transmission channel for monetary policy. The RBI’s 2015 “Corporate Bond Market Development” circular introduced a framework for market‑making by primary dealers, permitted repo in corporate bonds, and allowed banks to classify investment‑grade corporate bonds as Held‑to‑Maturity up to 25 % of their net demand and time liabilities. In 2018 the RBI operationalised a dedicated corporate bond repo platform on the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL), enabling banks and primary dealers to borrow against high‑rated corporate paper at rates closely linked to the policy repo. This repo window compresses the spread between the repo rate and corporate bond yields, so a 25‑basis‑point repo cut typically transmits 15‑20 bps to the 5‑year AAA corporate yield within two weeks, as documented in the RBI’s 2021 Monetary Policy Report.

Foreign portfolio investor (FPI) limits constitute a second transmission lever. The 2020 revision raised the overall FPI ceiling in corporate bonds to 15 % of outstanding stock, with a 9 % sub‑limit for short‑tenor (≤ 1 year) securities. When the RBI eases policy, the resulting decline in sovereign yields narrows the risk premium that FPIs demand, prompting inflows that push corporate yields lower. A 2022 RBI working paper estimated that a 1 % increase in FPI holdings of corporate bonds reduces the 10‑year AAA spread by 3‑4 bps over a quarter. Conversely, the 2021 tightening of the short‑term sub‑limit caused a temporary widening of 8‑10 bps as short‑horizon investors unwound positions.
