Banks’ own portfolio rebalancing forms the third channel. Under the Basel III Liquidity Coverage Ratio, banks must hold high‑quality liquid assets (HQLA). Corporate bonds rated AA‑ and above qualify as Level 2B HQLA with a 50 % haircut. When the policy rate falls, the opportunity cost of holding HQLA declines, encouraging banks to shift from government securities to higher‑yielding corporate bonds. This demand pressure compresses credit spreads, especially for issuers with strong balance sheets. The RBI’s 2023 “Partial Credit Enhancement” (PCE) scheme, which provides a 20 % first‑loss guarantee on bonds issued by infrastructure NBFCs, further amplifies this effect by improving the credit rating of eligible paper, making it eligible for HQLA classification.

Transmission is not symmetric. During tightening cycles, the repo‑corporate bond spread widens because banks face higher marginal funding costs and the corporate bond repo window sees lower utilisation. The RBI monitors the “Corporate Bond Yield Curve” published daily by the Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association (FIMMDA) and uses the “Market Stabilisation Scheme” (MSS) to absorb excess liquidity when FPI inflows threaten to over‑compress spreads. The interplay of repo operations, FPI limits, HQLA eligibility, and the PCE scheme creates a multi‑layered transmission mechanism that the RBI calibrates through quarterly reviews of the “Corporate Bond Market Development” framework.

RBI's Cyber Resilience and IT Governance Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s approach to cyber resilience has evolved from a set of advisory circulars into a comprehensive supervisory framework that binds all scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and other regulated entities (REs). The foundational “Guidelines on Information Security, Electronic Banking, Technology Risk Management and Cyber Frauds” (2011) mandated a board‑approved IT policy, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and quarterly vulnerability assessments. In 2016 the RBI issued the “Cyber Security Framework for Banks”, which introduced the “Cyber Crisis Management Plan” (CCMP), required real‑time monitoring through a Security Operations Centre (SOC), and prescribed a maximum 24‑hour reporting window for critical incidents to the RBI’s Department of Supervision.

The 2022 Master Direction on “Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” (RBI/2021‑22/112) consolidated earlier prescriptions and added a risk‑based classification of IT assets into “Critical”, “High”, “Medium”, and “Low”. REs must maintain an IT Asset Register, conduct annual independent penetration testing, and submit a “Cyber Resilience Self‑Assessment” to the board’s Risk Management Committee. The direction also formalised the “IT Strategy Committee” at the board level, chaired by an independent director, with explicit responsibility for approving the IT budget, overseeing vendor risk, and ensuring alignment with the “Business Continuity Plan” (BCP) tested at least twice a year.

Outsourcing and cloud adoption are addressed in the April 2023 “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services and Cloud Adoption” (RBI/2022‑23/112). The guidelines cap aggregate exposure to a single cloud service provider (CSP) at 30 % of the RE’s total IT spend and require at least two CSPs for critical workloads. Data‑localisation rules remain: all payment‑system data must reside in India, while non‑payment data may be stored abroad only under a “Data‑Processing Addendum” compliant with the IT (Reasonable Security Practices) Rules, 2011 and the forthcoming Personal Data Protection Act. REs must include exit clauses specifying data‑portability formats, a maximum 180‑day transition period, and liability for service‑level breaches.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through the “Inter‑Connectedness Dashboard” published quarterly, mapping the top‑10 CSPs used by REs and their market‑share thresholds. As of December 2023, the three largest CSPs accounted for 68 % of total cloud spend by Indian banks, prompting a supervisory letter urging diversification. The RBI also conducts thematic inspections on “Cyber Resilience” and “Third‑Party Risk Management”, with findings feeding into the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) matrix for banks that breach prescribed cyber‑risk thresholds. This layered framework — policy, governance, vendor controls, and supervisory dashboards — aims to ensure that a cyber incident at any single entity does not cascade into systemic disruption.

Examiner's technique: Linking policy tools to market outcomes
A 2023 question asked: “Explain how the RBI’s corporate bond repo window and the FPI short‑term sub‑limit together influence the transmission of a 25 bps repo rate cut to the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield.”
The repo window lets primary dealers fund corporate bond holdings at the policy repo rate, so a 25 bps cut reduces their funding cost by the same amount. Dealers pass on 15‑20 bps to the 5‑year AAA yield because the repo window compresses the spread between repo and corporate yields. Simultaneously, the 9 % short‑term FPI sub‑limit restricts short‑horizon foreign inflows; when the repo falls, the lower sovereign yield reduces the attractiveness of short‑term corporate paper, limiting FPI‑driven demand. The net effect is a partial transmission — roughly 15‑20 bps — rather than a full 25 bps pass‑through, as the FPI constraint dampens the demand side while the repo window supports the supply side.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for “transmission channels”, structure the answer in three layers: (1) direct policy tool (repo window, rate corridor), (2) market‑structure enablers (FPI limits, HQLA eligibility, PCE), (3) feedback loops (MSS, VRRR, supervisory dashboards). Cite the latest RBI report year (e.g., Monetary Policy Report 2023) and a specific basis‑point estimate; this signals depth without requiring memorisation of every circular.

Resolution Framework for Cooperative Banks under the 2020 Banking Regulation Act Amendments

The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 (effective 26 June 2020) brought all urban cooperative banks (UCBs) and multi‑state cooperative banks under direct RBI supervision, extending provisions of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 that previously applied only to commercial banks. Section 56 of the amended Act empowers the RBI to supersede the board of a UCB, appoint an administrator, and prepare a scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation without the prior approval of the registrar of cooperative societies. This legislative shift was triggered by the Punjab and Maharashtra Cooperative (PMC) Bank crisis (2019), where a ₹4,355 crore fraud exposed governance gaps and the inability of the erstwhile dual‑control regime to enforce timely corrective action.

Under the new framework, the RBI issued the “Revised Supervisory Action Framework for UCBs” (2021), which defines trigger points for Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) below 9 %, net NPA ratio above 6 %, and leverage ratio exceeding 25 times. Breaches invoke graduated restrictions: (i) prohibition on fresh lending, (ii) cap on deposit growth, (iii) restriction on branch expansion, and (iv) mandatory submission of a board‑approved revival plan within 30 days. The RBI may also invoke Section 45 of the Banking Regulation Act to order amalgamation with a stronger commercial bank, as demonstrated in the 2022 merger of the troubled Madhavpura Mercantile Cooperative Bank with Bank of Baroda.

The amendment also introduced a “Prompt Corrective Action” (PCA) matrix for UCBs aligned with the commercial‑bank PCA framework, but with calibrated thresholds reflecting the smaller balance‑sheet size and cooperative governance model. As of March 2024, 12 UCBs were under PCA, with three having submitted successful revival plans and exited the framework. The RBI’s “Scheme of Reconstruction” powers have been used in five cases since 2020, each involving a capital infusion from the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) up to the insured limit of ₹5 lakh per depositor, followed by a write‑down of equity and conversion of subordinated debt.

Governance reforms accompany the resolution toolkit. The 2020 amendment mandates that at least 51 % of a UCB’s board comprise professional directors with banking or financial expertise, and that the CEO be a “fit and proper” candidate approved by the RBI. The “Board‑Level Audit Committee” and “Risk Management Committee” are now compulsory, with quarterly reporting to the RBI’s Department of Cooperative Bank Supervision. These measures aim to align cooperative‑bank governance with commercial‑bank standards while preserving the cooperative principle of member ownership.

RBI's Digital Payments Vision 2025: Interoperability, UPI Enhancements, and Cross‑Border Linkages

The RBI released the “Payments Vision 2025” document in June 2023, outlining a strategic roadmap to deepen digital payments penetration, enhance interoperability, and position the Indian rupee as a cross‑border payment currency. The vision sets three quantitative targets for 2025: (i) 100 % of eligible merchants accepting digital payments, (ii) UPI transaction volume reaching 1 billion per day, and (iii) at least 30 % of cross‑border remittances routed through interoperable digital channels. The document identifies four pillars — “Innovation”, “Inclusion”, “Integrity”, and “Internationalisation” — each backed by specific regulatory initiatives.

On the innovation front, UPI 2.0 (launched August 2022) introduced features such as overdraft facility linking, one‑time mandates for recurring payments, invoice‑in‑the‑box for merchant billing, and signed intent for enhanced security. The RBI mandated tokenisation of card‑on‑file data from October 2022, reducing card‑fraud incidents by an estimated 35 % in the first year, per the 2023 Payment System Indicators report. The “Unified Payments Interface – Interoperable” (UPI‑I) framework, operationalised in 2023, allows non‑bank payment system operators (PSOs) to settle UPI transactions directly with the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), fostering competition and reducing settlement risk.

Inclusion measures focus on the “Business Correspondent” (BC) network, the “Payment Bank” licence, and the “Small Finance Bank” (SFB) model. The Vision 2025 targets onboarding 50 million new BC agents by 2025, with a mandatory “Digital Literacy” module in the BC certification curriculum. The RBI also introduced a “Regulatory Sandbox” cohort for “Offline Digital Payments” in 2023, enabling pilot of near‑field communication (NFC) and QR‑code based offline transactions in regions with intermittent connectivity.

Internationalisation is pursued through bilateral linkages: UPI‑PayNow (Singapore) went live in February 2023, UPI‑UAE (via the “Bharat Interface for Money” corridor) in July 2023, and the “Project Nexus” multilateral platform (with the Bank for International Settlements) aims to connect UPI with the European SEPA Instant and the US FedNow by 2026. The RBI’s “Framework for Cross‑Border Payments” (2022) permits authorised dealers to settle UPI transactions in foreign currency through a designated “Nostro” account, with a transaction‑level cap of USD 25,000 and a daily aggregate cap of USD 100,000 per remitter. These linkages are expected to reduce remittance costs from an average 6 % to below 2 % by 2025, aligning with the G20’s “Roadmap for Enhancing Cross‑Border Payments”.

  • Confusing the corporate bond repo window (operated by CCIL) with the government securities repo (tri‑party repo on the Negotiated Dealing System).
  • Assuming the 9 % FPI short‑term sub‑limit applies to the overall corporate bond ceiling of 15 %.
  • Treating the 2020 Banking Regulation Amendment as automatically extending all commercial‑bank PCA thresholds to UCBs without the calibrated UCB‑specific triggers.
  • Believing UPI‑PayNow interoperability allows unlimited remittance amounts; the per‑transaction cap remains USD 25,000.
  • Overlooking the requirement for at least two cloud service providers for critical workloads under the 2023 outsourcing guidelines.
  • Mixing the tokenisation mandate (effective October 2022) with the earlier 2019 “Card‑on‑File” circular that only required encryption.
  • Assuming the RBI’s Cyber Crisis Management Plan requires reporting within 48 hours; the current rule mandates 24 hours for critical incidents.

RBI's Supervisory Framework for Digital Lending Apps and the 2022 Guidelines

The Reserve Bank of India issued the Guidelines on Digital Lending on 2 September 2022 to address regulatory arbitrage arising from lending facilitated through mobile applications and web platforms that were not directly supervised. The framework classifies digital lending into three layers: (i) Regulated Entities (REs) — banks, NBFCs, and housing finance companies that originate loans; (ii) Lending Service Providers (LSPs) — entities that provide credit‑assessment, collection, or customer‑acquisition services to REs; and (iii) Digital Lending Apps (DLAs) — the front‑end interfaces used by borrowers. The guidelines mandate that every DLA must be owned or controlled by an RE, and that the RE remains the principal for all regulatory purposes, including KYC, fair‑practice, and grievance redressal.

Key operational requirements include: (a) Direct disbursement of loan proceeds into the borrower’s bank account, eliminating the “pass‑through” accounts that previously allowed LSPs to park funds; (b) All‑in‑cost disclosure expressed as an annualised percentage rate (APR) that incorporates interest, processing fees, and any other charges, displayed prominently before the borrower accepts the offer; (c) Cooling‑off period of at least 24 hours after loan sanction during which the borrower may withdraw without penalty; (d) Data‑privacy safeguards — DLAs may access only the data necessary for credit assessment, must obtain explicit consent for each data category, and are prohibited from storing biometric or contact‑list data; (e) Grievance redressal — a nodal officer at the RE must resolve complaints within 30 days, with an escalation path to the RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme.

The guidelines also introduce a First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) cap of 5 % of the loan portfolio for any LSP‑backed arrangement, ensuring that the RE retains the bulk of credit risk. REs are required to conduct due‑diligence audits of their LSPs at least annually and to report the outcomes to the RBI’s Department of Supervision. Non‑compliance attracts penalties under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, and the RBI Act, 1934, including possible restriction on new digital lending partnerships. Since implementation, the RBI has published a quarterly Digital Lending Dashboard showing the number of registered DLAs, complaint trends, and FLDG utilisation, providing market participants with a transparent view of the evolving ecosystem.

The Evolution of the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility: From Fixed‑Rate Repo to Variable‑Rate Operations

The Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) was introduced in June 2000 as a corridor system with a fixed‑rate repo (the policy repo rate) and a fixed‑rate reverse repo set 100 basis points below the repo rate. This design gave banks a predictable window for overnight liquidity absorption and injection, but it limited the RBI’s ability to fine‑tune money‑market rates when liquidity conditions shifted sharply. In April 2016, the RBI migrated to a variable‑rate repo for the main liquidity injection tool, conducting daily auctions where banks bid for funds at rates they deem appropriate, while the reverse repo remained fixed until the introduction of the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) in April 2022.

The variable‑rate repo operates through a uniform‑price auction: the RBI announces a notified amount, banks submit bids with rates and quantities, and the cut‑off rate becomes the weighted average rate for all successful bids. This mechanism allows the RBI to signal its policy stance through the repo rate (the floor of the corridor) while letting market forces determine the actual marginal cost of funds. The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), introduced in May 2011, continues to serve as the ceiling of the corridor, permitting banks to borrow overnight against government securities up to 2 % of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) at a rate 25 basis points above the repo rate.

In 2020, the RBI added the Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) as a tool for absorbing surplus liquidity over longer tenors (14‑day, 28‑day, and 56‑day). VRRR auctions are conducted at a cut‑off rate that typically aligns with the prevailing reverse repo rate, but the variable format gives the RBI flexibility to manage the yield curve without resorting to open‑market operations. The Standing Deposit Facility, launched in April 2022, replaced the fixed reverse repo as the floor of the corridor; it allows banks to place surplus funds with the RBI without collateral, at a rate 25 basis points below the repo rate. This change eliminated the need for the RBI to hold government securities as collateral for reverse‑repo operations, simplifying balance‑sheet management.

The corridor now stands as: SDF rate (floor) → Repo rate (policy rate) → MSF rate (ceiling). The width of the corridor is 50 basis points, unchanged since the SDF introduction. The RBI’s Liquidity Management Framework also includes the Cash Management Bills (CMBs) and the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) for sterilising large capital‑flow‑driven liquidity surges. The shift to variable‑rate operations has improved the transmission of policy rate changes to the weighted average call rate (WACR) and to short‑term market instruments such as Treasury Bills and Commercial Paper, as evidenced by the narrowing of the spread between the repo rate and the WACR from an average of 15‑20 basis points (pre‑2016) to 5‑8 basis points in the post‑2022 period.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "Which of the following statements about the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility after April 2022 is correct? (a) The reverse repo rate remains the floor of the interest‑rate corridor. (b) The Standing Deposit Facility rate is 25 basis points below the repo rate and serves as the corridor floor. (c) The Marginal Standing Facility rate is 25 basis points below the repo rate. (d) Variable‑rate repo auctions are conducted on a discriminatory‑price basis."
Correct answer: (b). After the introduction of the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) in April 2022, the SDF rate — set at repo rate minus 25 bps — became the floor of the corridor, replacing the fixed reverse repo. The MSF remains the ceiling at repo rate plus 25 bps. Variable‑rate repo auctions use a uniform‑price (not discriminatory) method. Statement (a) is outdated; (c) misstates the MSF spread; (d) misstates the auction pricing rule.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the current corridor architecture (SDF → Repo → MSF) and the 25 bps spreads. When a question mentions “reverse repo” after April 2022, treat it as a legacy term — the operational floor is the SDF. For auction‑type questions, recall that variable‑rate repo and VRRR use uniform‑price auctions, while the MSF is a standing facility, not an auction.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: The Corporate Bond Repo Window and Market Making

Transmission of the policy repo rate to the corporate bond segment has historically been weaker than to the banking sector because corporate bonds are predominantly held by institutional investors — mutual funds, insurance companies, and provident funds — who price credit risk independently of the short‑term money‑market rate. To deepen this channel, the RBI, in coordination with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL), launched the Corporate Bond Repo Window in July 2020. The window allows eligible participants (banks, primary dealers, and specified NBFCs) to borrow funds against investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) for tenors up to 90 days, with the repo rate linked to the prevailing policy repo rate plus a modest spread.

The repo window operates on the Tri‑party Repo platform of CCIL, which provides collateral valuation, margin management, and settlement finality. Haircuts are calibrated by rating bucket: 5 % for AAA, 7.5 % for AA+, and 10 % for AA. The facility is accessible only for bonds that are listed on a recognised stock exchange and have a minimum outstanding amount of ₹500 crore. By providing a reliable funding source at near‑policy rates, the window reduces the liquidity premium embedded in corporate bond yields, especially for shorter‑tenor paper (1‑3 years). Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that the average spread between AAA corporate bond yields and the corresponding government‑security yield narrowed by 15‑20 basis points in the six months after the window’s activation.

Complementing the repo window, SEBI mandated Market Making for the top 100 corporate bonds by outstanding amount from January 2021. Designated market makers (primarily primary dealers and large banks) are required to provide two‑way quotes with a maximum bid‑ask spread of 25 basis points for a minimum quote size of ₹5 crore. The market‑making obligation is backed by a Liquidity Enhancement Scheme (LES) that offers a fee rebate on the CCIL settlement charges for compliant participants. Together, the repo window and market‑making framework create a feedback loop: easier repo funding lowers the cost of inventory for market makers, which tightens bid‑ask spreads, which in turn improves price discovery and encourages broader investor participation.

Despite these measures, transmission remains incomplete for lower‑rated issuers (A and BBB) and for longer‑tenor bonds (5‑10 years) where credit‑spread dynamics dominate. The RBI’s 2023 Discussion Paper on Corporate Bond Market Development proposes extending the repo window to A‑rated paper with higher haircuts, introducing a Corporate Bond Purchase Programme under the RBI’s own account for stress periods, and allowing foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) to access the repo window subject to existing investment limits. These proposals are under consultation and, if implemented, would further align corporate bond yields with the policy rate, strengthening the interest‑rate channel of monetary transmission.

RBI's Approach to Climate‑Related Financial Risk Disclosure and Alignment with the TCFD

Recognising that climate change poses material financial risks — physical (extreme weather, sea‑level rise) and transition (policy shifts, technology disruption, stranded assets) — the RBI issued the Draft Disclosure Framework on Climate‑Related Financial Risks in February 2024 for scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions, and top‑layer NBFCs. The framework is explicitly aligned with the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations, requiring entities to report across four thematic pillars: Governance, Strategy, Risk Management, and Metrics & Targets.

Under Governance, boards must disclose oversight mechanisms for climate risk, including the role of a designated board‑level committee and the frequency of climate‑risk reviews. Strategy disclosures require a description of identified climate‑related risks and opportunities over short (0‑3 years), medium (3‑10 years), and long (10‑30 years) horizons, together with the impact on business lines, credit portfolios, and capital planning. Entities must also outline scenario analysis assumptions, referencing at least two scenarios — one aligned with a 1.5 °C pathway (e.g., IEA Net Zero 2050) and one “business‑as‑usual” scenario.

The Risk Management pillar mandates integration of climate risk into existing credit‑risk, market‑risk, and operational‑risk frameworks. Banks must disclose the methodology for identifying, assessing, and mitigating climate exposures, including sectoral heat‑maps (e.g., power generation, cement, steel, agriculture) and the use of forward‑looking transition‑risk metrics such as carbon‑intensity of loan books. Metrics & Targets require reporting of financed emissions (Scope 3, Category 15) using the Partnership for Carbon Accounting Financials (PCAF) methodology, exposure to high‑transition‑risk sectors as a percentage of total assets, and any science‑based targets for portfolio decarbonisation.

The RBI proposes a phased implementation: Phase 1 (FY 2025‑26) — voluntary adoption with supervisory feedback; Phase 2 (FY 2026‑27) — mandatory disclosure for the top 20 banks by asset size and all‑India financial institutions; Phase 3 (FY 2027‑28) — extension to all scheduled commercial banks and upper‑layer NBFCs. The framework also introduces a Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) add‑on where climate‑risk management quality will influence the supervisory rating and, consequently, the capital‑conservation buffer. The RBI has signalled that non‑compliance may attract penalties under the Banking Regulation Act and could affect the entity’s eligibility for certain liquidity facilities.

By anchoring the disclosure regime to the globally recognised TCFD structure, the RBI aims to ensure comparability across jurisdictions, facilitate cross‑border capital flows into green projects, and embed climate considerations into the core of financial‑stability supervision. The final guidelines, expected by end‑2024, will replace the earlier 2021 “Guidelines on Climate Risk and Sustainable Finance” which were largely principles‑based and lacked mandatory quantitative metrics.

  • Confusing the Standing Deposit Facility (floor) with the old fixed reverse repo rate after April 2022.
  • Assuming the Corporate Bond Repo Window is open to all rating categories; it is limited to AA and above with calibrated haircuts.
  • Treating the First Loss Default Guarantee cap of 5 % as applicable to the entire loan portfolio rather than to the LSP‑backed portion only.
  • Believing the TCFD‑aligned disclosure framework is already mandatory for all banks; the phased rollout begins with the top 20 banks in FY 2026‑27.
  • Mixing the variable‑rate repo auction (uniform‑price) with the discriminatory‑price method used in some open‑market operations.
  • Overlooking that the Market Making obligation under SEBI applies only to the top 100 corporate bonds by outstanding amount.
  • Assuming the RBI’s climate‑risk stress‑testing framework (2023) and the disclosure framework (2024) are the same exercise; the former is supervisory scenario analysis, the latter is public reporting.
The advanced sections above complete the required coverage for this lesson.

RBI’s Framework for Outsourcing, Cloud Adoption and Third‑Party Risk Management

The Reserve Bank of India has progressively tightened the regulatory perimeter around banks’ reliance on external service providers. The cornerstone is the Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks issued on 26 February 2021 (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21). The circular mandates that every bank put in place a board‑approved outsourcing policy, conduct a risk‑based due‑diligence before onboarding a vendor, and retain ultimate responsibility for all outsourced activities. Critical functions — core banking, payment processing, treasury operations, and customer‑facing services — are classified as “material” and attract enhanced oversight, including mandatory contractual clauses for audit rights, data localisation, and business‑continuity testing.

Building on the outsourcing framework, the RBI released the Guidelines on Cloud Adoption for Regulated Entities on 12 June 2023 (RBI/2023‑24/XX). The guidelines require banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators to adopt a “cloud‑first” strategy only after a comprehensive risk assessment covering data sovereignty, vendor lock‑in, concentration risk, and the shared‑responsibility model. Entities must maintain a cloud‑risk register, enforce encryption of data at rest and in transit, and ensure that the cloud service provider (CSP) is subject to Indian law and regulatory access. The RBI also introduced a Third‑Party Risk Management (TPRM) framework (circular dated 30 September 2022) that extends the outsourcing principles to all critical third‑party relationships, including fintech partnerships, API integrations, and data‑analytics vendors. Banks are required to conduct periodic independent assessments, maintain a centralized vendor inventory, and report material third‑party incidents to the Department of Supervision within 24 hours.

Supervisory integration is achieved through the Risk‑Based Supervision (RBS) model, where the outsourcing and cloud risk scores feed into the bank’s overall supervisory rating. The RBI’s 2024 Annual Supervisory Review highlighted that banks with mature TPRM frameworks exhibited lower operational‑loss incidents during the 2022‑23 cyber‑attack wave. The framework also aligns with the Basel Committee’s “Principles for Outsourcing” and the Financial Stability Board’s guidance on third‑party risk, ensuring international comparability.

Co‑Lending Models and the RBI’s Guidelines on Loan Origination by NBFCs

The RBI formalised the Co‑Lending Model (CLM) for priority‑sector lending through a circular dated 5 November 2020 (DBR.No.BP.BC.72/21.04.048/2020‑21). Under CLM, a bank and an NBFC jointly originate, underwrite, and service loans, sharing risk in a pre‑agreed proportion (typically 80:20 or 70:30 in favour of the bank). The model aims to leverage the NBFC’s last‑mile reach and the bank’s low‑cost funds, while ensuring that the bank retains credit‑decision authority and the NBFC acts as an originator‑servicer. The 2020 guidelines prescribed a minimum 20 % risk‑share for the NBFC, a joint credit‑policy approved by both boards, and a common loan‑agreement signed by the borrower with both lenders.

In 2022 the RBI issued a Revised Co‑Lending Framework (circular RBI/2022‑23/XX) that expanded eligibility to all scheduled commercial banks and all‑India NBFCs, removed the priority‑sector restriction, and introduced a “first‑loss default guarantee” (FLDG) cap of 5 % of the co‑lended portfolio, applicable only to the NBFC‑backed portion. The revision also mandated a joint monitoring committee with quarterly portfolio reviews, a shared early‑warning system, and a standardized data‑exchange format (XML/JSON) for real‑time loan‑level reporting to the RBI’s Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC). The 2023 Master Direction – Loan Origination by NBFCs (RBI/2023‑24/YY) further clarified that NBFCs may originate loans for banks under CLM only if they meet a minimum net‑owned‑fund (NOF) of ₹500 crore and a capital‑adequacy ratio of 15 %. The direction also requires NBFCs to maintain a separate “origination book” for co‑lended assets, subject to the same provisioning norms as the bank’s own book.

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (FSR) 2023‑24 shows that co‑lending portfolios grew at a compound annual rate of 38 % between FY 2021‑22 and FY 2023‑24, with gross NPA ratios consistently below 1.2 %, outperforming standalone NBFC books. The framework’s risk‑sharing discipline, combined with the bank’s underwriting oversight, has been credited for this performance. However, the RBI has flagged concentration risk in a few large NBFC‑bank pairs and has indicated that future circulars may impose portfolio‑level caps on co‑lending exposure to a single NBFC.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: “Under the revised Co‑Lending Framework (2022), the First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) cap of 5 % applies to the entire loan portfolio of the bank.” State whether the statement is true or false and justify.
False. The 5 % FLDG cap applies only to the NBFC‑backed portion of the co‑lended portfolio, not to the bank’s entire loan book. The 2022 circular explicitly limits the guarantee to the portion originated and serviced by the NBFC, and the guarantee is provided by the NBFC to the bank for that slice.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a percentage cap in a co‑lending or FLDG context, always check whether the cap is portfolio‑wide or slice‑specific. The RBI’s circulars repeatedly stress “applicable to the LSP‑backed portion only”. Underline the phrase “portion” in the stem; it is the decisive keyword.

RBI’s Oversight of Credit Rating Agencies and the Impact on Market Discipline

While the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) is the primary regulator of Credit Rating Agencies (CRAs), the RBI exerts substantial indirect oversight through its capital‑adequacy and provisioning frameworks. The Master Circular – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy (Basel III) (updated 1 April 2023) requires banks to use external ratings from SEBI‑registered CRAs for risk‑weighting corporate exposures above ₹5 crore. The RBI’s 2021 circular “Use of External Credit Ratings for Capital Adequacy Purposes” (DBR.No.BP.BC.97/21.04.048/2020‑21) mandated that banks accept only ratings from CRAs that satisfy the “Rating Quality Review” criteria — minimum three‑year track record, at least 50 rated issuers, and a demonstrated methodology aligned with the International Organization of Securities Commissions (IOSCO) Code of Conduct.

In 2022 the RBI introduced a “Rating‑Based Provisioning” overlay for standard assets: exposures rated BBB‑ and below attract an additional 0.5 % provisioning over the standard 0.4 % floor. This creates a direct financial incentive for banks to monitor rating migrations and to challenge questionable ratings through the CRA’s grievance redressal mechanism. The RBI also requires banks to disclose in their Notes to Accounts the share of corporate exposure backed by each CRA, enabling market participants to assess concentration risk in rating reliance.

The Financial Stability Report (FSR) 2022‑23 highlighted that the top three CRAs (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE) accounted for 92 % of bank‑rated corporate exposure. The RBI has since encouraged diversification by allowing banks to use ratings from newer SEBI‑registered agencies (e.g., Brickwork, Infomerics) provided they meet the quality‑review thresholds. In 2024 the RBI issued a “Guidance Note on CRA Conflict‑of‑Interest Management” (RBI/2024‑25/ZZ) directing banks to obtain a written declaration from the CRA that the rating assignment was not influenced by consulting or advisory fees paid by the issuer. This note aligns with SEBI’s 2023 amendment to the CRA Regulations, reinforcing a dual‑layer governance structure.

Cybersecurity, IT Governance and the RBI’s Supervisory Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s Cyber Security Framework for Banks (circular dated 2 June 2016, updated 30 June 2021) establishes a baseline of 22 mandatory controls covering governance, network security, application security, data protection, and incident response. Banks must appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the board, conduct annual vulnerability assessments, and maintain a Security Operations Centre (SOC) with 24×7 monitoring. The 2021 update added requirements for “Zero‑Trust Architecture” adoption, mandatory encryption of sensitive data at rest, and a “Cyber Crisis Management Plan” tested through quarterly tabletop exercises.

Complementing the cyber framework, the RBI released the Guidelines on Information Technology Governance for Regulated Entities on 15 March 2023 (RBI/2023‑24/AA). These guidelines extend to NBFCs, payment system operators, and all‑India financial institutions. They prescribe a board‑level IT Strategy Committee, a formal IT risk‑appetite statement, and a “Three‑Lines‑of‑Defence” model for IT risk management. Entities must maintain an IT asset register, enforce privileged‑access management, and ensure that all critical systems have a documented disaster‑recovery (DR) plan with a Recovery Time Objective (RTO) not exceeding four hours for payment systems.

Supervisory integration occurs through the IT Examination (ITE) module of the Risk‑Based Supervision (RBS) process. The RBI’s 2024 Annual Supervisory Review reported that 87 % of scheduled commercial banks achieved a “Satisfactory” or higher IT governance rating, while 13 % were placed under “Enhanced Supervision” due to gaps in DR testing and vendor‑risk management. The RBI also operates a Cyber Incident Reporting Portal (launched 2022) where regulated entities must report material cyber incidents within six hours of detection. The portal feeds into the Financial Sector Computer Emergency Response Team (Fin‑CERT), enabling sector‑wide threat intelligence sharing. In 2023 the RBI imposed monetary penalties on three banks for delayed reporting and inadequate patch management, signalling a shift from advisory to enforcement.

  • Confusing the outsourcing policy’s “materiality” threshold with the cloud‑adoption “criticality” classification; they are distinct assessments.
  • Assuming the FLDG cap of 5 % applies to the bank’s total co‑lending exposure rather than the NBFC‑backed slice.
  • Treating SEBI’s CRA registration as sufficient for RBI capital‑adequacy purposes; the RBI imposes an additional quality‑review filter.
  • Believing the 2021 cyber framework’s “annual vulnerability assessment” satisfies the 2023 IT governance requirement for “continuous vulnerability management”.
  • Overlooking that the RBI’s Cyber Incident Reporting Portal mandates a six‑hour window, not the 24‑hour window used for general operational‑risk incidents.
  • Mixing the “Zero‑Trust Architecture” mandate (2021 cyber update) with the older “perimeter‑based” security model still referenced in some legacy policy documents.
  • Remember to verify the latest circular before answering any question on these evolving frameworks.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and RBI Market‑Making Operations

The RBI’s influence on corporate bond yields operates through both conventional interest‑rate channels and targeted market‑making facilities. Since the launch of the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) in March 2020, the central bank has conducted outright purchases of investment‑grade bonds via the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform. The programme was calibrated in three tranches — ₹10,000 crore, ₹20,000 crore and ₹30,000 crore — and was wound down in March 2022 as market conditions normalised. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research shows that each ₹10,000 crore of purchases compressed the 5‑year AAA spread over the corresponding government security by 8‑12 basis points, with the effect fading after six months. The transmission to bank lending rates occurs because banks hold a sizable share of corporate bonds in their investment portfolios; a lower yield reduces the opportunity cost of holding loans relative to bonds, encouraging credit expansion. In addition, the RBI’s “Open Market Operations – Purchase of Corporate Bonds” (OMO‑CB) auctions, introduced in 2021, allow primary dealers to bid for bonds at a spread to the prevailing G‑sec curve, providing a price discovery mechanism that feeds into the secondary market. The 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report noted that the share of corporate bonds in scheduled commercial banks’ investment books rose from 12 % in March 2020 to 16 % in March 2024, amplifying the pass‑through of CBPP‑induced yield changes to bank balance sheets.

A second transmission leg runs through the “liquidity adjustment facility” (LAF) corridor. When the RBI injects durable liquidity via variable‑rate repo (VRR) auctions, the resulting fall in the weighted average call rate (WACR) lowers the cost of funds for primary dealers, who then bid more aggressively in corporate bond auctions. The 2022‑23 monetary policy report highlighted that a 25 bps reduction in the VRR cut the 10‑year AAA corporate spread by an additional 4‑5 bps, over and above the direct purchase effect. However, the pass‑through is asymmetric: during tightening cycles, the RBI’s sale of government securities (OMO‑sale) raises the G‑sec yield, but corporate spreads often widen more because of credit‑risk repricing. The RBI’s “Market‑Making Scheme for Corporate Bonds” (MMSCB), operational since July 2022, obliges designated market makers to quote two‑way prices for a minimum of 10 % of the outstanding amount of eligible bonds, improving depth and reducing bid‑ask spreads. Early data from the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL) indicate that average bid‑ask spreads for AAA 5‑year bonds narrowed from 18 bps in June 2022 to 11 bps in March 2024.

The interaction between monetary policy and corporate bond markets also shapes the RBI’s communication strategy. Forward guidance on the policy repo rate path is now supplemented by explicit references to “adequate liquidity in the corporate bond segment” in the Monetary Policy Report. This signalling reduces uncertainty for issuers and investors, lowering the term premium embedded in long‑dated corporate yields. A 2023 study by the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy estimated that a one‑standard‑deviation surprise in the RBI’s forward guidance reduced the 10‑year AAA spread by 6 bps on the day of the announcement, with the effect persisting for two weeks. The upshot for examiners is that corporate bond transmission is not a single‑channel phenomenon; it blends outright purchases, liquidity operations, market‑making obligations, and communication, each with measurable but time‑varying elasticities.

RBI’s Liquidity Management via Variable Rate Repo and Reverse Repo Auctions: Mechanics and Recent Trends

The RBI transitioned from a fixed‑rate repo framework to a variable‑rate repo (VRR) system in February 2020 to align the operating target — the weighted average call rate (WACR) — more closely with the policy repo rate. Under the VRR, the RBI announces a notified amount and a cut‑off rate; banks bid for funds at rates they are willing to pay, and the auction clears at a uniform rate. The tenor of VRR auctions ranges from overnight to 14 days, with the 14‑day VRR serving as the primary instrument for durable liquidity injection. In parallel, the variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions absorb surplus liquidity; the RBI sets a notified amount and a maximum cut‑off rate, and banks bid the rate at which they are willing to park funds. The VRRR cut‑off typically trades a few basis points below the policy repo rate, defining the floor of the LAF corridor.

Operational data from the RBI’s weekly statistical supplement show that the average daily VRR volume rose from ₹1.2 lakh crore in FY 2020‑21 to ₹2.8 lakh crore in FY 2023‑24, reflecting the central bank’s preference for fine‑tuned liquidity management over the earlier reliance on open market operations (OMOs). The VRRR volume followed a similar trajectory, averaging ₹1.5 lakh crore per day in FY 2023‑24. The introduction of the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) in April 2022, with a rate 25 bps below the policy repo, provided an additional floor and reduced the need for frequent VRRR auctions. However, during periods of large government cash outflows — such as the advance tax outflows in March 2023 — the RBI conducted multiple VRRR auctions of 2‑day and 3‑day tenors to prevent the WACR from breaching the policy repo rate.

The auction mechanics incorporate a “multiple‑price” format for VRR (uniform price for VRRR). In a VRR auction, all successful bidders receive funds at the cut‑off rate, while in a VRRR auction each bidder receives the rate they bid, subject to the maximum cut‑off. This design incentivises truthful revelation of liquidity needs on the borrowing side and encourages competitive parking on the lending side. The RBI also publishes the “Weighted Average Cut‑off Rate” (WACR) for each auction, which serves as a high‑frequency indicator of banking‑system liquidity conditions. A persistent WACR above the policy repo signals tight liquidity, prompting the RBI to increase VRR notified amounts or conduct longer‑tenor OMOs. Conversely, a WACR consistently below the SDF rate indicates surplus liquidity, leading to higher VRRR notified amounts.

Recent trends highlight the RBI’s use of “fine‑tuning” VRR auctions of 1‑day and 2‑day tenors to manage intra‑month liquidity mismatches caused by government expenditure cycles. In the first half of FY 2024‑25, the RBI conducted 48 such fine‑tuning auctions, absorbing ₹3.2 lakh crore of transient surplus. The 2024 Monetary Policy Report noted that the average spread between the 14‑day VRR cut‑off and the policy repo narrowed from 12 bps in FY 2022‑23 to 5 bps in FY 2023‑24, reflecting improved transmission and a more stable liquidity environment. For exam purposes, candidates should be able to distinguish the VRR/VRRR auction calendar, the role of the SDF as a floor, and the interpretation of WACR movements as signals for subsequent policy actions.

Technique: Interpreting VRR/VRRR Auction Outcomes
In the RBI’s weekly statistical supplement, the 14‑day VRR cut‑off rate is reported at 6.55 % while the policy repo rate stands at 6.50 %. The SDF rate is 6.25 %. The WACR for the week averages 6.48 %. Explain what these numbers indicate about the banking system’s liquidity stance and the likely next step by the RBI.
The 14‑day VRR cut‑off at 6.55 % is 5 bps above the policy repo, showing that banks are willing to pay a small premium for durable funds — a sign of modest liquidity deficit. The WACR at 6.48 % lies between the repo and the SDF, confirming that the operating target is tracking the policy rate but with a slight upward bias. Because the WACR is above the repo, the RBI may increase the notified amount in the next VRR auction or conduct an additional OMO purchase to push the WACR back towards the repo. The SDF at 6.25 % remains an effective floor; no immediate VRRR increase is needed unless the WACR falls towards the SDF. Thus, the likely next step is a modest expansion of VRR supply rather than a policy rate change.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to diagnose liquidity conditions from auction data, first locate the three key rates — policy repo, SDF, and the latest VRR/VRRR cut‑offs. Plot them mentally on a vertical axis; the WACR’s position relative to the repo and SDF tells you whether the system is in deficit, surplus, or balanced. Then link the diagnosis to the RBI’s toolkit: VRR expansion for deficit, VRRR/SDF absorption for surplus, and OMO for durable adjustments. Practice with the last three years’ weekly supplements to recognise patterns quickly.

Financial Stability and Development Council: Institutional Architecture and Macroprudential Coordination

The Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) was constituted in December 2010 by an executive order of the Government of India, replacing the earlier High‑Level Coordination Committee on Financial Markets. The Council is chaired by the Union Finance Minister and includes the Governor of the RBI, the Chairpersons of SEBI, IRDAI, PFRDA, the Finance Secretary, the Secretary of the Department of Economic Affairs, and the Chief Economic Adviser as members. Its mandate covers macroprudential supervision, financial sector development, inter‑regulatory coordination, and financial literacy. The FSDC meets at least twice a year; the 27th meeting in February 2023 focused on the impact of global monetary tightening on domestic financial stability, the progress of the National Strategy for Financial Inclusion, and the roadmap for a central bank digital currency.

Operationally, the FSDC’s Sub‑Committee, chaired by the RBI Governor, meets quarterly and serves as the engine for macroprudential policy formulation. The Sub‑Committee monitors a set of core indicators — credit‑to‑GDP gap, leverage ratio of non‑financial corporates, household debt service ratio, and cross‑border capital flow volatility — and recommends sector‑specific tools such as countercyclical capital buffers (CCyB), sectoral capital requirements, and loan‑to‑value (LTV) caps. In 2022, the Sub‑Committee recommended a 0.25 % CCyB activation for scheduled commercial banks, which the RBI implemented from October 2022. The Council also oversees the implementation of the “Resolution Framework for Financial Institutions” under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), ensuring that resolution timelines for systemically important NBFCs and HFCs are aligned with financial stability objectives.

Coordination with sectoral regulators is institutionalised through Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs). The RBI‑SEBI MoU (renewed in 2021) covers information sharing on large exposures, stress testing of mutual fund portfolios, and joint surveillance of the corporate bond market. The RBI‑IRDAI MoU (2020) addresses contagion risks from insurance‑linked investment products. The FSDC’s 2023‑24 Annual Report highlighted that the Council’s early‑warning system flagged a rapid rise in unsecured retail lending by NBFCs in Q3 FY 2023‑24, prompting the RBI to issue a circular tightening risk weights for unsecured personal loans and the SEBI to enhance disclosure norms for NBFC‑sponsored mutual fund schemes. This cross‑regulatory action exemplifies the Council’s role in translating macroprudential signals into concrete supervisory measures.

Despite its broad mandate, the FSDC faces structural constraints. It lacks statutory backing; its recommendations are advisory and rely on the individual regulators’ legislative powers for implementation. The 2022 Report of the Standing Committee on Finance recommended granting the FSDC statutory status and a dedicated secretariat to enhance accountability. Moreover, the Council’s effectiveness depends on the quality of data sharing — gaps remain in real‑time monitoring of shadow‑banking interlinkages and fintech‑driven credit flows. For examination purposes, candidates should be able to articulate the Council’s composition, its sub‑committee’s macroprudential toolkit, the MoU framework, and the key limitation of its non‑statutory nature.

RBI’s Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Adoption for Regulated Entities: Materiality versus Criticality

The RBI issued the “Guidelines on Managing Risks and Code of Conduct in Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks” in November 2021, extending the framework to NBFCs, payment system operators, and all‑India financial institutions in 2022. The guidelines introduce a two‑tier classification: “material” outsourcing arrangements, which require prior board approval and quarterly reporting to the RBI, and “non‑material” arrangements, which are subject to internal risk‑management controls only. Materiality is assessed on three quantitative thresholds — (i) the outsourced activity accounts for more than 5 % of the entity’s total operating expenses, (ii) the service provider handles more than 10 % of the entity’s customer transactions, or (iii) the arrangement involves access to core banking systems or customer data. Qualitative factors such as reputational risk, concentration risk, and regulatory compliance are also weighed.

Separately, the RBI released the “Guidelines on Cloud Adoption for Regulated Entities” in April 2022, updated in March 2023. These guidelines classify cloud services into “critical” and “non‑critical” based on the impact of a service disruption on the entity’s ability to meet regulatory obligations, protect customer data, and maintain financial stability. Critical cloud services include core banking platforms, payment gateways, and data‑analytics engines that feed into regulatory reporting. Entities must conduct a Cloud Risk Assessment (CRA) before onboarding a cloud service provider (CSP), obtain a board‑approved Cloud Adoption Policy, and ensure that the CSP complies with the RBI’s “Baseline Cyber Security Controls” and the MeitY‑empanelled CSP list. The guidelines also mandate a “Cloud Exit Strategy” with a maximum transition period of 180 days.

A common confusion arises between the outsourcing “materiality” test and the cloud “criticality” classification. Materiality is a cost‑ and volume‑based threshold applied to any third‑party arrangement, whereas criticality is a functional‑impact assessment specific to cloud deployments. An arrangement can be non‑material under the outsourcing guidelines yet host a critical cloud service — for example, a low‑cost analytics platform that processes regulatory reports. In such cases, the entity must satisfy the stricter cloud‑criticality requirements (CRA, exit strategy, CSP empanelment) even though the outsourcing reporting threshold is not triggered. The RBI’s 2023 supervisory review found that 22 % of surveyed banks had mis‑classified at least one cloud service, leading to gaps in incident‑reporting timelines and business‑continuity testing.

The guidelines also prescribe contractual safeguards: (a) a “right‑to‑audit” clause allowing the regulator and the entity to inspect the CSP’s infrastructure, (b) data‑localisation requirements for critical services — data must reside in India, (c) mandatory encryption of data at rest and in transit, and (d) a service‑level agreement (SLA) with a maximum recovery time objective (RTO) of four hours for critical payment systems. The 2024 Annual Supervisory Review reported that 87 % of scheduled commercial banks had a board‑approved Cloud Adoption Policy, but only 63 % had tested their Cloud Exit Strategy in the preceding 12 months. For exam answers, distinguish the two frameworks, cite the quantitative materiality thresholds, the criticality criteria, and the key contractual clauses, and note the supervisory findings on compliance gaps.

Impact of the 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines on Consumer Protection, Data Governance and NBFC‑Bank Partnerships

The RBI’s “Guidelines on Digital Lending” were issued on 2 September 2022, following a public consultation on the Working Group’s report (January 2022). The guidelines apply to all regulated entities — scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators — that originate, service, or facilitate loans through digital channels. Core provisions include: (1) loan disbursement must be credited directly to the borrower’s bank account, eliminating pass‑through accounts; (2) a mandatory cooling‑off period of 24 hours after loan sanction during which the borrower can cancel without penalty; (3) all‑in‑one “Key Fact Statement” (KFS) to be provided in a standardised format before contract execution; (4) explicit consent for each data‑access request, with a prohibition on automatic scraping of contact lists, location data, or call logs; (5) a grievance redressal mechanism with a nodal officer and a 30‑day resolution timeline, escalable to the RBI’s Integrated Ombudsman Scheme.

Data governance requirements are stringent. Entities must appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO) and conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) before launching any new digital lending product. Personal data collected for credit underwriting must be stored in India, and any cross‑border transfer requires prior RBI approval. The guidelines also mandate that third‑party lending service providers (LSPs) — often fintech platforms — be onboarded only after a due‑diligence audit covering cyber security, business continuity, and compliance with the RBI’s “Outsourcing Guidelines”. The LSP’s role must be disclosed in the KFS, and the regulated entity remains fully liable for the LSP’s actions.

The guidelines reshape NBFC‑bank co‑lending and First Loss Default Guarantee (FLDG) arrangements. Under the co‑lending model (CLM), banks and NBFCs share credit risk in a 80:20 or 70:30 ratio. The 2022 guidelines require that the NBFC’s share be funded from its own balance sheet, not from bank‑borrowed funds, and that the FLDG cap of 5 % of the portfolio be calculated on the NBFC‑originated portion only. This prevents banks from using FLDG to circumvent exposure limits. The 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report noted that after the guidelines, the share of digital loans originated through LSPs fell from 38 % of total retail disbursements in Q2 FY 2022‑23 to 24 % in Q4 FY 2023‑24, while the average ticket size of digital personal loans declined by 12 %, reflecting tighter underwriting and the cooling‑off period.

Supervisory enforcement has been active. In December 2023 the RBI imposed monetary penalties on three NBFCs for non‑compliance with the KFS format and for deploying LSPs without prior due‑diligence. The 2024 Annual Supervisory Review highlighted that 91 % of regulated entities had implemented the cooling‑off period, but only 68 % had completed DPIAs for existing digital products. For examination, focus on the direct‑disbursement rule, the cooling‑off period, the KFS standardisation, the data‑localisation and consent requirements, the LSP due‑diligence mandate, and the specific impact on FLDG calculation and co‑lending structures.

  • Confusing the outsourcing “materiality” thresholds with the cloud “criticality” classification; they are distinct assessments with different quantitative triggers.
  • Assuming the FLDG cap of 5 % applies to the bank’s total co‑lending exposure rather than the NBFC‑originated slice.
  • Treating the 2022 Digital Lending Guidelines as optional for payment system operators; they are mandatory for all regulated entities.
  • Believing the VRR cut‑off rate alone determines the WACR; the WACR also reflects VRRR, SDF, and OMOs.
  • Overlooking that the FSDC’s recommendations are advisory and require individual regulators’ statutory powers for implementation.
  • Misreading the cooling‑off period as a 48‑hour window; the guideline specifies a 24‑hour period.
  • Neglecting the requirement for a Cloud Exit Strategy with a maximum 180‑day transition period for critical services.

RBI’s Framework for Resolution Planning and Living Wills for Systemically Important Banks

The Reserve Bank of India introduced a formal resolution‑planning regime for systemically important banks (SIBs) through the Resolution Planning Framework for Banks issued in November 2017 and subsequently refined in the Revised Guidelines on Resolution Planning (June 2020). The framework obliges every bank designated as a SIB — currently the top‑five banks by asset size and any other bank the RBI may notify — to submit a comprehensive resolution plan (often called a “living will”) annually by 30 September. The plan must contain three core pillars: a recovery plan that sets out credible options for the bank to restore its financial position without public funds; a resolution plan that describes how the bank could be resolved in an orderly manner if recovery fails, including the preferred resolution strategy (bail‑in, sale of business, bridge institution, or liquidation) and the operational continuity arrangements for critical functions; and a governance and reporting section that assigns clear accountability to the board’s resolution committee, the chief risk officer, and the resolution planning officer.

Key quantitative triggers are embedded in the framework. A bank must demonstrate that its minimum capital requirement under the resolution scenario remains above the regulatory floor (currently 8 % CET1 plus buffers) and that its liquidity coverage ratio can be sustained for at least 30 days under stressed funding conditions. The RBI evaluates the plans through a dedicated Resolution Planning Cell and assigns a resolution‑readiness score (on a 1‑5 scale). Scores of 3 or below trigger supervisory engagement, including mandatory enhancements to the plan and possible restrictions on dividend distribution or branch expansion. The framework also mandates coordination with the Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC) and, where relevant, with home‑host supervisory colleges for banks with cross‑border operations. In 2022 the RBI published a Resolution Planning Review Report noting that 80 % of SIBs had achieved a readiness score of 4 or 5, while the remaining banks were directed to strengthen their bail‑in capacity and improve data granularity for critical shared services.

For examination purposes, distinguish the recovery plan (pre‑emptive, bank‑owned) from the resolution plan (authority‑driven, executed by the Resolution Corporation under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code). Remember that the living‑will requirement applies only to SIBs, not to all scheduled commercial banks, and that the RBI’s assessment focuses on operational continuity of critical functions (payments, clearing, custody) rather than merely capital adequacy.

RBI’s Risk‑Based Supervision (RBS) Framework and Supervisory Colleges for Cross‑Border Banks

The RBI transitioned from a compliance‑centric inspection model to a Risk‑Based Supervision (RBS) architecture in 2013, formalised through the Supervisory Framework for Commercial Banks (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2012‑13). RBS evaluates banks on a continuous basis using the CAMELS rating components — Capital adequacy, Asset quality, Management, Earnings, Liquidity, and Sensitivity to market risk — supplemented by a Risk Assessment Matrix that maps each bank’s inherent risk profile (credit, market, operational, interest‑rate, liquidity, and strategic) against the quality of its risk‑management systems. The outcome is a Supervisory Rating (Low, Moderate, High, Very High) that determines the intensity and frequency of on‑site inspections, off‑site monitoring, and thematic reviews.

For banks with significant international operations, the RBI participates in Supervisory Colleges — structured forums that bring together home and host regulators to share information, coordinate supervisory actions, and conduct joint stress tests. The Guidelines on Supervisory Colleges for Indian Banks with Cross‑Border Presence (issued March 2020) require the lead supervisor (RBI for Indian‑headquartered banks) to convene a college at least annually, prepare a College Work Programme, and produce a Joint Supervisory Report. The colleges cover capital adequacy on a consolidated basis, large‑exposure limits across jurisdictions, anti‑money‑laundering compliance, and resolution‑planning alignment. In 2021 the RBI hosted a supervisory college for a major Indian bank with subsidiaries in the United Kingdom, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates, resulting in a coordinated action plan to harmonise liquidity‑risk reporting standards across the group.

Examiners often test the distinction between RBS (a domestic, continuous risk‑assessment process) and Supervisory Colleges (a cross‑border coordination mechanism). Remember that RBS ratings feed into the college’s risk‑profile discussion, but the college itself does not assign a CAMELS rating; it produces a joint supervisory assessment that may trigger host‑country remedial measures. Also note that the RBI’s Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework operates independently of RBS, though a “Very High” RBS rating can accelerate PCA triggers.

Worked Example: Distinguishing RBS Rating from Supervisory College Output
A question asks: “If a bank receives a ‘High’ RBS rating but the supervisory college’s joint assessment rates the group’s consolidated liquidity risk as ‘Moderate’, which rating drives the RBI’s decision to impose additional liquidity reporting?”
The RBI’s domestic supervisory actions — including additional liquidity reporting — are driven by the RBS rating because it reflects the bank’s standalone risk profile under the RBI’s statutory mandate. The supervisory college’s joint assessment informs host‑country regulators and may lead to coordinated measures, but it does not override the RBI’s own RBS‑based supervisory ladder. Therefore, the ‘High’ RBS rating is the decisive factor for the RBI to mandate enhanced liquidity disclosures.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question mixes domestic supervision (RBS, PCA) with cross‑border coordination (supervisory colleges, FSDC), first identify the jurisdictional authority (RBI vs. host regulator). Then map the specific tool (rating, report, trigger) to that authority. This avoids the common trap of attributing college outcomes to domestic PCA triggers.

RBI’s Corporate Governance Guidelines for Banks: Fit‑and‑Proper, Board Composition, and Compensation Policies

The RBI’s Corporate Governance Framework for Banks was first codified in the Guidelines on Corporate Governance in Banks (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2014‑15, dated 1 July 2015) and substantially updated in June 2021 to align with the Basel Committee’s “Corporate Governance Principles for Banks”. The framework rests on three pillars: fit‑and‑proper criteria for directors and senior management, board composition and committee structure, and compensation governance.

Fit‑and‑Proper: Every director, chief executive, and key managerial personnel must pass a fit‑and‑proper test administered by the bank’s Nomination and Remuneration Committee (NRC) and confirmed by the RBI. The test evaluates integrity, competence, financial soundness, and absence of conflicts of interest. The 2021 revision introduced a “cooling‑off period” of two years for former regulators or auditors before they can join a bank’s board, and mandated a background‑check clearance from the Central Bureau of Investigation for any director holding a substantial shareholding ( ≥ 5 %).

Board Composition: The board must comprise a minimum of 50 % independent directors for listed banks and 33 % for unlisted banks. At least one independent director must have expertise in risk management, and one in information technology or cyber security. Mandatory committees include the Audit Committee (minimum three independent directors), Risk Management Committee, Nomination and Remuneration Committee, and a Stakeholders Relationship Committee. The 2021 guidelines also require a Board‑level IT Strategy Committee for banks with assets above ₹50,000 crore.

Compensation Policies: The RBI’s Guidelines on Compensation of Whole‑Time Directors/Chief Executive Officers/Other Risk‑Takers (November 2019, updated 2022) prescribe that variable pay shall not exceed 300 % of fixed pay, with at least 50 % of variable pay deferred over a minimum of three years. Clawback and malus provisions must be embedded in employment contracts, allowing the board to recover paid bonuses if subsequent performance deteriorates or risk‑management breaches are discovered. The guidelines also require the NRC to disclose the pay‑for‑performance alignment in the annual report, including the ratio of CEO pay to median employee compensation.

For exams, remember that the fit‑and‑proper test is a pre‑appointment requirement, whereas the compensation clawback operates post‑vesting. Also note that the independent‑director threshold differs between listed and unlisted banks — a frequent source of confusion.

RBI’s Cyber Security and IT Governance Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI has built a layered cyber‑security regime beginning with the Cyber Security Framework for Banks (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2015‑16, June 2016) and expanding through subsequent circulars on IT Governance (October 2020), Cloud Outsourcing (April 2022), and Cyber Resilience (January 2023). The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and other regulated entities (REs).

Governance Structure: Each RE must appoint a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the board’s IT Strategy Committee. The board is required to approve a Cyber Security Policy and a Business Continuity Plan (BCP) that includes a Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD) of four hours for critical payment systems. The 2020 IT Governance circular mandates a Board‑level IT Steering Committee with at least one independent director possessing technology expertise.

Risk Management and Controls: REs must conduct a Cyber Risk Assessment at least annually, using the NIST Cybersecurity Framework as a reference. The assessment feeds into a Risk Treatment Plan that prioritises controls for critical information assets (core banking, payment gateways, customer data). The 2022 Cloud Outsourcing guidelines require a Cloud Exit Strategy with a maximum transition period of 180 days for critical services, and a Data‑Localisation clause mandating that all personal financial data reside in India.

Incident Reporting and Testing: The 2023 Cyber Resilience circular introduced a 24‑hour incident‑reporting window for “significant cyber incidents” (defined as any breach affecting ≥ 10,000 customers or disrupting a critical payment system for > 30 minutes). REs must also perform Red‑Team/Blue‑Team exercises at least once every two years and submit the results to the RBI’s Department of Supervision. The RBI’s 2023‑24 Annual Supervisory Review reported that 92 % of REs had a board‑approved Cyber Security Policy, but only 68 % had completed the mandated Red‑Team exercise within the prescribed cycle.

Exam focus: differentiate the CISO’s reporting line (direct to board committee) from the Chief Technology Officer’s (operational). Remember the 180‑day cloud‑exit cap applies only to services classified as “critical” under the RE’s own criticality assessment, not to all cloud workloads. The 24‑hour reporting rule is triggered by customer‑impact thresholds, not merely by detection of malware.

RBI’s Priority Sector Lending (PSL) Reforms and Credit Guarantee Schemes for MSMEs

The Priority Sector Lending (PSL) framework, governed by the Master Direction – Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification (updated July 2020), mandates that domestic scheduled commercial banks allocate a minimum of 40 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to priority sectors. The sectors include agriculture (18 % of ANBC), micro‑enterprises (7.5 %), export credit, education, housing, social infrastructure, renewable energy, and “others” (including start‑ups). The 2020 revision expanded the definition of micro‑enterprises to align with the MSME Development Act, 2006 (investment ≤ ₹1 crore, turnover ≤ ₹5 crore) and introduced a sub‑target of 7.5 % for micro‑enterprises within the overall 40 % target.

To address credit‑risk aversion, the government and RBI have operationalised several credit‑guarantee schemes. The Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE), established in 2000, provides collateral‑free guarantees up to ₹2 crore for term loans and working‑capital facilities. In response to the COVID‑19 pandemic, the Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS) was launched in May 2020, offering a 100 % guarantee on additional working‑capital loans up to 20 % of outstanding credit (capped at ₹500 crore per borrower). ECLGS was extended through four tranches (ECLGS 1.0‑4.0) until March 2023, covering over 1.2 crore MSME accounts with guaranteed amounts exceeding ₹3.5 lakh crore.

The Revised PSL Guidelines (2021) introduced a “PSL‑linked incentive” for banks that exceed the micro‑enterprise sub‑target, allowing them to count excess lending toward the overall 40 % target in the subsequent year. The RBI also mandated that banks report PSL disbursement data on a quarterly basis through the Central Repository of Information on Large Credits (CRILC) to improve monitoring. The 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report highlighted that PSL compliance improved to 96 % of the target, driven largely by the ECLGS‑induced surge in micro‑enterprise lending, while the agriculture segment lagged at 89 % due to structural issues in tenant‑farmer credit access.

Key exam points: the 40 % ANBC target is a floor, not a ceiling; banks may lend more but must meet sub‑targets. The CGTMSE guarantee covers only collateral‑free loans, whereas ECLGS guarantees incremental working‑capital facilities irrespective of collateral. Confusing the two guarantee mechanisms is a common trap.

  • Assuming the living‑will requirement applies to all scheduled commercial banks; it is limited to systemically important banks designated by the RBI.
  • Conflating the RBS rating (domestic, continuous) with the supervisory college’s joint assessment (cross‑border, periodic).
  • Treating the fit‑and‑proper test as a post‑appointment review rather than a pre‑appointment gate.
  • Believing the 180‑day cloud‑exit cap applies to every cloud service; it applies only to services classified as critical by the regulated entity.
  • Mixing CGTMSE (collateral‑free guarantee for new loans) with ECLGS (guarantee on incremental working‑capital for existing borrowers).
  • Overlooking that the PSL 40 % target is measured against Adjusted Net Bank Credit, not total advances.
  • Thinking the supervisory college can impose PCA actions; only the RBI’s domestic PCA framework can trigger such restrictions.

These advanced sections complete the required coverage for the current pass.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The Reserve Bank of India has progressively strengthened the transmission channel from the policy repo rate to corporate bond yields, recognising that a deep corporate bond market reduces over‑reliance on bank credit and improves the interest‑rate pass‑through to the real economy. The 2021 “Corporate Bond Market Development Framework” introduced a dedicated repo window for corporate bonds, allowing primary dealers to pledge investment‑grade papers (rated AAA to BBB‑) as collateral for overnight liquidity at the repo rate. In 2022 the RBI mandated that all primary dealers maintain a minimum market‑making obligation of 5 % of the outstanding amount in each eligible ISIN, with a bid‑ask spread cap of 15 basis points, thereby compressing liquidity premiums. The 2023 “Liquidity Enhancement Scheme” permitted scheduled commercial banks to classify eligible corporate bonds as High Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) for LCR purposes, provided the bonds meet a minimum issue size of ₹500 crore and a residual maturity above one year. This regulatory re‑classification expanded the investor base to include banks’ treasury desks, which previously held only government securities for LCR compliance. Empirical evidence from the RBI’s 2024 Monetary Policy Report shows that a 25‑basis‑point repo cut in February 2024 transmitted to a 12‑basis‑point decline in the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield within two weeks, compared with a 6‑basis‑point move in the same tenor government security, indicating a stronger pass‑through once liquidity constraints are eased. The clearing and settlement infrastructure, operated by CCIL and NSDL, was upgraded in 2023 to support T+1 settlement for corporate bonds, reducing counterparty risk and encouraging intraday trading. However, the transmission remains uneven for lower‑rated issuers (BBB and below) where credit spreads dominate and the repo window is not accessible; the RBI’s 2024 consultation paper on a “Credit Risk Mitigation Facility” aims to address this gap by allowing partial guarantees from a proposed Credit Guarantee Fund for Corporate Bonds.

RBI’s Framework for Macroprudential Stress Testing of Non‑Banking Financial Companies

Following the IL&FS episode, the RBI issued the “Macroprudential Stress Testing Framework for NBFCs” in June 2021, extending the bank‑centric stress‑testing architecture to the shadow‑banking segment. The framework requires all Upper‑Layer NBFCs (as defined under the Scale‑Based Regulation) to conduct quarterly bottom‑up stress tests covering credit, market, liquidity, and operational risk, and to submit results to the Department of Supervision within 30 days of quarter‑end. The credit‑risk module uses a scenario‑based approach with three macro‑scenarios — baseline, adverse, and severely adverse — calibrated to GDP growth, CPI inflation, and sectoral default rates published in the RBI’s Financial Stability Report. The market‑risk module mandates a 99 % Value‑at‑Risk (VaR) over a 10‑day horizon for trading portfolios, while the liquidity module applies the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) and Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) templates adapted for NBFC balance sheets, with a minimum LCR of 100 % and NSFR of 100 % effective from March 2023. The 2022 circular on “Prompt Corrective Action for NBFCs” linked stress‑test breaches to graduated restrictions: a breach of the adverse‑scenario capital adequacy threshold (15 % CRAR) triggers a ban on dividend distribution and branch expansion; a breach under the severely adverse scenario (12 % CRAR) invokes a moratorium on fresh lending and mandatory capital infusion within 90 days. The RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report disclosed that 87 % of Upper‑Layer NBFCs met the adverse‑scenario CRAR requirement, but only 62 % cleared the severely adverse threshold, prompting the RBI to issue a 2024 directive for enhanced capital planning and contingency funding arrangements. The framework also introduced a “Systemic Risk Surcharge” of 0.5 % on risk‑weighted assets for NBFCs identified as Domestic Systemically Important NBFCs (D‑SIBs), aligning with the Basel III countercyclical capital buffer logic. Data from the 2024 stress‑test cycle indicate that the aggregate capital shortfall under the severely adverse scenario narrowed to ₹1.2 lakh crore from ₹1.8 lakh crore a year earlier, reflecting improved provisioning standards and the migration of several large NBFCs to bank‑led resolution under the IBC.

Worked Example: Stress‑Test Capital Shortfall Calculation
An Upper‑Layer NBFC reports risk‑weighted assets (RWA) of ₹50,000 crore and a Common Equity Tier‑1 (CET1) capital of ₹6,500 crore. Under the severely adverse scenario the RBI projects a 12 % increase in credit‑risk RWA and a 15 % decline in CET1 due to mark‑to‑market losses. Compute the post‑stress CET1 ratio and state whether the NBFC breaches the 12 % severely adverse threshold.
Step 1: Stressed RWA = ₹50,000 crore × 1.12 = ₹56,000 crore. Step 2: Stressed CET1 = ₹6,500 crore × 0.85 = ₹5,525 crore. Step 3: Stressed CET1 ratio = (₹5,525 crore ÷ ₹56,000 crore) × 100 = 9.87 %. Since 9.87 % < 12 %, the NBFC breaches the severely adverse threshold and would face PCA restrictions including a lending moratorium and mandatory capital infusion within 90 days.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the three macro‑scenario labels (baseline, adverse, severely adverse) and the exact CET1 thresholds (15 % adverse, 12 % severely adverse). In numerical questions, first adjust RWA and CET1 separately before computing the ratio; a common slip is to apply the percentage change to the ratio directly. Also recall that the LCR/NSFR minimums for NBFCs are 100 % each, identical to banks, but the reporting frequency is quarterly, not monthly.

Evolution of the RBI’s Foreign Exchange Reserves Management Strategy

The RBI’s reserves management has shifted from a passive accumulation model to an active, risk‑adjusted portfolio approach aligned with the IMF’s Assessing Reserve Adequacy (ARA) metric. In the early 1990s, reserves hovered around USD 5‑6 billion, primarily held in short‑term US Treasury bills. The 1993‑94 move to a market‑determined exchange rate and the 1997‑98 Asian Financial Crisis prompted the RBI to diversify into sovereign bonds of G‑7 countries and to initiate a gold acquisition programme, raising the gold share from 2 % to 5 % of total reserves by 2000. The 2008 Global Financial Crisis saw reserves peak at USD 314 billion; the RBI deployed a portion via the “Forex Swap Window” to provide dollar liquidity to banks, a tool reactivated during the 2020 COVID‑19 shock with a USD 30 billion swap facility.
