The 2013 Taper Tantrum triggered a sharp reserve drawdown of USD 30 billion in three months, leading the RBI to adopt a “strategic asset allocation” framework in 2014, capping exposure to any single currency at 55 % and to any single issuer at 10 %. The 2021 “Investment Guidelines for Foreign Exchange Reserves” formalised a three‑bucket structure: (i) Liquidity Bucket (30‑40 %) in highly rated short‑term sovereigns and SDR‑denominated assets; (ii) Investment Bucket (40‑50 %) in medium‑term government and agency bonds with a duration target of 3‑5 years; (iii) Strategic Bucket (10‑20 %) in gold, SDRs, and select high‑yield sovereigns for return enhancement. The 2022‑23 Annual Report disclosed that the reserve composition stood at 58 % USD, 22 % EUR, 8 % GBP, 5 % JPY, 4 % gold, and 3 % SDRs, with an overall portfolio duration of 4.2 years. The RBI’s 2023 “Reserve Adequacy Assessment” concluded that reserves at USD 642 billion (as of March 2024) covered 11.5 months of imports and 1.8 times the ARA metric, comfortably above the 100‑150 % adequacy range. Recent initiatives include the 2024 “Gold Repatriation and Domestic Storage” programme, moving 100 tonnes of gold from the Bank of England to RBI vaults to reduce custodial risk, and the exploration of a “Sovereign Wealth Fund” structure to manage a portion of reserves for long‑term developmental financing without compromising liquidity.

RBI’s Guidelines on Outsourcing and Cloud Services for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s regulatory stance on outsourcing evolved from the 2017 “Guidelines on Managing Risks and Code of Conduct in Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks” to a comprehensive 2021 “Outsourcing and Cloud Services Framework” that applies uniformly to banks, NBFCs, payment system operators, and other regulated entities (REs). The 2021 framework mandates that any outsourcing of “critical” functions — defined as those whose failure would materially impair the RE’s ability to meet regulatory obligations or serve customers — requires prior board approval, a documented risk‑assessment, and a contract containing explicit audit‑right clauses, data‑localisation provisions, and a 180‑day exit‑strategy clause. The 2022 “Critical Cloud Services” circular introduced a concentration limit: no single Cloud Service Provider (CSP) may host more than 10 % of an RE’s critical workloads, and the aggregate exposure to the top three CSPs must not exceed 25 %. REs must maintain a “Cloud Exit Plan” tested annually, with results reported to the RBI’s Department of Supervision. The 2023 “Cyber Resilience” circular (referenced in the existing lesson) added a 24‑hour incident‑reporting window for significant cyber incidents affecting ≥10,000 customers or disrupting a critical payment system for >30 minutes, and mandated Red‑Team/Blue‑Team exercises biennially. The 2024 “Third‑Party Risk Management” guidelines extended due‑diligence requirements to fourth‑party sub‑contractors, requiring REs to obtain assurance reports (SOC 2 Type II or equivalent) from all CSPs handling critical data. Compliance data from the 2023‑24 Annual Supervisory Review shows that 92 % of REs had a board‑approved Cyber Security Policy, but only 68 % completed the mandated Red‑Team exercise within the prescribed cycle. A frequent supervisory finding is the misclassification of “non‑critical” workloads, which exempts them from the 180‑day exit cap; the RBI clarifies that the cap applies solely to services classified as critical under the RE’s own criticality assessment, not to all cloud workloads.

Interaction Between Fiscal Deficit Financing and Monetary Policy: RBI’s Market Borrowing Programme

The RBI acts as the government’s debt manager under Section 21 of the RBI Act, 1934, and coordinates the annual Market Borrowing Programme (MBP) with the Ministry of Finance to ensure that gross market borrowing does not destabilise the yield curve or crowd out private credit. The MBP is announced in the Union Budget and detailed in a quarterly borrowing calendar; for FY 2024‑25 the centre’s gross borrowing target is ₹15.4 lakh crore, with net borrowing of ₹11.1 lakh crore after buybacks. During the COVID‑19 pandemic, the RBI launched the Government Securities Acquisition Programme (G‑SAP) in April 2021, purchasing ₹1 lakh crore of G‑secs in the secondary market to anchor yields; G‑SAP 2.0 (2021‑22) added another ₹1.2 lakh crore. These operations, combined with Variable Rate Repo (VRR) and Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions, kept the 10‑year benchmark yield within a 6.0‑6.5 % band despite a fiscal deficit of 9.5 % of GDP in FY 2020‑21. The RBI’s “Operation Twist” (simultaneous purchase of long‑dated and sale of short‑dated securities) was deployed in 2022‑23 to flatten the yield curve, reducing the 10‑year‑1‑year spread from 140 bps to 90 bps. The 2023 “Ways and Means Advances (WMA)” framework was revised, raising the normal WMA limit for the centre to ₹1.5 lakh crore and the special drawing facility to ₹50,000 crore, providing a liquidity buffer that reduces the need for ad‑hoc Treasury Bill issuances. The RBI’s 2024 Monetary Policy Report highlights that the fiscal‑monetary coordination framework — formalised through a quarterly “Fiscal‑Monetary Coordination Meeting” — has improved predictability: the centre’s net market borrowing in H1 FY 2024‑25 was ₹5.2 lakh crore, closely tracking the calendar, and the 10‑year yield remained stable at 7.05 % despite a 5.8 % fiscal deficit target. However, the report flags the risk of “fiscal dominance” if off‑budget borrowings (e.g., through the National Small Savings Fund) expand, as they bypass the MBP and increase the RBI’s sterilisation burden. The RBI’s ongoing “Debt Sustainability Analysis” uses the IMF’s Debt‑GDP threshold of 60 % for the general government; as of March 2024 the combined centre‑state debt‑GDP ratio stands at 84 %, underscoring the need for continued coordination to avoid upward pressure on long‑term rates.

  • Confusing the corporate bond repo window (eligible for AAA‑BBB‑ papers) with the government securities repo window (only sovereign collateral).
  • Assuming the NBFC stress‑test adverse‑scenario CET1 threshold is 12 %; it is 15 % — the 12 % threshold applies only to the severely adverse scenario.
  • Treating the RBI’s gold share in reserves as static; it has risen from 2 % (1990) to 5 % (2000) and stood at 4 % in the 2023‑24 composition.
  • Believing the 180‑day cloud‑exit cap applies to every outsourced service; it applies only to services the RE itself classifies as critical.
  • Overlooking that the RBI’s Operation Twist involves simultaneous purchase of long‑dated and sale of short‑dated securities, not a simple open‑market purchase.
  • Mixing the G‑SAP (secondary‑market G‑sec purchases) with the MBP (primary‑market borrowing calendar); they serve different liquidity‑management objectives.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the External Sector: Exchange Rate Pass‑Through and Trade Balance

The transmission of domestic monetary policy to the external sector operates primarily through the exchange rate channel. When the RBI tightens policy rates, the resulting rise in short‑term yields attracts foreign portfolio inflows, appreciating the rupee. A stronger rupee reduces the domestic currency price of imports, dampening imported inflation, but it also makes exports less competitive, widening the trade deficit. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research shows that the pass‑through coefficient for a 1 % change in the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) to the wholesale price index (WPI) is approximately 0.15 in the short run and rises to 0.30 over a twelve‑month horizon. The same studies estimate that a 1 % appreciation of the NEER reduces export volumes by 0.6 % and increases import volumes by 0.4 % within two quarters.

The magnitude of pass‑through depends on the degree of invoice currency pricing. A large share of India’s imports — especially crude oil, gold and electronic components — are invoiced in US dollars, so rupee movements translate almost one‑for‑one into import costs. Exports, by contrast, are more diversified across currencies, which dampens the export‑side response. The RBI’s 2023 Monetary Policy Report highlighted that during the 2022‑23 tightening cycle, the rupee appreciated 3.2 % against the dollar in real terms, contributing an estimated 30 basis points to the decline in headline CPI inflation, while the export‑growth momentum slowed from 18 % year‑on‑year to 9 % over the same period.

Policy makers therefore face a trade‑off: a tighter stance helps anchor inflation expectations but can exacerbate the current account deficit if the exchange rate appreciates sharply. The RBI manages this by intervening in the foreign exchange market — selling dollars when the rupee strengthens beyond a comfort band — and by using the standing deposit facility (SDF) and variable rate reverse repo (VRRR) to absorb excess liquidity without raising the policy rate further. The 2024 “Foreign Exchange Intervention Framework” circular formalised a rule‑based approach: intervention is triggered when the 30‑day moving average of the rupee‑dollar rate deviates more than 2 % from its 180‑day average, and the volume of intervention is capped at 0.5 % of reserves per month.

From an exam perspective, it is crucial to distinguish between the nominal exchange rate channel (direct impact on import prices) and the real exchange rate channel (impact on export competitiveness via relative price changes). Questions often ask candidates to calculate the net effect on the trade balance given a hypothetical 2 % policy‑rate hike, assuming a pass‑through of 0.25 to import prices and an export elasticity of –0.8. The correct approach is to compute the change in import value = import volume × (1 + pass‑through × ΔNEER) and export value = export volume × (1 + elasticity × ΔNEER), then compare the two.

India’s Capital Account Convertibility Roadmap: Tarapore Committee Recommendations and Current Status

The debate on full capital account convertibility (CAC) in India has been shaped by two high‑level committees chaired by S. S. Tarapore. The first committee (1997) laid out a three‑phase roadmap: Phase I (1997‑2000) focused on liberalising current account transactions and allowing limited portfolio inflows; Phase II (2000‑2005) envisaged opening up external commercial borrowings (ECBs) for corporates, permitting Indian firms to invest abroad up to USD 1 billion, and introducing a market‑determined exchange rate; Phase III (post‑2005) aimed at full freedom for residents and non‑residents to move capital, subject to prudential safeguards. The second committee (2006) refined the pre‑conditions, emphasising fiscal consolidation (fiscal deficit ≤ 3 % of GDP), a low and stable inflation rate (≤ 4 %), a comfortable current account deficit (≤ 1.5 % of GDP), and a robust banking sector with gross NPAs below 5 %.

As of March 2024, India has implemented most Phase I and Phase II measures. The Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) allows resident individuals to remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for any permissible capital or current account transaction. Corporate ECB limits have been raised to USD 750 million under the automatic route, and Indian companies can invest overseas up to 400 % of their net worth under the Overseas Direct Investment (ODI) framework. However, several Phase III elements remain incomplete: non‑residents still face restrictions on rupee‑denominated debt issuance (masala bonds are permitted but subject to a minimum maturity of three years), and the rupee is not fully freely convertible for capital outflows by residents beyond the LRS ceiling. The RBI’s 2023 “Framework for Capital Account Management” reaffirmed a calibrated approach, linking further liberalisation to the achievement of the macro‑prudential benchmarks set out by the second Tarapore committee.

Empirical evidence suggests that the incremental liberalisation has not triggered destabilising capital flight. Net portfolio inflows averaged USD 30 billion per annum during 2015‑2022, while the current account deficit narrowed from 4.8 % of GDP in FY 2013‑14 to 1.2 % in FY 2022‑23. The RBI’s foreign exchange reserves rose from USD 300 billion in 2013 to USD 640 billion in March 2024, providing a buffer against sudden stops. Nevertheless, the 2024 Monetary Policy Report cautioned that a rapid move to full CAC without meeting the fiscal‑inflation‑current‑account triad could expose the economy to volatile short‑term flows, especially in a global environment of rising US interest rates.

For examination purposes, candidates should be able to list the three phases, the key pre‑conditions, and the current status of each major liberalisation measure. A typical twist is to ask whether the LRS limit of USD 250,000 applies to both capital and current account transactions (it does) or whether masala bonds are considered a form of capital account liberalisation (they are, but with maturity and end‑use restrictions). Another common trap is confusing the ODI limit (400 % of net worth) with the ECB automatic route limit (USD 750 million).

Worked Example: Assessing CAC Readiness
Assume the following macro indicators for a hypothetical year: fiscal deficit 4.2 % of GDP, CPI inflation 5.1 %, current account deficit 2.3 % of GDP, gross NPA ratio 4.8 %. Based on the second Tarapore committee benchmarks, evaluate whether India satisfies the pre‑conditions for moving to Phase III of capital account convertibility.
The second Tarapore committee set four quantitative benchmarks: (1) fiscal deficit ≤ 3 % of GDP — not met (4.2 % > 3 %); (2) inflation ≤ 4 % — not met (5.1 % > 4 %); (3) current account deficit ≤ 1.5 % of GDP — not met (2.3 % > 1.5 %); (4) gross NPA ratio ≤ 5 % — met (4.8 % ≤ 5 %). Since three of the four conditions are violated, the economy does not satisfy the pre‑conditions for full capital account convertibility. The correct answer: India is not ready for Phase III.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to “evaluate readiness for full CAC”, first list the four Tarapore benchmarks, then compare each given indicator against its threshold. Do not simply state “not ready” — show the comparison for every benchmark; examiners award marks for the explicit mapping.

RBI’s Supervisory Framework for Payment Banks and Small Finance Banks: Capital, Leverage and Liquidity Requirements

Payment banks (PBs) and small finance banks (SFBs) occupy a distinct niche in India’s financial inclusion architecture. The RBI’s 2014 “Guidelines for Licensing of Payment Banks” and 2014 “Guidelines for Licensing of Small Finance Banks” established differentiated prudential norms that reflect their limited balance‑sheet activities. PBs are prohibited from lending; they can only accept deposits up to ₹2 lakh per customer and invest the proceeds in government securities and high‑quality liquid assets. Consequently, the capital adequacy requirement for PBs is a minimum common equity tier‑1 (CET1) ratio of 15 % of risk‑weighted assets (RWAs), higher than the 9 % applicable to universal banks. The leverage ratio floor for PBs is set at 3 % (Tier‑1 capital to total exposure), and they must maintain a liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) of 100 % from day one, given their reliance on short‑term deposits.

SFBs, by contrast, are required to extend at least 75 % of their adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) to priority sector lending (PSL) targets, with a minimum of 50 % of their loan portfolio to the agriculture and micro‑enterprise segments. Their capital framework mirrors that of universal banks: a minimum CET1 of 9 %, a total capital ratio of 11.5 % (including the capital conservation buffer), and a leverage ratio of 3.5 %. However, SFBs face an additional “small finance bank buffer” of 0.5 % CET1 that must be held above the regulatory minimum, reflecting their higher concentration risk. The RBI’s 2022 “Scale‑Based Regulation for NBFCs and HFCs” extended the same buffer concept to SFBs, requiring them to hold a countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) of up to 2.5 % when systemic credit growth exceeds the long‑term trend.

Liquidity management for SFBs is governed by the same LCR and net stable funding ratio (NSFR) standards as universal banks, but the RBI granted a transitional arrangement: SFBs were required to meet the LCR of 80 % by March 2020, 90 % by March 2021, and 100 % by March 2022. As of the 2023‑24 supervisory review, all ten SFBs reported LCR above 110 % and NSFR above 115 %, indicating comfortable liquidity positions. The RBI also conducts quarterly “Payment Bank Stress Tests” that simulate a 30 % deposit outflow over a 30‑day horizon; PBs must demonstrate that their high‑quality liquid assets (HQLA) cover at least 120 % of the stressed outflow.

A frequent examination question asks candidates to differentiate the capital requirements of PBs and SFBs and to explain why PBs, despite not lending, are subject to a higher CET1 ratio. The answer lies in the concentration of PB assets in sovereign securities and the absence of diversified loan income, which makes them more vulnerable to interest‑rate risk and mark‑to‑market losses on their investment portfolio. Another twist is to ask whether SFBs can issue certificates of deposit (CDs); the answer is yes, but only after they have completed three years of operations and meet the minimum net worth of ₹200 crore.

Interaction Between Monetary Policy and Priority Sector Lending: Credit Allocation and Financial Inclusion

Priority sector lending (PSL) norms, mandated under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949, require scheduled commercial banks to allocate a minimum share of their adjusted net bank credit (ANBC) to designated sectors — agriculture (18 %), micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) (7.5 %), export credit (2 %), education (1 %), housing (1 %), social infrastructure (1 %), renewable energy (1 %), and others. The RBI’s 2020 “Revised PSL Guidelines” expanded the definition of MSMEs to align with the MSME Development Act, 2006, and introduced a “PSL shortfall” penalty: banks that fail to meet the sub‑targets must deposit the shortfall amount in the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) at a penal interest rate of 2 % above the prevailing repo rate.

The interaction with monetary policy arises because PSL targets influence the marginal cost of funds for banks. When the RBI raises the policy repo rate, the cost of incremental deposits rises, but PSL loans are often priced at a spread over the base rate that is lower than the spread on non‑PSL corporate loans. This compresses the net interest margin (NIM) on the PSL portfolio, creating an incentive for banks to shift credit away from priority sectors toward higher‑yielding non‑priority assets. Empirical analysis by the RBI’s Financial Stability Unit (2022) found that a 100‑basis‑point increase in the repo rate reduces PSL disbursement growth by 3.2 % in the subsequent quarter, while non‑PSL credit growth falls by only 1.8 %.

To mitigate this distortion, the RBI introduced the “Interest Subvention Scheme” for short‑term crop loans (2 % subvention on loans up to ₹3 lakh) and the “Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE)” which provides a 75 % guarantee cover on collateral‑free loans up to ₹2 crore. These schemes effectively lower the risk‑adjusted cost of PSL credit, partially offsetting the transmission of higher policy rates. The 2023‑24 Union Budget allocated ₹19,500 crore for interest subvention and ₹7,500 crore for CGTMSE, reflecting the fiscal‑monetary coordination needed to preserve financial inclusion objectives during tightening cycles.

From a testing perspective, candidates should be able to calculate the PSL shortfall penalty: if a bank’s ANBC is ₹5 lakh crore and its agriculture lending is ₹70 000 crore (14 % of ANBC), the shortfall relative to the 18 % target is ₹20 000 crore, which must be placed in RIDF at the penal rate. Another common question asks how the “PSL sub‑target for small and marginal farmers” (8 % of ANBC) interacts with the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) scheme; the answer is that KCC loans count toward the sub‑target, and the interest subvention applies only to the first ₹3 lakh of each KCC account.

Global Monetary Policy Spillovers and the RBI’s Policy Space: Managing Imported Inflation and Capital Flows

India’s monetary policy does not operate in a vacuum; decisions by the US Federal Reserve, the European Central Bank, and the Bank of Japan transmit through capital flows, exchange rates, and commodity prices. The RBI’s 2024 “Monetary Policy Report” quantified the spillover elasticity: a 100‑basis‑point increase in the US federal funds rate is associated with a 30‑basis‑point rise in India’s 10‑year government bond yield, a 1.5 % depreciation of the rupee against the dollar, and a 0.2 % increase in headline CPI inflation via higher imported oil prices. The report also noted that the sensitivity has risen since 2020 because foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) now hold about 22 % of outstanding government securities, up from 14 % in 2015.

The RBI’s toolkit for managing spillovers includes (i) foreign exchange intervention, (ii) variable rate repo/reverse repo auctions to calibrate domestic liquidity, (iii) the standing deposit facility (SDF) to absorb surplus rupee liquidity without affecting the policy rate, and (iv) macro‑prudential measures such as the “Capital Flow Management Measures (CFM)” framework introduced in 2021, which allows temporary restrictions on non‑resident inflows into specific debt segments. During the 2022‑23 Fed tightening cycle, the RBI sold USD 45 billion in the spot market, conducted VRRR auctions totalling ₹8 lakh crore, and raised the SDF rate from 3.75 % to 6.25 % to keep the weighted average call rate (WACR) anchored near the policy repo rate.

Empirical work by the IMF (2023) suggests that India’s “managed float” regime, combined with a credible inflation‑targeting framework, has reduced the pass‑through of external shocks to domestic inflation by roughly 40 % compared with the pre‑2016 period. However, the RBI’s 2024 “Financial Stability Report” warned that a sustained divergence between US and Indian policy rates could trigger a “sudden stop” in FPI flows, leading to a sharp rupee depreciation and a spike in bond yields. The report recommended building a larger foreign exchange reserve buffer (targeting 15 % of GDP) and deepening the domestic investor base — particularly insurance and pension funds — to reduce reliance on volatile foreign capital.

Examination questions often present a scenario: “The US Fed raises rates by 75 bps while the RBI keeps the repo rate unchanged. Explain the likely impact on (a) the rupee‑dollar rate, (b) the 10‑year G‑sec yield, (c) CPI inflation, and (d) the RBI’s policy options.” A high‑scoring answer traces the chain: higher US yields → capital outflows → rupee depreciation → higher import prices → upward pressure on CPI → RBI may intervene, raise the SDF rate, or conduct VRRR to tighten rupee liquidity without a formal repo hike. Candidates should also mention the role of the “Fiscal‑Monetary Coordination Meeting” in aligning government borrowing with the altered liquidity environment.

  • Confusing the PSL sub‑target for agriculture (18 % of ANBC) with the small‑and‑marginal‑farmer sub‑target (8 % of ANBC).
  • Assuming payment banks can lend to micro‑enterprises; they are explicitly prohibited from any lending activity.
  • Treating the LRS limit of USD 250,000 as applicable only to current account transactions; it covers both capital and current account remittances.
  • Believing the countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) is automatically activated at 2.5 % for all banks; it is deployed only when the RBI declares a buffer based on the credit‑to‑GDP gap.
  • Mixing up the SDF rate with the reverse repo rate; the SDF is a standing facility for absorbing liquidity at a rate below the policy repo, while the reverse repo is the floor of the LAF corridor.
  • Overlooking that the RBI’s foreign exchange intervention rule triggers on a 2 % deviation of the 30‑day moving average from the 180‑day average, not on daily spot movements.

RBI's Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process and Supervisory Review Process

The Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP) is the cornerstone of Pillar 2 of the Basel framework as implemented in India. The RBI first issued ICAAP guidelines in 2007, revised them comprehensively in 2015, and further sharpened expectations through the 2021 “Guidelines on ICAAP and Supervisory Review Process (SRP)”. Banks must prepare a forward‑looking capital plan covering a minimum three‑year horizon, incorporating stress‑test results for credit, market, operational and liquidity risks. The board of directors is explicitly responsible for approving the ICAAP document, setting risk appetite limits, and ensuring that capital buffers above the regulatory minimum (including the Capital Conservation Buffer, Countercyclical Capital Buffer and any Pillar 2 add‑ons) are maintained at all times.

Key Components of ICAAP

  • Risk Identification and Measurement – Banks must map all material risks, including concentration risk, interest‑rate risk in the banking book (IRRBB), and reputational risk, and quantify them using internal models approved by the RBI.
  • Stress Testing – At least two macro‑scenarios (baseline and adverse) and one idiosyncratic scenario are required annually. The adverse scenario typically assumes a 300‑basis‑point rise in policy rates, a 15 % fall in GDP growth and a 20 % depreciation of the rupee.
  • Capital Planning – The plan must demonstrate that the Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio remains above the sum of the minimum 5.5 % (including CCB) plus any Pillar 2 add‑on throughout the projection period.
  • Governance and Documentation – The ICAAP report, board minutes, and model validation records are subject to on‑site inspection and off‑site supervisory review.

Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP)

The RBI’s SREP translates the ICAAP into supervisory action. The process follows a four‑step cycle: (i) assessment of the bank’s risk profile, (ii) evaluation of the adequacy of capital and risk‑management frameworks, (iii) determination of any Pillar 2 capital add‑on, and (iv) communication of supervisory expectations through a “Supervisory Letter”. Since 2020 the RBI has published aggregate SREP outcomes in its Financial Stability Report, revealing that the median Pillar 2 add‑on for scheduled commercial banks stood at 0.75 % of risk‑weighted assets in FY 2023‑24. Banks that fail to meet the supervisory capital expectation are placed under the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework, which imposes restrictions on dividend distribution, branch expansion and high‑cost deposits.

Cybersecurity and Technology Risk Management Framework for Regulated Entities

The RBI’s cybersecurity framework has evolved through a series of circulars: the 2016 “Cyber Security Framework in Banks”, the 2018 “Baseline Cyber Security and Resilience Requirements”, the 2021 “Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices”, and the 2023 “Guidelines on Cyber Security for Payment System Operators”. Together they mandate a board‑level Cyber Security Committee, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), and a minimum set of baseline controls aligned with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover).

Baseline Controls and Reporting

  • Asset Inventory and Classification – All information assets must be catalogued and classified by sensitivity within 30 days of onboarding.
  • Multi‑Factor Authentication (MFA) – Mandatory for all privileged access and for customer‑facing digital channels since July 2022.
  • Incident Reporting – Entities must report a “significant cyber incident” (defined as any breach affecting confidentiality, integrity or availability of critical systems) to the RBI within 6 hours of detection and submit a root‑cause analysis within 15 days.
  • Annual Independent Audit – A CERT‑IN empanelled auditor must conduct a comprehensive penetration test and vulnerability assessment each financial year; the report is submitted to the RBI’s Department of Supervision.

Technology Risk Governance

The 2021 Master Direction requires banks to adopt an IT Strategy Committee at the board level, approve an IT Risk Appetite Statement, and maintain a Technology Risk Register that is reviewed quarterly. The RBI’s 2023 guidelines for payment system operators extend these requirements to non‑bank payment aggregators, mandating a “Zero Trust” architecture for API gateways and a maximum 4‑hour recovery time objective (RTO) for core payment switches. In FY 2023‑24 the RBI reported 1,842 cyber incidents across regulated entities, of which 27 % were ransomware attacks; the average downtime for affected payment systems was 2.3 hours, well within the prescribed RTO.

Examiner's technique
A 2023 Mains question asked: “Explain the key differences between the RBI’s 2016 Cyber Security Framework and the 2021 Master Direction on IT Governance. How do these differences affect a bank’s board‑level responsibilities?”
The 2016 framework was prescriptive, listing 14 specific controls (e.g., firewall configuration, anti‑malware updates) and assigning operational responsibility to the CISO. The 2021 Master Direction shifts to a principles‑based governance model: it requires a board‑approved IT Strategy Committee, an IT Risk Appetite Statement, and a Technology Risk Register reviewed quarterly. Consequently, the board moves from a monitoring role to an active decision‑making role, approving capital allocation for cyber resilience and overseeing the annual independent audit. The answer should contrast “control‑list compliance” with “governance‑framework accountability” and cite the specific circular numbers (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2015‑16 and DOR.No.BP.BC.57/21.04.048/2020‑21).
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks for “evolution” of a regulatory framework, structure the answer chronologically: (1) first circular, (2) major amendment, (3) current master direction, (4) key shift in philosophy (prescriptive → principles‑based). Use a two‑column table in the answer sheet to contrast board responsibilities before and after the 2021 Master Direction; this visual cue earns easy marks for clarity.

Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s “Master Direction – Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks” (2017) and the parallel “Guidelines on Outsourcing of Financial Services by NBFCs” (2022) create a unified risk‑management regime for third‑party arrangements. The framework classifies outsourcing into “material” and “non‑material” based on the impact on the entity’s risk profile, customer service, and regulatory compliance. Material outsourcing agreements require prior RBI approval for banks and board approval for NBFCs, and must contain mandatory clauses on data localisation, audit rights, business continuity, and sub‑contracting restrictions.

Due‑Diligence and Contractual Safeguards

  • Vendor Assessment – Entities must conduct a comprehensive due‑diligence covering financial health, information‑security posture, concentration risk (no single vendor > 10 % of total outsourced spend), and legal compliance (including KYC/AML).
  • Data Sovereignty – All customer data processed by the vendor must reside in India; cross‑border data flow is permitted only with explicit RBI approval and a data‑processing agreement meeting the 2022 “Data Localisation” circular.
  • Exit Strategy – Contracts must specify a transition plan with a maximum 180‑day wind‑down period, including data return in a machine‑readable format.
  • Continuous Monitoring – Quarterly performance dashboards, annual on‑site audits, and immediate incident escalation (within 2 hours for cyber incidents) are mandatory.

Supervisory Oversight

The RBI conducts thematic inspections on outsourcing risk every two years. In the 2023‑24 inspection cycle, 12 % of banks were found non‑compliant with the sub‑contracting clause, leading to supervisory letters and, in three cases, a temporary ban on new outsourcing agreements until remediation. NBFCs are subject to a lighter touch: the 2022 guidelines require only board‑level oversight and half‑yearly reporting to the RBI’s Department of Non‑Banking Supervision.

Credit Risk Transfer, Securitisation and the RBI's 2021 Securitisation Framework

Securitisation in India is governed by the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act (SARFAESI) 2002, the RBI’s 2006 “Guidelines on Securitisation of Standard Assets”, the 2012 revision, and the comprehensive 2021 “Framework for Securitisation of Standard Assets”. The 2021 framework introduced a Minimum Retention Requirement (MRR) of 5 % for originators and 10 % for sponsors, measured at the time of issuance, to align incentives. It also mandated a Simple, Transparent and Comparable (STC) label for qualifying securitisations, which enjoy a 20 % risk‑weight under the Basel III standardised approach.

Key Structural Features

  • Asset Eligibility – Only standard assets with a minimum seasoning of 6 months (for retail) or 12 months (for corporate) may be securitised; NPA‑backed structures remain prohibited.
  • Credit Enhancement – Over‑collateralisation, cash collateral accounts, and excess spread are permitted; however, the total credit enhancement cannot exceed 30 % of the pool balance.
  • Disclosure and Reporting – Originators must publish a monthly investor report (pool performance, delinquency, prepayment) on the stock exchange platform within 15 days of month‑end.
  • Regulatory Capital Relief – Banks achieving STC status can apply a 20 % risk weight to the senior tranche; non‑STC tranches attract a 100 % risk weight.

Market Development

Since the 2021 framework, the volume of rated securitisation issuances rose from ₹0.9 lakh crore in FY 2020‑21 to ₹2.3 lakh crore in FY 2023‑24, with the share of STC‑labelled deals crossing 65 %. The RBI’s 2023 “Review of Securitisation Market” highlighted that the MRR has improved originator skin‑in‑the‑game, reducing early‑payment defaults by 18 % compared with pre‑2021 vintages.

Financial Literacy, Consumer Protection and the RBI's Ombudsman Scheme Enhancements

The National Strategy for Financial Education (NSFE) 2020‑25, launched jointly by the RBI, SEBI, IRDAI and PFRDA, sets a target of reaching 500 million adults through the “Financial Literacy Week” and the “Centre for Financial Literacy” network. On the consumer‑protection front, the RBI’s “Consumer Protection Code” (2017) and the “Internal Ombudsman Scheme” (2018) require every bank to appoint an Internal Ombudsman (IO) with a minimum tenure of three years and direct reporting to the board’s Customer Service Committee.

Ombudsman Scheme 2021 Amendments

  • Unified Ombudsman – The 2021 amendment merged the Banking Ombudsman, NBFC Ombudsman and Digital Transactions Ombudsman into a single “Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme” (RB‑IOS), operational from November 2021.
  • Compensation Limits – The scheme caps compensation at ₹20 lakh for deficiency in service and ₹1 lakh for mental agony; the IO can recommend higher amounts subject to RBI approval.
  • Turnaround Time – The ombudsman must issue an award within 90 days of receipt of a complete complaint; the 2023 annual report shows a median disposal time of 68 days.
  • Appeal Mechanism – Dissatisfied parties may approach the RBI’s Appellate Authority within 30 days; the Authority’s decision is final and binding.

Impact Metrics

In FY 2023‑24 the RB‑IOS received 1.42 lakh complaints, a 22 % increase over the previous year, with 78 % resolved in favour of the complainant. The most frequent grievances related to unauthorised electronic transactions (31 %), loan‑account mismanagement (24 %) and non‑adherence to the Fair Practices Code (18 %). The RBI’s “Consumer Confidence Index” rose from 58.3 in March 2022 to 62.7 in March 2024, reflecting improved trust in grievance redressal.

  • Confusing the ICAAP capital planning horizon (minimum three years) with the stress‑testing horizon (one year for regulatory reporting).
  • Assuming the 2021 Master Direction on IT Governance replaces the 2016 Cyber Security Framework; they operate in parallel, the former governing governance, the latter prescribing controls.
  • Treating all outsourcing as “material” – only arrangements exceeding the 10 % concentration threshold or affecting core banking functions trigger prior RBI approval.
  • Believing the Minimum Retention Requirement applies uniformly at 10 % for both originators and sponsors; the framework differentiates (5 % for originators, 10 % for sponsors).
  • Overlooking that the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme’s compensation ceiling for mental agony is ₹1 lakh, not ₹20 lakh.
  • Candidates should internalise these traps to avoid losing marks.

RBI's Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets (2019): Resolution Timeline Discipline and the End of Regulatory Forbearance

The Reserve Bank of India's 7 June 2019 "Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets" replaced the entire architecture of resolution schemes — Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR), Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR), Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A), and the 12 February 2018 circular (later struck down by the Supreme Court in Dharani Sugars v. Union of India, 2019) — with a single, principles-based framework. The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs), all-India financial institutions, and NBFCs (including HFCs). Its central innovation is a strict 30-day review period from the date of default (defined as non-payment of any interest or principal beyond 30 days) during which lenders must undertake a prima facie review of the borrower account and decide on a resolution strategy. If a resolution plan (RP) is not implemented within 180 days from the end of the review period (i.e., 210 days from default), the account must be referred to the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), unless the lenders holding 75% by value and 60% by number agree to extend the timeline by a further 90 days with documented justification.

The framework mandates an Inter-Creditor Agreement (ICA) among all lenders, making the decision of lenders representing 75% by value and 60% by number binding on all. This replaced the earlier "super-majority" thresholds that varied across schemes. The RP may involve restructuring (change in ownership, debt-equity swap, haircut, moratorium), sale to an ARC, or change in management. Crucially, the framework prohibits evergreening by requiring that any restructuring must be accompanied by a bona fide change in ownership or management control, except in cases of "genuine business failure" certified by an independent credit evaluation. The 2021 "Resolution Framework for COVID-19 Related Stress" (and its 2022 extension for MSMEs) operated as a parallel, time-bound window under Section 35AA of the Banking Regulation Act, but the 2019 framework remains the general regime. The RBI's 2023 "Review of the Prudential Framework" noted that 78% of accounts entering the review period were either resolved or referred to NCLT within the prescribed timeline, a sharp improvement from the pre-2019 experience where cases lingered for years under CDR/SDR.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Credit Spreads, Liquidity Premia, and the Role of Partial Credit Enhancement

While the interest rate channel transmits policy rate changes to bank lending rates, the corporate bond market channel operates through shifts in credit spreads, term premia, and liquidity premia on non-government securities. In India, the corporate bond market remains bank-dominated (banks hold ~40% of outstanding corporate bonds), but the transmission mechanism has distinct features. A policy rate cut reduces the risk-free yield curve (G-sec yields), but the credit spread — the yield differential between a corporate bond and a G-sec of matching maturity — may widen or narrow depending on risk perception, liquidity conditions, and the monetary policy stance's signalling effect. The RBI's 2019 "Framework for Partial Credit Enhancement (PCE)" permits banks to provide credit enhancement up to 20% of the bond issue size (capped at 50% of the issue for infra bonds) to improve the credit rating of bonds issued by infrastructure and non-infra companies. This directly lowers the credit spread at issuance. However, the liquidity premium — the additional yield investors demand for holding less liquid corporate bonds — remains significant; the bid-ask spread on AAA-rated corporate bonds in the secondary market averages 15-25 basis points versus 1-2 bps for G-secs.

The RBI's Operation Twist (open market purchase of long-term G-secs funded by sale of short-term G-secs) and Targeted Long-Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) (2020-21) were explicitly designed to compress term premia and improve corporate bond market liquidity. TLTRO 1.0 and 2.0 required banks to deploy funds in investment-grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non-convertible debentures, with at least 50% in primary issuances. The 2022 "Framework for Market Making in Corporate Bonds" mandated designated market makers (primary dealers and scheduled commercial banks) to provide two-way quotes for specified ISINs, with a maximum bid-ask spread of 25 bps for AAA/AA bonds and 50 bps for A/BBB bonds. The RBI's 2023 "Review of Corporate Bond Market Development" reported that the share of corporate bonds in total financial system credit rose from 14.2% (March 2019) to 18.7% (March 2024), while the average credit spread for AAA 5-year paper compressed from 115 bps to 78 bps over the same period. However, transmission remains asymmetric: policy rate hikes transmit faster to primary market yields (via higher G-sec yields) than rate cuts, because credit spreads exhibit counter-cyclical behaviour — they widen during downturns, offsetting the fall in risk-free rates.

Examiner's Trap: Asymmetric Transmission and the Credit Spread Channel
A question states: "Monetary policy transmission to the corporate bond market in India is symmetric — rate cuts and hikes affect corporate bond yields equally." Evaluate this statement with reference to the behaviour of credit spreads and liquidity premia over the monetary policy cycle.
The statement is false. Transmission is asymmetric. During tightening cycles, policy rate hikes raise the risk-free curve (G-sec yields) almost immediately; credit spreads may initially compress due to "flight to quality" but then widen as default risk rises. The net effect on corporate yields is a rapid increase. During easing cycles, G-sec yields fall, but credit spreads typically widen (counter-cyclical) because risk aversion rises and liquidity premia increase in uncertain environments. This offsets part of the risk-free rate decline. Empirical RBI studies (2021, 2023) show that a 100 bps policy rate cut transmits only 40-55 bps to AAA corporate bond yields within 6 months, whereas a 100 bps hike transmits 75-90 bps. The asymmetry arises from: (1) counter-cyclical credit spreads, (2) persistent liquidity premia in thin secondary markets, (3) bank-dominated investor base with mark-to-market constraints, and (4) the absence of a deep derivatives market for hedging duration risk. PCE and market-making frameworks mitigate but do not eliminate this asymmetry.
Exam-Day Strategy: Corporate Bond Transmission
When a question asks about "monetary transmission beyond banks", structure the answer in three layers: (1) risk-free rate channel (G-sec yields), (2) credit spread channel (counter-cyclical behaviour, PCE role), (3) liquidity premium channel (market-making, TLTRO, bid-ask spreads). Cite the 2022 Market Making Framework and the 2023 RBI Review data (spread compression from 115 to 78 bps for AAA 5Y). Always mention the asymmetry — it is the examiner's favourite twist.

RBI's Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs: The 2023 Guidelines and Board-Level Accountability

The Reserve Bank's 8 June 2023 "Framework for Compromise Settlements and Technical Write-offs" replaced the 2007 guidelines and introduced a governance-first architecture for resolving stressed assets outside the IBC and the Prudential Framework. The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks (excluding RRBs), all-India financial institutions, and NBFCs (Middle and Upper Layers). A compromise settlement is defined as a negotiated settlement with a borrower (including wilful defaulters and fraud accounts) involving a sacrifice (haircut) by the lender, where the account is not referred to NCLT. The framework mandates that every compromise settlement must be approved by the Board of the lending institution (or a Board-level committee with a minimum of three directors, including one independent director), and the minutes must record the rationale for the sacrifice, the recovery estimate versus liquidation value, and a confirmation that the settlement is not detrimental to the institution's long-term interests. For wilful defaulters and fraud accounts, an additional cooling period of 12 months applies before the borrower can access fresh credit from any regulated entity, and the settlement requires approval by the majority of independent directors on the Board.

Technical write-offs — the removal of NPAs from the balance sheet without waiving the legal right to recover — now require a Board-approved policy specifying the minimum ageing (typically 4 years for secured, 2 years for unsecured), the provisioning coverage threshold (minimum 100% of the outstanding), and the recovery efforts undertaken. The framework caps the aggregate technical write-offs in a financial year at 5% of the gross NPAs at the beginning of the year, unless the Board provides a detailed justification recorded in minutes. Crucially, the 2023 guidelines introduced a "cooling-off" period for senior management: the Managing Director & CEO, Chief Risk Officer, and Head of the Stressed Assets Vertical cannot be part of the compromise settlement approval process for accounts where they were the sanctioning authority at the time of original lending. The RBI's 2024 supervisory data shows that in FY 2023-24, compromise settlements accounted for ₹1.2 lakh crore of stressed asset resolution (18% of total resolution), with an average haircut of 52%, while technical write-offs stood at ₹2.1 lakh crore. The framework also mandates quarterly reporting to the RBI of all compromise settlements and technical write-offs, including borrower-wise details, enabling supervisory detection of patterns indicative of evergreening or governance failures.

The RBI's Regulatory Framework for Fintech Self-Regulatory Organisations: The 2024 Draft Framework and Industry-Led Governance

In January 2024, the RBI released the Draft Framework for Self-Regulatory Organisations (SROs) in the Fintech Sector, marking a shift from direct regulation of individual fintech entities to industry-led governance under RBI oversight. The framework proposes that an SRO be recognised by the RBI as a Section 8 company (non-profit) with a minimum net worth of ₹10 crore, broad-based membership (at least 50 fintech entities across categories — payments, lending, wealth-tech, insurtech, regtech), and a governing board comprising independent directors (minimum 50%), RBI nominees, and member-elected directors. The SRO's core functions include: (1) developing a Code of Conduct covering fair practices, data privacy, algorithmic transparency, and outsourcing standards; (2) operating a grievance redressal mechanism with a 30-day turnaround, escalable to the RBI's Integrated Ombudsman Scheme; (3) maintaining a public registry of member fintechs with their regulatory status, complaint history, and compliance ratings; (4) conducting independent audits of members' technology stacks, data security, and business practices annually; and (5) reporting systemic risk indicators (concentration, interconnectedness, herding behaviour) to the RBI quarterly.

The framework introduces a tiered membership structure: "Full Members" (regulated entities or those partnering with regulated entities) and "Associate Members" (unregulated fintechs seeking guidance). Only Full Members have voting rights. The SRO must establish a Disciplinary Committee (chaired by an independent director) with powers to impose monetary penalties (up to ₹1 crore per violation), suspend membership, or recommend RBI action including cancellation of the fintech's partnership with regulated entities. The RBI retains reserve powers to issue directions to the SRO, inspect its records, and withdraw recognition if the SRO fails to act against errant members. The 2024 draft follows the 2022 "Recommendations of the Working Group on Digital Lending" and the 2023 "Guidelines on Default Loss Guarantee (DLG) in Digital Lending", which already mandated that fintech lending apps must be hosted on a verified repository (the RBI's proposed "FinTech Repository" launched in beta in April 2024). The SRO framework aims to address the regulatory arbitrage where unregulated fintechs operate at the periphery of the financial system, creating consumer protection and systemic risk gaps. The final framework, expected by end-2024, will likely mandate that all fintechs partnering with REs must join an RBI-recognised SRO within 12 months of notification.

RBI's Prompt Corrective Action Framework for Non-Banking Financial Companies: The 2022 Framework and Its Divergence from the Bank PCA

The RBI's 13 October 2022 "Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for NBFCs" (effective 1 October 2022) introduced a separate, calibrated regime for NBFCs in the Middle and Upper Layers under the Scale-Based Regulation (SBR), distinct from the bank PCA framework (2017, revised 2021). The NBFC PCA triggers on three tracked indicators: (1) Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) — breach of the regulatory minimum (15% for Upper Layer, 12% for Middle Layer) or a decline of 300 bps below the minimum in a single quarter; (2) Net NPA Ratio — exceeding 6% for Upper Layer, 7% for Middle Layer; and (3) Leverage Ratio — exceeding 7x for Upper Layer, 10x for Middle Layer (total outside liabilities / owned funds). Unlike the bank PCA, which has three risk thresholds (Threshold 1, 2, 3), the NBFC PCA has two stages: Stage 1 (early warning) and Stage 2 (corrective action). Stage 1 triggers when any one indicator breaches; Stage 2 triggers when two or more indicators breach, or a single indicator breaches severely (CRAR below 9%, Net NPA above 12%, Leverage above 10x for UL).

The mandatory corrective actions at Stage 1 include: submission of a board-approved capital restoration plan (for CRAR breach), restriction on dividend distribution, and enhanced monitoring by the RBI. At Stage 2, mandatory actions expand to: restriction on branch expansion, cap on incremental lending to high-risk sectors (real estate, capital market exposure), requirement to reduce leverage within a board-approved timeline, and prior RBI approval for any acquisition or merger. Discretionary actions (at RBI's direction) include: restriction on management compensation, change in ownership/management, and supersession of the Board. A critical divergence from the bank PCA is the explicit linkage to the SBR layers: an Upper Layer NBFC entering PCA Stage 2 faces enhanced supervisory scrutiny including mandatory engagement with a resolution adviser, while a Middle Layer NBFC may be directed to downsize its balance sheet to exit the Upper Layer thresholds. The framework also introduces a "exit criteria": the NBFC must meet all three indicators for four consecutive quarters without any breach, verified by statutory auditor certification. The RBI's 2023-24 Financial Stability Report noted that as of March 2024, three Upper Layer NBFCs and seven Middle Layer NBFCs were under PCA Stage 1, with one Upper Layer NBFC in Stage 2 — the first activation since the framework's inception.

  • Confusing the 2019 Prudential Framework's 180-day resolution timeline (from end of 30-day review period) with the IBC's 180-day CIRP timeline (extendable by 90 days); they run sequentially, not concurrently.
  • Assuming credit spreads narrow during rate cuts; they typically widen (counter-cyclical), causing asymmetric transmission — a favourite examiner twist.
  • Overlooking that the 2023 Compromise Settlement Framework requires Board approval for every settlement and a 12-month cooling period for wilful defaulters before fresh credit access.
  • Treating the Fintech SRO as a voluntary industry body; the 2024 draft makes SRO membership effectively mandatory for fintechs partnering with REs, with RBI reserve powers to enforce compliance.
  • Equating NBFC PCA with Bank PCA — the NBFC version has two stages (not three), uses leverage ratio as a tracked indicator (banks use Tier 1 leverage), and links exit to four clean quarters with auditor certification.
  • Missing that the 2019 Prudential Framework's ICA voting threshold (75% value, 60% number) is binding on all lenders, including dissenting ones — a key difference from the earlier CDR/SDR schemes.
  • Believing Operation Twist and TLTRO are conventional monetary policy tools; they are unconventional liquidity management operations targeting specific segments of the yield curve and corporate bond market.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with issuance concentrated in high‑rated public sector entities and a limited secondary‑market turnover. Since 2015 the Reserve Bank has introduced a series of targeted operations to improve the pass‑through of policy rates to corporate borrowing costs. The first major step was the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) announced in March 2020, which provided three‑year funds at the prevailing repo rate to banks on the condition that the proceeds were deployed in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper and non‑convertible debentures. The TLTRO window was calibrated in three tranches (TLTRO 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0) with progressively tighter end‑use restrictions, ensuring that liquidity reached the intended segments rather than being parked in government securities.

In parallel, the RBI launched the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) in October 2020, authorising the central bank to buy up to ₹1 lakh crore of investment‑grade corporate bonds in the secondary market through a transparent auction mechanism. The purchases were conducted on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, and the eligible universe was limited to bonds rated AA and above with a residual maturity of up to ten years. The CBPP was wound down in March 2022 after the targeted amount was absorbed, but its signalling effect persisted: spreads on AAA‑rated bonds compressed by 30‑40 basis points relative to the pre‑programme period, and primary issuance volumes rose 18 per cent year‑on‑year in FY 2021‑22.

A third transmission channel operates through the market‑making framework for corporate bonds introduced in 2021. Designated market makers (primarily primary dealers and large banks) are required to quote two‑way prices for a prescribed basket of liquid corporate bonds, with a maximum bid‑ask spread of 15 basis points. The RBI provides a back‑stop liquidity facility — the Standing Liquidity Facility for Corporate Bonds (SLFCB) — at the repo rate plus a modest margin, which market makers can draw upon to honour their quotes. This arrangement reduces the liquidity premium embedded in corporate bond yields and aligns them more closely with the policy corridor.

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that the combined effect of TLTRO, CBPP and market‑making has shortened the average lag between a repo‑rate change and the movement in the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield from 6‑8 months (pre‑2015) to 2‑3 months in the 2021‑23 window. However, transmission remains asymmetric: during rate‑cut cycles spreads tend to widen as risk aversion rises, while during tightening cycles the pass‑through is faster because banks substitute away from corporate bonds toward higher‑yielding government securities. The examiner often tests this asymmetry by asking candidates to explain why a 50 bps repo cut may not translate into an equivalent decline in corporate bond yields.

RBI's Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio Implementation

The Reserve Bank adopted the Basel III liquidity standards in a phased manner. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) became applicable to all scheduled commercial banks (excluding regional rural banks) from 1 January 2015, with a minimum requirement of 60 per cent that was raised by 10 percentage points each year until it reached 100 per cent on 1 January 2019. The LCR mandates that banks hold a stock of High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) — primarily government securities, cash and central bank reserves — sufficient to cover net cash outflows over a 30‑day stress scenario. The RBI’s LCR framework classifies HQLA into Level 1 (zero haircut) and Level 2A/2B (15 per cent and 50 per cent haircuts respectively) and prescribes a cap of 40 per cent on Level 2 assets within the HQLA pool.

The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) was introduced later, with the final guidelines issued on 17 May 2018 and a compliance date of 1 October 2020 for all banks (including small finance banks and payment banks). The NSFR requires that the amount of Available Stable Funding (ASF) — weighted liabilities and capital — be at least 100 per cent of Required Stable Funding (RSF) — weighted assets and off‑balance‑sheet exposures — over a one‑year horizon. The RBI assigned ASF factors of 100 per cent to regulatory capital and retail deposits with a maturity above one year, 90 per cent to stable retail deposits, and 50 per cent to less stable wholesale funding. On the RSF side, residential mortgages with a risk weight of 35 per cent receive a 65 per cent factor, while performing corporate loans attract an 85 per cent factor.

Both ratios are reported on a consolidated basis for banking groups and on a solo basis for individual entities. The RBI conducts quarterly on‑site inspections and off‑site surveillance using the LCR/NSFR Monitoring Template submitted through the Centralised Information Management System (CIMS). Breaches trigger a supervisory response that may include a capital‑add‑on, restriction on dividend distribution, or a directive to submit a funding‑plan. As of March 2024, the system‑wide LCR stood at 138 per cent and the NSFR at 115 per cent, comfortably above the regulatory minima, reflecting the abundant liquidity injected through pandemic‑era measures and the subsequent gradual normalisation.

An examiner favourite is to ask for the difference in horizon between the two ratios (30 days vs. one year) and the implication for asset‑liability management: LCR drives short‑term HQLA holdings, while NSFR forces banks to lengthen the maturity profile of liabilities and to avoid over‑reliance on short‑term wholesale funding. Candidates should also be able to calculate the impact of a ₹500 crore increase in retail term deposits (ASF factor 90 per cent) on the NSFR numerator.

Worked Example: NSFR Impact Calculation
A bank reports Available Stable Funding (ASF) of ₹1,20,000 crore and Required Stable Funding (RSF) of ₹1,10,000 crore. It raises an additional ₹500 crore of retail term deposits with a maturity of two years. Assuming the ASF factor for such deposits is 90 per cent and the RSF remains unchanged, compute the new NSFR and state whether the bank meets the 100 per cent minimum.
Additional ASF = ₹500 crore × 0.90 = ₹450 crore. New ASF = ₹1,20,000 crore + ₹450 crore = ₹1,20,450 crore. New NSFR = (₹1,20,450 crore ÷ ₹1,10,000 crore) × 100 = 109.5 per cent. Since 109.5 per cent ≥ 100 per cent, the bank continues to satisfy the NSFR requirement.
Exam‑Day Strategy
Memorise the LCR phase‑in timeline (60 % → 100 % by Jan 2019) and the NSFR compliance date (Oct 2020). Keep a mental table of ASF/RSF factors for the most common liability and asset classes; a quick‑reference sheet saves 2‑3 minutes on calculation questions. When a question asks for “the ratio that addresses structural funding mismatches”, answer NSFR; for “the ratio that ensures survival of a 30‑day liquidity shock”, answer LCR.

Fintech Self‑Regulatory Organisations: Governance, Enforcement and RBI Oversight

The rapid proliferation of fintech entities — lending apps, payment aggregators, account aggregators and wealth‑tech platforms — created a regulatory perimeter problem: many operated without a direct licence but interacted closely with regulated entities (REs) such as banks and NBFCs. In response, the RBI released a Draft Framework for Self‑Regulatory Organisations (SROs) for Fintechs in April 2024, building on the 2022 “Guidelines on Digital Lending” that mandated fintech lending apps to be hosted on a verified repository. The draft defines an SRO as a non‑profit body recognised by the RBI, with a governing board comprising independent directors, industry representatives and a nominee of the central bank. Membership is effectively compulsory for any fintech that partners with an RE; the RE must ensure that its fintech partners join an RBI‑recognised SRO within 12 months of the final notification.

Governance standards require the SRO to frame a Code of Conduct covering data privacy, fair‑lending practices, grievance redressal, and transparency in algorithmic credit scoring. The SRO must maintain a public register of members, conduct periodic audits, and submit quarterly compliance reports to the RBI. Enforcement powers include the ability to impose monetary penalties (up to ₹1 crore per violation), suspend or expel members, and recommend regulatory action by the RBI. The RBI retains reserve powers to direct an SRO to take specific corrective measures, to dissolve an SRO that fails to meet its obligations, or to directly supervise a fintech that remains outside any SRO.

The framework also addresses cross‑border data flows by requiring SROs to ensure that member fintechs comply with the RBI’s data localisation norms (storage of payment data in India) and the Personal Data Protection Bill provisions once enacted. A notable feature is the “sandbox‑to‑SRO” pathway: fintechs that graduate from the RBI’s Regulatory Sandbox can obtain expedited SRO membership, reducing the time to market for innovative products while preserving supervisory oversight.

As of the beta launch in April 2024, two industry‑led consortia — the Fintech Association for Consumer Empowerment (FACE) and the Digital Lending Self‑Regulatory Body (DLSRB) — have applied for recognition. The final framework, expected by end‑2024, will likely prescribe a minimum capital requirement for SROs (₹10 crore net owned funds) and a mandatory independent audit of the SRO’s own governance every two years. Examiners may ask candidates to contrast the SRO model with the traditional “licensing‑only” approach, highlighting the shift from ex‑ante licensing to ex‑post behavioural regulation.

RBI's Framework for Climate Risk Disclosure and Green Taxonomy

Recognising that climate change poses material financial risks — physical (extreme weather, sea‑level rise) and transition (policy shifts, technology disruption) — the RBI issued a Draft Disclosure Framework on Climate‑Related Financial Risks in February 2023, aligned with the Task Force on Climate‑Related Financial Disclosures (TCFD) recommendations. The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks, all‑India financial institutions, and top‑layer NBFCs (Upper Layer under the Scale‑Based Regulation). It requires entities to disclose governance arrangements, strategy, risk management, and metrics/targets in their annual reports from FY 2024‑25 onward.

In parallel, the RBI constituted a Green Taxonomy Working Group (chaired by the Deputy Governor in charge of regulation) to develop a classification system for “green” economic activities. The interim taxonomy, released in July 2023, lists 12 sectors — renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, green buildings, clean transportation, and climate‑resilient infrastructure — with technical screening criteria (e.g., solar PV projects must have a life‑cycle emission intensity below 50 gCO₂/kWh). The taxonomy is intended to guide banks’ green‑loan tagging, facilitate the issuance of green bonds, and enable the RBI to monitor the flow of credit to sustainable activities.

The disclosure framework mandates scenario analysis using at least two climate pathways: a “Net‑Zero 2050” scenario (consistent with the IEA’s Net Zero by 2050 roadmap) and a “Delayed Transition” scenario (reflecting a 2 °C pathway with policy action postponed to 2030). Banks must estimate the impact on credit‑risk parameters (probability of default, loss given default) for exposed portfolios and report the results to the RBI’s Department of Supervision. The RBI’s 2023‑24 Financial Stability Report noted that 68 per cent of scheduled commercial banks had initiated scenario‑analysis exercises, but only 22 per cent had integrated the outputs into capital‑planning processes.

Supervisory integration is progressing through the Climate Risk Stress Testing (CRST) programme launched in January 2024. The CRST uses a top‑down macro‑financial model linking climate shocks to GDP, sectoral output, and bank balance sheets. Preliminary results indicate that under a severe physical‑risk shock (once‑in‑100‑year flood in the Ganga basin), the system‑wide CET1 ratio could decline by 45 bps, while a disorderly transition shock (sudden carbon price jump to US$100/tCO₂) could erode CET1 by 70 bps. The RBI has signalled that banks with material exposure to high‑carbon sectors may face additional Pillar 2 capital add‑ons from FY 2025‑26.

Digital Rupee Retail Pilot: Design, Adoption and Interoperability

The RBI’s retail Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC‑R), branded as the Digital Rupee (e₹‑R), entered a closed‑user‑group pilot on 1 December 2022 with four banks (State Bank of India, ICICI Bank, Yes Bank and IDFC First Bank) in four cities (Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and Bhubaneswar). The pilot was expanded in phases: by March 2023 it covered 13 banks and 15 cities, and by October 2023 the user base exceeded 1.2 million retail wallets with a cumulative transaction volume of ₹3,500 crore. The design follows a token‑based, account‑less model where each e₹‑R unit is a cryptographically signed digital bearer instrument denominated in rupees, stored in a wallet app provided by the participating bank.

Key architectural choices include: (i) a two‑tier distribution — the RBI issues e₹‑R to banks (wholesale leg), banks distribute to end‑users (retail leg); (ii) offline capability using near‑field communication (NFC) for peer‑to‑peer transfers without internet connectivity, with a per‑transaction limit of ₹2,000 and a daily wallet limit of ₹10,000; (iii) interoperability with UPI — users can load e₹‑R from a UPI‑linked bank account and redeem e₹‑R back to the same account instantly, leveraging the Unified Payments Interface’s existing settlement rails; (iv) privacy tiers — transaction metadata is visible to the issuing bank and the RBI, but not to merchants, preserving a degree of anonymity akin to cash for low‑value payments.

Adoption metrics from the pilot show that 62 per cent of transactions were person‑to‑person (P2P), 28 per cent person‑to‑merchant (P2M) via QR codes, and 10 per cent offline NFC transfers. The average ticket size was ₹1,150, well below the ₹2,000 offline ceiling, indicating that the offline feature is being used for everyday retail purchases. Merchant onboarding relied on existing UPI QR infrastructure; no separate POS hardware was required, which accelerated acceptance.

Interoperability testing with the Digital Rupee Wholesale (e₹‑W) pilot (launched November 2022 for government securities settlement) demonstrated atomic cross‑leg settlement: a bank could simultaneously deliver e₹‑W to the Clearing Corporation of India and receive e₹‑R in its retail wallet, eliminating settlement risk. The RBI has indicated that a full‑scale launch will await the finalisation of the CBDC‑R Legal Framework (expected to be introduced as an amendment to the RBI Act, 1934) and the resolution of cross‑border interoperability standards being discussed at the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Innovation Hub.

  • Confusing the LCR’s 30‑day horizon with the NSFR’s one‑year horizon and mis‑identifying which ratio drives HQLA holdings versus stable funding.
  • Assuming the fintech SRO framework is voluntary; the 2024 draft makes membership effectively mandatory for any fintech partnering with a regulated entity.
  • Treating the Green Taxonomy as a binding regulatory capital rule; it is currently a classification tool for disclosure and green‑loan tagging, not a capital‑charge framework.
  • Overlooking that the Digital Rupee retail pilot uses a token‑based bearer model, not an account‑based ledger, and that offline NFC transfers have a hard ₹2,000 per‑transaction cap.
  • Believing the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme is a permanent facility; it was a time‑bound, ₹1 lakh crore programme wound down in March 2022.
  • Mixing up the TLTRO end‑use restrictions across its three tranches; each tranche had distinct eligible instruments and maturity caps.
  • Neglecting the scenario‑analysis requirement of two distinct climate pathways (Net‑Zero 2050 and Delayed Transition) in the RBI’s climate‑risk disclosure framework.

The advanced sections above equip candidates with the granular operational detail that distinguishes a competent answer from a merely descriptive one.

RBI's Digital Lending Guidelines (2022) and the Lending Service Provider Ecosystem

The Reserve Bank of India issued the Guidelines on Digital Lending on 2 September 2022, effective from 1 December 2022 for new loans and 31 March 2023 for existing exposures. The framework targets the entire digital lending value chain — regulated entities (banks, NBFCs, HFCs), lending service providers (LSPs), and digital lending apps (DLAs). It mandates that all loan origination, credit assessment, disbursement, and recovery must be conducted through the regulated entity's own digital platform or through an LSP that is contractually bound to the regulated entity. The regulated entity remains the principal and bears full responsibility for compliance, customer protection, and data privacy.

Key operational requirements include: (i) a key facts statement (KFS) in a standardized format disclosed to the borrower before contract execution; (ii) an all‑in‑cost (AIC) disclosure that captures interest, processing fees, and any other charges, expressed as an annualised percentage; (iii) a cooling‑off period of at least 24 hours after loan sanction during which the borrower may withdraw without penalty; (iv) data localisation — all borrower data must be stored on servers located in India; (v) grievance redressal — a dedicated nodal officer and a 30‑day resolution timeline; and (vi) algorithmic transparency — credit‑scoring models must be documented, auditable, and free from discriminatory variables.

The guidelines also define the LSP registration process. An LSP must be a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, with a minimum net owned fund of ₹2 crore, and must enter into a written agreement with the regulated entity specifying service levels, data‑sharing protocols, and liability clauses. The regulated entity is required to conduct due‑diligence on the LSP's technology stack, information‑security practices, and business continuity plans before onboarding. The RBI has clarified that outsourcing of core lending functions — such as credit appraisal, KYC verification, and loan monitoring — to an LSP does not dilute the regulated entity's statutory obligations.

Enforcement actions since the guidelines' commencement include penalties on three NBFCs for non‑disclosure of AIC, suspension of a DLA for unauthorised data harvesting, and a directive to a major bank to re‑engineer its loan‑origination workflow to eliminate “pre‑filled” consent screens. The framework is expected to curb predatory pricing, improve borrower literacy, and create a level playing field between bank‑led and fintech‑led digital credit.

National Asset Reconstruction Company (NARCL) and the Resolution of Legacy Stressed Assets

The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was incorporated on 7 July 2021 under the Companies Act, 2013, as a government‑backed asset reconstruction company (ARC) to acquire and resolve legacy non‑performing assets (NPAs) from scheduled commercial banks. The Union Cabinet approved a capital infusion of ₹6,000 crore, with the Government of India holding a 51 % stake through the Department of Financial Services and the remaining 49 % held by a consortium of public‑sector banks led by State Bank of India. NARCL operates alongside the India Debt Resolution Company Limited (IDRCL), a separate entity tasked with operational management, valuation, and resolution of the acquired assets.

The acquisition mechanism follows a 15‑85 structure: NARCL pays 15 % of the agreed purchase price upfront in cash (funded by the government‑backed capital) and issues security receipts (SRs) for the remaining 85 %. The SRs are subscribed by the selling banks, which thereby retain an economic interest in the recovery. The SRs are tradable on the stock exchanges, providing liquidity to banks. The RBI has granted NARCL a special dispensation under the Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest (SARFAESI) Act, 2002, allowing it to acquire assets without the usual 15 % minimum cash requirement for ARCs.

As of March 2024, NARCL has acquired 12 accounts with an aggregate gross book value of ₹82,000 crore, covering sectors such as power, steel, textiles, and infrastructure. The resolution strategy emphasises asset‑level restructuring — including debt‑equity swaps, promoter buy‑outs, and sale to strategic investors — rather than immediate liquidation. IDRCL has engaged external turnaround advisors and has set up a resolution monitoring committee comprising representatives from the selling banks, NARCL, and independent experts.

The initiative addresses the “legacy NPA overhang” that persisted after the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) process, where many large accounts remained unresolved due to litigation, valuation disputes, or lack of viable resolution applicants. By concentrating these assets in a single, well‑capitalised vehicle, the framework aims to achieve economies of scale in resolution, reduce the provisioning burden on banks, and free up capital for fresh lending. The RBI monitors NARCL's progress through quarterly returns and has mandated a minimum recovery rate of 40 % on the SR portfolio within five years, failing which the government may consider additional capital support.

Technique: Mapping Institutional Architecture to Exam Questions
A question asks: “Explain the 15‑85 acquisition structure of NARCL and its implications for bank balance sheets.”
The 15‑85 structure means NARCL pays 15 % cash upfront (funded by government capital) and issues security receipts (SRs) for 85 % of the purchase price. Banks subscribe to SRs, converting a non‑performing loan into a tradable instrument. On the balance sheet, the NPA is derecognised; the SR appears as an investment (fair‑value through OCI or FVTPL depending on classification). Provisioning on the original NPA is reversed, improving the bank’s CET1 ratio. However, the bank retains recovery risk via SR valuation. The SR’s market price reflects expected recovery; if recovery falls below 40 % over five years, the SR value declines, creating a future provisioning need. The structure thus provides immediate capital relief while preserving upside participation.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question references a newly created institution (NARCL, IDRCL, NARCL‑IDRCL nexus), first identify the statutory basis (SARFAESI amendment, Cabinet approval), then trace the capital flow (government → NARCL → SRs → banks). Use a two‑column table: “Before acquisition” vs “After acquisition” to show balance‑sheet impact. This visual cue earns full marks for “analysis” and “evaluation” components.

Sovereign Green Bonds and the RBI's Role in Climate Finance Mobilisation

In January 2023, the Government of India issued its first Sovereign Green Bonds (SGrBs) under the Framework for Sovereign Green Bonds released by the Ministry of Finance in November 2022. The inaugural tranche comprised two securities — a 5‑year bond of ₹8,000 crore and a 10‑year bond of ₹8,000 crore — aggregating ₹16,000 crore. The proceeds are earmarked for public‑sector projects that meet the Green Bond Principles of the International Capital Market Association (ICMA): renewable energy, energy efficiency, pollution prevention, sustainable agriculture, and climate‑resilient infrastructure.

The RBI acts as the issuance agent and market maker for SGrBs. It conducts the primary auction on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, manages the order book, and provides secondary‑market liquidity through its Open Market Operations (OMO) and the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) corridor. The RBI also monitors the use‑of‑proceeds reporting — the Ministry of Finance publishes an annual allocation report verified by an external reviewer (currently the Climate Bonds Initiative). The RBI’s Monetary Policy Report now includes a box on green‑bond issuance, yields, and investor composition, signalling the central bank’s commitment to integrating climate finance into monetary operations.

Investor response has been dominated by domestic institutional investors — insurance companies, provident funds, and mutual funds — which together absorbed over 85 % of the inaugural issuance. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) participated within the Fully Accessible Route (FAR) limits, reflecting the bonds’ eligibility under the Voluntary Retention Route (VRR) for government securities. The yield spread over comparable conventional G‑secs was 3‑5 basis points, indicating a modest “greenium”. The RBI has indicated that future tranches will be calibrated to the National Green Taxonomy (under finalisation) and may include transition bonds for hard‑to‑abate sectors.

From a monetary‑policy perspective, SGrBs expand the high‑quality liquid asset (HQLA) pool for banks, supporting Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) compliance. They also provide a benchmark for pricing corporate green bonds, thereby deepening the domestic green‑bond market. The RBI’s Climate Risk Stress Testing (CRST) framework, launched in January 2024, incorporates SGrB holdings as a mitigant for transition‑risk exposures on bank balance sheets.

Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Regulation and Consumer Credit Protection Framework

The rapid proliferation of Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) products — short‑term, interest‑free instalment facilities offered at point‑of‑sale by fintech platforms — prompted the RBI to extend its Digital Lending Guidelines (2022) to cover BNPL arrangements.
