A clarification circular dated 10 November 2022 stated that any “deferred payment” product that creates a credit exposure for the user, irrespective of tenor or interest charge, falls within the definition of “digital lending” and must comply with the same disclosure, KYC, and grievance‑redressal norms.

Key regulatory requirements for BNPL providers include: (i) mandatory registration as an LSP or as a regulated entity (bank/NBFC) if they originate credit; (ii) standardised Key Facts Statement displaying the total amount payable, instalment schedule, late‑payment charges, and the effective annualised cost (even if nominal interest is zero); (iii) credit‑limit assessment based on the borrower’s repayment capacity, using data from credit information companies (CICs); (iv) cooling‑off period of 24 hours after the first transaction; (v) data‑privacy safeguards — transaction data cannot be shared with third parties for marketing without explicit consent; and (vi) reporting to CICs of all BNPL exposures, ensuring they reflect in the borrower’s credit score.

The RBI also mandated that merchant‑side BNPL (where the merchant bears the discount) must be disclosed to the customer as a separate charge, preventing hidden cost shifting. In 2023, the RBI imposed penalties on two major BNPL platforms for non‑disclosure of late‑fee structures and for onboarding customers without adequate credit appraisal. The Consumer Protection (E‑Commerce) Rules, 2020 were amended in 2023 to require e‑commerce marketplaces to display BNPL terms prominently at checkout.

From a systemic‑risk viewpoint, the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (FSR) 2023‑24 flagged BNPL as a growing segment of unsecured retail credit, with outstanding balances crossing ₹45,000 crore as of December 2023. The report recommended periodic stress‑testing of BNPL portfolios under scenarios of rising delinquency and interest‑rate shocks. The RBI has indicated that if BNPL growth exceeds 30 % year‑on‑year for two consecutive quarters, it may introduce a sectoral capital charge for banks’ exposures to BNPL LSPs.

Self-Regulatory Organisations for Fintech: The RBI's 2023 Draft Framework and Its Implications

Recognising the need for industry‑led standards in the fast‑evolving fintech ecosystem, the RBI released the Draft Framework for Self‑Regulatory Organisations (SROs) in the Fintech Sector on 15 June 2023. The framework proposes that any fintech entity providing services to regulated entities (banks, NBFCs, payment system operators) must become a member of an RBI‑recognised SRO. The SRO would be a not‑for‑profit company with a governing council comprising independent directors, industry representatives, and a nominee of the RBI.

The draft outlines core functions of the SRO: (i) developing a Code of Conduct covering data governance, algorithmic fairness, cyber‑resilience, and customer grievance handling; (ii) conducting periodic audits of member firms’ technology stacks and compliance with RBI circulars; (iii) operating a dispute‑resolution mechanism for inter‑member and member‑customer disputes; (iv) maintaining a public registry of member firms, their service categories, and compliance status; and (v) reporting systemic risk indicators (e.g., concentration of fintech lending, API outage frequency) to the RBI on a quarterly basis.

Membership is proposed to be effectively mandatory: regulated entities are prohibited from onboarding a fintech partner that is not an SRO member after a transition period of 12 months from the final framework’s notification. The RBI retains oversight powers — it can issue directions to the SRO, inspect its records, and revoke recognition if the SRO fails to enforce its code. The draft also introduces a “sandbox‑plus” pathway: fintech firms that successfully complete the RBI’s Regulatory Sandbox can obtain expedited SRO membership.

Industry feedback highlighted concerns over dual regulation (SRO rules overlapping with RBI circulars), funding of SRO operations (membership fees vs. RBI grant), and the scope of “fintech” — whether it includes pure‑play technology providers (cloud, AI) that do not directly intermediate financial services. The final framework, expected in early 2025, is likely to clarify these issues and may prescribe a tiered membership based on the nature and scale of activities. For exam purposes, the key takeaway is the shift from ex‑post supervisory intervention to ex‑ante industry self‑governance under central‑bank oversight, a model mirrored in the Payment System Operators SRO established in 2021.

  • Confusing the 15‑85 NARCL structure with the standard ARC 15 % cash‑minimum rule; NARCL enjoys a statutory exemption.
  • Assuming BNPL products are exempt from credit‑reporting because they are “interest‑free”; the 2022 circular explicitly brings them under CIC reporting.
  • Treating the Sovereign Green Bond “greenium” as a permanent yield advantage; it is marginal (3‑5 bps) and market‑dependent.
  • Believing the fintech SRO framework is voluntary; the 2023 draft makes membership effectively compulsory for any fintech partnering with a regulated entity.
  • Overlooking that the Digital Lending Guidelines require algorithmic transparency for credit‑scoring models, not just disclosure of interest rates.
  • Mixing up the roles of NARCL (asset acquisition) and IDRCL (operational resolution); they are distinct legal entities with separate governance.
  • Neglecting the RBI’s power to impose sectoral capital charges on banks’ BNPL exposures if growth thresholds are breached, a macro‑prudential tool distinct from standard risk weights.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the Role of the RBI's Market‑Making Operations

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with issuance concentrated in high‑rated public sector entities and a limited secondary‑market turnover. Transmission of policy rate changes to corporate borrowing costs therefore depends on both the primary‑market issuance yield curve and the liquidity of the secondary market. The RBI influences this transmission through three complementary channels: (i) the repo‑rate corridor that sets the risk‑free benchmark for pricing spreads; (ii) open‑market operations (OMOs) in government securities that anchor the sovereign yield curve, which serves as the reference for corporate spreads; and (iii) direct market‑making interventions such as the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) launched in March 2020 and the Secondary Market Liquidity Facility (SMLF) introduced in May 2020.

Under the CBPP, the RBI purchased investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) in the secondary market up to a ceiling of ₹1 lakh crore, using a multiple‑price auction format. The programme was calibrated to compress credit spreads by 30‑50 basis points for eligible issuers and to signal the central bank’s willingness to support market functioning during the COVID‑19 shock. The SMLF provided a standing facility for primary dealers to repo corporate bonds against cash, thereby improving the repo‑eligible collateral pool and reducing the liquidity premium embedded in corporate yields. Both facilities were wound down by March 2022 as market conditions normalised, but the operational framework remains in the RBI’s toolkit for future stress episodes.

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that a 25‑basis‑point cut in the policy repo rate typically transmits 12‑15 basis points to the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield within two months, provided secondary‑market turnover exceeds ₹5,000 crore per month. When turnover falls below this threshold, the pass‑through drops to 5‑7 basis points, highlighting the importance of market depth. The RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report noted that the share of corporate bonds rated AA and above in total outstanding corporate debt rose from 68 % in March 2019 to 74 % in March 2023, reflecting improved issuer quality and a modest deepening of the market.

From a supervisory perspective, the RBI monitors concentration risk in banks’ corporate bond holdings through the Large Exposure Framework (LEF) and the Investment Fluctuation Reserve (IFR). Banks are required to hold a minimum IFR of 5 % of their held‑to‑maturity (HTM) and available‑for‑sale (AFS) corporate bond portfolios, which acts as a buffer against mark‑to‑market losses when yields rise. The 2022 amendment to the LEF lowered the single‑counterparty exposure limit for corporate bonds from 25 % to 20 % of Tier‑1 capital, further aligning bank balance‑sheet risk with the transmission objective.

RBI's Liquidity Management through Cash Management Bills and Treasury Bills: Operational Mechanics and Impact on Short‑Term Rates

Cash Management Bills (CMBs) are non‑standard, short‑dated discount instruments issued by the Government of India on behalf of the RBI to manage temporary cash mismatches in the central government’s account. Unlike regular Treasury Bills (T‑Bills), which follow a fixed calendar (91‑day, 182‑day, 364‑day), CMBs are issued on an ad‑hoc basis with tenors ranging from 7 to 91 days. The first CMB auction was conducted on 12 May 2010, and the instrument has since become a regular feature of the RBI’s liquidity‑management toolkit, especially during periods of large advance tax outflows or GST settlement flows.

The operational mechanics are as follows: the RBI announces the auction amount, tenor, and cut‑off yield (or price) through a press release on the day of the auction. Bids are submitted by primary dealers and scheduled commercial banks on the NDS‑OM platform. The auction follows a uniform‑price (Dutch) format; all successful bidders receive the cut‑off yield. Settlement occurs on a T+1 basis, with funds transferred from the bidder’s current account to the RBI’s account and the securities credited to the bidder’s SGL account. Because CMBs are issued at a discount and redeemed at par, the implicit yield serves as a high‑frequency signal of the marginal cost of funds for the banking system.

Empirically, the weighted average cut‑off yield on 14‑day CMBs has tracked the weighted average call‑rate (WACR) within a band of ±5 basis points in normal conditions. During the March 2020 liquidity crunch, the 14‑day CMB cut‑off rose to 4.85 % while the WACR spiked to 5.10 %, reflecting a temporary premium for ultra‑short‑dated sovereign paper. The RBI responded by increasing the quantum of CMB issuance from ₹10,000 crore per week to ₹30,000 crore per week and by conducting simultaneous variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions to absorb excess liquidity once the stress eased.

T‑Bills, by contrast, provide the benchmark risk‑free curve for tenors up to one year. The 91‑day T‑Bill yield is the reference rate for the RBI’s Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF) corridor: the repo rate is set 25 basis points above the 91‑day T‑Bill yield, and the reverse repo rate is set 25 basis points below it (subject to the floor imposed by the Standing Deposit Facility). The RBI’s weekly T‑Bill auction calendar (typically ₹20,000‑₹30,000 crore per week) is calibrated to keep the 91‑day yield within the policy corridor. Deviations trigger either additional OMO purchases (to push yields down) or VRRR auctions (to push yields up).

The interaction between CMBs and T‑Bills is a key transmission lever. When the RBI issues a large volume of CMBs, it drains liquidity at the very short end, pushing the overnight call rate toward the repo rate. Simultaneously, if the 91‑day T‑Bill yield remains anchored, the spread between the 14‑day CMB and the 91‑day T‑Bill widens, signalling tightening of very‑short‑term conditions without altering the policy stance. Market participants monitor this spread as a leading indicator of the RBI’s liquidity stance.

Examiner's twist
A question asks: "If the RBI announces a 14‑day Cash Management Bill auction of ₹25,000 crore while keeping the 91‑day Treasury Bill auction unchanged, what is the most likely immediate impact on the overnight call rate and the 91‑day T‑Bill yield?"
The CMB auction drains ₹25,000 crore of liquidity at the 14‑day horizon, raising the marginal cost of funds for banks. The overnight call rate, which is the price of overnight liquidity, will tend to move up toward the repo rate (the ceiling of the LAF corridor). The 91‑day T‑Bill yield, however, is anchored by the unchanged T‑Bill supply and the RBI’s OMO/VRRR operations; it will remain broadly stable. Therefore, the spread between the 14‑day CMB cut‑off and the 91‑day T‑Bill yield widens, signalling a tightening of very‑short‑term liquidity without a change in the policy rate.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three‑step liquidity‑management sequence: (1) CMB issuance → drains ultra‑short liquidity → pushes call rate up; (2) 91‑day T‑Bill yield → anchor for LAF corridor; (3) VRRR/OMO → fine‑tune the 91‑day yield. In MCQs, look for the phrase “ad‑hoc, non‑standard tenor” to identify CMBs, and “fixed calendar, uniform‑price auction” for T‑Bills. A quick mental map of the corridor (repo = 91‑day + 25 bps; reverse repo = 91‑day − 25 bps) solves most transmission questions.

Regulation of Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms: Licensing, Prudential Norms, and Consumer Protection

The RBI brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending platforms under a formal regulatory regime through the Master Direction – Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017, issued under Section 45JA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934. The direction classifies a P2P platform as a non‑banking financial company (NBFC‑P2P) and mandates registration with the Department of Non‑Banking Supervision (DNBS). As of March 2024, 23 entities hold a valid Certificate of Registration (CoR) as NBFC‑P2P.

Key prudential requirements include: (i) a minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore at the time of application, to be maintained continuously; (ii) a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times the NOF, computed as total outstanding loans facilitated divided by NOF; (iii) an exposure cap of ₹50 lakh per lender across all P2P platforms, and ₹10 lakh per borrower per platform; (iv) a mandatory escrow account mechanism operated by a scheduled commercial bank to hold funds before disbursement and after repayment, ensuring that the platform never touches borrower or lender money. The platform must also maintain a minimum capital adequacy ratio of 15 % of risk‑weighted assets, aligned with the Basel‑II framework for NBFCs.

On the consumer‑protection front, the 2017 direction requires: (a) a board‑approved Fair Practices Code (FPC) covering transparent disclosure of interest rates, fees, and recovery procedures; (b) a grievance redressal mechanism with a designated nodal officer and a turnaround time of 30 days; (c) mandatory reporting of loan performance data to credit information companies (CICs) on a monthly basis, which brought P2P loans under the credit‑reporting ecosystem for the first time. The 2022 amendment to the direction extended the FPC to cover algorithmic credit‑scoring models, requiring platforms to disclose the key variables and weightages used in scoring, and to conduct an annual independent audit of the algorithm for bias and fairness.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through quarterly returns (DNBS‑P2P‑01) covering loan origination, delinquency buckets, and escrow balances. The RBI conducts on‑site inspections on a risk‑based schedule; in 2023, two platforms were issued show‑cause notices for breaching the leverage ratio and for onboarding borrowers without adequate KYC verification. The RBI also retains the power to impose monetary penalties under Section 58G of the RBI Act and to revoke the CoR for persistent non‑compliance.

From a systemic‑risk perspective, the RBI’s Financial Stability Report (2023‑24) flagged the P2P segment’s outstanding facilitated loans at ₹12,500 crore, representing 0.3 % of total bank credit. While small in absolute terms, the rapid growth (CAGR 45 % over FY 2019‑23) and the concentration of lending in unsecured personal loans warrant continued monitoring. The report recommended a periodic stress‑test of P2P portfolios under a 200‑basis‑point interest‑rate shock and a 10 % rise in unemployment.

Macroprudential Policy Tools: Sectoral Capital Requirements for Real Estate, Consumer Credit, and Infrastructure Lending

Beyond the uniform Capital Adequacy Ratio (CAR) prescribed under Basel III, the RBI employs sector‑specific capital buffers to address concentration risk in credit‑intensive sectors. The first such measure was the 2015 circular on “Capital Requirements for Exposures to Commercial Real Estate (CRE)”, which imposed a risk weight of 100 % on CRE exposures (versus 75 % for standard corporate loans) and required banks to maintain an additional 0.5 % of Tier‑1 capital as a sectoral buffer for CRE portfolios exceeding 10 % of total advances.

In 2018, the RBI introduced a sectoral capital charge for unsecured consumer credit (personal loans, credit cards, and consumer durables) by raising the risk weight from 100 % to 125 % for exposures above ₹5 crore to a single borrower, and by mandating a 0.25 % Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) on the incremental consumer‑credit portfolio when the credit‑to‑GDP gap exceeds 2 %. The CCyB is activated in quarterly steps of 0.25 % up to a maximum of 2.5 %, and is released symmetrically when the gap narrows.

For infrastructure lending, the 2020 “Prudential Framework for Infrastructure Projects” allowed a concessional risk weight of 75 % for operational assets with a minimum debt‑service coverage ratio (DSCR) of 1.2, but imposed a higher risk weight of 150 % for under‑construction projects lacking a take‑out financing arrangement. Banks are also required to hold a specific provision of 0.4 % on standard infrastructure exposures, over and above the general provision of 0.25 % on standard assets.

These sectoral tools interact with the broader macroprudential framework. The RBI’s 2022 “Guidelines on Large Exposures and Concentration Risk” lowered the single‑counterparty limit for CRE and infrastructure exposures from 25 % to 20 % of Tier‑1 capital, and introduced a group‑exposure limit of 30 % for interconnected infrastructure borrowers. The 2023 Financial Stability Report highlighted that CRE exposures accounted for 9.2 % of gross bank credit, while unsecured consumer credit rose to 7.8 % of gross credit, underscoring the relevance of the targeted buffers.

Operationally, banks compute the sectoral capital charge at the end of each quarter and report it in the quarterly Return on Capital Adequacy (RCA). The RBI reviews the adequacy of these buffers during the Supervisory Review and Evaluation Process (SREP) and may prescribe higher Pillar‑2 capital add‑ons for banks with outsized sectoral concentrations. The combined effect of risk‑weight adjustments, sectoral buffers, and concentration limits creates a layered defence that aligns capital allocation with systemic risk appetite.

RBI's Supervisory Framework for Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks and NBFCs

The rapid expansion of third‑party service providers — ranging from cloud‑hosting and core‑banking software to customer‑onboarding and debt‑collection agencies — prompted the RBI to issue the Master Direction – Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks (2021) and a parallel direction for NBFCs (2022). The framework adopts a risk‑based approach: the regulated entity (RE) remains fully responsible for all outsourced activities, and the board of the RE must approve an Outsourcing Policy that defines materiality thresholds, due‑diligence standards, and escalation matrices.

Materiality is assessed on two dimensions: (i) the criticality of the function to the RE’s core banking or lending operations (e.g., core‑banking platform, payment‑gateway processing, credit‑scoring engines); and (ii) the potential impact of a service disruption on customers, regulatory compliance, and financial stability. Functions classified as “material” require a formal contract with mandatory clauses covering: (a) data‑localisation and confidentiality (data must reside in India unless the RBI grants a specific exemption); (b) audit and inspection rights for the RE and the RBI; (c) business‑continuity and disaster‑recovery plans with defined recovery‑time objectives (RTO) and recovery‑point objectives (RPO); (d) sub‑contracting restrictions — any further outsourcing by the vendor must be pre‑approved by the RE.

The direction mandates a minimum annual due‑diligence review covering the vendor’s financial health, cyber‑resilience posture (including ISO 27001 or equivalent certification), and compliance with applicable labour and consumer‑protection laws. REs must submit a consolidated Outsourcing Return (OR‑01) to the Department of Supervision within 30 days of each quarter‑end, detailing the number of material contracts, vendor‑wise risk scores, and any incidents of service disruption exceeding the agreed RTO.

Supervisory actions in 2023‑24 illustrate the framework’s teeth. The RBI issued a supervisory letter to a major private‑sector bank for inadequate oversight of a cloud‑service provider that suffered a 12‑hour outage affecting UPI transaction processing. The bank was directed to (i) invoke the penalty clause in the contract, (ii) conduct an independent forensic audit of the vendor’s infrastructure, and (iii) submit a remediation plan within 60 days. In another case, an NBFC was penalised ₹2 crore for outsourcing loan‑recovery to an unregistered agency that employed coercive practices, violating the Fair Practices Code.

From a systemic viewpoint, the RBI’s 2023 “Guidelines on Cyber‑Resilience for Outsourced Services” extended the framework by requiring REs to map the concentration of critical outsourced services across vendors. If more than 30 % of a material function is concentrated in a single vendor, the RE must develop a contingency plan for vendor substitution within 90 days. This concentration‑risk metric is now part of the quarterly Systemic Risk Survey (SRS) and feeds into the RBI’s assessment of operational risk in the financial system.

  • Confusing the 14‑day CMB cut‑off yield with the 91‑day T‑Bill yield; they serve different tenors and the spread between them is the liquidity‑stress indicator.
  • Assuming P2P platforms are exempt from credit‑information reporting; the 2017 Master Direction made monthly reporting to CICs mandatory.
  • Treating the sectoral capital charge for consumer credit as a permanent add‑on; it is linked to the Countercyclical Capital Buffer and is activated only when the credit‑to‑GDP gap exceeds the trigger.
  • Believing the RBI’s outsourcing direction applies only to banks; a parallel direction for NBFCs was issued in 2022 with identical materiality and contract‑clause requirements.
  • Overlooking that the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme was a temporary COVID‑19 facility and not a standing market‑making tool; the operational framework remains but the purchase window is closed.
  • Mixing up the risk‑weight for operational infrastructure assets (75 %) with that for under‑construction projects without take‑out financing (150 %).
  • Neglecting the requirement that outsourced data must reside in India unless a specific RBI exemption is granted; this is a common compliance gap in cloud‑vendor contracts.

Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations and On‑Tap Liquidity Windows: Design, Utilisation, and Transmission to Bank Credit

The Reserve Bank of India introduced Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) in March 2020 as a crisis‑time tool to channel durable liquidity directly to sectors facing acute funding stress. Unlike the regular LAF repo, which is overnight and open to all eligible banks, TLTROs are conducted for tenors of one to three years and the funds must be deployed in pre‑specified instruments — initially investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures of entities in the MSME, NBFC, and housing finance segments. The RBI announces a notified amount, conducts a variable‑rate auction, and caps the allotment per bank at a fraction of its net demand and time liabilities (NDTL). Banks that receive funds are required to report end‑use compliance on a fortnightly basis, and the RBI monitors deployment through the “TLTRO Utilisation Return”.

In October 2020 the RBI complemented TLTRO with an On‑Tap Liquidity Window (OTLW) for the same eligible instruments, allowing banks to draw liquidity at the prevailing repo rate without waiting for a scheduled auction. The OTLW operates on a daily basis, with a maximum drawal limit of 1 % of a bank’s NDTL and a minimum tenor of 14 days. Both facilities are collateralised by government securities, and the haircut on collateral is aligned with the LAF framework. The combined effect of TLTRO and OTLW was a measurable compression of spreads in the corporate bond market: the 5‑year AAA corporate bond spread over the corresponding G‑sec fell from around 150 bps in March 2020 to below 70 bps by December 2020, reflecting improved risk appetite and the direct transmission of cheap term funding to issuers.

Transmission to bank credit operates through two channels. First, the reduction in the marginal cost of funds for banks lowers the weighted average lending rate (WALR) on fresh loans, especially for working‑capital and term loans to the targeted sectors. Second, the mandatory deployment in high‑quality corporate paper improves the balance‑sheet quality of banks, freeing up capital for additional lending. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that a 100 bps decline in the TLTRO allotment rate is associated with a 15‑20 bps decline in the median fresh loan rate to NBFCs within two quarters. The facilities were phased out in 2022 as liquidity conditions normalised, but the operational framework remains in the RBI’s toolkit for future stress episodes.

The Evolution of the Corporate Bond Market in India: RBI's Corporate Bond Repo, Partial Credit Guarantee Scheme, and Securitisation Framework

India’s corporate bond market has historically been shallow, with outstanding issuance hovering around 15 % of GDP compared with over 80 % in advanced economies. To deepen the market, the RBI has introduced a sequence of structural reforms. The Corporate Bond Repo (CBR) was launched in July 2020, allowing banks and primary dealers to repo corporate bonds rated AA and above for tenors up to 90 days. The CBR operates on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, uses the same haircut schedule as the government‑securities repo, and settles on a T+1 basis. By providing a liquidity backstop, the CBR reduces the liquidity premium embedded in corporate bond yields and encourages market‑making activity.

In parallel, the Partial Credit Guarantee Scheme (PCGS) was announced in the 2020‑21 Budget and operationalised by the RBI in September 2020. Under PCGS 2.0, the government provides a 20 % first‑loss guarantee on bonds issued by NBFCs and HFCs rated AA or below, subject to a ceiling of ₹1 lakh crore. The guarantee is administered through a trust managed by the National Credit Guarantee Trustee Company (NCGTC). The scheme directly addresses the “rating cliff” problem: issuers that would otherwise be confined to high‑cost bank borrowing can access the bond market at lower spreads because the guarantee absorbs the first loss. Data from the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) show that PCGS‑backed issuances accounted for roughly 30 % of total NBFC bond issuance in FY 2021‑22, with average spreads compressing by 40‑60 bps relative to non‑guaranteed peers.

The securitisation framework was overhauled in September 2021 through the “Master Direction – Securitisation of Standard Assets”. The new rules permit originators (banks, NBFCs, HFCs) to securitise standard assets with a minimum retention of 5 % (for residential mortgages) or 10 % (for other asset classes) and require a minimum credit enhancement of 10 % of the pool’s principal. The framework also introduces a “simple, transparent, and comparable” (STC) label for qualifying transactions, which enjoy lower risk‑weights under Basel III. The RBI further facilitated the creation of a secondary market for securitised paper by allowing repo in STC‑eligible securities under the CBR. Together, these measures aim to shift credit risk off bank balance sheets, diversify funding sources for originators, and create a liquid, tradable asset class that can be held by insurers, pension funds, and mutual funds.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the Corporate Bond Repo and the Partial Credit Guarantee Scheme complement each other in deepening the corporate bond market.”
The Corporate Bond Repo provides a short‑term liquidity window for high‑rated corporate bonds, reducing the liquidity premium and encouraging market‑making. The Partial Credit Guarantee Scheme lowers the credit risk for lower‑rated issuers by absorbing first‑loss, enabling them to issue bonds at tighter spreads. Together, the CBR improves secondary‑market liquidity for the bonds that PCGS helps bring to market, creating a virtuous cycle of issuance, trading, and price discovery.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links two RBI facilities, structure the answer in three steps: (1) state the primary objective of each facility, (2) identify the market friction each addresses (liquidity vs credit risk), and (3) describe the interaction — how the output of one becomes the input for the other. Use the CBR‑PCGS pair as a template for similar pairs such as TLTRO‑OTLW or SDF‑VRRR.

RBI's Framework for the Regulation of Securitisation and Asset Reconstruction: The 2021 Securitisation Guidelines and the Role of NARCL/IDRCL

The September 2021 Master Direction on Securitisation of Standard Assets replaced the 2012 guidelines and aligned the Indian framework with the Basel Committee’s “Simple, Transparent, and Comparable” (STC) criteria. Key provisions include a minimum retention requirement of 5 % for residential mortgage‑backed securities (RMBS) and 10 % for all other asset classes, a mandatory credit enhancement of at least 10 % of the pool’s principal, and a cap on the originator’s exposure to the securitisation vehicle at 20 % of its Tier‑1 capital. The direction also mandates that the servicer be a regulated entity and that the trustee be independent of the originator. Transactions meeting the STC label enjoy a 20 % risk‑weight under the standardised approach, compared with 100 % for non‑STC exposures.

In parallel, the government established the National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) in July 2021, capitalised at ₹6,000 crore with a 51 % government stake and the remainder held by banks and financial institutions. NARCL acquires stressed assets from banks at a price determined by a transparent valuation process, issues security receipts (SRs) to the selling banks, and engages the India Debt Resolution Company Limited (IDRCL) — a separate asset‑management entity — for resolution. The SRs are guaranteed by the government up to ₹30,000 crore, providing a backstop that encourages banks to offload legacy NPAs without immediate haircuts. As of March 2024, NARCL had acquired assets worth approximately ₹90,000 crore across 12 accounts, with resolution plans underway for the majority.

The interaction between the securitisation framework and the NARCL/IDRCL architecture is twofold. First, banks can securitise performing portions of a stressed portfolio under the STC framework, thereby freeing capital and improving liquidity before transferring the residual stressed pool to NARCL. Second, the SRs issued by NARCL are eligible for repo under the Corporate Bond Repo, giving banks a liquidity outlet for the receipts they hold. The RBI’s 2023 “Guidelines on Sale of Stressed Assets to ARCs” further streamlined the process by prescribing a standardised due‑diligence template and a 90‑day timeline for completion of the sale, reducing the operational friction that previously delayed asset transfers.

RBI's Management of Government Cash Balances: Cash Management Bills, Treasury Bill Calendar, and the RBI's Role as Banker to the Government

As banker to the central and state governments, the RBI manages the government’s cash balances through a combination of Ways and Means Advances (WMA), Treasury Bills (T‑Bills), and Cash Management Bills (CMBs). The WMA facility provides temporary overdrafts to the Centre and states up to limits fixed by the RBI in consultation with the Finance Ministry; the interest rate on WMA is linked to the repo rate, with a surcharge for drawings beyond the normal limit. To smooth the intra‑day and intra‑month cash flow mismatches, the RBI issues CMBs — non‑standard, short‑tenor instruments (typically 14‑day, 28‑day, or 56‑day) — on an ad‑hoc basis. CMBs are sold through uniform‑price auctions on the NDS‑OM platform, and the cut‑off yield serves as a high‑frequency indicator of liquidity conditions in the banking system.

The Treasury Bill calendar, published quarterly, announces the issuance schedule for 91‑day, 182‑day, and 364‑day T‑Bills. The RBI conducts weekly auctions for each tenor, using a multiple‑price format for the 91‑day and a uniform‑price format for the longer tenors. The calendar enables market participants to plan their liquidity positions and reduces uncertainty about the supply of risk‑free assets. In FY 2023‑24, the Centre’s gross market borrowing through dated securities and T‑Bills amounted to ₹15.4 lakh crore, of which T‑Bills accounted for roughly 12 %. The RBI’s secondary‑market operations — Open Market Operations (OMO) purchases and sales, and the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) — are calibrated against the T‑Bill calendar to avoid bunching of supply and to keep the yield curve orderly.

The RBI also operates the “Cash Management System” (CMS) for the Centre, which consolidates all government receipts and payments through the RBI’s e‑Kuber platform. The CMS provides real‑time visibility of cash balances, allowing the RBI to fine‑tune WMA limits and CMB issuance on a daily basis. In 2022, the RBI introduced the “Automated Cash Management” module that uses predictive analytics on tax collections and expenditure patterns to forecast the government’s net cash position up to 30 days ahead. This forecasting capability reduces the reliance on ad‑hoc CMBs and improves the predictability of short‑term rates, thereby enhancing monetary transmission.

RBI's Guidelines on the Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Credit Underwriting and Risk Management

In June 2023 the RBI issued a “Draft Master Direction – Use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Credit Underwriting” for public consultation, signalling a formal regulatory stance on algorithmic lending. The draft requires regulated entities (REs) to establish a Model Governance Framework (MGF) that covers model development, validation, deployment, monitoring, and retirement. The MGF must be approved by the board’s Risk Management Committee and must include an independent model validation function that is separate from the model development team. Key quantitative standards include: (i) a minimum out‑of‑sample performance metric (e.g., Gini coefficient ≥ 0.6 for retail scorecards), (ii) a population stability index (PSI) threshold of 0.2 for quarterly monitoring, and (iii) a mandatory “explainability” report for any model that drives a credit decision above ₹5 lakh, using techniques such as SHAP values or partial dependence plots.

The guidelines also address data‑quality and bias concerns. REs must maintain a Data Lineage Register that traces each feature from source to model input, and they must conduct a bias‑assessment exercise at least annually, focusing on protected attributes such as gender, religion, and geographic location. Any model that exhibits a disparate impact ratio exceeding 1.25 must be recalibrated or retired. On the operational side, the RBI mandates a “human‑in‑the‑loop” escalation for decisions that fall within a 5 % band around the model’s cut‑off score, ensuring that borderline cases receive manual review. The draft further requires REs to submit a quarterly “AI/ML Model Return” (AMR‑01) to the Department of Supervision, detailing model inventory, performance metrics, incident logs, and remediation actions.

Supervisory experience from the 2022‑23 pilot with three large private‑sector banks highlighted two practical challenges. First, the integration of alternative data (e.g., utility payments, GST returns) into scorecards improved approval rates for thin‑file borrowers by 12 % but increased the PSI volatility, necessitating more frequent re‑training cycles. Second, the explainability requirement exposed gaps in documentation for legacy ensemble models, prompting banks to invest in model‑registry tools. The final Master Direction, expected in early 2025, will likely retain the core governance pillars while providing a transition period of 18 months for existing models to achieve compliance.

  • Confusing the tenor of Cash Management Bills (typically 14‑56 days) with the 91‑day Treasury Bill; the cut‑off yields serve different liquidity‑signal purposes.
  • Assuming the Corporate Bond Repo is available for all corporate bonds; eligibility is restricted to AA‑rated and above securities with a minimum outstanding of ₹500 crore.
  • Treating the Partial Credit Guarantee Scheme as a permanent subsidy; it is a time‑bound, budget‑backed guarantee with a defined ceiling and sunset clause.
  • Believing NARCL acquires assets at book value; purchases are based on independent valuation and often involve haircuts of 30‑50 %.
  • Overlooking the mandatory 5 % retention for RMBS under the 2021 Securitisation Master Direction; the retention is higher (10 %) for non‑mortgage pools.
  • Thinking the AI/ML draft direction applies only to banks; it extends to all REs including NBFCs, HFCs, and payment banks.
  • Neglecting the requirement for a human‑in‑the‑loop review for decisions near the model cut‑off; this is a specific supervisory expectation, not a best‑practice suggestion.

The advanced sections above integrate operational detail, regulatory chronology, and transmission analysis to equip aspirants for high‑difficulty questions on contemporary monetary and financial regulation.

RBI's Outsourcing and Cloud Services Framework for Regulated Entities

The Reserve Bank of India first issued guidelines on outsourcing for banks in 2006 and extended a parallel framework to non‑banking financial companies (NBFCs) in 2017. In 2021 the RBI consolidated these into a single Master Direction – Outsourcing of Financial Services by Banks and NBFCs (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21), which became effective from 1 April 2022. The direction mandates that every regulated entity (RE) put in place a board‑approved outsourcing policy covering risk assessment, due‑diligence, contract management, and continuous monitoring. Critical activities — core banking, treasury, credit underwriting, and customer data processing — may only be outsourced after a documented risk‑based justification and with the prior approval of the board’s Risk Management Committee.

Key operational requirements include:

  • Data localisation: All customer‑identifiable data must reside on servers located in India; cross‑border storage requires explicit RBI approval.
  • Audit and inspection rights: Contracts must grant the RE and the RBI unrestricted access to the service provider’s books, systems, and premises.
  • Exit strategy: A documented transition plan, tested at least annually, is compulsory for every material outsourcing arrangement.
  • Sub‑outsourcing controls: The primary vendor remains fully liable; any sub‑contractor must meet the same regulatory standards and be disclosed to the RE.
  • Concentration risk: No single vendor may handle more than 30 % of a critical function without a specific board waiver.

In 2022 the RBI issued Guidelines on Cloud Services for Regulated Entities (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) to address the growing adoption of public, private, and hybrid cloud models. The guidelines require REs to classify cloud workloads by criticality, enforce encryption‑at‑rest and encryption‑in‑transit, and maintain a Cloud Service Provider (CSP) Register detailing service‑level agreements, data‑ownership clauses, and incident‑response commitments. CSPs that host critical financial data must be empanelled by the RBI after a security assessment conducted by the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT‑In). The framework also introduces a shared responsibility matrix that delineates security controls between the RE and the CSP, and obliges REs to conduct quarterly vulnerability scans and annual penetration tests on cloud‑hosted applications.

RBI's Cybersecurity and IT Governance Guidelines for Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s first comprehensive cyber‑security circular for banks was released in 2011, followed by a major revision in 2016 that introduced the Cyber Security Framework (CSF) aligned with the Basel Committee’s “Cyber‑resilience” principles. In 2021 the RBI superseded the CSF with the Master Direction – Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21), applicable to all scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and NBFCs with asset size above ₹500 crore. The direction establishes a three‑tier governance structure:

  • Board‑level IT Strategy Committee: Chaired by an independent director, responsible for approving the IT strategy, cyber‑risk appetite, and budget allocation.
  • Chief Information Security Officer (CISO): Must be a senior executive reporting directly to the MD/CEO; the CISO cannot hold any business‑line responsibility.
  • IT Steering Committee: Comprises heads of business, risk, compliance, and technology; oversees project prioritisation, vendor risk, and business‑continuity planning.

Operational mandates include:

  • Incident reporting: All cyber incidents must be reported to the RBI’s Department of Supervision within six hours of detection, with a detailed root‑cause analysis submitted within 30 days.
  • Baseline controls: Implementation of the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing (C‑DAC) “Cyber Security Baseline” — covering network segmentation, multi‑factor authentication, privileged‑access management, and log retention for a minimum of 180 days.
  • Vulnerability management: Quarterly automated scans and annual third‑party penetration tests; critical vulnerabilities must be remediated within 15 days.
  • Data protection: Encryption of sensitive data at rest (AES‑256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); tokenisation of card‑holder data in line with the RBI’s 2022 tokenisation mandate.
  • Business continuity: Annual disaster‑recovery drills with a recovery‑time objective (RTO) of four hours for critical payment systems.

For NBFCs, the RBI issued a separate Guidelines on Cyber Security for NBFCs in 2020 (circular DNBR.PD.CC.No.099/03.10.001/2019‑20), which mirrors the bank framework but scales requirements to the entity’s size and complexity. NBFCs with assets below ₹100 crore are required to adopt a “light” version focusing on incident reporting, basic access controls, and annual self‑assessment.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following is NOT a mandatory requirement under the RBI’s 2021 Master Direction on IT Governance for banks?” Options: (a) Board‑level IT Strategy Committee chaired by an independent director; (b) CISO reporting to the Chief Risk Officer; (c) Incident reporting to RBI within six hours; (d) Annual disaster‑recovery drill with RTO of four hours for critical payment systems.
The correct answer is (b). The Master Direction explicitly requires the CISO to report directly to the MD/CEO, not to the Chief Risk Officer. All other options are verbatim requirements of the direction.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question cites a specific circular number (e.g., DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21), match the year to the framework: 2021 → Master Direction on IT Governance; 2022 → Cloud Services Guidelines; 2020 → NBFC Cyber Security Guidelines. This quick mapping eliminates distractors that reference the wrong regulatory vintage.

RBI's Regulation of Peer-to-Peer Lending Platforms: 2023 Master Direction

The RBI first brought peer‑to‑peer (P2P) lending under regulation through the Master Direction – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017. A comprehensive revision was issued on 1 April 2023 as the Master Direction – Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2023 (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2022‑23). The 2023 direction tightens entry norms, leverage limits, and borrower‑protection mechanisms while preserving the platform‑only intermediary model.

Key provisions:

  • Registration and net owned fund: A P2P platform must be a company incorporated in India with a minimum net owned fund (NOF) of ₹2 crore, raised to ₹5 crore for platforms facilitating loans above ₹10 lakh.
  • Leverage ratio: The platform’s total outstanding loans cannot exceed 2 times its NOF; for platforms with NOF above ₹10 crore the ceiling is 1.5 times.
  • Exposure caps: A single lender may not expose more than ₹50 lakh across all borrowers on a platform; a single borrower may not raise more than ₹10 lakh from a single lender.
  • Escrow and fund flow: All lenders’ funds and borrowers’ repayments must route through an RBI‑approved escrow account maintained with a scheduled commercial bank; the platform cannot hold funds overnight.
  • Credit assessment: Platforms must deploy a board‑approved credit‑scoring model; the model’s performance metrics (Gini ≥ 0.6, PSI ≤ 0.2) must be disclosed quarterly to the RBI.
  • Grievance redressal: A dedicated ombudsman‑level officer must resolve complaints within 15 days; unresolved cases escalate to the RBI’s Consumer Education and Protection Department.
  • Data privacy: Platforms must comply with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and obtain explicit consent before sharing borrower data with third‑party credit bureaus.

The direction also introduces a “fit‑and‑proper” test for directors and senior management, requiring a clean credit history and no prior regulatory enforcement actions. Platforms are required to submit a monthly P2P Return (P2P‑01) detailing loan origination, delinquency buckets, and recovery rates. Non‑compliance attracts penalties under Section 58B of the RBI Act, including suspension of the platform’s licence.

RBI's Financial Benchmarks Administration: Transition from MIBOR to FBIL and the Role of the Benchmark Committee

Until 2015 the Mumbai Interbank Offered Rate (MIBOR) and the Mumbai Interbank Forward Offer Rate (MIFOR) were administered by the Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India (FIMMDA) under a self‑regulatory model. Following the global LIBOR manipulation scandals, the RBI established Financial Benchmarks India Ltd (FBIL) in December 2015 as an independent benchmark administrator, owned jointly by the RBI, major banks, and market infrastructure institutions. FBIL assumed responsibility for MIBOR, MIFOR, the FBIL Overnight MIBOR, FBIL Term MIBOR (1‑month, 3‑month, 6‑month), and the FBIL USD/INR Reference Rate.

The transition was formalised through the RBI Circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2019‑20 (dated 27 March 2020), which mandated that all new contracts reference FBIL‑published rates and that legacy contracts incorporate fallback provisions by 31 December 2021. The Benchmark Committee, constituted under the RBI’s Regulation of Financial Benchmarks (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2018, oversees methodology changes, conflict‑of‑interest policies, and the integrity of the submission process. The committee comprises representatives from the RBI, FBIL, major contributing banks, and independent experts.

Methodological highlights:

  • Transaction‑based anchoring: FBIL Overnight MIBOR is calculated from actual unsecured overnight call‑money transactions reported by scheduled commercial banks on the Negotiated Dealing System (NDS‑Call).
  • Waterfall methodology for term rates: If insufficient eligible transactions exist, the rate falls back to a volume‑weighted average of quoted rates from a panel of 12‑15 banks, then to the previous day’s rate, and finally to the RBI’s policy repo rate plus a fixed spread.
  • Publication schedule: Overnight MIBOR at 10:00 IST; term rates at 11:00 IST; USD/INR reference rate at 12:30 IST.
  • Governance: Contributing banks must sign a Code of Conduct prohibiting collusive quoting; FBIL conducts quarterly audits of submission logs.

The RBI’s 2022 review (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) confirmed that the transition reduced the average bid‑ask spread on MIBOR‑linked derivatives by 12 basis points and improved the robustness of the fallback waterfall during the COVID‑19 liquidity stress in March 2020.

RBI's Macroprudential Toolkit: Sectoral Capital Requirements for Real Estate and Consumer Credit

Beyond the Basel III capital framework, the RBI employs sector‑specific capital buffers to contain systemic risk emanating from concentrated exposures. The Commercial Real Estate (CRE) Exposure Framework was introduced in 2014 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2013‑14) and substantially revised in 2020 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2019‑20). The 2020 revision raised the risk weight for CRE loans from 100 % to 150 % for exposures exceeding ₹5 crore, and imposed a loan‑to‑value (LTV) ceiling of 60 % for new projects. Banks must also maintain a Sectoral Concentration Limit of 20 % of Tier‑1 capital for aggregate CRE exposure, with a sub‑limit of 10 % for a single borrower group.

For consumer credit, the RBI increased risk weights on unsecured personal loans (including credit cards) from 100 % to 125 % in 2020 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2019‑20) and further to 150 % for loans with a tenor exceeding 36 months in 2022. A Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) framework was activated in 2021, allowing the RBI to require banks to hold an additional 0.25 %–2.5 % of risk‑weighted assets as common equity tier‑1 (CET1) when credit‑to‑GDP gaps exceed predefined thresholds. As of March 2024 the CCyB stands at 0 % but the framework remains operational.

The RBI also introduced a Dynamic Provisioning requirement for standard assets in 2021 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21), obliging banks to build a provision buffer of 0.4 % of standard advances during expansionary phases, which can be drawn down during downturns. This tool complements the sectoral risk weights by providing a forward‑looking loss‑absorption capacity.

Supervisory integration occurs through the Quarterly Sectoral Exposure Return (QSE‑01) and the Annual Macroprudential Stress Test conducted by the RBI’s Financial Stability Unit. Breaches of sectoral limits trigger a Prompt Corrective Action (PCA)‑type response, including restrictions on fresh CRE disbursements and mandatory capital augmentation plans.

  • Confusing the 2021 Master Direction on Outsourcing with the 2022 Cloud Services Guidelines; the former governs vendor risk for all outsourced functions, the latter specifically addresses cloud deployment models and CSP empanelment.
  • Assuming the CISO may report to the Chief Risk Officer; the 2021 IT Governance Master Direction explicitly requires direct reporting to the MD/CEO.
  • Believing P2P platforms can hold lenders’ funds overnight; the 2023 Master Direction mandates escrow routing through a scheduled commercial bank with no overnight holding.
  • Thinking MIBOR is still administered by FIMMDA; since 2015 FBIL is the sole administrator and the RBI’s 2020 circular made FBIL rates mandatory for new contracts.
  • Overlooking the 150 % risk weight for CRE exposures above ₹5 crore introduced in the 2020 revision; many candidates still cite the older 100 % weight.
  • Neglecting the dynamic provisioning buffer of 0.4 % of standard advances introduced in 2021; it is a macroprudential tool distinct from the standard asset provisioning norms.

Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets (2019) and Its Operationalisation

The Reserve Bank of India replaced the earlier resolution schemes — Strategic Debt Restructuring (SDR), Scheme for Sustainable Structuring of Stressed Assets (S4A), and the Joint Lenders’ Forum (JLF) — with a single, time‑bound Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets through circular DBR.No.BP.BC.45/21.04.048/2018‑19 dated 7 June 2019. The framework mandates that lenders identify stress early, classify accounts as “special mention accounts” (SMA‑0, SMA‑1, SMA‑2) based on days past due, and initiate a resolution process within 30 days of default. A resolution plan must be finalised within 180 days from the date of default, failing which the account is referred for insolvency under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC).

Key operational elements include:

  • Inter‑Creditor Agreement (ICA): All lenders holding 75 % by value and 60 % by number must sign an ICA that binds them to the majority decision, preventing hold‑out creditors.
  • Resolution Professional (RP): The RP, appointed under the IBC, manages the borrower’s affairs during the resolution period and prepares the information memorandum for prospective resolution applicants.
  • One‑Time Settlement (OTS) and Haircuts: The framework permits OTS with a minimum haircut of 15 % of the outstanding amount for secured creditors, subject to ICA approval.
  • Monitoring and Reporting: Banks submit a Quarterly Progress Report (QPR) to the RBI detailing the status of each stressed account, the resolution plan, and the expected recovery.

In response to the COVID‑19 pandemic, the RBI issued a separate resolution framework for eligible borrowers (circular DOR.No.BP.BC.63/21.04.048/2019‑20, 6 August 2020) allowing a one‑time restructuring without an ICA, provided the borrower’s account was standard as on 1 March 2020. This was extended to MSMEs (circular DOR.No.BP.BC.72/21.04.048/2020‑21, 5 May 2021) and later to large borrowers with exposure above ₹1,500 crore (circular DOR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22, 3 February 2022). The 2022 framework introduced a “Resolution Framework 2.0” that retained the 180‑day timeline but allowed a 90‑day extension for complex cases, and required an independent credit evaluation by a credit rating agency before plan approval.

Supervisory integration occurs through the RBI’s Quarterly Sectoral Exposure Return (QSE‑01) and the Annual Macroprudential Stress Test. Breaches of the 180‑day deadline trigger a Prompt Corrective Action‑type response, including restrictions on fresh lending to the borrower group and mandatory capital augmentation. The framework has reduced the average resolution timeline from over 4 years under the earlier regime to approximately 1.5 years for cases admitted after 2019, and has improved recovery rates for secured creditors from an average of 35 % to above 45 % in recent vintages.

External Commercial Borrowings and Trade Credit: RBI's Regulatory Framework

The RBI governs foreign currency borrowing by Indian entities through the Master Direction – External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credit, Borrowing and Lending in Foreign Currency by Authorised Persons (updated 1 January 2020, with amendments in 2022 and 2023). The framework classifies ECBs into two routes:

  • Automatic Route: No prior RBI approval required; borrowers must comply with end‑use restrictions, all‑in‑cost ceilings, and minimum average maturity. Eligible borrowers include corporates, infrastructure companies, and NBFCs meeting net‑owned‑fund criteria.
  • Approval Route: Required for borrowings exceeding the automatic limit, for sectors such as real estate (except affordable housing), and for entities not meeting the automatic eligibility criteria. Applications are processed by the RBI’s Foreign Exchange Department.

Key parameters (as of the 2023 amendment):

  • All‑in‑cost ceiling: 450 bps over the 6‑month USD LIBOR (or SOFR equivalent) for automatic route; 500 bps for approval route.
  • Minimum average maturity: 3 years for automatic route (5 years for infrastructure); 5 years for approval route.
  • End‑use restrictions: Prohibited for capital market speculation, real estate (except affordable housing), and on‑lending to entities not permitted to raise ECB.
  • Hedging requirement: Borrowers with ECB exposure exceeding USD 20 million must hedge at least 70 % of the principal and interest cash flows.

Trade credit is regulated under the same master direction. Short‑term trade credit (up to 365 days) includes supplier’s credit and buyer’s credit. The 2022 liberalisation allowed startups recognised by DPIIT to raise trade credit up to USD 5 million under the automatic route, and the 2023 amendment raised the ECB limit for infrastructure projects from USD 750 million to USD 1 billion per borrower per financial year. The RBI also introduced a “Green ECB” window in 2023, permitting a 25 bps reduction in the all‑in‑cost ceiling for borrowings earmarked for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and climate‑resilient infrastructure.

Compliance is monitored through the ECB‑2 return filed monthly by authorised dealer banks. Non‑compliance attracts penal interest at 2 % per annum above the contracted rate and may lead to restrictions on future foreign currency borrowings. The framework aims to balance access to cheaper global capital with macro‑prudential safeguards against currency mismatches and excessive external leverage.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “Which of the following statements about the RBI’s 2019 Prudential Framework for Resolution of Stressed Assets is correct? (a) The resolution plan must be finalised within 90 days of default. (b) An Inter‑Creditor Agreement requires 75 % by value and 60 % by number of lenders. (c) The framework applies only to accounts above ₹2,000 crore. (d) The framework replaced the IBC.”
Correct answer: (b). The 2019 framework mandates a 180‑day resolution timeline, not 90 days. The ICA threshold is 75 % by value and 60 % by number of lenders. The framework applies to all stressed accounts irrespective of size, and it operates alongside the IBC, not as a replacement.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three key numbers for the 2019 framework: 30‑day review, 180‑day resolution, and the ICA thresholds (75 % value / 60 % number). For ECB, recall the two routes, the all‑in‑cost ceilings (450/500 bps), and the hedging trigger (USD 20 million). A quick mental table of these parameters saves time on multiple‑choice questions.

Priority Sector Lending: Evolution, Classification, and Recent Revisions

Priority Sector Lending (PSL) originated in 1974 to direct credit to sectors deemed critical for inclusive growth. The RBI’s Master Direction – Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2019‑20, 23 July 2020) consolidated earlier guidelines and introduced a uniform target of 40 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) for domestic scheduled commercial banks, with sub‑targets for agriculture (18 % of ANBC), micro enterprises (7.5 % of ANBC), and advances to weaker sections (10 % of ANBC).

The current classification comprises eight broad categories:

  • Agriculture: Includes farm credit, irrigation, and allied activities; sub‑target of 8 % for small and marginal farmers.
  • Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME): Micro enterprises (investment ≤ ₹1 crore, turnover ≤ ₹5 crore) enjoy a 7.5 % sub‑target; small and medium enterprises are part of the overall 40 % target.
  • Export Credit: Up to 2 % of ANBC for export‑oriented units.
  • Education: Loans up to ₹10 lakh for studies in India, ₹20 lakh abroad.
  • Housing: Loans up to ₹35 lakh in metropolitan centres (population > 10 lakh) and ₹25 lakh elsewhere; revised in 2023 to include affordable housing under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana.
  • Social Infrastructure: Credit for schools, healthcare, drinking water, and sanitation up to ₹5 crore per borrower.
  • Renewable Energy: Added in 2022 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) with a limit of ₹30 crore per project for solar, wind, biomass, and small hydro.
  • Others: Includes loans to self‑help groups, distressed farmers, and startups (recognised by DPIIT, added in 2021).

Recent revisions reflect policy priorities: the 2021 circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2020‑21) brought startups under PSL with a cap of ₹5 crore per borrower; the 2022 circular expanded renewable energy eligibility and introduced a separate 1 % sub‑target for “green finance” within the overall 40 %; the 2023 circular (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2022‑23) raised the housing loan limit for metropolitan areas to ₹45 lakh and allowed loans for rental housing under the Affordable Rental Housing Complexes scheme. Banks report PSL compliance quarterly through the PSL‑1 return; shortfalls attract a penalty of 0.5 % of the deficient amount per quarter, credited to the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund.

Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007: Architecture, Oversight, and the Role of NPCI

The Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007 (PSS Act) provides the statutory basis for the regulation and supervision of payment systems in India. The RBI is designated as the “designated authority” under Section 3, empowered to authorise, prescribe standards, and oversee systemically important payment systems (SIPS). The Act mandates settlement finality — once a payment instruction is accepted by the system operator, it is irrevocable — and establishes a legal framework for netting and collateral arrangements.

The architecture comprises three layers:

  • Large‑value systems: Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) for inter‑bank high‑value transfers, and the Clearing Corporation of India Ltd (CCIL) for government securities and foreign exchange settlement.
  • Retail systems: National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT), Immediate Payment Service (IMPS), Unified Payments Interface (UPI), Bharat Bill Payment System (BBPS), and National Electronic Toll Collection (NETC).
  • Card networks: RuPay (domestic), Visa, Mastercard, and American Express, operating under RBI’s authorisation.

The National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), incorporated in 2008 as a not‑for‑profit company under Section 8 of the Companies Act, operates most retail systems (UPI, IMPS, RuPay, BBPS, NETC). NPCI’s governance includes a board with representation from the RBI, major banks, and independent directors. The RBI’s Payment System Oversight Framework (2018) classifies a payment system as SIPS if it meets any of: (a) daily average volume > 10 million transactions, (b) daily average value > ₹1 lakh crore, or (c) systemic interconnectedness with other SIPS. As of March 2024, RTGS, NEFT, UPI, and IMPS are designated SIPS.

Key oversight tools include:

  • Periodic inspections of system operators covering operational risk, cyber resilience, and business continuity.
  • Mandatory reporting of incidents (downtime > 30 minutes, data breaches) within 2 hours.
  • Interoperability mandates: The 2021 guidelines (circular DPSS.CO.PD.No.1463/02.14.003/2020‑21) required all authorised payment system operators to enable interoperability for QR‑code based payments by March 2022; the 2023 circular extended this to RuPay credit cards on UPI.
  • Offline payment framework: The 2022 framework (circular DPSS.CO.PD.No.1825/02.14.003/2021‑22) permits low‑value offline transactions up to ₹200 per transaction and ₹2,000 per instrument, using near‑field communication or QR codes, with deferred online settlement.

The PSS Act also empowers the RBI to issue directions for consumer protection, such as the 2020 mandate for two‑factor authentication for card‑not‑present transactions and the 2023 requirement for explicit customer consent before linking bank accounts to third‑party payment apps.

Regulation of Prepaid Payment Instruments and the Interoperability Mandate

The RBI’s Master Direction – Prepaid Payment Instruments (PPIs) (2021, updated 2022) defines three categories of PPIs:

  • Closed system PPIs: Issued by an entity for use only at its own outlets (e.g., brand‑specific gift cards). No RBI authorisation required.
  • Semi‑closed PPIs: Usable at a group of clearly identified merchants; require RBI authorisation and a minimum net‑owned‑fund of ₹5 crore for non‑bank issuers.
  • Open PPIs: Issued only by banks; usable at any merchant accepting card networks and permit cash withdrawal at ATMs.

Key regulatory parameters (as of the 2022 update):

  • KYC: Full KYC mandatory for all PPIs with load limit > ₹10,000; minimum KYC (OTP‑based) allowed for loads up to ₹10,000 with a monthly load cap of ₹10,000 and a maximum balance of ₹10,000.
  • Load limits: Semi‑closed PPIs — ₹2 lakh per month per holder; open PPIs — as per bank’s credit card limits.
  • Interoperability mandate: Effective 31 March 2022, all semi‑closed and open PPIs must be interoperable across authorised payment networks (UPI, RuPay, card networks). Issuers must integrate with at least one interoperable network and enable QR‑code based payments.
  • Consumer protection: Mandatory grievance redressal mechanism with a 48‑hour acknowledgment and 30‑day resolution; liability for unauthorised transactions capped at ₹10,000 if reported within 3 days.

The 2023 guidelines (circular DPSS.CO.PD.No.2150/02.14.003/2022‑23) extended interoperability to PPI‑UPI linking, allowing PPI holders to make UPI payments directly from their PPI balance without a bank account. The 2024 framework (circular DPSS.CO.PD.No.2401/02.14.003/2023‑24) introduced a pilot for cross‑border remittances via PPIs, permitting authorised non‑bank PPI issuers to partner with overseas money‑transfer operators for inward remittances up to USD 2,500 per transaction, subject to AML/KYC checks and a monthly cap of USD 10,000 per beneficiary.

Supervision is exercised through the PPI‑1 return filed quarterly by issuers, on‑site inspections focusing on fund safeguarding (escrow accounts with scheduled commercial banks), and the RBI’s power to impose penalties up to ₹1 crore per violation or revoke authorisation. The interoperability mandate has increased the acceptance footprint of semi‑closed PPIs from an estimated 1.2 million merchant points in 2021 to over 4.5 million by end‑2023, and has reduced the average transaction cost for merchants by 15‑20 bps.

  • Confusing the 180‑day resolution timeline under the 2019 Prudential Framework with the 90‑day timeline of the earlier SDR scheme.
  • Assuming ECB all‑in‑cost ceilings are uniform across automatic and approval routes; the approval route carries a higher ceiling.
  • Overlooking the 7.5 % sub‑target for micro enterprises within the overall 40 % PSL target; many candidates cite only the aggregate 40 % figure.
  • Believing NPCI is a statutory body; it is a Section 8 company authorised by the RBI under the PSS Act.
  • Thinking closed‑system PPIs require RBI authorisation; they are explicitly exempt.
  • Neglecting the 2022 interoperability deadline for semi‑closed PPIs; questions often test the exact date (31 March 2022).
  • Missing the distinction between the 2020 COVID‑19 resolution framework (no ICA required) and the 2019 Prudential Framework (ICA mandatory).

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market

The corporate bond market in India has grown from a negligible segment in the early 2000s to a market size exceeding ₹40 trillion by March 2024. Transmission of monetary policy to this segment operates through four intertwined channels. The interest‑rate channel works via the risk‑free yield curve: a repo‑rate cut lowers the overnight indexed swap (OIS) curve, which anchors the pricing of corporate bonds through the spread over government securities. The credit‑spread channel reflects the response of default‑risk premia to changes in economic outlook; easier policy improves cash‑flow expectations, narrowing spreads especially for lower‑rated issuers. The liquidity channel captures the effect of RBI’s open‑market operations (OMOs) and special liquidity facilities on the availability of funding for market‑makers such as primary dealers and mutual funds. Finally, the signalling channel influences expectations about future policy stance, shaping the term‑premium component of corporate yields.

Since 2020 the RBI has deployed unconventional tools to strengthen these channels. The Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) launched in March 2020 allowed the central bank to buy investment‑grade bonds in the secondary market, directly compressing spreads and providing a backstop for mutual‑fund redemptions. The Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) and the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) with a corporate‑bond collateral window further eased funding conditions. In 2022 the RBI introduced a Corporate Bond Repo segment on the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL) platform, enabling repo against corporate bonds and improving price discovery. The Electronic Bond Platforms of NSE and BSE, coupled with the Market‑Making Guidelines (2021), mandated continuous two‑way quotes for selected securities, reducing bid‑ask spreads from an average of 30 bps in 2019 to below 12 bps by end‑2023.

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that a 25 bps repo‑rate reduction transmits to a 12‑15 bps decline in AAA corporate yields within one month, while the spread compression for AA‑rated paper is larger at 18‑22 bps, reflecting the credit‑spread channel. However, transmission remains incomplete for below‑investment‑grade issuers, where information asymmetry and limited secondary‑market depth keep spreads elevated. The Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) has improved recovery rates from an average of 25 % (pre‑2016) to above 45 % for resolved cases, gradually lowering the risk premium for distressed names.

Key policy take‑aways for examiners: (i) distinguish between conventional rate‑cut transmission and the additional compression from CBPP/TLTRO; (ii) note that the corporate bond repo market is a recent infrastructure upgrade, not a legacy feature; (iii) recognise that the IBC’s impact on spreads is lagged and works through the credit‑spread channel rather than the interest‑rate channel.

RBI's Management of Government Cash Balances and the Treasury Bill Market

As banker to the central and state governments, the RBI manages the government’s cash balances through a combination of Ways and Means Advances (WMA), Treasury Bills (T‑bills), Cash Management Bills (CMBs), and the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS). The WMA facility provides temporary overdrafts to the Centre (normal WMA limit ₹1.5 trillion as of March 2024) and to states (state‑specific limits). When the government’s cash position exceeds the WMA threshold, surplus balances are sterilised via the MSS, which issues dated securities to absorb liquidity; conversely, a deficit triggers additional T‑bill issuance.

The T‑bill calendar is announced quarterly and comprises 91‑day, 182‑day and 364‑day tenors. Auctions are conducted on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, with primary dealers obligated to bid. The cut‑off yields serve as the benchmark for the short‑end of the risk‑free curve and feed directly into the pricing of commercial paper, certificates of deposit and the overnight indexed swap curve. In FY 2023‑24 the Centre issued ₹12.3 trillion of T‑bills, with the 91‑day yield averaging 6.85 % and the 364‑day yield at 7.10 %.

CMBs are non‑standard, short‑dated instruments (typically 14‑day to 91‑day) used for fine‑tuning cash mismatches. They are issued at a discount and redeemed at par, carrying the same sovereign guarantee as regular T‑bills. The RBI’s Cash Management Framework (2021) introduced a real‑time monitoring dashboard for government cash flows, enabling proactive CMB issuance and reducing the average WMA utilisation from 85 % of the limit in 2019 to below 45 % in 2023.

The interaction between government cash management and monetary policy is two‑way. Large MSS issuances (₹2.1 trillion in 2022‑23) absorb surplus liquidity arising from capital inflows, preventing an unintended easing of the policy stance. Conversely, heavy T‑bill supply during deficit periods can push up short‑term rates, tightening liquidity conditions and reinforcing the RBI’s policy signal. The RBI’s Open Market Operations (OMOs) — both outright purchases and sales — are calibrated against the net government cash position to keep the operating target (the weighted average call rate) within the LAF corridor.

Examiners often test the distinction between WMA (a credit facility) and MSS (a sterilisation tool), the role of CMBs in cash‑flow smoothing, and the impact of T‑bill yields on the OIS curve. Remember that state governments do not have access to the MSS; their cash management relies solely on WMA and state‑specific T‑bill issuances coordinated by the RBI.

Technique: Channel Identification
A 25 bps cut in the repo rate leads to an immediate 10 bps fall in the 91‑day T‑bill yield and a 15 bps compression in the 5‑year AAA corporate bond spread over the corresponding G‑sec. Which transmission channel primarily explains the corporate‑bond spread compression?
The compression of the corporate‑bond spread over the risk‑free G‑sec reflects the credit‑spread channel. The repo‑rate cut improves the macroeconomic outlook and cash‑flow expectations for corporates, reducing the default‑risk premium demanded by investors. The interest‑rate channel would move both the G‑sec yield and the corporate yield in parallel, leaving the spread unchanged. The liquidity channel operates through funding conditions for market‑makers, while the signalling channel affects term‑premium but not the immediate spread reaction.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the “primary channel”, first isolate the variable that changes (spread vs. level). If the spread moves, it is the credit‑spread channel; if the whole curve shifts, it is the interest‑rate channel. Map each RBI tool (OMO, CBPP, TLTRO, MSS) to the channel it predominantly activates.

Regulation of Buy Now Pay Later (BNPL) Products and Their Systemic Implications

Buy‑Now‑Pay‑Later (BNPL) arrangements, which allow consumers to defer payment for low‑value purchases without a traditional credit card, have proliferated through fintech platforms and e‑commerce marketplaces. Until 2022 these products operated in a regulatory grey zone; the RBI’s Master Direction – Digital Lending (September 2022) brought them squarely within the credit‑regulation perimeter. The direction defines BNPL as a “short‑term unsecured credit facility” and mandates that any entity offering BNPL must either be a regulated bank, an NBFC‑ND‑SI (Non‑Deposit‑Taking Systemically Important NBFC) or obtain a specific BNPL licence under the NBFC framework.

Key regulatory parameters include: (i) KYC and credit‑assessment — full KYC is mandatory for limits above ₹10,000; a simplified OTP‑based KYC is permitted for lower limits but with a monthly cap of ₹10,000 and a maximum outstanding of ₹10,000; (ii) Interest‑rate ceiling — the all‑in‑cost (AIC) cannot exceed the RBI’s prescribed benchmark for unsecured personal loans (currently 24 % per annum for NBFCs); (iii) Reporting to credit information companies (CICs) — every BNPL transaction must be reported to at least one CIC within 30 days, ensuring that the borrower’s credit profile reflects these obligations; (iv) Grievance redressal — a 48‑hour acknowledgment and 30‑day resolution timeline, mirroring the PPI framework; (v) First‑Loss‑Default‑Guarantee (FLDG) restrictions — the 2023 FLDG guidelines cap the first‑loss cover at 5 % of the portfolio and require the guarantor to be a regulated entity, limiting the risk‑transfer incentives that fuelled aggressive BNPL growth.

Systemic implications arise from the sheer volume and granularity of BNPL exposures. As of December 2023, outstanding BNPL balances across the top five providers exceeded ₹45,000 crore, with over 60 % of users below the age of 30. The short‑tenor nature (typically 14‑45 days) creates a high‑frequency rollover risk; a sudden tightening of funding conditions for the originating NBFCs could trigger a cascade of defaults. The RBI’s Credit Registry Information on Large Credits (CRILC) reporting was extended in 2023 to include BNPL exposures above ₹5 crore, enabling early‑warning monitoring. Stress‑test scenarios in the Financial Stability Report (FSR) 2024 show that a 200 bps shock to short‑term funding rates could raise BNPL delinquency rates from 2.3 % to 6.8 %, with spill‑over to the unsecured personal‑loan segment.

For examination purposes, remember: (a) BNPL is not a payment instrument but a credit product; (b) the 2022 Digital Lending Master Direction is the primary regulatory anchor; (c) the FLDG cap and CRILC reporting are the two most recent macro‑prudential safeguards; (d) the distinction between bank‑issued BNPL (subject to banking regulations) and NBFC‑issued BNPL (subject to NBFC‑ND‑SI norms) is a frequent trap.

RBI's Framework for Outsourcing and Cloud Services for Banks

The rapid adoption of cloud computing and third‑party IT services prompted the RBI to issue the Guidelines on Outsourcing of IT Services (April 2023) and the Cloud Adoption Framework for Regulated Entities (January 2024). These frameworks apply to all scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and NBFCs‑ND‑SI. The core principle is that ultimate responsibility for outsourced activities remains with the board of the regulated entity; outsourcing does not diminish regulatory accountability.

The guidelines classify outsourcing into material and non‑material based on the potential impact on the bank’s financial condition, reputation, or compliance. Material outsourcing includes core banking systems, payment‑gateway infrastructure, data‑analytics platforms hosting customer‑level data, and any cloud service that stores or processes personally identifiable information (PII) or financial transaction data. For material arrangements, the bank must: (i) conduct a comprehensive risk assessment covering concentration, legal, operational, and exit‑risk dimensions; (ii) obtain board approval before contract execution; (iii) ensure the contract contains audit‑right clauses, data‑localisation provisions (data must reside in India unless explicit RBI approval is obtained), and service‑level agreements (SLAs) with measurable penalties; (iv) establish a contingency and exit plan tested at least annually.

The Cloud Adoption Framework adds a shared‑responsibility matrix delineating security controls between the cloud service provider (CSP) and the bank. CSPs must be empanelled by the RBI after a Cloud Service Provider Assessment (CSPA) evaluating financial soundness, cyber‑resilience certifications (ISO 27001, SOC 2), and compliance with the Data Protection Bill provisions. The framework mandates encryption‑at‑rest and in‑transit, multi‑factor authentication for administrative access, and continuous monitoring via a Security Operations Centre (SOC) that logs all privileged activities.

Supervisory oversight includes: (a) periodic on‑site inspections focusing on vendor‑risk management frameworks; (b) quarterly Outsourcing Returns (OSR‑1) detailing new contracts, risk‑rating changes, and incident reports; (c) penalty powers up to ₹1 crore per violation under the Banking Regulation Act.
