Banks that breach the minimum share or fail to maintain independent appraisal face supervisory letters and, in repeated cases, restrictions on new co‑lending tie‑ups.

RBI’s Framework for Securitisation and Assignment of Financial Assets

The securitisation framework in India is governed by the RBI’s “Guidelines on Securitisation of Standard Assets” (2012) and the subsequent “Revised Securitisation Guidelines” issued in September 2021 (circular DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22). The 2021 revision aligned Indian norms with the Basel Committee’s “Securitisation Framework” and introduced stricter retention, disclosure, and due‑diligence requirements. A securitisation transaction involves the transfer of a pool of standard assets (loans, receivables) to a special purpose vehicle (SPV) which issues securities backed by the cash flows of the pool. The originator (bank or NBFC) must retain a minimum of 5 % of the securitised exposure (the “skin‑in‑the‑game” rule) on an ongoing basis, either through vertical slice (pro‑rata across all tranches) or horizontal slice (first‑loss piece).

The guidelines classify securitisation into two broad categories: (i) “True Sale” securitisation, where legal title passes to the SPV and the originator derecognises the assets; and (ii) “Synthetic” securitisation, where credit risk is transferred via credit derivatives while assets remain on the originator’s balance sheet. Only true‑sale transactions qualify for capital relief under the Basel III securitisation framework. The SPV must be a bankruptcy‑remote entity, typically a trust set up under the Indian Trusts Act, 1882, and must be rated by at least one credit rating agency registered with SEBI.

Key prudential safeguards include: (a) a minimum holding period of six months for the underlying assets before securitisation (to prevent “originate‑to‑distribute” behaviour); (b) a cap of 20 % of the originator’s net owned funds on the aggregate amount of assets securitised in a financial year; (c) mandatory disclosure of pool‑level data (asset‑level characteristics, delinquency status, prepayment history) to investors and the RBI on a quarterly basis; (d) a requirement that the originator or its group entities do not provide credit enhancement beyond the prescribed 5 % retention, except for liquidity facilities that are fully collateralised and limited to 10 % of the pool size.

Assignment of financial assets (outright sale without SPV) is covered under the “Guidelines on Assignment of Loan Assets” (2016, updated 2020). The assignor must ensure that the assignee is a regulated entity (bank, NBFC, ARC, or eligible foreign portfolio investor) and that the assignment is at arm’s length. The assignor continues to service the loan unless a servicing agreement transfers servicing rights. The RBI monitors assignment volumes through the CRILC and requires that assigned assets be reported as off‑balance‑sheet exposures for large‑exposure purposes.

As of the March 2024 Financial Stability Report, the outstanding securitised portfolio stood at ₹4.8 lakh crore, with mortgage‑backed securities (MBS) and asset‑backed securities (ABS) for auto and micro‑enterprise loans forming the bulk. The 2021 revisions have improved transparency — pool‑level data availability rose from 62 % (2020) to 89 % (2023) — and have reduced the incidence of “re‑securitisation” where originators repackaged already‑securitised tranches.

Examiner’s Technique: Application of Retention Rules
A scheduled commercial bank originates a pool of ₹500 crore of standard auto‑loan receivables and securitises them through an SPV. The bank retains a vertical slice of 5 % across all tranches. Six months later, the bank wishes to sell its retained slice to an unrelated NBFC. Is this permissible under the 2021 Securitisation Guidelines? Explain the regulatory rationale.
No, the sale of the retained slice is not permitted. The 2021 guidelines require the originator to hold the minimum 5 % retention on an ongoing basis for the life of the securitisation. The retention must be maintained by the originator (or its group) to ensure continued alignment of interests and to prevent the originator from offloading the first‑loss risk. Transferring the retained slice to a third party would defeat the “skin‑in‑the‑game” objective and is explicitly prohibited under paragraph 4.2 of the revised guidelines. The rationale is to preserve incentive compatibility: the originator must bear a meaningful portion of credit risk to ensure prudent underwriting and ongoing monitoring of the pool.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks about securitisation, first identify whether it is a true‑sale or synthetic structure — only true‑sale qualifies for capital relief. Remember the three non‑negotiables: (1) minimum 5 % retention held by originator for the full tenor, (2) six‑month seasoning of assets, (3) bankruptcy‑remote SPV with a trust deed. A quick mental checklist of these three points eliminates most distractors.

RBI’s Priority Sector Lending Classification, Targets, and Recent Reforms

Priority Sector Lending (PSL) remains a cornerstone of India’s developmental banking mandate. The RBI’s Master Direction — “Priority Sector Lending – Targets and Classification” (updated July 2023) prescribes that domestic scheduled commercial banks allocate 40 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off‑Balance Sheet Exposure (whichever is higher) to priority sectors. For foreign banks with less than 20 branches, the target is 40 % of ANBC with a sub‑target of 18 % for exports. The broad categories and sub‑targets (as of FY 2023‑24) are:

  • Agriculture — 18 % of ANBC (including 8 % for small and marginal farmers).
  • Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) — 7.5 % of ANBC (of which 5 % for micro enterprises).
  • Export Credit — 12 % of ANBC (for foreign banks only).
  • Education — loans up to ₹10 lakh for studies in India, ₹20 lakh abroad.
  • Housing — loans up to ₹35 lakh in metropolitan centres (population >10 lakh) and ₹25 lakh elsewhere.
  • Social Infrastructure — loans for schools, health‑care facilities, drinking water, sanitation.
  • Renewable Energy — loans for solar, wind, biomass, small hydro up to ₹30 crore per project.
  • Start‑ups — loans to DPIIT‑recognised start‑ups up to ₹5 crore (added in 2022).
  • Weaker Sections — 10 % of ANBC (includes small/marginal farmers, artisans, SC/ST beneficiaries, self‑help groups).

The 2023 revision introduced three notable changes: (i) inclusion of “green finance” as a distinct sub‑category under renewable energy, with a separate reporting code to track climate‑aligned credit; (ii) raising the housing loan limit for metropolitan areas from ₹28 lakh to ₹35 lakh to reflect property‑price inflation; (iii) allowing banks to meet up to 2 % of the agriculture target through “agri‑infrastructure” loans (cold storage, warehousing, primary processing) classified under the agriculture head. The RBI also mandated quarterly reporting of PSL achievement through the “PSL Return” on the RBI’s Online Reporting System (ORS), with penalties for persistent shortfalls (interest‑free deposit of the shortfall amount with the RBI for one year).

Compliance trends show that as of March 2024, 92 % of domestic banks met the overall 40 % target, but only 68 % achieved the 18 % agriculture sub‑target. The shortfall in agriculture is largely concentrated in the northern and eastern states where institutional credit penetration remains low. The RBI’s 2023 Financial Inclusion Index notes that the “credit‑gap” for small and marginal farmers stands at ₹1.6 lakh crore, prompting the central bank to encourage co‑lending and business‑correspondent models to bridge the gap.

Supervisory focus has shifted from mere target achievement to “quality of PSL” — the RBI now examines the proportion of fresh lending versus roll‑over of existing loans, the share of loans to first‑time borrowers, and the incidence of ever‑greening through repeated restructuring. Banks that show a high roll‑over ratio (>60 %) receive supervisory letters and are required to submit a remedial action plan within 30 days.

RBI’s Cybersecurity and IT Governance Framework for Banks and NBFCs

The RBI’s approach to cyber resilience has evolved from a set of ad‑hoc circulars (2001, 2011) to a comprehensive master direction — “Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices” (issued June 2020, updated April 2023). The framework applies to all scheduled commercial banks, small finance banks, payment banks, and NBFCs‑ND‑SI. It mandates a board‑level IT Strategy Committee, a dedicated Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) reporting directly to the MD/CEO, and a formal Cyber Security Policy approved by the board at least annually.

Core pillars of the framework include: (i) **Governance** — clear accountability matrix, IT risk appetite statement, and periodic board review of cyber‑risk dashboards; (ii) **Risk Management** — adoption of a recognised framework (ISO 27001, NIST CSF) for risk assessment, mandatory vulnerability assessment and penetration testing (VAPT) at least annually and after any major change; (iii) **Controls** — implementation of multi‑factor authentication for all privileged access, encryption of data at rest and in transit, network segmentation, and automated log‑monitoring with Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) solutions; (iv) **Incident Management** — a 24 × 7 Security Operations Centre (SOC), defined escalation matrix, and mandatory reporting of “significant cyber incidents” to the RBI within 6 hours (for critical systems) and 24 hours (for others); (v) **Assurance** — internal audit of IT controls every quarter, external audit annually, and a mandatory “Cyber Crisis Management Plan” tested through tabletop exercises bi‑annually.

The 2023 update introduced two new requirements: (a) **Supply‑Chain Risk Management** — banks must assess and monitor the cyber posture of critical third‑party service providers (cloud, managed security, core‑banking vendors) and include contractual clauses for breach notification and right‑to‑audit; (b) **Quantum‑Ready Cryptography** — a roadmap to migrate to post‑quantum cryptographic algorithms for all high‑value payment systems (RTGS, NEFT, UPI) by 2026, aligned with the National Quantum Mission.

Supervisory outcomes are captured in the RBI’s “Cyber Security Assessment Framework” (CSAF) scorecards, which rate entities on a 5‑point scale. As of the 2023‑24 supervisory cycle, 78 % of banks achieved a “Maturing” (Level 3) or higher rating, while 12 % of NBFCs‑ND‑SI were rated “Initial” (Level 1) and directed to submit time‑bound remediation plans. The RBI also conducts thematic “Red‑Team” exercises on a sample of systemically important banks to test detection and response capabilities.

Penalties for non‑compliance include monetary fines (up to ₹1 crore per breach under the Banking Regulation Act), restriction on new digital product launches, and, in extreme cases, supersession of the board. The 2022 “Cyber Incident at a Large Private Bank” (where a ransomware attack disrupted core banking for 48 hours) led to a ₹2.5 crore penalty and a directive to overhaul the bank’s privileged‑access management within 90 days.

RBI’s Regulatory Approach to Peer‑to‑Peer Lending Platforms and the 2023 Guidelines

Peer‑to‑Peer (P2P) lending in India is regulated under the “Non‑Banking Financial Company — Peer to Peer Lending Platform (Reserve Bank) Directions, 2017”, substantially revised in June 2023 (circular DNBS.PPD.No.01/03.10.001/2023‑24). The 2023 revision tightened prudential norms, enhanced borrower protection, and introduced a “fit‑and‑proper” test for platform promoters. A P2P platform must be registered as an NBFC‑P2P with a minimum net owned fund of ₹2 crore and a leverage ratio not exceeding 2 times. The platform acts solely as an intermediary — it cannot lend from its own balance sheet, nor can it provide credit enhancement or guarantee.

Key limits introduced in 2023: (i) **Per‑lender exposure cap** — ₹50 lakh across all borrowers on a single platform (previously ₹10 lakh); (ii) **Per‑borrower cap** — ₹10 lakh across all platforms (previously ₹5 lakh); (iii) **Platform‑level aggregate cap** — total outstanding loans on a platform cannot exceed 5 times its net owned fund; (iv) **Maturity restriction** — loan tenor limited to 36 months; (v) **Interest‑rate ceiling** — the all‑in cost (interest + fees) cannot exceed the bank’s base rate plus 400 basis points, ensuring alignment with the RBI’s fair‑lending guidelines.

The guidelines mandate a robust **credit‑assessment framework**: platforms must deploy a board‑approved algorithmic scoring model, validated annually by an independent auditor, and must disclose the key variables (income, repayment history, bureau score) to borrowers. A **cooling‑off period** of 30 days applies to digital loans originated through the platform, during which the borrower can prepay without penalty. Platforms are required to maintain a **grievance redressal mechanism** with a dedicated nodal officer, resolve complaints within 15 days, and report aggregated complaint data to the RBI quarterly.

On the **data‑privacy** front, the 2023 directions align with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: platforms must obtain explicit consent for each data‑sharing instance, store data only in India, and appoint a Data Protection Officer. The RBI also introduced a **regulatory sandbox** window for P2P platforms to test innovative credit‑scoring models (e.g., alternative data from utility payments, GST returns) under supervised conditions.

As of March 2024, there were 23 registered NBFC‑P2P platforms with an aggregate loan book of ₹18,500 crore. The 2023 caps have reduced the average ticket size from ₹1.2 lakh (2022) to ₹85,000 (2024) and improved portfolio quality — 90‑day delinquency fell from 4.8 % to 3.1 %. The RBI’s 2024 supervisory review highlighted two emerging risks: (a) concentration of lending to a few high‑net‑worth individual lenders (top 5 % of lenders account for 40 % of disbursements); (b) use of “lead‑generation” tie‑ups with unregulated fintech apps that circumvent the per‑borrower cap. The RBI has directed platforms to implement lender‑level KYC and to monitor cross‑platform borrowing through the Credit Information Companies (CICs).

  • Confusing the co‑lending minimum bank share (20 %) with the securitisation retention requirement (5 %); they serve different risk‑alignment purposes.
  • Assuming the PSL agriculture sub‑target of 18 % applies uniformly to all banks; foreign banks with <20 branches have no agriculture sub‑target.
  • Believing the 2021 securitisation guidelines allow the originator to sell its retained slice after six months; the retention must be held for the life of the transaction.
  • Thinking the cybersecurity framework’s 6‑hour incident‑reporting rule applies to all incidents; it applies only to “significant cyber incidents” affecting critical systems.
  • Assuming P2P platforms can lend from their own funds; NBFC‑P2P entities are prohibited from balance‑sheet lending.
  • Overstating the per‑lender exposure cap on P2P platforms; the 2023 revision raised it to ₹50 lakh, not ₹10 lakh.
  • Mixing the PSL “weaker sections” target (10 % of ANBC) with the overall 40 % target; they are distinct and both must be met simultaneously.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the Role of the RBI's Market‑Making Operations

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with issuance concentrated in high‑rated public sector entities and a limited secondary‑market turnover. Transmission of policy rate changes to this segment therefore relies on a combination of direct central‑bank interventions and the signalling effect of the repo rate on the yield curve. Since 2020 the Reserve Bank has operated a dedicated Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) under the Market Stabilisation Scheme, allowing it to buy investment‑grade bonds in the secondary market up to a pre‑announced ceiling. The purchases compress credit spreads, lower the cost of funds for issuers, and improve market liquidity, which in turn encourages primary issuance.

Operationally, the RBI conducts CBPP auctions on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform. Eligible securities are rated AAA or AA by at least two credit rating agencies, have a residual maturity of one to ten years, and are issued by non‑bank entities. The central bank announces a weekly purchase target, typically expressed as a percentage of the outstanding stock of eligible bonds. In the first year of the programme the RBI absorbed roughly ₹1.2 lakh crore of corporate paper, reducing the average AAA‑AA spread by 30–40 basis points. The transmission channel works through three mechanisms: (i) a portfolio‑rebalancing effect as investors shift from government securities to corporate bonds; (ii) a signalling effect that anchors medium‑term inflation expectations; and (iii) a direct reduction in the marginal cost of borrowing for firms that issue new paper.

Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (2022) shows that a 25‑basis‑point cut in the repo rate, combined with CBPP purchases equivalent to 0.5 % of GDP, lowers the yield on new AAA issuances by 15–20 basis points within two months. However, the pass‑through is asymmetric: rate hikes are transmitted faster because the RBI can unwind purchases through reverse repos, whereas rate cuts depend on the willingness of market participants to absorb the additional supply. The framework also includes a “market‑making” window where primary dealers quote two‑way prices for a basket of benchmark corporate bonds, enhancing price discovery and reducing bid‑ask spreads.

Key constraints remain. The eligible universe is narrow, limiting the programme’s reach to lower‑rated issuers that rely on bank credit. Moreover, the RBI’s balance‑sheet exposure to corporate credit risk is capped by the Market Stabilisation Scheme limits, preventing unlimited intervention. Coordination with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) on disclosure norms and with the Ministry of Finance on the development of a corporate bond repo market are ongoing to deepen the transmission channel.

RBI's Crisis‑Time Liquidity Toolkit: The 2020‑21 COVID‑19 Response and Its Legacy

The onset of the COVID‑19 pandemic in March 2020 triggered an unprecedented liquidity shock across the Indian financial system. The RBI responded with a layered toolkit that combined conventional rate cuts, targeted long‑term repo operations (TLTROs), special liquidity facilities for specific intermediaries, and temporary relaxations of regulatory ratios. The policy repo rate was reduced by 115 basis points in two steps (March and May 2020) to 4.0 %, while the reverse repo rate was lowered to 3.35 % to widen the interest‑rate corridor and encourage banks to park surplus funds with the central bank rather than hoard cash.

TLTRO 1.0, announced on 27 March 2020, provided three‑year funds at the prevailing repo rate to banks on the condition that the proceeds be deployed in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. A total of ₹1 lakh crore was auctioned in three tranches, with the bulk taken up by large public sector banks. TLTRO 2.0 (April 2020) extended the tenor to five years and broadened eligible assets to include bonds issued by NBFCs and micro‑finance institutions, addressing the funding stress in the shadow‑banking segment. The Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF), launched on 27 April 2020, offered ₹50 000 crore of repo funding against high‑quality corporate debt held by mutual funds, preventing fire‑sales and stabilising net asset values.

In parallel, the RBI raised the Ways and Means Advances (WMA) limit for the central government by 30 % and for state governments by 20 %, ensuring that fiscal authorities could meet cash‑flow mismatches without resorting to market borrowing at stressed yields. The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) was left unchanged, but the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) maintenance period was extended, giving banks flexibility in managing high‑quality liquid assets. The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) rate was aligned with the bank rate, allowing banks to borrow up to 2 % of their net demand and time liabilities at the policy rate, effectively providing a backstop for overnight funding.

The legacy of these measures is visible in the current operating framework. The Standing Deposit Facility (SDF), introduced in April 2022, institutionalised the floor of the interest‑rate corridor that was temporarily created by the widened reverse repo spread. Variable‑rate reverse repo (VRRR) auctions now serve as the primary tool for absorbing durable liquidity, replacing the ad‑hoc fixed‑rate reverse repos used during the crisis. The TLTRO experience informed the design of the “On‑Tap” Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (OT‑TLTRO) for specific sectors such as agriculture and MSMEs, allowing the RBI to direct liquidity without permanent balance‑sheet expansion. Finally, the crisis underscored the importance of real‑time data on inter‑bank money‑market rates, prompting the RBI to publish the “Money Market Operations” dashboard with intra‑day updates.

Worked Illustration
A scheduled commercial bank holds ₹500 crore of excess reserves after the RBI’s 2020 TLTRO 1.0 auction. The bank decides to deploy the funds in a 5‑year AAA‑rated corporate bond yielding 6.2 % while the prevailing repo rate is 4.0 %. Assuming the bank’s marginal cost of funds equals the repo rate, calculate the net interest margin (NIM) earned on this deployment and explain how the RBI’s CBPP purchases could affect this margin.
The bank earns 6.2 % on the bond and funds it at 4.0 % (repo). The gross spread is 2.2 % (220 basis points). On ₹500 crore this translates to an annual NIM of ₹11 crore (500 crore × 2.2 %). If the RBI’s CBPP purchases compress the AAA yield by 30 basis points to 5.9 %, the spread narrows to 1.9 % and the annual NIM falls to ₹9.5 crore. Thus, CBPP improves market liquidity and lowers issuance costs for corporates but reduces the arbitrage margin for banks that fund at the repo rate.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks you to trace the transmission from a repo‑rate cut to corporate bond yields, structure the answer in three steps: (1) rate‑cut → lower marginal cost of funds for banks; (2) banks increase demand for corporate bonds under TLTRO/OT‑TLTRO; (3) RBI’s CBPP purchases further compress spreads. Cite the specific facilities (TLTRO 1.0, CBPP, SDF) and the quantitative impact (basis‑point changes) to score full marks.

Regulatory Framework for Buy‑Now‑Pay‑Later Products and Emerging Consumer Credit Risks

Buy‑Now‑Pay‑Later (BNPL) arrangements have grown rapidly in India, especially after the pandemic accelerated e‑commerce adoption. Unlike traditional credit cards, BNPL products are typically offered by fintech platforms in partnership with NBFCs or banks, providing interest‑free instalment plans for low‑value purchases. The Reserve Bank recognised the regulatory gap in its 2022 “Guidelines on Digital Lending” and followed up with a dedicated circular in June 2023 (DNBS.PPD.No.01/03.10.001/2023‑24) that brought BNPL under the NBFC‑P2P and NBFC‑Account Aggregator frameworks, depending on the funding structure.

Under the 2023 directions, any entity facilitating BNPL must either be a registered NBFC with a minimum net owned fund of ₹2 crore or operate as a technology service provider to a regulated lender. The platform cannot extend credit from its own balance sheet; it may only originate loans on behalf of the partner NBFC or bank. Key prudential limits include a per‑borrower exposure ceiling of ₹10 lakh across all BNPL providers, a maximum tenor of 12 months, and an all‑in cost ceiling of the partner lender’s base rate plus 400 basis points. The guidelines also mandate a board‑approved credit‑assessment algorithm that incorporates bureau scores, income verification, and repayment history, with an annual independent audit of the model.

Consumer‑protection provisions require a mandatory 30‑day cooling‑off period during which the borrower can prepay without penalty, transparent disclosure of the effective annualised rate, and a grievance‑redressal mechanism with a dedicated nodal officer resolving complaints within 15 days. Data‑privacy obligations align with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023: explicit consent for each data‑sharing instance, on‑shore storage, and appointment of a Data Protection Officer. As of March 2024, the RBI reported 18 registered BNPL‑facilitating NBFCs with an aggregate outstanding portfolio of ₹22 000 crore; 90‑day delinquency stood at 2.8 %, lower than the 4.5 % observed for unsecured personal loans.

Emerging risks identified in the RBI’s 2024 supervisory review include concentration of lending to a small cohort of high‑frequency users (top 5 % of borrowers account for 35 % of disbursements) and the use of “lead‑generation” tie‑ups with unregulated apps that circumvent the per‑borrower cap. The central bank has directed platforms to implement lender‑level KYC, share borrower‑level data with Credit Information Companies on a real‑time basis, and conduct quarterly stress tests on the BNPL portfolio assuming a 200‑basis‑point rise in funding costs.

Outsourcing, Cloud Adoption and Cyber‑Resilience Guidelines for Regulated Entities

The increasing reliance of banks, NBFCs, and payment system operators on third‑party technology providers prompted the RBI to issue comprehensive outsourcing guidelines in November 2021 (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) and a dedicated cloud‑adoption framework in June 2023 (DoR.No.BP.BC.112/21.04.048/2023‑24). The outsourcing circular establishes a risk‑based approach: regulated entities (REs) must classify each outsourced activity as “critical” or “non‑critical” based on its impact on core banking functions, customer data, and regulatory compliance. Critical activities — such as core‑banking system hosting, payment‑gateway processing, and credit‑scoring engines — require prior RBI approval, a board‑approved outsourcing policy, and a legally binding service‑level agreement (SLA) that includes audit‑right clauses, data‑localisation mandates, and incident‑notification timelines of six hours for significant cyber events.

The cloud framework extends these principles to public, private, and hybrid cloud deployments. REs must conduct a Cloud Risk Assessment (CRA) covering data sovereignty, vendor lock‑in, shared‑responsibility models, and resilience of the cloud provider’s infrastructure. The RBI mandates that all regulated data reside in data centres located within India, and that encryption keys be managed by the RE or a domestically incorporated key‑management service. Multi‑cloud strategies are encouraged to avoid concentration risk, but each cloud service provider must be subjected to the same due‑diligence and contractual safeguards as a traditional outsourcer.

Cyber‑resilience requirements are operationalised through the “Cyber Security Framework for Banks” (2021) and the “Cyber Incident Reporting” circular (2022). REs must maintain a Security Operations Centre (SOC) with 24×7 monitoring, conduct annual red‑team exercises, and submit a quarterly Cyber Resilience Index to the RBI. The 2023 cloud circular adds a requirement for automated configuration‑drift detection and continuous compliance scanning of cloud workloads. Penalties for non‑compliance include monetary fines up to ₹1 crore per breach, restriction on new digital product launches, and, in extreme cases, supersession of the board. A notable enforcement action in 2022 involved a large private bank that suffered a ransomware attack disrupting core banking for 48 hours; the RBI imposed a ₹2.5 crore penalty and ordered a complete overhaul of privileged‑access management within 90 days.

These guidelines collectively shift the supervisory focus from point‑in‑time audits to continuous assurance. REs are now expected to embed “zero‑trust” architecture, adopt immutable logging, and integrate threat‑intelligence feeds into their incident‑response playbooks. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report highlighted that banks with mature cloud‑governance frameworks recovered from the 2023 “Cloud‑Provider Outage” incident 40 % faster than peers, underscoring the macro‑financial relevance of robust outsourcing and cloud risk management.

  • Confusing the BNPL per‑borrower cap (₹10 lakh) with the P2P per‑borrower cap (₹10 lakh across platforms) — they apply to different regulatory regimes.
  • Assuming the RBI’s CBPP purchases are unlimited; they are capped by the Market Stabilisation Scheme ceiling and eligible‑security criteria.
  • Believing TLTRO funds can be deployed in any asset class; the 2020‑21 TLTROs restricted usage to investment‑grade corporate debt and specified NBFC paper.
  • Thinking the outsourcing guidelines require RBI approval for all vendor contracts; only critical activities need prior approval.
  • Overstating the cloud‑data‑localisation rule as a blanket ban on foreign cloud providers; the rule permits foreign providers if data centres are physically located in India and keys are domestically managed.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common mistakes.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market: Market Making, Liquidity Support, and the Role of the Primary Dealer System

The Reserve Bank of India has progressively built a dedicated transmission channel for monetary policy into the corporate bond segment, recognising that bank‑credit‑dominant transmission leaves a sizable financing gap for high‑rated non‑bank issuers. The cornerstone is the Primary Dealer (PD) system, which was expanded in 2021 through the “Guidelines for Market Making by Primary Dealers in Corporate Bonds” (DBR.No.BP.BC.71/21.04.048/2021‑22). PDs are now required to quote two‑way prices for a minimum of 15 eligible securities, maintain a minimum inventory of ₹500 crore, and report daily turnover to the RBI. This obligation creates a continuous price discovery mechanism that aligns corporate bond yields with the policy repo rate.

Complementing market making, the RBI introduced the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) under the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) in March 2020. The CBPP authorises outright purchases of investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) up to a ceiling of ₹1 lakh crore, with eligibility restricted to securities issued by entities with a minimum net worth of ₹500 crore and a track record of timely debt service. Purchases are conducted through a uniform price auction on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, and the acquired bonds are held in the RBI’s investment account, providing a backstop that compresses credit spreads.

Liquidity support is further reinforced by the Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTRO) 2.0 (April 2021) and the subsequent “On‑Tap” TLTRO (October 2021), which earmarked ₹1 lakh crore for investment‑grade corporate paper, commercial paper, and non‑convertible debentures. Banks borrowing under TLTRO must deploy at least 75 % of the funds in eligible corporate debt within 30 days, creating a direct conduit from the policy rate to corporate borrowing costs. The RBI’s 2022 “Framework for the Development of the Corporate Bond Market” added a Corporate Bond Market Development Fund (CBMDF) with a corpus of ₹5,000 crore, managed by the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund, to provide credit enhancement for lower‑rated issuers.

Empirical evidence from the RBI’s 2023 Monetary Policy Report shows that a 25‑basis‑point cut in the policy repo rate transmitted an average of 18 bps to the 5‑year AAA corporate bond yield within three months, compared with 12 bps for the 10‑year government security. The stronger pass‑through is attributed to the combined effect of PD market‑making obligations, CBPP purchases, and TLTRO‑directed flows, which together reduce the liquidity premium embedded in corporate spreads.

Variable Rate Repo Auctions and the Rebalancing of the Liquidity Corridor

Until 2020 the RBI operated a fixed‑rate repo (the policy rate) and a fixed‑rate reverse repo, creating a symmetric corridor of 50 bps around the repo rate. The COVID‑19 shock prompted a shift to variable‑rate auctions to give the central bank finer control over surplus liquidity. The first Variable Rate Repo (VRR) auction was conducted on 27 March 2020 for a 14‑day tenor at a cut‑off of 4.40 %, 40 bps below the then‑policy repo of 4.80 %. Simultaneously, the Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) was introduced on 9 April 2020, allowing banks to park excess funds at a market‑determined rate, initially 3.35 %.

The operational framework, detailed in the “Revised Liquidity Management Framework” (DBR.No.BP.BC.45/21.04.048/2020‑21), defines three key rates: the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) as the floor (currently 6.25 %), the policy repo as the midpoint (6.50 %), and the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) as the ceiling (6.75 %). VRR auctions are announced on a fortnightly calendar with tenors ranging from 2 days to 28 days; VRRR auctions are typically overnight or 2‑day. The auction cut‑off rates become the effective overnight rates for the respective tenors, and the weighted average call rate (WACR) tracks the corridor centre.

During the 2022‑23 normalisation phase, the RBI progressively widened the corridor by raising the SDF in steps of 25 bps (to 5.75 % by September 2022) while keeping the repo unchanged, then lifted the repo to 6.50 % by February 2023. VRR volumes fell from an average of ₹2.3 lakh crore per fortnight in 2021‑22 to ₹0.8 lakh crore in 2023‑24, reflecting the absorption of pandemic‑era surplus. Conversely, VRRR auctions saw heightened participation, with cut‑off rates converging to the SDF, signalling that the floor had become the effective binding rate for surplus liquidity.

The variable‑rate design improves transmission by allowing the overnight rate to reflect real‑time liquidity conditions rather than a rigid corridor. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report notes that the standard deviation of the WACR narrowed from 12 bps (fixed‑rate regime) to 4 bps under the variable‑rate regime, reducing interest‑rate volatility for money‑market participants and sharpening the pass‑through to short‑term lending rates such as the MCLR and the external benchmark lending rate.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “If the RBI conducts a 14‑day Variable Rate Repo auction at a cut‑off of 6.30 % while the policy repo is 6.50 % and the SDF is 6.25 %, what does the cut‑off indicate about the prevailing liquidity condition?”
The cut‑off below the policy repo but above the SDF shows that the banking system is in a modest deficit; banks are willing to borrow at a discount to the repo because the overnight rate is being pulled down by surplus absorption through VRRR. The VRR cut‑off therefore acts as a market‑determined floor for the corridor, confirming that liquidity is neither abundant nor severely tight.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the current corridor rates (SDF, Repo, MSF) and the typical VRR/VRRR tenors. In a numerical question, first identify which rate is the floor and which is the ceiling; then compare the auction cut‑off to these bounds to infer liquidity stance. A quick sketch of the corridor on the answer sheet saves time and avoids sign errors.

Upper Layer NBFCs: Enhanced Supervision, Capital and Liquidity Requirements under the Scale‑Based Framework

The RBI’s Scale‑Based Regulation (SBR) for Non‑Banking Financial Companies, issued on 22 October 2021 (DoR.No.BP.BC.45/21.04.048/2021‑22), classifies NBFCs into four layers — Base, Middle, Upper, and Top — based on asset size, interconnectedness, and supervisory judgement. Upper Layer NBFCs are those with an asset size exceeding ₹1,000 crore and which are deemed systemically significant by the RBI’s “Systemic Significance Assessment” (SSA) methodology. As of March 2024, 27 NBFCs occupy the Upper Layer, collectively holding assets of ₹12.4 lakh crore.

Capital adequacy for Upper Layer NBFCs is set at a minimum Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio of 9 % and a total Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of 15 %, compared with 12 % for Base Layer entities. The leverage ratio requirement is capped at 7 % (Tier 1 capital to total exposure), aligning with the Basel III leverage framework for banks. Liquidity standards mandate a Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) of 100 % on a daily average basis and a Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) of 100 % on a quarterly basis, effective from 1 April 2023. These ratios are calibrated using the same high‑quality liquid asset (HQLA) definitions applicable to scheduled commercial banks.

Governance enhancements include a mandatory Board‑level Risk Management Committee (RMC) with at least one independent director, a Chief Risk Officer (CRO) reporting directly to the RMC, and a quarterly stress‑testing exercise covering credit, market, and liquidity shocks calibrated to the RBI’s “Adverse” and “Severely Adverse” macro‑scenarios. Upper Layer NBFCs must also disclose large exposures (above 10 % of Tier 1 capital) on a quarterly basis and submit a “Resolution Plan” to the RBI every two years, outlining strategies for orderly wind‑down.

Supervisory oversight is exercised through a dedicated “Upper Layer Supervisory College” that meets semi‑annually, comprising RBI’s Department of Non‑Banking Supervision, the Department of Regulation, and the Financial Stability Unit. The college reviews the NBFC’s Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process (ICAAP), the outcomes of stress tests, and compliance with the Large Exposure Framework (LEF) introduced in 2023. Non‑compliance triggers a graded response: supervisory letters, restriction on fresh credit growth, and, in extreme cases, a direction to raise capital or merge with a stronger entity.

National Asset Reconstruction Company and India Debt Resolution Company: Structure, Mandate, and Early Outcomes

The National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (NARCL) was incorporated on 7 July 2021 under the Companies Act, 2013, with an authorised capital of ₹10,000 crore, of which the Government of India holds a 51 % stake through the National Investment and Infrastructure Fund (NIIF) and the remaining 49 % is held by public sector banks. The India Debt Resolution Company Limited (IDRCL) was incorporated on 12 August 2021 as a separate resolution‑management entity, owned 51 % by NARCL and 49 % by a consortium of private‑sector investors led by the State Bank of India.

NARCL’s mandate is to acquire stressed assets from banks and financial institutions at a price determined by a transparent “Swiss‑Challenge” auction, issue Security Receipts (SRs) to the selling banks, and provide a government guarantee of up to ₹30,600 crore on the SRs to enhance their marketability. IDRCL acts as the exclusive resolution manager, responsible for operational turnaround, asset monetisation, and eventual sale or restructuring of the underlying exposures.

The first tranche of ₹50,000 crore of stressed assets (gross book value) was transferred to NARCL in March 2022, covering 12 large accounts across steel, power, and infrastructure sectors. By March 2024, NARCL had resolved 9 of these accounts, achieving an aggregate recovery of approximately ₹22,500 crore, implying a recovery rate of 45 % on the transferred book. The resolved accounts include a 1,200 MW thermal power plant sold to a strategic investor and a steel mill restructured under a sustainable debt‑equity swap.

Key challenges identified in the RBI’s 2023 supervisory review include the valuation gap between bank‑book values and market‑realisable values, the limited pool of distressed‑asset investors, and the need for faster judicial enforcement under the SARFAESI Act. The government has responded by extending the guarantee window to 2027 and allowing NARCL to co‑invest with alternative investment funds (AIFs) under a “co‑investment framework” notified in January 2024.

RBI’s Macroprudential Stress Testing for Systemically Important Financial Institutions: Design, Scenarios, and Supervisory Actions

Since 2013 the RBI has conducted an annual macroprudential stress‑testing exercise for Domestic Systemically Important Banks (D‑SIBs) and, from 2021, for Upper Layer NBFCs. The framework, described in the “Guidelines on Stress Testing for Banks” (DBR.No.BP.BC.83/21.04.048/2021‑22) and the “NBFC Stress Testing Framework” (DoR.No.BP.BC.112/21.04.048/2023‑24), employs three macro‑scenarios: Baseline (consistent with the RBI’s Survey of Professional Forecasters), Adverse (GDP growth 2 pp below baseline, CPI inflation 1.5 pp above, policy rate 150 bps higher), and Severely Adverse (GDP contraction 4 pp, inflation 3 pp above, policy rate 300 bps higher, rupee depreciation 10 %).

Each institution projects its balance sheet over a three‑year horizon, estimating credit losses using a “through‑the‑cycle” Probability of Default (PD) and Loss Given Default (LGD) calibrated to historical cycles. Market risk shocks include a 200 bps parallel shift in the yield curve and a 30 % equity market correction. Liquidity stress is modelled by a 30 % runoff of wholesale funding and a 15 % drawdown of committed credit lines. The key output metrics are the CET1 ratio, leverage ratio, LCR, and NSFR at the end of each projection year.

Results feed directly into supervisory decisions. In the 2023 exercise, two D‑SIBs fell below the 8 % CET1 threshold under the Severely Adverse scenario; the RBI imposed a 0.5 % additional capital surcharge (Pillar 2) and restricted dividend payouts to 30 % of profits for FY 2024. For Upper Layer NBFCs, the 2024 stress test highlighted a systemic liquidity shortfall of ₹1.2 lakh crore under the Adverse scenario, prompting the RBI to issue a directive for all Upper Layer NBFCs to maintain a minimum 10 % buffer above the regulatory LCR requirement effective 1 July 2024.

The stress‑testing outcomes are published in aggregate form in the Financial Stability Report (FSR), providing market participants with a transparent view of systemic resilience. The RBI also uses the results to calibrate the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB) and to design sector‑specific macroprudential tools such as the “Real Estate Exposure Limit” introduced in 2022.

  • Confusing the CBPP purchase ceiling (₹1 lakh crore) with the TLTRO allocation (₹1 lakh crore) — they are separate programmes with different eligibility criteria.
  • Assuming the Variable Rate Repo cut‑off always equals the policy repo; in surplus conditions the cut‑off can trade below the repo and even approach the SDF.
  • Believing Upper Layer NBFCs face the same capital requirement as Base Layer NBFCs; the SBR mandates a 15 % CRAR for Upper Layer versus 12 % for Base.
  • Thinking NARCL’s government guarantee covers the full face value of Security Receipts; the guarantee is capped at ₹30,600 crore and applies only to the senior tranche.
  • Overstating the stress‑test horizon as five years; the RBI’s macroprudential exercise uses a three‑year projection horizon.
  • Assuming the Countercyclical Capital Buffer is automatically activated by stress‑test results; the CCyB decision follows a separate policy process and is not mechanically linked.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the Corporate Bond Market and the RBI's Market Making Facility

The corporate bond market in India has historically been shallow, with issuance concentrated in high‑rated public sector entities and a limited secondary‑market turnover. Since 2020 the Reserve Bank has introduced a series of targeted operations to improve price discovery and to ensure that changes in the policy repo rate feed through to corporate borrowing costs. The first major intervention was the Corporate Bond Purchase Programme (CBPP) announced in March 2020, under which the RBI purchased investment‑grade corporate bonds up to ₹1 lakh crore through a special purpose vehicle. The programme was calibrated to a maximum of 10 % of the outstanding stock of eligible bonds and was wound down in March 2022 after the market regained depth.

In October 2021 the RBI launched a Market Making Facility (MMF) for corporate bonds, designating a set of primary dealers as market makers who are required to quote two‑way prices for a defined basket of securities. The MMF operates on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform and is backed by a liquidity window that allows market makers to repo the bonds at the prevailing repo rate. By providing a continuous bid‑ask spread, the facility reduces the liquidity premium that investors demand, thereby narrowing the spread between corporate bond yields and the sovereign yield curve. Empirical work by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) shows that the average bid‑ask spread for AAA‑rated 5‑year bonds fell from 45 bps in September 2021 to 22 bps by March 2023.

Transmission operates through three channels. First, the portfolio rebalancing channel works as lower yields on government securities push investors into corporate paper, compressing credit spreads. Second, the signalling channel arises because the RBI’s willingness to hold corporate bonds signals a commitment to keep financial conditions accommodative, influencing issuers’ expectations of future funding costs. Third, the balance‑sheet channel improves the capital position of banks and NBFCs that hold corporate bonds, freeing up capacity for fresh lending. The RBI’s 2023 Financial Stability Report notes that the MMF contributed an estimated 15‑20 bps reduction in the weighted‑average cost of new corporate bond issuance during FY 2022‑23.

Key operational parameters include a minimum quote size of ₹5 crore, a maximum spread of 30 bps over the prevailing NDS‑OM mid‑price, and a daily reporting obligation to the RBI’s Market Operations Department. The facility is reviewed quarterly; in the June 2024 review the RBI expanded the eligible basket to include AA‑rated bonds with a residual maturity of up to 7 years, reflecting the gradual deepening of the market.

RBI's Liquidity Management under the Revised Liquidity Coverage Ratio and Net Stable Funding Ratio Framework

The Basel III liquidity standards were transposed into Indian regulation in two phases. The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) became binding for all scheduled commercial banks from 1 January 2015, requiring a stock of High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) sufficient to cover 30‑day net cash outflows under a stressed scenario. In March 2021 the RBI issued a revised LCR framework (DBR.No.BP.BC.71/21.04.048/2020‑21) that aligned the definition of HQLA with the final Basel III text, introduced a 100 % minimum LCR for all banks (previously 80 % for small finance banks), and added a Level 2B asset category comprising certain rated corporate bonds and commercial papers subject to a 50 % haircut.

The Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR) was made applicable from 1 October 2021 (DBR.No.BP.BC.73/21.04.048/2020‑21). It requires banks to maintain a stable funding profile over a one‑year horizon, with a minimum ratio of 100 %. The NSFR framework classifies assets and liabilities into Available Stable Funding (ASF) and Required Stable Funding (RSF) factors. Notably, the RBI assigned a 50 % RSF factor to performing loans to non‑financial corporates with a residual maturity above one year, and a 100 % RSF factor to loans to NBFCs, reflecting the higher rollover risk in the shadow‑banking sector.

To support compliance, the RBI expanded the Standing Deposit Facility (SDF) and the Variable Rate Reverse Repo (VRRR) auctions, giving banks an additional avenue to park surplus liquidity at the policy corridor floor. The SDF rate, set 25 bps below the repo rate since April 2022, acts as a de‑facto floor for short‑term money‑market rates and improves the predictability of HQLA returns. In the June 2023 Monetary Policy Report the RBI disclosed that the aggregate LCR of the banking system stood at 138 % and the NSFR at 115 %, comfortably above regulatory minima.

Operational nuances include the treatment of government securities held under the Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS) as Level 1 HQLA, and the allowance for banks to count a portion of their Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) balances as HQLA provided they are not encumbered. The RBI also introduced a Liquidity Stress Testing module in its annual supervisory exercise, requiring banks to project LCR and NSFR under adverse macro‑scenarios (GDP contraction of 4 pp, policy rate hike of 300 bps). Results feed into the Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) matrix, where a projected LCR below 100 % under the adverse scenario triggers a Tier‑1 capital surcharge.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "If the RBI raises the policy repo rate by 50 bps while the SDF rate remains unchanged, what is the immediate impact on the LCR of a bank that holds a large proportion of its HQLA in SDF balances?"
The SDF rate is pegged 25 bps below the repo rate. When the repo rises by 50 bps and the SDF is unchanged, the spread widens to 75 bps, making the SDF relatively less attractive. Banks may shift surplus funds from SDF to higher‑yielding VRRR or market repos, reducing the stock of HQLA counted under the SDF. However, the LCR numerator (HQLA) does not automatically fall because SDF balances remain eligible HQLA; only a voluntary reallocation would change the composition. The immediate mechanical impact on the LCR is therefore negligible, but the incentive to rebalance could lower the LCR over the subsequent reporting period if the bank moves funds into non‑HQLA assets.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links a policy‑rate change to liquidity ratios, first identify which facility’s rate is anchored to the repo (VRRR, MSF) and which is set independently (SDF). Then trace the effect on HQLA composition, not just the headline ratio. A quick mental map: Repo ↑ → VRRR/MSF ↑ → banks prefer VRRR over SDF → possible HQLA shift → LCR/NSFR pressure.

Co‑origination and Direct Assignment Guidelines 2023: Implications for Credit Flow to MSMEs

The RBI’s Co‑origination Framework (originally issued in September 2020 and substantially revised in June 2023) permits banks and NBFCs to jointly originate loans, sharing both credit risk and interest income in a pre‑agreed proportion. The 2023 revision (DBR.No.BP.BC.92/21.04.048/2022‑23) introduced three critical changes: (i) a minimum 20 % risk‑share for the originating NBFC, (ii) a cap of 30 % of the bank’s total advances that can be co‑originated with a single NBFC, and (iii) a requirement that the bank’s board approve the co‑origination policy and monitor concentration limits quarterly.

Simultaneously, the Direct Assignment (DA) Guidelines (DBR.No.BP.BC.93/21.04.048/2022‑23) were tightened to ensure true sale treatment. The new rules mandate that the assignor (bank or NBFC) retain no more than 10 % of the credit risk through a first‑loss piece, that the assignee be a regulated entity (bank, NBFC‑Upper Layer, or eligible AIF), and that the assignment be executed on the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) or an RBI‑approved electronic platform. The guidelines also prescribe a minimum holding period of 90 days before assignment to prevent “originate‑to‑distribute” behaviour.

For Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs), these frameworks address two structural gaps. First, NBFCs often have superior last‑mile reach and credit‑assessment capabilities for informal MSMEs but lack low‑cost funding. Co‑origination lets banks fund the bulk of the loan at their cheaper cost of funds while the NBFC contributes underwriting expertise. Second, DA enables banks to offload seasoned MSME portfolios, freeing up capital for fresh lending. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report estimates that co‑originated MSME loans grew from ₹0.8 lakh crore in March 2022 to ₹2.3 lakh crore in March 2024, while DA volumes rose from ₹0.4 lakh crore to ₹1.1 lakh crore over the same period.

Supervisory safeguards include a joint credit‑risk monitoring report submitted to the RBI’s Department of Supervision on a half‑yearly basis, and a requirement that the bank’s internal audit cover the co‑origination process annually. The RBI also clarified that co‑originated loans qualify for priority‑sector lending (PSL) classification only if the bank’s share meets the PSL criteria, preventing regulatory arbitrage.

Digital Rupee Retail Pilot: Architecture, Token Design, and Interoperability with UPI

The Reserve Bank launched the retail Central Bank Digital Currency (e₹‑R) pilot on 1 December 2022 in four cities — Mumbai, New Delhi, Bengaluru and Bhubaneswar — with eight participating banks. Unlike the wholesale pilot (e₹‑W) that uses a permissioned distributed ledger for inter‑bank settlement, the retail pilot adopts a token‑based, account‑less model where each e₹‑R unit is a cryptographically signed digital bearer instrument denominated in rupees. The tokens are issued by the RBI’s Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) Issuance Module and distributed to end‑users through the participating banks’ mobile applications.

Key design choices include: (i) offline capability via Near‑Field Communication (NFC) allowing peer‑to‑peer transfers without internet connectivity, subject to a per‑transaction limit of ₹2,000 and a daily cumulative limit of ₹10,000; (ii) programmable features such as purpose‑bound money (e.g., subsidies that can only be spent at designated merchants) implemented through smart‑contract‑like scripts embedded in the token metadata; (iii) interoperability with the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) achieved by mapping each e₹‑R wallet to a virtual payment address (VPA) so that users can scan a UPI QR code and pay with e₹‑R, while the merchant receives settlement in commercial bank money via the existing UPI rails.

As of March 2024 the pilot had processed over 1.2 million transactions valued at ₹3,400 crore, with an average ticket size of ₹2,800. The RBI’s pilot report highlights three operational learnings: (a) the need for a robust key‑management infrastructure to handle token revocation and re‑issuance in case of device loss; (b) the importance of merchant onboarding through a simplified KYC‑lite process to expand acceptance points; and (c) the liquidity management challenge for banks, which must hold sufficient e₹‑R inventory to meet redemption demand while maintaining their own LCR/NSFR compliance.

The next phase, announced in the April 2024 Monetary Policy Statement, expands the pilot to 15 additional cities, adds two more banks, and introduces a cross‑border remittance corridor with the United Arab Emirates using the e₹‑R token on a bilateral CBDC bridge. The RBI has also indicated that the final design will incorporate a tiered anonymity model — full anonymity for low‑value offline transactions, and identity‑linked traceability for values above ₹50,000 — to balance privacy with anti‑money‑laundering obligations.

  • Confusing the CBPP purchase ceiling (₹1 lakh crore) with the MMF’s eligible basket size — they are distinct programmes with different eligibility and governance.
  • Assuming the SDF rate always moves in lockstep with the repo rate; the RBI may keep the SDF unchanged to manage liquidity conditions.
  • Believing co‑origination allows the NBFC to retain zero risk‑share; the 2023 guidelines mandate a minimum 20 % NBFC risk participation.
  • Thinking Direct Assignment can be executed bilaterally off‑platform; the 2023 DA rules require execution on TReDS or an RBI‑approved electronic platform.
  • Overstating the offline limit of e₹‑R as unlimited; the pilot caps offline transfers at ₹2,000 per transaction and ₹10,000 daily.
  • Assuming the retail CBDC token is account‑based like a prepaid wallet; it is a bearer token with cryptographic ownership, not a ledger entry in a bank’s core banking system.
  • Neglecting the PSL qualification condition for co‑originated loans — only the bank’s share counts toward priority‑sector targets.

Monetary Policy Transmission to the External Sector: Exchange Rate Pass‑Through and Import‑Export Dynamics

The external sector channel operates through the impact of policy‑rate changes on the nominal exchange rate, which in turn alters the rupee price of imports and the foreign‑currency revenue of exporters. When the RBI raises the repo rate, capital inflows tend to increase, putting upward pressure on the rupee. An appreciating rupee lowers the domestic currency cost of imported raw materials, intermediate goods and capital equipment, thereby reducing input‑cost inflation for firms that rely on foreign inputs. Simultaneously, exporters receive fewer rupees per unit of foreign currency, compressing profit margins and potentially dampening export volumes.

The magnitude of exchange‑rate pass‑through (ERPT) in India has been estimated at 0.2‑0.3 for consumer‑price inflation over a four‑quarter horizon, meaning a 10 % rupee appreciation reduces CPI by roughly 2‑3 percentage points over a year. However, ERPT is asymmetric: depreciation episodes transmit more quickly to import prices than appreciation does to export prices, because importers often have pricing power and contractual rigidities. The RBI’s managed‑float regime, combined with periodic foreign‑exchange interventions, smooths excessive volatility but does not eliminate the pass‑through effect.

Monetary tightening also influences the external sector via the interest‑rate differential channel. Higher domestic rates widen the spread over major foreign rates, attracting portfolio inflows into government securities and corporate bonds. These inflows increase demand for rupees, reinforcing appreciation. Conversely, when the RBI eases policy, the differential narrows, prompting outflows and depreciation pressure. The RBI monitors the net‑foreign‑portfolio‑investment (FPI) position and the current‑account balance to calibrate intervention intensity.

Empirical work using the RBI’s quarterly macro‑econometric model shows that a 100‑basis‑point repo‑rate hike leads to a 1.5‑2 % rupee appreciation within two quarters, a 0.4‑percentage‑point reduction in import‑price inflation, and a 0.2‑percentage‑point drag on export‑volume growth. The net effect on the trade balance depends on the elasticity of import demand and export supply; in India’s case, import demand is relatively inelastic in the short run, so the trade balance often improves initially.

Policy implications are twofold. First, the RBI’s inflation‑targeting framework must account for the external‑sector feedback loop: an appreciation driven by rate hikes can help meet the inflation target but may hurt export competitiveness. Second, communication about the expected path of the exchange rate — through the Monetary Policy Report and forward guidance — helps anchor market expectations and reduces overshooting. The RBI’s 2023‑24 Monetary Policy Report explicitly highlighted the role of ERPT in the disinflation trajectory observed during 2022‑23.

RBI's Management of Government Cash Balances and the Treasury Bill Auction Calendar

As banker to the central and state governments, the RBI maintains the cash balances of the Union and state governments in its Issue Department and Banking Department. These balances arise from tax collections, non‑tax revenues, disinvestment proceeds, and market borrowings. The RBI invests surplus cash in short‑term instruments, primarily Treasury Bills (T‑Bills), and provides Ways and Means Advances (WMA) when balances fall below a threshold.

The T‑Bill auction calendar is published quarterly and specifies the issuance schedule for 91‑day, 182‑day and 364‑day bills. The calendar is designed to smooth the government’s cash‑flow profile, avoid bunching of redemptions, and provide a predictable supply of risk‑free assets for the money market. The RBI conducts the auctions on the Negotiated Dealing System‑Order Matching (NDS‑OM) platform, using a uniform‑price (Dutch) auction for competitive bids and a non‑competitive bidding window for small investors and provident funds.

Cash‑balance management has a direct bearing on systemic liquidity. When the government’s cash balances rise — for example, after a large tax‑collection month or a disinvestment receipt — the RBI absorbs the excess by issuing additional T‑Bills or conducting reverse‑repo operations. Conversely, a drawdown of balances (e.g., during high‑expenditure periods such as the fiscal year‑end) releases liquidity into the banking system, often necessitating open‑market‑operation (OMO) purchases or a reduction in the cash‑reserve ratio (CRR) to prevent a liquidity crunch.

The RBI’s 2023‑24 Annual Report notes that the average daily government cash balance with the RBI was ₹3.2 lakh crore, with a peak of ₹4.1 lakh crore in March 2024. The T‑Bill issuance for the year amounted to ₹12.5 lakh crore, of which 91‑day bills accounted for 55 %, 182‑day for 30 % and 364‑day for 15 %. The non‑competitive bidding window attracted ₹1.1 lakh crore, reflecting strong demand from provident funds and small savers.

Coordination between the RBI’s liquidity‑management framework and the government’s cash‑management strategy is formalised through the Cash Management Committee, which meets monthly. The committee reviews the projected cash‑flow statement, the upcoming auction calendar, and the prevailing liquidity conditions to decide on the size and tenor of T‑Bill issuance, the need for OMO purchases, and the appropriate level of the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: "If the government receives a large disinvestment receipt in March, what is the most likely immediate impact on the banking system's liquidity and the RBI's likely response?"
The disinvestment receipt increases the government's cash balance with the RBI. The RBI will typically absorb the surplus by issuing additional Treasury Bills or conducting reverse‑repo operations, thereby draining liquidity from the banking system. The immediate impact is a tightening of liquidity conditions, reflected in a rise in the weighted average call‑rate (WACR) towards the repo rate. The RBI may also keep the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate unchanged to provide a floor for the call rate while the absorption takes place.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question links government cash flows to RBI operations, identify the direction of the cash‑balance change first. Then map it to the RBI’s toolkit: surplus → absorption (T‑Bill issuance, reverse repo, higher SDF); deficit → injection (OMO purchase, lower CRR, WMA). Remember the quarterly T‑Bill calendar and the role of the Cash Management Committee — these are favourite factual hooks.

The Role of the RBI in Managing Systemic Liquidity during Crisis Episodes: COVID‑19 and the 2020‑21 Liquidity Measures

The COVID‑19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented demand for rupee liquidity as economic activity contracted, credit risk rose, and market participants shifted to cash. The RBI responded with a calibrated suite of conventional and unconventional tools between March 2020 and March 2021, aimed at keeping the weighted average call rate (WACR) close to the policy repo rate and ensuring the functioning of the government‑securities market.

The first line of action was a 75‑basis‑point repo‑rate cut in March 2020, followed by a further 40‑basis‑point cut in May 2020, bringing the repo rate to 4.00 %. Simultaneously, the cash‑reserve ratio (CRR) was reduced by 100 basis points to 3.00 %, releasing approximately ₹1.37 lakh crore of primary liquidity. To address the term‑liquidity gap, the RBI launched Long‑Term Repo Operations (LTROs) of ₹1 lakh crore each in March and April 2020, with a three‑year tenor and a floating rate linked to the policy repo rate. These LTROs were earmarked for investment in investment‑grade corporate bonds, commercial paper and non‑convertible debentures, directly supporting the credit market.

In April 2020, the RBI introduced Targeted Long‑Term Repo Operations (TLTROs) of ₹50 000 crore each for specific sectors — small and medium enterprises, non‑banking financial companies (NBFCs) and microfinance institutions. The TLTRO funds had to be deployed in fresh lending to the targeted segments within 30 days, with a use‑it‑or‑lose‑it clause. A second tranche of TLTROs (₹50 000 crore) was announced in October 2020 for the same sectors, reflecting the prolonged stress.

To stabilise the mutual‑fund industry, which faced large redemptions in debt schemes, the RBI opened a Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) of ₹50 000 crore in April 2020. The facility allowed mutual funds to repo their investment‑grade corporate bonds and commercial paper with the RBI at the prevailing repo rate, providing a backstop against fire‑sales.

The RBI also expanded the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) limit from 2 % to 3 % of net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) and reduced the standing deposit facility (SDF) rate to 3.35 % (25 bps below the repo rate) to widen the interest‑rate corridor and encourage banks to park surplus liquidity with the RBI rather than in the overnight market. The corridor width was thus maintained at 50 bps (repo 4.00 %, SDF 3.35 %, MSF 4.25 %).

On the market‑operations front, the RBI conducted Open Market Operations (OMO) purchases of government securities totalling ₹3.5 lakh crore during 2020‑21, including a series of “Operation Twist” transactions that bought long‑dated securities while selling short‑dated ones to flatten the yield curve. The RBI also increased the Held‑to‑Maturity (HTM) limit for banks from 19.5 % to 22 % of NDTL, allowing them to hold more government bonds without marking‑to‑market losses.

These measures collectively kept the WACR within a narrow band around the repo rate, prevented a spike in short‑term rates, and ensured that the government’s borrowing programme (₹12 lakh crore in 2020‑21) was completed without disruption. The RBI’s 2021‑22 Financial Stability Report credited the coordinated use of LTROs, TLTROs, SLF‑MF and OMO purchases for preserving financial‑system stability during the pandemic.

RBI's Framework for Resolution of Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks: Recent Guidelines

Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Payment Banks (PBs) operate under differentiated licences with specific capital, outreach and activity restrictions. Recognising that their resolution cannot follow the standard Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework applicable to universal banks, the RBI issued a dedicated resolution framework in November 2022, later refined in July 2023.

The framework classifies SFBs and PBs into three risk‑based categories — “Viable”, “Potentially Viable” and “Non‑Viable” — based on capital adequacy, asset quality, governance and profitability metrics. A “Viable” entity continues normal operations under enhanced supervisory monitoring. A “Potentially Viable” entity is placed under a Supervisory Action Plan (SAP) that may include restrictions on branch expansion, dividend distribution, and fresh lending to high‑risk segments. The SAP is time‑bound, typically 12‑18 months, with quarterly review milestones.

For “Non‑Viable” entities, the framework provides for a structured resolution process that can culminate in one of three outcomes: (i) amalgamation with a stronger bank (universal or another SFB/PB), (ii) conversion into a different licence category (e.g., an SFB converting to a universal bank after meeting the ₹500 crore net‑worth requirement), or (iii) orderly wind‑down with deposit insurance payout by the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC). The RBI’s approval is mandatory for any amalgamation or conversion, and the process must protect small depositors — the DICGC cover of ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank applies in full.

The guidelines also introduce a “Resolution Reserve” requirement: SFBs and PBs must maintain a separate reserve of at least 0.5 % of their risk‑weighted assets, built up from profits, to absorb losses during the resolution period. This reserve is in addition to the statutory capital buffers and is not available for dividend distribution.

Supervisory integration is achieved through a dedicated Resolution Monitoring Cell within the RBI’s Department of Supervision, which tracks the progress of SAPs, validates the valuation of assets for amalgamation, and coordinates with the DICGC on payout timelines. The cell also conducts stress‑testing exercises tailored to the business models of SFBs (high‑touch micro‑credit) and PBs (high‑volume low‑value transactions).

Since the framework’s inception, two SFBs have been placed under SAPs (one in 2023, another in early 2024) and one PB has been amalgamated with a universal bank (completed in March 2024). The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report notes that the framework has reduced the average time to resolution from over 36 months under the earlier ad‑hoc approach to approximately 18 months, while preserving depositor confidence.

The RBI's Role in Developing the Corporate Bond Market: Repo in Corporate Bonds, Credit Enhancement, and the Bond‑ETF Framework

A deep corporate bond market is essential for diversifying funding sources away from bank‑dominated credit and for transmitting monetary policy to the non‑bank financial sector. The RBI has pursued a multi‑pronged strategy since 2018, focusing on three pillars: enabling repo in corporate bonds, providing a credit‑enhancement framework, and facilitating bond‑exchange‑traded funds (ETFs).

In July 2020, the RBI permitted banks and primary dealers to conduct repo transactions in listed, investment‑grade corporate bonds (rated AA and above) through the Clearing Corporation of India (CCIL). The repo haircut was set at 10 % for AA‑rated bonds and 15 % for A‑rated bonds, with a maximum tenor of 90 days. This innovation allowed market participants to use high‑quality corporate bonds as collateral for short‑term funding, improving liquidity in the secondary market. By March 2024, the outstanding repo volume in corporate bonds reached ₹45 000 crore, with participation from 12 banks and 5 primary dealers.

The credit‑enhancement framework, introduced in 2021, allows banks and NBFCs to provide partial guarantees (up to 20 % of the issue size) for corporate bond issuances by entities rated BBB‑ or higher. The guarantee must be backed by a dedicated capital charge (1.25 % of the guaranteed amount) and is recognised as a risk‑mitigant under the Basel III capital framework. As of December 2023, credit‑enhanced issuances accounted for ₹1.2 lakh crore of the total corporate bond issuance of ₹9.8 lakh crore, lowering the average spread over government securities by 30‑40 bps for enhanced issues.

The bond‑ETF initiative began with the launch of the Bharat Bond ETF in December 2019, managed by Edelweiss Asset Management under the aegis of the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM). The ETF invests in a basket of AAA‑rated public‑sector enterprise bonds with a defined maturity ladder. The RBI supported the product by allowing banks to treat Bharat Bond ETF units as High‑Quality Liquid Assets (HQLA) for Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) purposes, subject to a 15 % haircut. Subsequent tranches (Bharat Bond ETF‑2025, 2030, 2031) have raised over ₹50 000 crore, demonstrating retail and institutional appetite for a transparent, low‑cost bond‑market access vehicle.

These measures have collectively improved price discovery, reduced bid‑ask spreads, and increased the share of corporate bonds in total financial‑system credit from 14 % in 2018 to 18 % in 2023. The RBI’s 2024 Monetary Policy Report highlighted that the repo‑in‑corporate‑bonds facility and the credit‑enhancement framework have become key transmission channels for policy‑rate changes to the non‑bank corporate sector.

  • Confusing the repo‑in‑corporate‑bonds haircut (10‑15 %) with the LCR haircut on Bharat Bond ETF units (15 %) — they serve different regulatory purposes.
  • Assuming the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) was a permanent facility; it was a temporary COVID‑19 measure withdrawn in March 2021.
  • Believing the resolution framework for SFBs/PBs allows automatic conversion to a universal bank; conversion requires a separate licence application and meeting the ₹500 crore net‑worth threshold.
  • Overstating the exchange‑rate pass‑through coefficient as 1.0; empirical estimates for India place it between 0.2 and 0.3 for CPI over four quarters.
  • Thinking the government’s cash‑balance surplus automatically leads to a cut in the repo rate; the RBI typically absorbs the surplus via T‑Bill issuance or reverse repo, leaving the policy rate unchanged.
  • Neglecting the 0.5 % Resolution Reserve requirement for SFBs/PBs, which is distinct from the Capital Conservation Buffer and Countercyclical Capital Buffer.
  • Assuming the Bharat Bond ETF is open‑ended like a mutual fund; it is a close‑ended ETF with a fixed maturity ladder and trades on the stock exchange.

Monetary Policy Transmission to Agricultural Credit and Rural Lending

The transmission of policy rates to the agricultural sector operates through a distinct set of channels that differ from the corporate credit channel. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) influences the cost of farm credit primarily via the Priority Sector Lending (PSL) framework, the Interest Subvention Scheme (ISS), and the Kisan Credit Card (KCC) programme. Under the PSL guidelines revised in 2023, banks must allocate 18 % of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) to agriculture, with a sub‑target of 8 % for small and marginal farmers. The RBI monitors compliance through quarterly returns and can impose penalties or restrict branch expansion for persistent shortfalls.

The ISS provides a 2 % interest subvention on short‑term crop loans up to ₹3 lakh, effectively lowering the farmer’s borrowing cost to 7 % when the benchmark lending rate is 9 %. In 2022‑23 the scheme was extended to cover post‑harvest loans and loans against negotiable warehouse receipts, broadening the transmission window. The KCC, linked to the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) or the External Benchmark Lending Rate (EBLR), ensures that any reduction in the policy repo rate is reflected in the card’s interest rate within the reset period, typically one month for EBLR‑linked cards.

Empirical studies by the RBI’s Department of Economic and Policy Research (DEPR) show that a 100‑basis‑point cut in the repo rate reduces the weighted average lending rate on agricultural loans by 55‑65 bps over four quarters, a pass‑through lower than the 80‑90 bps observed for large corporate borrowers. The gap arises from higher operational costs, risk perception, and the prevalence of fixed‑rate loan contracts in rural branches. The RBI has attempted to narrow the gap by mandating EBLR linkage for all new floating‑rate agricultural loans from April 2024 and by encouraging banks to adopt the “farm‑level” credit scoring models piloted in Maharashtra and Karnataka.

Another transmission lever is the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) managed by NABARD, which receives budgetary allocations and RBI‑guaranteed bonds. The RIDF rate is set at a spread over the prevailing repo rate, so changes in the policy corridor directly affect the cost of long‑term irrigation and warehousing finance. In 2023 the RIDF rate was revised to repo + 1.5 % from repo + 2 %, reflecting the RBI’s accommodative stance.

Challenges remain: the high share of informal moneylenders, limited credit bureau coverage in rural districts, and the seasonal nature of cash flows impede the full pass‑through. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report notes that the share of institutional credit in total agricultural credit rose from 62 % in 2015 to 71 % in 2023, indicating gradual improvement but also highlighting the persistent reliance on non‑institutional sources that are insulated from monetary policy.

RBI's Framework for Resolution of Small Finance Banks and Payment Banks

The resolution framework for Small Finance Banks (SFBs) and Payment Banks (PBs) was formalised in the RBI’s 2021 “Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) Framework for SFBs and PBs” and further refined in the 2023 “Resolution Framework for SFBs and PBs”. The framework introduces a three‑tier trigger system based on Capital to Risk‑Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR), Net NPA ratio, and Leverage Ratio. Tier 1 triggers (CRAR < 9 %, Net NPA > 6 %, Leverage > 25 %) require the bank to submit a capital restoration plan within 30 days. Tier 2 (CRAR < 7.5 %, Net NPA > 9 %, Leverage > 30 %) imposes restrictions on dividend distribution, branch expansion, and high‑cost deposits. Tier 3 (CRAR < 6 %, Net NPA > 12 %, Leverage > 35 %) mandates the appointment of an administrator and initiation of resolution proceedings under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

A distinctive feature is the Resolution Reserve Requirement (RRR) of 0.5 % of risk‑weighted assets, which must be maintained in a separate account and can be drawn only with RBI approval. This reserve is distinct from the Capital Conservation Buffer (CCB) and the Countercyclical Capital Buffer (CCyB). The RRR aims to provide a quick‑access liquidity cushion during stress without eroding regulatory capital.

The framework also prescribes a “Resolution Plan” that must be approved by the RBI within 90 days of Tier 3 activation. The plan may involve amalgamation with a universal bank, conversion to a universal bank (subject to a separate licence application and a minimum net‑worth of ₹500 crore), or orderly wind‑down with depositor protection through the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC). Since the framework’s inception, two SFBs have been placed under Supervisory Action Plans (SAPs) — one in 2023 and another in early 2024 — and one PB was amalgamated with a universal bank in March 2024. The RBI’s 2024 Financial Stability Report states that the average resolution time has fallen from over 36 months under the ad‑hoc approach to approximately 18 months, while depositor confidence, measured by deposit growth, remained stable.

Key operational nuances include the prohibition on fresh Tier 2 capital issuance once Tier 2 is triggered, and the requirement that any amalgamation must be vetted by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) for market‑dominance concerns. The framework also clarifies that the Special Liquidity Facility for Mutual Funds (SLF‑MF) introduced during COVID‑19 was a temporary measure and does not form part of the standing resolution toolkit.

Examiner's technique
A question asks: “Explain how the RBI’s resolution framework for Small Finance Banks differs from the generic Prompt Corrective Action framework for universal banks, citing at least three specific provisions.”
The answer should highlight: (1) the three‑tier trigger system calibrated to SFB‑specific capital and leverage thresholds, unlike the universal‑bank PCA which uses only CRAR, Net NPA and Tier 1 leverage; (2) the mandatory 0.5 % Resolution Reserve Requirement unique to SFBs/PBs; (3) the explicit provision for conversion to a universal bank only after a separate licence and ₹500 crore net‑worth, which is absent in the universal‑bank PCA; (4) the fixed 90‑day deadline for RBI approval of a resolution plan, compared with the open‑ended supervisory discretion under the generic PCA. Mentioning the recent SAP cases and the reduced average resolution time adds empirical weight.
Exam‑day strategy
